Vāseṭṭha, a Samaṇa also, having practiced good conduct by body, having practiced good conduct by speech, having practiced good conduct by mind, is of right view and undertakes actions based on right view; because of undertaking actions based on right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.

137. “Khattiyopi kho, vāseṭṭha, kāyena dvayakārī, vācāya dvayakārī, manasā dvayakārī, vimissadiṭṭhiko vimissadiṭṭhikammasamādāno vimissadiṭṭhikammasamādānahetu vimissadiṭṭhiko vimissakammasamādāno vimissakammasamādānahetu (syā.), vītimissadiṭṭhiko vītimissadiṭṭhikammasamādānahetu (sī. pī.) kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī hoti. Brāhmaṇopi kho, vāseṭṭha [P 3.0097] …pe… vessopi kho, vāseṭṭha… suddopi kho, vāseṭṭha… samaṇopi kho, vāseṭṭha, kāyena dvayakārī[T 3.0106], vācāya dvayakārī, manasā dvayakārī, vimissadiṭṭhiko vimissadiṭṭhikammasamādāno vimissadiṭṭhikammasamādānahetu kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī hoti.

137. Vāseṭṭha, a Khattiya also is one who acts in two ways by body, one who acts in two ways by speech, one who acts in two ways by mind; he is of mixed view and undertakes actions based on mixed view. Because of undertaking actions based on mixed view, with the breakup of the body, after death, he becomes one who experiences pleasure and pain. Vāseṭṭha, a Brahmin also... Vāseṭṭha, a Vessa also... Vāseṭṭha, a Sudda also... Vāseṭṭha, a Samaṇa also is one who acts in two ways by body, one who acts in two ways by speech, one who acts in two ways by mind; he is of mixed view and undertakes actions based on mixed view. Because of undertaking actions based on mixed view, with the breakup of the body, after death, he becomes one who experiences pleasure and pain.

Bodhipakkhiyabhāvanā

The Development of the Factors of Enlightenment

138. “Khattiyopi kho, vāseṭṭha, kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto sattannaṃ bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanamanvāya diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyati parinibbāti (ka.). Brāhmaṇopi kho, vāseṭṭha…pe… vessopi kho vāseṭṭha… suddopi kho, vāseṭṭha [V 3.0072]… samaṇopi kho, vāseṭṭha, kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto [T 3.0107] manasā saṃvuto sattannaṃ bodhipakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhāvanamanvāya diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyati.

138. Vāseṭṭha, a Khattiya also, being restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind, on account of developing the seven factors of enlightenment, attains final Nibbāna in this very life. Vāseṭṭha, a Brahmin also... a Vessa also... a Sudda also... a Samaṇa also, being restrained in body, restrained in speech, and restrained in mind, on account of developing the seven factors of enlightenment, attains final Nibbāna in this very life.

139. “Imesañhi, vāseṭṭha, catunnaṃ vaṇṇānaṃ yo hoti bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano [M 3.0081] sammadaññā vimutto so nesaṃ aggamakkhāyati dhammeneva. No adhammena. Dhammo hi, vāseṭṭha, seṭṭho janetasmiṃ diṭṭhe ceva dhamme abhisamparāyañca.

139. Vāseṭṭha, among these four classes, whichever bhikkhu is an Arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, who has done what was to be done, who has laid down the burden, who has attained his own goal, whose fetter of existence is destroyed, and who is liberated through perfect knowledge—he is declared the foremost among them by Dhamma itself, not by what is not-Dhamma. For, Vāseṭṭha, the Dhamma is the best among this populace, both in this present life and in the life to come.

140. “Brahmunā pesā, vāseṭṭha, sanaṅkumārena gāthā bhāsitā –

140. Vāseṭṭha, this verse was also spoken by the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra:

‘Khattiyo seṭṭho janetasmiṃ, ye gottapaṭisārino;

Vijjācaraṇasampanno, so seṭṭho devamānuse’ti.

‘The Khattiya is the best among this populace, for those who rely on lineage; one accomplished in knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.’

“Sā kho panesā, vāseṭṭha, brahmunā sanaṅkumārena gāthā sugītā, no duggītā. Subhāsitā, no dubbhāsitā. Atthasaṃhitā, no anatthasaṃhitā. Anumatā mayā. Ahampi, vāseṭṭha, evaṃ vadāmi –

Indeed, Vāseṭṭha, that verse was well sung by the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, not poorly sung; well spoken, not poorly spoken; connected with benefit, not unconnected with benefit. It is approved by me. I too, Vāseṭṭha, say this:

‘Khattiyo [P 3.0098] seṭṭho janetasmiṃ, ye gottapaṭisārino;

Vijjācaraṇasampanno, so seṭṭho devamānuse’ti.

‘The Khattiya is the best among this populace, for those who rely on lineage; one accomplished in knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans.’

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā vāseṭṭhabhāradvājā bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One spoke this. Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, with delighted minds, rejoiced in what was spoken by the Blessed One.

Aggaññasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Aggañña Sutta, the fourth, is concluded.

5. Sampasādanīyasuttaṃ

5. 5. The Sampasādanīya Sutta

Sāriputtasīhanādo

Sāriputta’s Lion’s Roar

141. Evaṃ [M 3.0082][P 3.0099][V 3.0073][T 3.0108] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nāḷandāyaṃ viharati pāvārikambavane. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā sāriputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “evaṃpasanno ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati, na cāhu na ca bhavissati na cetarahi vijjati añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro yadidaṃ sambodhiya”nti.

141. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Nāḷandā, in Pāvārika’s mango grove. Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, I am confident in the Blessed One in this way: there has not been, nor will there be, nor is there at present, any other ascetic or brahmin more exceedingly knowledgeable than the Blessed One with respect to enlightenment.”

142. “Uḷārā kho te ayaṃ, sāriputta, āsabhī vācā bhāsitā, ekaṃso gahito, sīhanādo nadito – ‘evaṃpasanno ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati; na cāhu na ca bhavissati na cetarahi vijjati añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro yadidaṃ sambodhiya’nti. Kiṃ te kiṃ nu (sī. pī.), kiṃ nu kho te (syā.), sāriputta, ye te ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, sabbe te bhagavanto cetasā ceto paricca viditā – ‘evaṃsīlā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃdhammā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi[P 3.0100], evaṃpaññā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃvihārī te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipi, evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto ahesuṃ itipī’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

142. “Sāriputta, this magnificent and unshakeable speech has been spoken by you, a definitive statement has been made, a lion’s roar has been roared: ‘Venerable Sir, I have such confidence in the Blessed One that there has not been, nor will there be, nor is there at present, any other ascetic or brahmin more exceedingly knowledgeable than the Blessed One with respect to enlightenment.’ Sāriputta, as for those Blessed Ones of the past, who were Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones—were all those Blessed Ones known to you, having encompassed their minds with your mind, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such virtue,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such Dhamma,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such wisdom,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones were of such an abiding,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones were so liberated’?” “No, Venerable Sir.”

“Kiṃ pana te kiṃ pana (sī. pī.), sāriputta, ye te bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā[T 3.0109], sabbe te bhagavanto cetasā ceto paricca viditā, `evaṃsīlā te bhagavanto bhavissanti itipi, evaṃdhammā…pe… evaṃpaññā… evaṃvihārī… evaṃvimuttā te bhagavanto bhavissanti itipī’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Sāriputta, what about those who will be Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones in the future? Are all those Blessed Ones known to you, having encompassed their minds with your mind, thus: ‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such virtue,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such Dhamma,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such wisdom,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones will be of such an abiding,’ and ‘Those Blessed Ones will be so liberated’?” “No, Venerable Sir.”

“Kiṃ [V 3.0074] pana te kiṃ pana (sī. pī.), sāriputta, ahaṃ etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho cetasā ceto paricca vidito – ‘evaṃsīlo bhagavā itipi, evaṃdhammo…pe… evaṃpañño [M 3.0083]… evaṃvihārī… evaṃvimutto bhagavā itipī’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Sāriputta, am I, who am at present an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, known to you, having encompassed my mind with your mind, thus: ‘The Blessed One is of such virtue,’ and ‘of such Dhamma,’ and ‘of such wisdom,’ and ‘of such an abiding,’ and ‘The Blessed One is so liberated’?” “No, Venerable Sir.”

“Ettha ca hi te, sāriputta, atītānāgatapaccuppannesu arahantesu sammāsambuddhesu cetopariyañāṇaṃ natthi. Atha kiṃ carahi te ayaṃ, sāriputta, uḷārā āsabhī vācā bhāsitā, ekaṃso gahito, sīhanādo nadito – ‘evaṃpasanno ahaṃ, bhante, bhagavati, na cāhu na ca bhavissati na cetarahi vijjati añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro yadidaṃ sambodhiya’”nti?

“Sāriputta, in this matter, you have no knowledge of encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present. That being so, why then, Sāriputta, has this magnificent and unshakeable speech been spoken by you, this definitive statement been made, this lion’s roar been roared: ‘Venerable Sir, I have such confidence in the Blessed One that there has not been, nor will there be, nor is there at present, any other ascetic or brahmin more exceedingly knowledgeable than the Blessed One with respect to enlightenment’?”

143. “Na kho me na kho panetaṃ (syā. ka.), bhante, atītānāgatapaccuppannesu arahantesu sammāsambuddhesu cetopariyañāṇaṃ atthi. Api ca, me me bhante (sī. pī. ka.) dhammanvayo vidito. Seyyathāpi, bhante[P 3.0101], rañño paccantimaṃ nagaraṃ daḷhuddhāpaṃ daḷhuddāpaṃ (sī. pī. ka.) daḷhapākāratoraṇaṃ ekadvāraṃ. Tatrassa dovāriko paṇḍito byatto medhāvī aññātānaṃ nivāretā, ñātānaṃ pavesetā. So tassa nagarassa samantā anupariyāyapathaṃ anukkamamāno na passeyya pākārasandhiṃ vā pākāravivaraṃ vā antamaso biḷāranikkhamanamattampi. Tassa evamassa – ‘ye kho keci oḷārikā pāṇā imaṃ nagaraṃ [T 3.0110] pavisanti vā nikkhamanti vā, sabbe te imināva dvārena pavisanti vā nikkhamanti vā’ti. Evameva kho me, bhante, dhammanvayo vidito. Ye te, bhante, ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, sabbe te bhagavanto pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā, satta sambojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhiṃsu. Yepi te, bhante, bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā, sabbe te bhagavanto pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacittā, satta sambojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhissanti. Bhagavāpi, bhante, etarahi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho pañca nīvaraṇe pahāya cetaso upakkilese paññāya dubbalīkaraṇe catūsu satipaṭṭhānesu suppatiṭṭhitacitto [M 3.0084] satta sambojjhaṅge yathābhūtaṃ bhāvetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho.

143. “Venerable sir, I do not have the knowledge encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present. However, the principle of the Dhamma is known to me. Just as, venerable sir, a king's frontier city might have strong foundations, strong ramparts and gates, and a single gate. There, a gatekeeper would be wise, competent, and intelligent, one who prevents the unknown and admits the known. As he patrols the path all around that city, he would not see a joint in the rampart or a gap in the rampart, not even one large enough for a cat to exit. It would occur to him: ‘Whatever larger beings enter or leave this city, all of them enter or leave by this very gate.’ In the very same way, venerable sir, the principle of the Dhamma is known to me. Venerable sir, those Blessed Ones who were Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones in the past, all those Blessed Ones, having abandoned the five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. Venerable sir, those Blessed Ones who will be Arahants, Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones in the future, all those Blessed Ones, having abandoned the five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, will fully awaken to the unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment. The Blessed One, too, venerable sir, being at present an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, having abandoned the five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—with his mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, is fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment.”

144. “Idhāhaṃ, bhante, yena bhagavā [P 3.0102] tenupasaṅkamiṃ dhammassavanāya. Tassa me, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti uttaruttaraṃ paṇītapaṇītaṃ kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ. Yathā yathā me, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ desesi uttaruttaraṃ paṇītapaṇītaṃ kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāgaṃ, tathā tathāhaṃ tasmiṃ dhamme abhiññā [V 3.0075] idhekaccaṃ dhammaṃ dhammesu niṭṭhamagamaṃ; satthari pasīdiṃ – ‘sammāsambuddho bhagavā, svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, suppaṭipanno sāvakasaṅgho’ti.

144. “Here, venerable sir, I approached the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma. To me, venerable sir, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, progressively higher, progressively more sublime, with its dark and bright counterparts. In whatever way, venerable sir, the Blessed One taught me the Dhamma—progressively higher, progressively more sublime, with its dark and bright counterparts—in that same way, I, by direct knowledge in that Dhamma, came to a conclusion about a certain teaching among the teachings. I gained confidence in the Teacher, thinking: ‘The Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well.’”

Kusaladhammadesanā

Discourse on Wholesome Dhammas

145. “Aparaṃ [T 3.0111] pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti kusalesu dhammesu. Tatrime kusalā dhammā seyyathidaṃ, cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā, ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Idha, bhante, bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, kusalesu dhammesu. Taṃ bhagavā asesamabhijānāti, taṃ bhagavato asesamabhijānato uttari abhiññeyyaṃ natthi, yadabhijānaṃ añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro assa, yadidaṃ kusalesu dhammesu.

145. “Furthermore, venerable sir, this is unsurpassed: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma with regard to wholesome states. And what are these wholesome states? They are: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right strivings, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, enters upon and abides in it. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed with regard to wholesome states. The Blessed One knows this completely. For the Blessed One who knows this completely, there is nothing further to be known beyond it, by knowing which another ascetic or brahmin could be of greater direct knowledge than the Blessed One, that is, with regard to wholesome states.”

Āyatanapaṇṇattidesanā

The Discourse on the Designation of the Sense Bases

146. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti āyatanapaṇṇattīsu. Chayimāni, bhante, ajjhattikabāhirāni āyatanāni. Cakkhuñceva rūpā rūpāni (ka.) ca, sotañceva saddā ca, ghānañceva gandhā ca, jivhā ceva rasā ca, kāyo ceva phoṭṭhabbā ca, mano ceva dhammā ca. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, āyatanapaṇṇattīsu. Taṃ bhagavā asesamabhijānāti, taṃ bhagavato asesamabhijānato uttari abhiññeyyaṃ natthi, yadabhijānaṃ [P 3.0103] añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro assa yadidaṃ āyatanapaṇṇattīsu.

146. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the designation of the sense bases. Venerable Sir, there are these six internal and external sense bases: the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental objects. This, Venerable Sir, is unsurpassed in the designation of the sense bases. The Blessed One directly knows this completely. For the Blessed One who directly knows this completely, there is nothing further to be known beyond it. There is no other ascetic or brahmin who could be more knowledgeable than the Blessed One by directly knowing anything further regarding this, that is, the designation of the sense bases.

Gabbhāvakkantidesanā

The Discourse on Entry into the Womb

147. “Aparaṃ [M 3.0085] pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti gabbhāvakkantīsu. Catasso imā, bhante, gabbhāvakkantiyo. Idha[T 3.0112], bhante, ekacco asampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati; asampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti; asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati. Ayaṃ paṭhamā gabbhāvakkanti.

147. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning entry into the womb. There are, Venerable Sir, these four kinds of entry into the womb. Here, Venerable Sir, a certain being enters the mother's womb without clear comprehension; remains in the mother's womb without clear comprehension; and emerges from the mother's womb without clear comprehension. This is the first kind of entry into the womb.

“Puna [V 3.0076] caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati; asampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti; asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati. Ayaṃ dutiyā gabbhāvakkanti.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain being enters the mother's womb with clear comprehension; remains in the mother's womb without clear comprehension; and emerges from the mother's womb without clear comprehension. This is the second kind of entry into the womb.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati; sampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti; asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati. Ayaṃ tatiyā gabbhāvakkanti.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain being enters the mother's womb with clear comprehension; remains in the mother's womb with clear comprehension; and emerges from the mother's womb without clear comprehension. This is the third kind of entry into the womb.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati; sampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti; sampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati. Ayaṃ catutthā gabbhāvakkanti. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, gabbhāvakkantīsu.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain being enters the mother's womb with clear comprehension; remains in the mother's womb with clear comprehension; and emerges from the mother's womb with clear comprehension. This is the fourth kind of entry into the womb. This, Venerable Sir, is unsurpassed concerning entry into the womb.

Ādesanavidhādesanā

The Discourse on the Modes of Declaration

148. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti ādesanavidhāsu. Catasso imā, bhante, ādesanavidhā. Idha, bhante, ekacco nimittena ādisati – ‘evampi te mano, itthampi te mano, itipi te citta’nti. So [T 3.0113] bahuṃ cepi ādisati, tatheva taṃ hoti, no aññathā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā ādesanavidhā.

148. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: the way the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the modes of declaration. There are, Venerable Sir, these four modes of declaration. Here, Venerable Sir, a certain person declares by means of a sign: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is in this way, your thought is like this.’ And however much he declares, it is exactly so and not otherwise. This is the first mode of declaration.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco na heva kho nimittena ādisati. Api ca kho manussānaṃ vā amanussānaṃ vā devatānaṃ vā saddaṃ sutvā ādisati – ‘evampi te mano, itthampi te mano, itipi te citta’nti. So bahuṃ cepi ādisati, tatheva taṃ hoti, no aññathā. Ayaṃ dutiyā ādesanavidhā.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain person does not declare by means of a sign. Rather, having heard a sound from humans, non-humans, or devas, he declares: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is in this way, your thought is like this.’ And however much he declares, it is exactly so and not otherwise. This is the second mode of declaration.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco na heva kho nimittena ādisati, nāpi manussānaṃ vā amanussānaṃ vā devatānaṃ vā saddaṃ sutvā ādisati. Api [P 3.0104] ca kho vitakkayato vicārayato vitakkavipphārasaddaṃ sutvā ādisati [M 3.0086] – ‘evampi te mano, itthampi te mano, itipi te citta’nti. So bahuṃ cepi ādisati, tatheva taṃ hoti, no aññathā. Ayaṃ tatiyā ādesanavidhā.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain person does not declare by means of a sign, nor does he declare having heard a sound from humans, non-humans, or devas. Rather, having heard the sound of the spreading of thought from one who is thinking and pondering, he declares: ‘Your mind is thus, your mind is in this way, your thought is like this.’ And however much he declares, it is exactly so and not otherwise. This is the third mode of declaration.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco na heva kho nimittena ādisati, nāpi manussānaṃ vā amanussānaṃ vā devatānaṃ vā saddaṃ sutvā ādisati, nāpi vitakkayato vicārayato vitakkavipphārasaddaṃ [V 3.0077] sutvā ādisati. Api ca kho avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhiṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārasamādhisamāpannassa (syā. ka.) a. ni. 3.61 passitabbaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāti – ‘yathā imassa bhoto manosaṅkhārā paṇihitā. Tathā imassa cittassa anantarā imaṃ nāma vitakkaṃ vitakkessatī’ti. So bahuṃ cepi ādisati, tatheva taṃ hoti, no aññathā. Ayaṃ catutthā ādesanavidhā. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, ādesanavidhāsu.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain person does not declare by means of a sign, nor does he declare having heard a sound from humans, non-humans, or devas, nor does he declare having heard the sound of the spreading of thought from one who is thinking and pondering. Rather, he knows the mind of a person who has attained a concentration without thought and examination, encompassing it with his own mind: ‘As the mental formations of this venerable one are directed, so, immediately following this state of mind, he will think such-and-such a thought.’ And however much he declares, it is exactly so and not otherwise. This is the fourth mode of declaration. This, Venerable Sir, is unsurpassed among the modes of declaration.

Dassanasamāpattidesanā

The Discourse on the Attainment of Vision

149. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti dassanasamāpattīsu. Catasso imā, bhante, dassanasamāpattiyo. Idha, bhante, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya padhānamanvāya anuyogamanvāya appamādamanvāya sammāmanasikāramanvāya tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā [T 3.0114] adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā nakhā dantā taco maṃsaṃ nhāru aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ vakkaṃ hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsaṃ antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ karīsaṃ pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medo assu vasā kheḷo siṅghānikā lasikā mutta’nti. Ayaṃ paṭhamā dassanasamāpatti.

149. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the attainments of vision. There are, Venerable Sir, these four attainments of vision. Here, Venerable Sir, a certain ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardor, striving, application, diligence, and right attention, attains such a concentration of mind that, with the mind thus concentrated, he reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by skin and full of various kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, undigested food, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, solid fat, tears, liquid fat, saliva, nasal mucus, synovial fluid, and urine.’ This is the first attainment of vision.

“Puna caparaṃ[P 3.0105], bhante, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā [M 3.0087] lomā…pe… lasikā mutta’nti. Atikkamma ca purisassa chavimaṃsalohitaṃ aṭṭhiṃ paccavekkhati. Ayaṃ dutiyā dassanasamāpatti.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, here a certain ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardor… attains such a concentration of mind that, with the mind thus concentrated, he reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by skin, and full of various kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs… synovial fluid, and urine.’ And transcending a person’s skin, flesh, and blood, he reviews the bones. This is the second attainment of vision.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… lasikā mutta’nti. Atikkamma ca purisassa chavimaṃsalohitaṃ aṭṭhiṃ paccavekkhati. Purisassa ca viññāṇasotaṃ pajānāti, ubhayato abbocchinnaṃ idha loke patiṭṭhitañca paraloke patiṭṭhitañca. Ayaṃ tatiyā dassanasamāpatti.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardor… attains such a concentration of mind that, with the mind thus concentrated, he reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by skin, and full of various kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs… synovial fluid, and urine.’ And transcending a person’s skin, flesh, and blood, he reviews the bones. And he discerns a person’s stream of consciousness, unbroken on both sides, established in this world and established in the next world. This is the third attainment of vision.

“Puna [V 3.0078] caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhati – ‘atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā…pe… lasikā mutta’nti. Atikkamma ca purisassa [T 3.0115] chavimaṃsalohitaṃ aṭṭhiṃ paccavekkhati. Purisassa ca viññāṇasotaṃ pajānāti, ubhayato abbocchinnaṃ idha loke appatiṭṭhitañca paraloke appatiṭṭhitañca. Ayaṃ catutthā dassanasamāpatti. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, dassanasamāpattīsu.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here a certain ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardor… attains such a concentration of mind that, with the mind thus concentrated, he reviews this very body upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the crown of the head, bounded by skin and full of various kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head hairs, body hairs… synovial fluid, and urine.’ And transcending a person’s skin, flesh, and blood, he reviews the bones. And he discerns a person’s stream of consciousness, unbroken on both sides, unestablished in this world and unestablished in the next world. This is the fourth attainment of vision. This, venerable sir, is the unsurpassed in the attainments of vision.

Puggalapaṇṇattidesanā

The Exposition on the Designation of Persons

150. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti puggalapaṇṇattīsu. Sattime, bhante, puggalā. Ubhatobhāgavimutto paññāvimutto kāyasakkhī diṭṭhippatto saddhāvimutto dhammānusārī saddhānusārī. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, puggalapaṇṇattīsu.

150. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the designations of persons. These seven persons, Venerable Sir, are: one liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained to view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, and a faith-follower. This, Venerable Sir, is the unsurpassed teaching concerning the designations of persons.

Padhānadesanā

The Exposition on the Supreme Efforts

151. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ [P 3.0106] deseti padhānesu. Sattime, bhante sambojjhaṅgā satisambojjhaṅgo dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo vīriyasambojjhaṅgo pītisambojjhaṅgo passaddhisambojjhaṅgo samādhisambojjhaṅgo [M 3.0088] upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, padhānesu.

151. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the supreme efforts. These, Venerable Sir, are the seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. This, Venerable Sir, is the unsurpassed teaching concerning the supreme efforts.

Paṭipadādesanā

The Exposition on the Ways of Practice

152. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti paṭipadāsu. Catasso imā, bhante, paṭipadā dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā, dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā, sukhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā, sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññāti. Tatra, bhante, yāyaṃ paṭipadā dukkhā dandhābhiññā, ayaṃ, bhante, paṭipadā ubhayeneva hīnā akkhāyati dukkhattā ca dandhattā ca. Tatra, bhante, yāyaṃ paṭipadā dukkhā khippābhiññā, ayaṃ pana, bhante, paṭipadā dukkhattā hīnā [V 3.0079] akkhāyati[T 3.0116]. Tatra, bhante, yāyaṃ paṭipadā sukhā dandhābhiññā, ayaṃ pana, bhante, paṭipadā dandhattā hīnā akkhāyati. Tatra, bhante, yāyaṃ paṭipadā sukhā khippābhiññā, ayaṃ pana, bhante, paṭipadā ubhayeneva paṇītā akkhāyati sukhattā ca khippattā ca. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, paṭipadāsu.

152. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the ways of practice. These, Venerable Sir, are the four ways of practice: the difficult practice with slow direct knowledge, the difficult practice with quick direct knowledge, the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge. Among these, Venerable Sir, the practice that is difficult with slow direct knowledge is declared to be inferior on both accounts: because of its difficulty and because of its slowness. Among these, Venerable Sir, the practice that is difficult with quick direct knowledge is declared to be inferior because of its difficulty. Among these, Venerable Sir, the practice that is pleasant with slow direct knowledge is declared to be inferior because of its slowness. Among these, Venerable Sir, the practice that is pleasant with quick direct knowledge is declared to be sublime on both accounts: because of its pleasantness and because of its quickness. This, Venerable Sir, is the unsurpassed teaching concerning the ways of practice.

Bhassasamācārādidesanā

The Exposition beginning with Good Conduct in Speech

153. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti bhassasamācāre. Idha, bhante, ekacco na ceva musāvādupasañhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati na ca vebhūtiyaṃ na ca pesuṇiyaṃ na ca sārambhajaṃ jayāpekkho; mantā mantā ca vācaṃ bhāsati nidhānavatiṃ kālena. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, bhassasamācāre.

153. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning good conduct in speech. Here, Venerable Sir, a certain person does not speak words connected with falsehood, nor words that cause discord, nor slanderous words, nor does he, expecting victory, speak contentious words. He speaks, having reflected with wisdom, words that are worth treasuring, at a suitable time. This, Venerable Sir, is the unsurpassed teaching concerning good conduct in speech.

“Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti purisasīlasamācāre. Idha, bhante, ekacco sacco cassa saddho ca, na ca kuhako, na ca lapako, na ca nemittiko, na ca nippesiko, na ca lābhena [P 3.0107] lābhaṃ nijigīsanako jijigiṃsanako (syā.), nijigiṃsitā (sī. pī.), indriyesu guttadvāro, bhojane mattaññū, samakārī, jāgariyānuyogamanuyutto, atandito, āraddhavīriyo, jhāyī, satimā, kalyāṇapaṭibhāno, gatimā, dhitimā, matimā, na ca kāmesu giddho, sato ca nipako ca. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, purisasīlasamācāre.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is unsurpassed: how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning a man's virtuous conduct. Here, Venerable Sir, a certain person is truthful and faithful; he is not a boaster, not a flatterer, not one who hints for gain, not one who is importunate, and not one who seeks gain with gain. He has the doors of his sense faculties guarded, knows the right measure in food, acts rightly, is devoted to wakefulness, is not lazy, has aroused energy, is meditative, mindful, of eloquent speech, intelligent, resolute, and wise. He is not greedy for sensual pleasures, and is both mindful and prudent. This, Venerable Sir, is the unsurpassed teaching concerning a man's virtuous conduct.

Anusāsanavidhādesanā

The Exposition on the Varieties of Instruction

154. “Aparaṃ [M 3.0089] pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti anusāsanavidhāsu. Catasso imā bhante anusāsanavidhā – jānāti[T 3.0117], bhante, bhagavā aparaṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā ‘ayaṃ puggalo yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamāno tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno bhavissati avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo’ti. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā – ‘ayaṃ puggalo yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamāno tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī bhavissati, sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karissatī’ti. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā – ‘ayaṃ puggalo yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamāno pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā opapātiko bhavissati tattha parinibbāyī anāvattidhammo tasmā [V 3.0080] lokā’ti. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā – ‘ayaṃ puggalo yathānusiṭṭhaṃ tathā paṭipajjamāno āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatī’ti. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, anusāsanavidhāsu.

154. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is an unsurpassed excellence: that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma in the varieties of instruction. These, venerable sir, are four varieties of instruction. Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows a certain person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Practicing in accordance with the instruction given, this person, through the destruction of the three fetters, will become a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into states of woe, assured, and bound for supreme enlightenment.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Practicing in accordance with the instruction given, this person, through the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, will become a once-returner; returning to this world just once, he will make an end of suffering.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Practicing in accordance with the instruction given, this person, through the destruction of the five lower fetters, will be of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Practicing in accordance with the instruction given, this person, through the destruction of the taints, will, in this very life, realize for himself through direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, will abide therein.’ This, venerable sir, is the unsurpassed excellence in the varieties of instruction.

Parapuggalavimuttiñāṇadesanā

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Liberation of Other Persons

155. “Aparaṃ [P 3.0108] pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti parapuggalavimuttiñāṇe. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā – ‘ayaṃ puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno bhavissati avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo’ti. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā [T 3.0118] – ‘ayaṃ puggalo tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī bhavissati, sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ karissatī’ti. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā – ‘ayaṃ puggalo pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā opapātiko bhavissati tattha parinibbāyī anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā’ti. Jānāti, bhante, bhagavā paraṃ puggalaṃ paccattaṃ yonisomanasikārā – ‘ayaṃ puggalo āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ [M 3.0090] diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharissatī’ti. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, parapuggalavimuttiñāṇe.

155. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is an unsurpassed excellence: that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma in the knowledge of the liberation of other persons. Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Through the destruction of the three fetters, this person will become a stream-enterer, not subject to falling into states of woe, assured, and bound for supreme enlightenment.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Through the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, this person will become a once-returner; returning to this world just once, he will make an end of suffering.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Through the destruction of the five lower fetters, this person will be of spontaneous birth, attaining final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.’ Venerable sir, the Blessed One knows another person individually through wise attention thus: ‘Through the destruction of the taints, this person will, in this very life, realize for himself through direct knowledge the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, will abide therein.’ This, venerable sir, is the unsurpassed excellence in the knowledge of the liberation of other persons.

Sassatavādadesanā

The Exposition of Eternalist Doctrines

156. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti sassatavādesu. Tayome, bhante, sassatavādā. Idha, bhante, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi anekānipi jātisatāni anekānipi jātisahassāni anekānipi jātisatasahassāni, ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī [T 3.0119][P 3.0109] evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro [V 3.0081] evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. So evamāha – ‘atītaṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ jānāmi – saṃvaṭṭi vā loko vivaṭṭi vāti. Anāgataṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ jānāmi – saṃvaṭṭissati vā loko vivaṭṭissati vāti. Sassato attā ca loko ca vañjho kūṭaṭṭho esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito. Te ca sattā sandhāvanti saṃsaranti cavanti upapajjanti, atthitveva sassatisama’nti. Ayaṃ paṭhamo sassatavādo.

156. Furthermore, venerable sir, this is an unsurpassed excellence: that the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning eternalist doctrines. Venerable sir, there are these three eternalist doctrines. Here, venerable sir, some ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardour... attains such a concentration of mind that with the mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past existences. That is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many hundreds of births, many thousands of births, many hundreds of thousands of births: ‘In that existence I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life span. Passing away from there, I reappeared in another existence; and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life span. Passing away from there, I have been reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past existences with their aspects and details. He says thus: ‘I know the past eon—that the world contracted or expanded. I also know the future eon—that the world will contract or expand. The self and the world are eternal, barren, steadfast as a mountain peak, standing firm like a stone pillar. And those beings transmigrate, wander on, pass away, and are reborn, but there is that which is eternal.’ This is the first eternalist doctrine.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ dvepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni tīṇipi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni cattāripi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni pañcapi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni dasapi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni, ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto [M 3.0091] evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. So evamāha – ‘atītaṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ jānāmi saṃvaṭṭi vā loko vivaṭṭi vāti[T 3.0120]. Anāgataṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ jānāmi [P 3.0110] saṃvaṭṭissati vā loko vivaṭṭissati vāti. Sassato attā ca loko ca vañjho kūṭaṭṭho esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito. Te ca sattā sandhāvanti saṃsaranti cavanti upapajjanti, atthitveva sassatisama’nti. Ayaṃ dutiyo sassatavādo.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here some ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardour... attains such a concentration of mind that with the mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past existences. That is, one aeon of contraction and expansion, two aeons of contraction and expansion, three aeons of contraction and expansion, four aeons of contraction and expansion, five aeons of contraction and expansion, ten aeons of contraction and expansion: ‘In that existence I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life span. Passing away from there, I was reborn in another existence; and there too I had such a name... and such a life span. Passing away from there, I have been reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past existences with their aspects and details. He says thus: ‘I know the past time—that the world contracted or expanded. I also know the future time—that the world will contract or expand. The self and the world are eternal, barren, steadfast as a mountain peak, standing firm like a stone pillar. And those beings transmigrate, wander on, pass away, and are reborn, while that which is eternal remains the same.’ This is the second eternalist doctrine.

“Puna caparaṃ, bhante, idhekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ, dasapi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni vīsampi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni tiṃsampi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni cattālīsampi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭāni, ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. So evamāha – ‘atītaṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ jānāmi saṃvaṭṭipi loko vivaṭṭipīti; anāgataṃpāhaṃ addhānaṃ jānāmi saṃvaṭṭissatipi loko vivaṭṭissatipīti. Sassato attā ca loko ca vañjho kūṭaṭṭho [V 3.0082] esikaṭṭhāyiṭṭhito. Te ca sattā sandhāvanti saṃsaranti cavanti upapajjanti, atthitveva sassatisama’nti. Ayaṃ tatiyo sassatavādo, etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, sassatavādesu.

Furthermore, venerable sir, here some ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardour... attains such a concentration of mind that, with a mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past existences. That is: ten aeons of contraction and expansion, twenty aeons of contraction and expansion, thirty aeons of contraction and expansion, and forty aeons of contraction and expansion: ‘In that existence I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life span. Passing away from there, I was reborn in another existence; and there too I had such a name... and such a life span. Passing away from there, I have been reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past existences with their aspects and details. He says thus: ‘I know the past time: the world contracted and it expanded. I also know the future time: the world will contract and it will expand. The self and the world are eternal, barren, steadfast as a mountain peak, standing firm like a stone pillar. And those beings transmigrate, wander on, pass away, and are reborn, while that which is eternal remains the same.’ This is the third eternalist doctrine. Venerable sir, among the eternalist doctrines, this is the unsurpassed.

Pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇadesanā

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Recollection of Past Lives

157. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇe. Idha, bhante, ekacco samaṇo vā [T 3.0121] brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Seyyathidaṃ, ekampi jātiṃ dvepi jātiyo tissopi jātiyo catassopi jātiyo pañcapi jātiyo dasapi jātiyo vīsampi jātiyo tiṃsampi jātiyo cattālīsampi [M 3.0092] jātiyo paññāsampi jātiyo jātisatampi jātisahassampi jātisatasahassampi anekepi saṃvaṭṭakappe anekepi vivaṭṭakappe [P 3.0111] anekepi saṃvaṭṭavivaṭṭakappe, ‘amutrāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto amutra udapādiṃ; tatrāpāsiṃ evaṃnāmo evaṃgotto evaṃvaṇṇo evamāhāro evaṃsukhadukkhappaṭisaṃvedī evamāyupariyanto, so tato cuto idhūpapanno’ti. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Santi, bhante, devā sattā (syā.), yesaṃ na sakkā gaṇanāya vā saṅkhānena vā āyu saṅkhātuṃ. Api ca, yasmiṃ yasmiṃ attabhāve abhinivuṭṭhapubbo abhinivutthapubbo (sī. syā. pī.) hoti yadi vā rūpīsu yadi vā arūpīsu yadi vā saññīsu yadi vā asaññīsu yadi vā nevasaññīnāsaññīsu. Iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇe.

157. Furthermore, venerable sir, it is unsurpassed how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the knowledge of the recollection of past lives. Here, venerable sir, some ascetic or brahmin, by means of ardour... attains such a concentration of mind that, with the mind thus concentrated, he recollects his manifold past lives. That is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many aeons of contraction, many aeons of expansion, and many aeons of contraction and expansion: ‘In that existence I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a life span. Passing away from there, I was reborn in another existence; and there too I had such a name... and such a life span. Passing away from there, I have been reborn here.’ Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. There are, venerable sir, gods whose lifespan cannot be reckoned by counting or calculation. And furthermore, whatever state of existence he has formerly dwelt in—whether among those with form, or those without form, or those with perception, or those without perception, or those with neither perception nor non-perception—thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their aspects and details. This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed in regard to the knowledge of the recollection of past lives.

Cutūpapātañāṇadesanā

The Discourse on the Knowledge of the Passing Away and Rebirth of Beings

158. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇe. Idha, bhante, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti – ‘ime [T 3.0122] vata bhonto sattā kāyaduccaritena samannāgatā vacīduccaritena samannāgatā manoduccaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ upavādakā micchādiṭṭhikā micchādiṭṭhikammasamādānā. Te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ [V 3.0083] nirayaṃ upapannā. Ime vā pana bhonto sattā kāyasucaritena samannāgatā vacīsucaritena samannāgatā manosucaritena samannāgatā ariyānaṃ anupavādakā sammādiṭṭhikā sammādiṭṭhikammasamādānā. Te kāyassa bhedā paraṃ [P 3.0112] maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapannā’ti. Iti dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte [M 3.0093] suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, sattānaṃ cutūpapātañāṇe.

158. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, it is unsurpassed how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma regarding the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. Here, Venerable Sir, some ascetic or brahmin, through ardent striving... attains such a concentration of mind that with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands beings who fare according to their kamma: ‘Indeed, these venerable beings were endowed with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views, and undertaking actions based on wrong views. After the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. But these other venerable beings were endowed with good conduct of body, speech, and mind, not revilers of the noble ones, holding right views, and undertaking actions based on right views. After the breakup of the body, after death, they have been reborn in a good destination, in the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands beings who fare according to their kamma. This, Venerable Sir, is unsurpassed in regard to the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

Iddhividhadesanā

The Exposition on Psychic Powers

159. “Aparaṃ pana, bhante, etadānuttariyaṃ, yathā bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti iddhividhāsu. Dvemā, bhante, iddhividhāyo – atthi, bhante, iddhi sāsavā saupadhikā, ‘no ariyā’ti vuccati. Atthi, bhante, iddhi anāsavā anupadhikā ‘ariyā’ti vuccati. “Katamā ca, bhante, iddhi sāsavā saupadhikā, ‘no ariyā’ti vuccati? Idha, bhante, ekacco samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā ātappamanvāya…pe… tathārūpaṃ cetosamādhiṃ phusati, yathāsamāhite citte anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti. Ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti, bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti; āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvaṃ [T 3.0123] tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati seyyathāpi ākāse. Pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti, seyyathāpi udake. Udakepi abhijjamāne gacchati, seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ. Ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamati, seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo. Imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parāmasati parimajjati. Yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti. Ayaṃ, bhante, iddhi sāsavā saupadhikā, ‘no ariyā’ti vuccati.

159. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, this is an unsurpassed quality, how the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma concerning the kinds of psychic power. There are, Venerable Sir, these two kinds of psychic power. There is, Venerable Sir, a psychic power that is with taints and with acquisitions, which is called ‘not noble.’ There is, Venerable Sir, a psychic power that is without taints and without acquisitions, which is called ‘noble.’ And what, Venerable Sir, is the psychic power that is with taints and with acquisitions, which is called ‘not noble’? Here, Venerable Sir, some ascetic or brahmin, through ardor… attains such a concentration of mind that, with the mind thus concentrated, he experiences various kinds of psychic power. Being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one. He appears and vanishes. He goes unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space. He dives in and out of the earth as if it were water. He walks on water without breaking it, as if on earth. He travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird. With his hand, he touches and strokes even these sun and moon, so mighty and powerful. He wields bodily mastery even as far as the Brahmā world. This, Venerable Sir, is the psychic power that is with taints and with acquisitions, which is called ‘not noble.’

“Katamā pana, bhante, iddhi anāsavā anupadhikā, ‘ariyā’ti vuccati? Idha, bhante, bhikkhu sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati. Sace ākaṅkhati – ‘appaṭikūle paṭikūlasaññī [P 3.0113] vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati. Sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca appaṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, appaṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati. Sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūle ca appaṭikūle ca paṭikūlasaññī vihareyya’nti, paṭikūlasaññī tattha viharati. Sace ākaṅkhati – ‘paṭikūlañca appaṭikūlañca tadubhayaṃ abhinivajjetvā upekkhako vihareyyaṃ sato sampajāno’ti, upekkhako tattha viharati sato sampajāno. Ayaṃ, bhante, iddhi anāsavā anupadhikā ‘ariyā’ti vuccati. Etadānuttariyaṃ, bhante, iddhividhāsu[V 3.0084]. Taṃ bhagavā asesamabhijānāti, taṃ bhagavato asesamabhijānato uttari abhiññeyyaṃ natthi, yadabhijānaṃ añño samaṇo [M 3.0094] vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro assa yadidaṃ iddhividhāsu.

And what, Venerable Sir, is the psychic power that is without taints and without acquisitions, which is called ‘noble’? Here, Venerable Sir, if a bhikkhu wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the unrepulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both the repulsive and the unrepulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘Having avoided both the repulsive and the unrepulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells there equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. This, Venerable Sir, is the psychic power that is without taints and without acquisitions, which is called ‘noble.’ This, Venerable Sir, is the unsurpassed quality in regard to the kinds of psychic power. The Blessed One fully knows this without remainder. Since the Blessed One fully knows this without remainder, there is nothing further to be known beyond it, by knowing which another ascetic or brahmin could be more greatly knowledgeable than the Blessed One with respect to the kinds of psychic power.

Aññathāsatthuguṇadassanaṃ

Seeing the Teacher's Qualities in Another Way

160. “Yaṃ [T 3.0124] taṃ, bhante, saddhena kulaputtena pattabbaṃ āraddhavīriyena thāmavatā purisathāmena purisavīriyena purisaparakkamena purisadhorayhena, anuppattaṃ taṃ bhagavatā. Na ca, bhante, bhagavā kāmesu kāmasukhallikānuyogamanuyutto hīnaṃ gammaṃ pothujjanikaṃ anariyaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, na ca attakilamathānuyogamanuyutto dukkhaṃ anariyaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ. Catunnañca bhagavā jhānānaṃ ābhicetasikānaṃ diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārānaṃ nikāmalābhī akicchalābhī akasiralābhī.

160. Venerable Sir, whatever is to be attained by a faithful clansman with aroused energy, endowed with strength, with manly strength, with manly energy, with manly exertion, and with manly perseverance—that has been attained by the Blessed One. And, Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is not given to the practice of indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is low, of village-folk, of ordinary people, ignoble, and unbeneficial; nor is he given to the practice of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. And the Blessed One is an obtainer at will, an obtainer without difficulty, an obtainer without trouble, of the four jhānas which belong to the higher mind and are pleasant abidings in this very life.

Anuyogadānappakāro

The Manner of Responding to Interrogation

161. “Sace maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyya – ‘kiṃ nu kho, āvuso sāriputta, ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ aññe samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññatarā sambodhiya’nti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ, bhante, ‘no’ti vadeyyaṃ. ‘Kiṃ panāvuso sāriputta, bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ aññe samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññatarā sambodhiya’nti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ, bhante, ‘no’ti vadeyyaṃ[P 3.0114]. ‘Kiṃ panāvuso sāriputta, atthetarahi añño samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā bhagavatā bhiyyobhiññataro sambodhiya’nti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ, bhante, ‘no’ti vadeyyaṃ.

161. Venerable Sir, if I were to be asked thus: ‘Friend Sāriputta, were there in the past other ascetics or brahmins more profoundly enlightened than the Blessed One in respect to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would say, ‘No.’ ‘And what, Friend Sāriputta, will there be in the future other ascetics or brahmins more profoundly enlightened than the Blessed One in respect to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would say, ‘No.’ ‘And what, Friend Sāriputta, is there at present another ascetic or brahmin more profoundly enlightened than the Blessed One in respect to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would say, ‘No.’

“Sace pana maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyya – ‘kiṃ nu kho, āvuso sāriputta, ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ aññe samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhagavatā samasamā sambodhiya’nti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ, bhante, ‘eva’nti vadeyyaṃ. ‘Kiṃ panāvuso sāriputta, bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ aññe samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhagavatā samasamā sambodhiya’nti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ, bhante, “eva”nti vadeyyaṃ[T 3.0125]. ‘Kiṃ panāvuso sāriputta, atthetarahi aññe samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā bhagavatā samasamā sambodhiya’nti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ bhante ‘no’ti vadeyyaṃ.

“But if, Venerable Sir, I were to be asked thus: ‘Friend Sāriputta, were there in the past other ascetics or brahmins equal to the Blessed One in respect to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would say, ‘Yes.’ ‘And what, friend Sāriputta, will there be in the future other ascetics or brahmins equal to the Blessed One in respect to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would say, ‘Yes.’ ‘And what, friend Sāriputta, are there at present other ascetics or brahmins equal to the Blessed One in respect to enlightenment?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would say, ‘No.’”

“Sace pana maṃ, bhante, evaṃ puccheyya – ‘kiṃ panāyasmā sāriputto ekaccaṃ abbhanujānāti[V 3.0085], ekaccaṃ na abbhanujānātī’ti, evaṃ puṭṭho ahaṃ, bhante, evaṃ byākareyyaṃ [M 3.0095] – ‘sammukhā metaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato sutaṃ, sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ – “ahesuṃ atītamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā mayā samasamā sambodhiya”nti. Sammukhā metaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato sutaṃ, sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ – “bhavissanti anāgatamaddhānaṃ arahanto sammāsambuddhā mayā samasamā sambodhiya”nti. Sammukhā metaṃ, āvuso, bhagavato sutaṃ sammukhā paṭiggahitaṃ – “aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ ekissā lokadhātuyā dve arahanto sammāsambuddhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ uppajjeyyuṃ, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī’”ti.

“But if, Venerable Sir, I were to be asked thus: ‘For what reason does the Venerable Sāriputta assent in one case and not assent in another?’—being asked thus, Venerable Sir, I would explain thus: ‘Friend, this has been heard by me in the Blessed One’s presence, received in his presence: “In the past, there were Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, equal to me in respect to enlightenment.” Friend, this has been heard by me in the Blessed One’s presence, received in his presence: “In the future, there will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, equal to me in respect to enlightenment.” Friend, this has been heard by me in the Blessed One’s presence, received in his presence: “It is impossible, it cannot be, that in one world-system two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones, should arise neither one before nor one after the other; that condition does not exist.”’”

“Kaccāhaṃ, bhante, evaṃ [P 3.0115] puṭṭho evaṃ byākaramāno vuttavādī ceva bhagavato homi, na ca bhagavantaṃ abhūtena abbhācikkhāmi, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākaromi, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo vādānupāto (sī.) gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchatī”ti? “Taggha tvaṃ, sāriputta, evaṃ puṭṭho evaṃ byākaramāno vuttavādī ceva me hosi, na ca maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkhasi, dhammassa cānudhammaṃ byākarosi, na ca koci sahadhammiko vādānuvādo gārayhaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgacchatī”ti.

“Venerable Sir, in being asked thus and explaining thus, do I speak in accordance with what has been said by the Blessed One, and do I not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue? Do I explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no reasonable, co-doctrinal line of reasoning would provide a basis for censure?” “Indeed, Sāriputta, in being asked thus and explaining thus, you do speak in accordance with what has been said by me, and you do not misrepresent me with what is untrue. You explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no reasonable, co-doctrinal line of reasoning provides a basis for censure.”

Acchariyaabbhutaṃ

Marvelous and Amazing

162. Evaṃ [T 3.0126] vutte, āyasmā udāyī bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante, tathāgatassa appicchatā santuṭṭhitā sallekhatā. Yatra hi nāma tathāgato evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo, atha ca pana nevattānaṃ pātukarissati! Ekamekañcepi ito, bhante, dhammaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā attani samanupasseyyuṃ, te tāvatakeneva paṭākaṃ parihareyyuṃ. Acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante, tathāgatassa appicchatā santuṭṭhitā sallekhatā. Yatra hi nāma tathāgato evaṃ mahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo. Atha ca pana nevattānaṃ pātukarissatī”ti!

162. When this was said, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One: 'It is marvelous, venerable sir, it is amazing, venerable sir, this fewness of wishes, this contentment, this effacement of the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata, who is of such great psychic power and such great might, does not make himself manifest! If, venerable sir, wanderers of other sects were to perceive in themselves even a single one of these qualities, they would carry it about like a banner. It is marvelous, venerable sir, it is amazing, venerable sir, this fewness of wishes, this contentment, this effacement of the Tathāgata. For the Tathāgata is of such great psychic power and such great might, yet he does not make himself manifest!'

“Passa kho tvaṃ, udāyi, ‘tathāgatassa appicchatā santuṭṭhitā sallekhatā. Yatra hi nāma tathāgato evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo, atha ca pana nevattānaṃ pātukarissati’! Ekamekañcepi ito, udāyi, dhammaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā attani samanupasseyyuṃ, te tāvatakeneva paṭākaṃ [M 3.0096] parihareyyuṃ. Passa kho tvaṃ, udāyi, ‘tathāgatassa appicchatā santuṭṭhitā sallekhatā. Yatra hi nāma tathāgato evaṃmahiddhiko evaṃmahānubhāvo, atha ca pana nevattānaṃ pātukarissatī’”ti!

“See indeed, Udāyī, the Tathāgata's fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement. For the Tathāgata, who is of such great psychic power and such great might, does not make himself manifest! If, Udāyī, wanderers of other sects were to perceive in themselves even a single one of these qualities, they would carry it about like a banner. See indeed, Udāyī, the Tathāgata's fewness of wishes, contentment, and effacement. For the Tathāgata is of such great psychic power and such great might, yet he does not make himself manifest!”

163. Atha [P 3.0116][V 3.0086] kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi – “tasmā tiha tvaṃ, sāriputta, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ abhikkhaṇaṃ bhāseyyāsi bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ. Yesampi hi, sāriputta, moghapurisānaṃ bhavissati tathāgate kaṅkhā vā vimati vā, tesamimaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ sutvā tathāgate kaṅkhā vā vimati vā, sā pahīyissatī”ti. Iti hidaṃ āyasmā sāriputto [T 3.0127] bhagavato sammukhā sampasādaṃ pavedesi. Tasmā imassa veyyākaraṇassa sampasādanīyaṃ tveva adhivacananti.

163. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: 'Therefore, Sāriputta, you should frequently speak this discourse on the Dhamma to the monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers. For, Sāriputta, whatever foolish persons may have doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata, for them, upon hearing this discourse on the Dhamma, that doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata will be abandoned.' Thus, in the presence of the Blessed One, the Venerable Sāriputta made known this expression of serene faith. Therefore, 'The Inspiring of Confidence' is the name for this exposition.

Sampasādanīyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Sampasādanīya Sutta, the fifth, is concluded.

6. Pāsādikasuttaṃ

6. The Pāsādika Sutta

164. Evaṃ [P 3.0117][M 3.0097][V 3.0087][T 3.0128] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati vedhaññā nāma sakyā, tesaṃ ambavane pāsāde.

164. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans, in the long-halled building in the mango grove of the Sakyans named Vedhaññā.

Nigaṇṭhanāṭaputtakālaṅkiriyā

The Passing Away of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta

Tena kho pana samayena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto nāthaputto (sī. pī.) pāvāyaṃ adhunākālaṅkato hoti. Tassa kālaṅkiriyāya bhinnā nigaṇṭhā dvedhikajātā bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharanti – “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi, ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmi, kiṃ tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānissasi? Micchāpaṭipanno tvamasi, ahamasmi sammāpaṭipanno. Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te. Purevacanīyaṃ pacchā avaca, pacchāvacanīyaṃ pure avaca. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ, āropito te vādo, niggahito tvamasi, cara vādappamokkhāya, nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosī”ti. Vadhoyeva kho vadhoyeveko (ka.) maññe nigaṇṭhesu nāṭaputtiyesu vattati anuvattati (syā. ka.). Yepi nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa sāvakā gihī odātavasanā[P 3.0118], tepi te tesu (ka.) nigaṇṭhesu nāṭaputtiyesu nibbinnarūpā nibbindarūpā (ka.) virattarūpā paṭivānarūpā, yathā taṃ durakkhāte dhammavinaye duppavedite aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite bhinnathūpe appaṭisaraṇe.

At that time, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta had recently passed away in Pāvā. With his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas became divided, split into two factions, quarrelsome, contentious, and fallen into dispute; they went about piercing each other with verbal spears: ‘You do not know this Dhamma and Vinaya; I know this Dhamma and Vinaya. How could you know this Dhamma and Vinaya? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. My words are coherent; yours are incoherent. What should be said before, you said after; what should be said after, you said before. What you have long practiced has been overturned. Your doctrine has been refuted. You are censured. Go, try to save your doctrine, or disentangle yourself if you can!’ It seems that only slaughter prevails among the Nigaṇṭhas, the followers of Nāṭaputta. Even the lay disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta, who wear white clothes, have become disgusted, disaffected, and have turned away from the Nigaṇṭhas, the followers of Nāṭaputta, as is to be expected in a Dhamma and Vinaya that is badly proclaimed, badly taught, not leading to release, not conducive to peace, not made known by a Perfectly Enlightened One, with a broken foundation, and without refuge.

165. Atha kho cundo samaṇuddeso pāvāyaṃ vassaṃvuṭṭho vassaṃvuttho (sī. syā. pī.) yena sāmagāmo, yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno [T 3.0129] kho cundo samaṇuddeso āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “nigaṇṭho, bhante, nāṭaputto pāvāyaṃ adhunākālaṅkato. Tassa kālaṅkiriyāya bhinnā nigaṇṭhā dvedhikajātā…pe… bhinnathūpe appaṭisaraṇe”ti.

165. Then the novice Cunda, having completed the rains residence in Pāvā, went to Sāmagāma, to where the Venerable Ānanda was, and approached him. Having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the novice Cunda said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "Venerable sir, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta has recently passed away in Pāvā. With his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas have become divided... with a broken foundation, and without refuge."

Evaṃ [V 3.0088] vutte, āyasmā ānando cundaṃ samaṇuddesaṃ etadavoca – “atthi kho idaṃ, āvuso cunda, kathāpābhataṃ bhagavantaṃ dassanāya. Āyāmāvuso [M 3.0098] cunda, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamissāma; upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocessāmā”ti āroceyyāmāti (syā.). “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho cundo samaṇuddeso āyasmato ānandassa paccassosi.

When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the novice Cunda: "Friend Cunda, this is a topic to be brought to the Blessed One for an audience. Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we will report this matter to the Blessed One." "Yes, venerable sir," the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.

Atha kho āyasmā ca ānando cundo ca samaṇuddeso yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ayaṃ, bhante, cundo samaṇuddeso evamāha, ‘nigaṇṭho, bhante, nāṭaputto pāvāyaṃ adhunākālaṅkato, tassa kālaṅkiriyāya bhinnā nigaṇṭhā…pe… bhinnathūpe appaṭisaraṇe’”ti.

Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice Cunda approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, this novice Cunda says: ‘Venerable sir, Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta has recently passed away in Pāvā. With his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas have become divided... with a broken foundation, and without refuge.’”

Asammāsambuddhappaveditadhammavinayo

The Dhamma-Vinaya Proclaimed by One Who Is Not a Perfectly Enlightened One

166. “Evaṃ hetaṃ, cunda, hoti durakkhāte dhammavinaye duppavedite [P 3.0119] aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite. Idha, cunda, satthā ca hoti asammāsambuddho, dhammo ca durakkhāto duppavedito aniyyāniko anupasamasaṃvattaniko asammāsambuddhappavedito, sāvako ca tasmiṃ dhamme na dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharati na sāmīcippaṭipanno na anudhammacārī, vokkamma ca tamhā dhammā vattati. So [T 3.0130] evamassa vacanīyo – ‘tassa te, āvuso, lābhā, tassa te suladdhaṃ, satthā ca te asammāsambuddho, dhammo ca durakkhāto duppavedito aniyyāniko anupasamasaṃvattaniko asammāsambuddhappavedito. Tvañca tasmiṃ dhamme na dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharasi, na sāmīcippaṭipanno, na anudhammacārī, vokkamma ca tamhā dhammā vattasī’ti. Iti kho, cunda, satthāpi tattha gārayho, dhammopi tattha gārayho, sāvako ca tattha evaṃ pāsaṃso. Yo kho, cunda, evarūpaṃ sāvakaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘etāyasmā tathā paṭipajjatu, yathā te satthārā dhammo desito paññatto’ti. Yo ca samādapeti samādāpeti (sī. ṭṭha.), yañca samādapeti, yo ca samādapito samādāpito (sī. ṭṭha.) tathattāya paṭipajjati. Sabbe te bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evaṃ hetaṃ, cunda, hoti durakkhāte dhammavinaye duppavedite aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite.

166. “So it is, Cunda, in a Dhamma and Vinaya that is badly proclaimed, badly taught, not leading to release, not conducive to peace, and not made known by a Perfectly Enlightened One. Here, Cunda, the teacher is not a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is badly proclaimed, badly taught, not leading to release, not conducive to peace, and not made known by a Perfectly Enlightened One; and a disciple in that Dhamma does not dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, does not practice properly, does not conduct himself in accordance with the Dhamma, but deviates from that Dhamma. He should be spoken to thus: ‘It is your gain, friend, it is well-gained by you that your teacher is not a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is badly proclaimed, badly taught, not leading to release, not conducive to peace, and not made known by a Perfectly Enlightened One; and that you, in that Dhamma, do not dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, do not practice properly, do not conduct yourself in accordance with the Dhamma, but deviate from that Dhamma.’ Thus, Cunda, in that case the teacher is blameworthy, the Dhamma is blameworthy, and the disciple is, in this way, praiseworthy. Whoever, Cunda, should say to such a disciple, ‘Come, venerable one, practice in such a way as the Dhamma has been taught and laid down by your teacher,’ and whoever persuades him, and whoever, being persuaded, practices for that purpose—all of them generate much demerit. For what reason? Because so it is, Cunda, in a Dhamma and Vinaya that is badly proclaimed, badly taught, not leading to release, not conducive to peace, and not made known by a Perfectly Enlightened One.”

167. “Idha [M 3.0099] pana, cunda, satthā ca hoti asammāsambuddho, dhammo ca durakkhāto duppavedito aniyyāniko anupasamasaṃvattaniko asammāsambuddhappavedito, sāvako ca tasmiṃ dhamme [V 3.0089] dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharati sāmīcippaṭipanno anudhammacārī, samādāya taṃ dhammaṃ vattati. So evamassa vacanīyo – ‘tassa te, āvuso, alābhā, tassa te dulladdhaṃ, satthā ca te asammāsambuddho[P 3.0120], dhammo ca durakkhāto duppavedito aniyyāniko anupasamasaṃvattaniko asammāsambuddhappavedito. Tvañca [T 3.0131] tasmiṃ dhamme dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharasi sāmīcippaṭipanno anudhammacārī, samādāya taṃ dhammaṃ vattasī’ti. Iti kho, cunda, satthāpi tattha gārayho, dhammopi tattha gārayho, sāvakopi tattha evaṃ gārayho. Yo kho, cunda, evarūpaṃ sāvakaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘addhāyasmā ñāyappaṭipanno ñāyamārādhessatī’ti. Yo ca pasaṃsati, yañca pasaṃsati, yo ca pasaṃsito bhiyyoso mattāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati. Sabbe te bahuṃ apuññaṃ pasavanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, cunda, hoti durakkhāte dhammavinaye duppavedite aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite.

167. Furthermore, Cunda, a teacher is not a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is poorly expounded, badly proclaimed, not leading to liberation, not conducive to peace, and proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One. And in that Dhamma, a disciple dwells practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, acting in accordance with the Dhamma, having undertaken that Dhamma. He should be told: ‘Friend, it is your loss, it is your misfortune that your teacher is not a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is poorly expounded, badly proclaimed, not leading to liberation, not conducive to peace, and proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One. And you, in that Dhamma, dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, acting in accordance with the Dhamma, having undertaken that Dhamma.’ Thus, Cunda, in that case, the teacher is blameworthy, the Dhamma is blameworthy, and the disciple is also blameworthy. The one who would say to such a disciple, ‘Surely, the venerable one is practicing the right way and will realize the right goal,’ as well as the one who praises, the one who is praised, and that same one who, being praised, exerts even greater effort—all of them generate much demerit. For what reason? Because so it is, Cunda, in a Dhamma and Discipline that is poorly expounded, badly proclaimed, not leading to liberation, not conducive to peace, and proclaimed by one who is not a Perfectly Enlightened One.

Sammāsambuddhappaveditadhammavinayo

The Dhamma and Discipline Proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One

168. “Idha pana, cunda, satthā ca hoti sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito, sāvako ca tasmiṃ dhamme na dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharati, na sāmīcippaṭipanno, na anudhammacārī, vokkamma ca tamhā dhammā vattati. So evamassa vacanīyo – ‘tassa te, āvuso, alābhā, tassa te dulladdhaṃ, satthā ca te sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito. Tvañca tasmiṃ dhamme na dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharasi, na sāmīcippaṭipanno, na anudhammacārī, vokkamma ca tamhā dhammā vattasī’ti. Iti kho, cunda, satthāpi tattha pāsaṃso, dhammopi tattha pāsaṃso, sāvako ca tattha evaṃ gārayho. Yo kho, cunda, evarūpaṃ [T 3.0132] sāvakaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘etāyasmā tathā paṭipajjatu yathā te satthārā dhammo desito paññatto’ti. Yo ca samādapeti, yañca samādapeti, yo ca samādapito tathattāya paṭipajjati. Sabbe te bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ[M 3.0100], cunda, hoti svākkhāte dhammavinaye suppavedite niyyānike upasamasaṃvattanike sammāsambuddhappavedite.

168. Furthermore, Cunda, a teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. Yet in that Dhamma, a disciple does not dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, does not practice properly, does not act in accordance with the Dhamma, but deviates from that Dhamma. He should be told: ‘Friend, it is your loss, it is your misfortune that your teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One; yet you, in that Dhamma, do not dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, do not practice properly, do not act in accordance with the Dhamma, but deviate from that Dhamma.’ Thus, Cunda, in that case, the teacher is praiseworthy, the Dhamma is praiseworthy, but the disciple is blameworthy. The one who would say to such a disciple, ‘Come, venerable one, practice in such a way as the Dhamma has been taught and laid down by your teacher,’ as well as the one who encourages him, the one who is encouraged, and that same one who, being encouraged, practices for that purpose—all of them generate much merit. For what reason? Because so it is, Cunda, in a Dhamma and Discipline that is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.
