169. “Idha [P 3.0121] pana, cunda, satthā ca hoti sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito, sāvako ca tasmiṃ dhamme dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharati sāmīcippaṭipanno anudhammacārī, samādāya taṃ dhammaṃ vattati. So evamassa vacanīyo – ‘tassa te, āvuso, lābhā, tassa te suladdhaṃ, satthā ca te satthā ca te arahaṃ (syā.) sammāsambuddho[V 3.0090], dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito. Tvañca tasmiṃ dhamme dhammānudhammappaṭipanno viharasi sāmīcippaṭipanno anudhammacārī, samādāya taṃ dhammaṃ vattasī’ti. Iti kho, cunda, satthāpi tattha pāsaṃso, dhammopi tattha pāsaṃso, sāvakopi tattha evaṃ pāsaṃso. Yo kho, cunda, evarūpaṃ sāvakaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘addhāyasmā ñāyappaṭipanno ñāyamārādhessatī’ti. Yo ca pasaṃsati, yañca pasaṃsati, yo ca pasaṃsito pasattho (syā.) bhiyyoso mattāya vīriyaṃ ārabhati. Sabbe te bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavanti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Evañhetaṃ, cunda, hoti svākkhāte [T 3.0133] dhammavinaye suppavedite niyyānike upasamasaṃvattanike sammāsambuddhappavedite.

169. Furthermore, Cunda, a teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. And in that Dhamma, a disciple dwells practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, acting in accordance with the Dhamma, having undertaken that Dhamma. He should be told: ‘Friend, it is your gain, it is your good fortune that your teacher is a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. And you, in that Dhamma, dwell practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, practicing properly, acting in accordance with the Dhamma, having undertaken that Dhamma.’ Thus, Cunda, in that case, the teacher is praiseworthy, the Dhamma is praiseworthy, and the disciple is also praiseworthy. The one who would say to such a disciple, ‘Surely, the venerable one is practicing the right way and will realize the right goal,’ as well as the one who praises, the one who is praised, and that same one who, being praised, strives with even greater diligence—all of them generate much merit. For what reason? Because so it is, Cunda, in a Dhamma and Discipline that is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One.

Sāvakānutappasatthu

The Teacher Who Causes Regret for the Disciples

170. “Idha pana, cunda, satthā ca loke udapādi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito, aviññāpitatthā cassa honti sāvakā saddhamme, na ca tesaṃ kevalaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ āvikataṃ hoti uttānīkataṃ sabbasaṅgāhapadakataṃ sappāṭihīrakataṃ [P 3.0122] yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ. Atha nesaṃ satthuno antaradhānaṃ hoti. Evarūpo kho, cunda, satthā sāvakānaṃ kālaṅkato anutappo hoti. Taṃ kissa hetu? Satthā ca no loke udapādi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito, aviññāpitatthā camha saddhamme, na ca no kevalaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ āvikataṃ hoti [M 3.0101] uttānīkataṃ sabbasaṅgāhapadakataṃ sappāṭihīrakataṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ. Atha no satthuno antaradhānaṃ hotīti. Evarūpo kho, cunda, satthā sāvakānaṃ kālaṅkato anutappo hoti.

170. Furthermore, Cunda, a teacher has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. But his disciples have not been made to understand the meaning of the true Dhamma, and for them the holy life has not been made manifest in its completeness and purity, made plain, established with comprehensive terms, made into a teaching of deliverance, and well-proclaimed to gods and humans. Then their teacher passes away. Such a teacher, Cunda, having passed away, causes regret for his disciples. For what reason? ‘A teacher has arisen in the world for us, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading to liberation, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by a Perfectly Enlightened One. But we have not been made to understand the meaning of the true Dhamma, and for us the holy life has not been made manifest in its completeness and purity, made plain, established with comprehensive terms, made into a teaching of deliverance, and well-proclaimed to gods and humans. Then our teacher passed away.’ Such a teacher, Cunda, having passed away, causes regret for his disciples.

Sāvakānanutappasatthu

The Teacher Who is Not a Cause of Regret for Disciples

171. “Idha pana, cunda, satthā ca loke udapādi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito. Viññāpitatthā cassa honti [T 3.0134] sāvakā saddhamme, kevalañca tesaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ āvikataṃ hoti uttānīkataṃ sabbasaṅgāhapadakataṃ sappāṭihīrakataṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ. Atha nesaṃ satthuno antaradhānaṃ hoti. Evarūpo kho, cunda, satthā sāvakānaṃ kālaṅkato ananutappo hoti[V 3.0091]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Satthā ca no loke udapādi arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito. Viññāpitatthā camha saddhamme, kevalañca no paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ āvikataṃ hoti uttānīkataṃ sabbasaṅgāhapadakataṃ sappāṭihīrakataṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ[P 3.0123]. Atha no satthuno antaradhānaṃ hotīti. Evarūpo kho, cunda, satthā sāvakānaṃ kālaṅkato ananutappo hoti.

171. Furthermore, Cunda, a Teacher has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. And the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, well-expounded, leading to deliverance, conducive to peace, proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One. And his disciples are made to understand the meaning of the true Dhamma, and for them the holy life, complete in its entirety, has been made manifest, made plain, established with all-encompassing terms, made liberating, and well-proclaimed as far as devas and humans. Then their Teacher passes away. Such a Teacher, Cunda, having passed away, is not a cause of regret for his disciples. For what reason? ‘A Teacher has arisen in the world for us, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. And the Dhamma is well-proclaimed, well-expounded, leading to deliverance, conducive to peace, proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One. We have been made to understand the meaning of the true Dhamma, and for us the holy life, complete in its entirety, has been made manifest, made plain, established with all-encompassing terms, made liberating, and well-proclaimed as far as devas and humans. Then our Teacher passed away.’ Such a Teacher, Cunda, having passed away, is not a cause of regret for his disciples.

Brahmacariyaaparipūrādikathā

Discourse on the Incomplete Holy Life, and so forth

172. “Etehi cepi, cunda, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ hoti, no ca kho satthā hoti thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto. Evaṃ taṃ brahmacariyaṃ aparipūraṃ hoti tenaṅgena.

172. Even if, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these factors, but the Teacher is not an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, then that holy life is incomplete in that respect.

“Yato ca kho, cunda, etehi ceva aṅgehi samannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ hoti, satthā ca hoti thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto. Evaṃ taṃ brahmacariyaṃ paripūraṃ hoti tenaṅgena.

And when, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these very factors, and the Teacher is an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, then that holy life is complete in that respect.

173. “Etehi cepi, cunda, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ hoti, satthā ca hoti thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto[T 3.0135], no ca khvassa therā bhikkhū sāvakā honti viyattā vinītā visāradā pattayogakkhemā. Alaṃ samakkhātuṃ saddhammassa, alaṃ uppannaṃ [M 3.0102] parappavādaṃ sahadhammehi suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ. Evaṃ taṃ brahmacariyaṃ aparipūraṃ hoti tenaṅgena.

173. Even if, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these factors, and the Teacher is an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, but his elder monk disciples are not accomplished, disciplined, confident, having attained security from the bonds, are not competent to proclaim the good Dhamma, and are not competent, having thoroughly refuted an arisen opposing doctrine in accordance with principle, to teach the Dhamma that leads to deliverance—then that holy life is incomplete in that respect.

“Yato ca kho, cunda, etehi ceva aṅgehi samannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ hoti, satthā ca hoti thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto, therā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti viyattā vinītā visāradā pattayogakkhemā. Alaṃ samakkhātuṃ saddhammassa, alaṃ uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammehi suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ. Evaṃ taṃ brahmacariyaṃ paripūraṃ hoti tenaṅgena.

And when, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these very factors, and the Teacher is an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, and his elder monk disciples are accomplished, disciplined, confident, having attained security from the bonds, are competent to proclaim the good Dhamma, and are competent, having thoroughly refuted an arisen opposing doctrine in accordance with principle, to teach the Dhamma that leads to deliverance—then that holy life is complete in that respect.

174. “Etehi cepi, cunda, aṅgehi samannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ hoti, satthā ca hoti thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto, therā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti viyattā [V 3.0092] vinītā visāradā pattayogakkhemā. Alaṃ samakkhātuṃ saddhammassa, alaṃ uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammehi suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ. No ca khvassa majjhimā bhikkhū sāvakā honti…pe… majjhimā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti, no ca khvassa navā bhikkhū sāvakā honti…pe… navā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti, no ca khvassa therā bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti…pe… therā cassa bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti, no ca khvassa majjhimā [P 3.0124] bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti…pe… majjhimā cassa bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti[T 3.0136], no ca khvassa navā bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti…pe… navā cassa bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti, no ca khvassa upāsakā sāvakā honti gihī odātavasanā brahmacārino…pe… upāsakā cassa sāvakā honti gihī odātavasanā brahmacārino, no ca khvassa upāsakā sāvakā honti gihī odātavasanā kāmabhogino…pe… upāsakā cassa sāvakā honti gihī odātavasanā kāmabhogino, no ca khvassa upāsikā sāvikā honti gihiniyo odātavasanā brahmacāriniyo…pe… upāsikā cassa sāvikā honti gihiniyo odātavasanā brahmacāriniyo, no ca khvassa upāsikā sāvikā honti gihiniyo odātavasanā kāmabhoginiyo…pe… upāsikā cassa sāvikā honti gihiniyo odātavasanā kāmabhoginiyo, no ca khvassa brahmacariyaṃ hoti iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ…pe… brahmacariyañcassa hoti iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva [M 3.0103] devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ, no ca kho lābhaggayasaggappattaṃ. Evaṃ taṃ brahmacariyaṃ aparipūraṃ hoti tenaṅgena.

174. Even if, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these factors, and the Teacher is an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, and his elder monk disciples are accomplished, disciplined, confident, having attained security from the bonds, competent to proclaim the good Dhamma, and competent, having thoroughly refuted an arisen opposing doctrine in accordance with principle, to teach the Dhamma that leads to deliverance; but if his monk disciples of middle standing are not so... or if his monk disciples of middle standing are so, but his newly ordained monk disciples are not so... or if his newly ordained monk disciples are so, but his elder nun disciples are not so... or if his elder nun disciples are so, but his nun disciples of middle standing are not so... or if his nun disciples of middle standing are so, but his newly ordained nun disciples are not so... or if his newly ordained nun disciples are so, but his male lay disciples—householders in white who practice the holy life—are not so... or if those male lay disciples are so, but his male lay disciples—householders in white who enjoy sensual pleasures—are not so... or if those male lay disciples are so, but his female lay disciples—householders in white who practice the holy life—are not so... or if those female lay disciples are so, but his female lay disciples—householders in white who enjoy sensual pleasures—are not so... or if those female lay disciples are so, but the holy life is not prosperous, flourishing, extensive, widely known, populous, and well-proclaimed as far as devas and humans... or if the holy life is so, but it has not attained the summit of gain and renown—then that holy life is incomplete in that respect.

“Yato ca kho, cunda, etehi ceva aṅgehi samannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ hoti, satthā ca hoti thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto, therā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti viyattā vinītā visāradā pattayogakkhemā. Alaṃ samakkhātuṃ saddhammassa, alaṃ uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammehi suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ. Majjhimā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti…pe… navā cassa bhikkhū sāvakā honti…pe… therā cassa bhikkhuniyo sāvikā [T 3.0137] honti…pe… majjhimā cassa bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti…pe… navā cassa bhikkhuniyo sāvikā honti…pe… upāsakā cassa sāvakā honti…pe… gihī odātavasanā brahmacārino[P 3.0125]. Upāsakā cassa sāvakā honti gihī odātavasanā kāmabhogino…pe… upāsikā cassa sāvikā honti gihiniyo odātavasanā brahmacāriniyo…pe… upāsikā cassa sāvikā honti gihiniyo odātavasanā kāmabhoginiyo…pe… brahmacariyañcassa hoti iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ [V 3.0093] bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ, lābhaggappattañca yasaggappattañca. Evaṃ taṃ brahmacariyaṃ paripūraṃ hoti tenaṅgena.

And when, Cunda, the holy life is endowed with these very factors, and the Teacher is an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life, and his elder monk disciples are accomplished, disciplined, confident, having attained security from the bonds, competent to proclaim the good Dhamma, and competent, having thoroughly refuted an arisen opposing doctrine in accordance with principle, to teach the Dhamma that leads to deliverance; and his monk disciples of middle standing are so... and his newly ordained monk disciples are so... and his elder nun disciples are so... and his nun disciples of middle standing are so... and his newly ordained nun disciples are so... and his male lay disciples—householders in white who practice the holy life—are so... and his male lay disciples—householders in white who enjoy sensual pleasures—are so... and his female lay disciples—householders in white who practice the holy life—are so... and his female lay disciples—householders in white who enjoy sensual pleasures—are so... and the holy life is prosperous, flourishing, extensive, widely known, populous, and well-proclaimed as far as devas and humans, and has attained the summit of gain and the summit of renown—then that holy life is complete in that respect.

175. “Ahaṃ kho pana, cunda, etarahi satthā loke uppanno arahaṃ sammāsambuddho. Dhammo ca svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito. Viññāpitatthā ca me sāvakā saddhamme, kevalañca tesaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ āvikataṃ uttānīkataṃ sabbasaṅgāhapadakataṃ sappāṭihīrakataṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ. Ahaṃ kho pana, cunda, etarahi satthā thero rattaññū cirapabbajito addhagato vayoanuppatto.

175. Cunda, I have now arisen in the world as a Teacher, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. And the Dhamma is well-expounded, well-proclaimed, leading out, conducive to peace, and proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One. My disciples have understood the meaning in the good Dhamma, and for them the holy life, complete in its entirety, is made manifest, made plain, made comprehensive, made to lead to deliverance, and well-elucidated as far as gods and humans. Cunda, I am now a Teacher who is an elder, long-experienced, long gone forth, advanced in years, and has reached the final stage of life.

“Santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi therā bhikkhū sāvakā honti viyattā vinītā visāradā pattayogakkhemā. Alaṃ samakkhātuṃ saddhammassa, alaṃ uppannaṃ parappavādaṃ sahadhammehi suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā sappāṭihāriyaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ. Santi kho pana me, cunda[T 3.0138], etarahi majjhimā bhikkhū sāvakā…pe… santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi navā bhikkhū sāvakā…pe… santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi therā bhikkhuniyo sāvikā…pe… santi kho [M 3.0104] pana me, cunda, etarahi majjhimā bhikkhuniyo sāvikā…pe… santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi navā bhikkhuniyo sāvikā…pe… santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi upāsakā sāvakā gihī odātavasanā brahmacārino…pe… santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi upāsakā sāvakā gihī odātavasanā kāmabhogino…pe… santi kho pana me, cunda, etarahi upāsikā sāvikā gihiniyo odātavasanā brahmacāriniyo…pe… santi kho pana [P 3.0126] me, cunda, etarahi upāsikā sāvikā gihiniyo odātavasanā kāmabhoginiyo…pe… etarahi kho pana me, cunda, brahmacariyaṃ iddhañceva phītañca vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ puthubhūtaṃ yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ.

Cunda, I now have elder bhikkhus who are my disciples; they are skilled, disciplined, confident, and have attained security from the bonds. They are capable of expounding the good Dhamma; capable of, having rightly and thoroughly refuted an arisen opposing doctrine, teaching the Dhamma that leads to deliverance. Cunda, I now have middle bhikkhus who are my disciples… new bhikkhus who are my disciples… elder bhikkhunīs who are my disciples… middle bhikkhunīs who are my disciples… new bhikkhunīs who are my disciples… male lay disciples who are householders wearing white clothes and observing the holy life… male lay disciples who are householders wearing white clothes and enjoying sensual pleasures… female lay disciples who are householders wearing white clothes and observing the holy life… female lay disciples who are householders wearing white clothes and enjoying sensual pleasures… Cunda, my holy life is now successful and flourishing, widespread, known to many, populous, and well-elucidated as far as gods and humans.

176. “Yāvatā kho, cunda, etarahi satthāro loke uppannā, nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ ekasatthārampi samanupassāmi evaṃlābhaggayasaggappattaṃ yatharivāhaṃ. Yāvatā kho pana, cunda, etarahi saṅgho vā gaṇo vā loke uppanno; nāhaṃ, cunda, aññaṃ ekaṃ saṃghampi samanupassāmi evaṃlābhaggayasaggappattaṃ yatharivāyaṃ, cunda, bhikkhusaṅgho. Yaṃ kho taṃ, cunda, sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘sabbākārasampannaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ anūnamanadhikaṃ svākkhātaṃ kevalaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ suppakāsita’nti. Idameva taṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘sabbākārasampannaṃ…pe… suppakāsita’nti.

176. Cunda, of all the teachers that have arisen in the world at this time, I do not see even one other teacher who has attained the pinnacle of gain and renown as I have. Cunda, of all the saṅghas or groups that have arisen in the world at this time, I do not see even one other saṅgha that has attained the pinnacle of gain and renown as this Bhikkhu Saṅgha has. Cunda, that which one speaking rightly would say is: ‘The holy life is complete in all aspects, perfect in all aspects, not deficient and not excessive, well-expounded, entirely complete, and well-elucidated.’ It is this very thing that one speaking rightly would say: ‘The holy life is complete in all aspects… well-elucidated.’

“Udako [V 3.0094] uddako (sī. syā. pī.) sudaṃ, cunda, rāmaputto evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘passaṃ na passatī’ti. Kiñca [T 3.0139] passaṃ na passatīti? Khurassa sādhunisitassa talamassa passati, dhārañca khvassa na passati. Idaṃ vuccati – ‘passaṃ na passatī’ti. Yaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, udakena rāmaputtena bhāsitaṃ hīnaṃ gammaṃ pothujjanikaṃ anariyaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ khurameva sandhāya. Yañca taṃ yañcetaṃ (syā. ka.), cunda, sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘passaṃ [P 3.0127] na passatī’ti, idameva taṃ idamevetaṃ (ka.) sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘passaṃ na passatī’ti. Kiñca passaṃ na passatīti? Evaṃ sabbākārasampannaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ anūnamanadhikaṃ svākkhātaṃ kevalaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ suppakāsitanti, iti hetaṃ passati suppakāsitaṃ, iti hetaṃ na passatīti (syā. ka.). Idamettha apakaḍḍheyya, evaṃ taṃ parisuddhataraṃ assāti, iti hetaṃ na passati na passatīti (syā. ka.). Idamettha upakaḍḍheyya, evaṃ taṃ paripūraṃ parisuddhataraṃ (syā. ka.), paripūrataraṃ (?) assāti, iti [M 3.0105] hetaṃ na passati. Idaṃ vuccati cunda – ‘passaṃ na passatī’ti. Yaṃ kho taṃ, cunda, sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘sabbākārasampannaṃ…pe… brahmacariyaṃ suppakāsita’nti. Idameva taṃ sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘sabbākārasampannaṃ sabbākāraparipūraṃ anūnamanadhikaṃ svākkhātaṃ kevalaṃ paripūraṃ brahmacariyaṃ suppakāsita’nti.

Cunda, Udaka, the son of Rāma, used to say this: ‘Seeing, one does not see.’ And what is it that seeing, one does not see? One sees the surface of a well-sharpened razor, but one does not see its edge. This is what is meant by: ‘Seeing, one does not see.’ But that which was spoken by Udaka, the son of Rāma, Cunda, is low, of the village, of ordinary people, ignoble, and unbeneficial, concerning merely a razor. But, Cunda, that which one speaking rightly would say—‘Seeing, one does not see’—it is this very thing that one speaking rightly would say: ‘Seeing, one does not see.’ And what is it that seeing, one does not see? One sees this: ‘The holy life is thus complete in all aspects, perfect in all aspects, not deficient and not excessive, well-expounded, entirely complete, and well-elucidated.’ But one does not see this: ‘This should be removed from it, so that it would be purer.’ And one does not see this: ‘This should be added to it, so that it would be complete.’ This, Cunda, is what is meant by: ‘Seeing, one does not see.’ Cunda, that which one speaking rightly would say—‘The holy life is complete in all aspects… well-elucidated’—it is this very thing that one speaking rightly would say: ‘The holy life is complete in all aspects, perfect in all aspects, not deficient and not excessive, well-expounded, entirely complete, and well-elucidated.’

Saṅgāyitabbadhammo

The Dhamma to be Recited in Council

177. Tasmātiha, cunda, ye vo mayā dhammā abhiññā desitā, tattha sabbeheva saṅgamma samāgamma atthena atthaṃ byañjanena byañjanaṃ saṅgāyitabbaṃ na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame ca te, cunda[T 3.0140], dhammā mayā abhiññā desitā, yattha sabbeheva saṅgamma samāgamma atthena atthaṃ byañjanena byañjanaṃ saṅgāyitabbaṃ na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ? Seyyathidaṃ – cattāro satipaṭṭhānā, cattāro sammappadhānā, cattāro iddhipādā, pañcindriyāni, pañca balāni, satta bojjhaṅgā[P 3.0128], ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Ime kho te, cunda, dhammā mayā abhiññā desitā. Yattha sabbeheva saṅgamma samāgamma atthena atthaṃ byañjanena byañjanaṃ saṅgāyitabbaṃ na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

177. Therefore, Cunda, regarding those teachings I have taught to you after having directly known them, you should all, having assembled and come together in concord, recite them together—comparing meaning with meaning and phrasing with phrasing—and you should not dispute. This is so that this holy life may be long-lasting and may endure for a long time, for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. And what, Cunda, are those teachings I have taught to you after having directly known them, regarding which you should all, having assembled and come together in concord, recite them together—comparing meaning with meaning and phrasing with phrasing—and you should not dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and may endure for a long time, for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans? They are these: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right exertions, the four bases of spiritual power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. These, Cunda, are the teachings I have taught to you after having directly known them, regarding which you should all, having assembled and come together in concord, recite them together—comparing meaning with meaning and phrasing with phrasing—and you should not dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and may endure for a long time, for the welfare and happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

Saññāpetabbavidhi

The Method of Instruction

178. “Tesañca [V 3.0095] vo, cunda, samaggānaṃ sammodamānānaṃ avivadamānānaṃ sikkhataṃ sikkhitabbaṃ (bahūsu) aññataro sabrahmacārī saṅghe dhammaṃ bhāseyya. Tatra ce tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā atthañceva micchā gaṇhāti, byañjanāni ca micchā ropetī’ti. Tassa neva abhinanditabbaṃ na paṭikkositabbaṃ, anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘imassa nu kho, āvuso, atthassa imāni vā byañjanāni etāni vā byañjanāni katamāni opāyikatarāni, imesañca imesaṃ vā (syā. pī. ka.), imesaṃ (sī.) byañjanānaṃ ayaṃ vā attho eso vā attho [M 3.0106] katamo opāyikataro’ti[T 3.0141]? So ce evaṃ vadeyya – ‘imassa kho, āvuso, atthassa imāneva byañjanāni opāyikatarāni, yā ceva yañceva (sī. ka.), ṭīkā oloketabbā etāni; imesañca imedaṃ (sabbattha) byañjanānaṃ ayameva attho opāyikataro, yā ceva yañceva (sī. ka.), ṭīkā oloketabbā eso’ti. So neva ussādetabbo na apasādetabbo, anussādetvā anapasādetvā sveva sādhukaṃ saññāpetabbo tassa ca atthassa tesañca byañjanānaṃ nisantiyā.

178. Cunda, while you are training united, in harmony, and without dispute, a certain fellow in the holy life might speak on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha. Therein, if it should occur to you: ‘This venerable one grasps the meaning wrongly and applies the phrasing wrongly,’ his words should neither be approved of nor rejected. Without approving or rejecting, he should be spoken to thus: ‘Friend, for this meaning, which phrasing is more suitable: this or that? And for this phrasing, which meaning is more suitable: this or that?’ If he should reply: ‘Friend, for this meaning, this very phrasing is more suitable; and for this phrasing, this very meaning is more suitable,’ he should be neither censured nor disparaged. Without censuring or disparaging him, he himself should be well and thoroughly instructed for the firm establishing of that meaning and that phrasing.

179. “Aparopi ce, cunda, sabrahmacārī saṅghe dhammaṃ bhāseyya. Tatra ce tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā atthañhi kho micchā gaṇhāti byañjanāni sammā [P 3.0129] ropetī’ti. Tassa neva abhinanditabbaṃ na paṭikkositabbaṃ, anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘imesaṃ nu kho, āvuso, byañjanānaṃ ayaṃ vā attho eso vā attho katamo opāyikataro’ti? So ce evaṃ vadeyya – ‘imesaṃ kho, āvuso, byañjanānaṃ ayameva attho opāyikataro, yā ceva eso’ti. So neva ussādetabbo na apasādetabbo, anussādetvā anapasādetvā sveva sādhukaṃ saññāpetabbo tasseva atthassa nisantiyā.

179. Furthermore, Cunda, a fellow in the holy life might speak on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha. Therein, if it should occur to you: ‘This venerable one grasps the meaning wrongly, but applies the phrasing correctly,’ his words should neither be approved of nor rejected. Without approving or rejecting, he should be spoken to thus: ‘Friend, for this phrasing, which meaning is more suitable: this or that?’ If he should reply: ‘Friend, for this phrasing, this very meaning is more suitable,’ he should be neither censured nor disparaged. Without censuring or disparaging him, he himself should be well and thoroughly instructed for the firm establishing of that very meaning.

180. “Aparopi ce, cunda, sabrahmacārī saṅghe dhammaṃ bhāseyya. Tatra ce tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā atthañhi kho sammā gaṇhāti byañjanāni micchā ropetī’ti. Tassa neva abhinanditabbaṃ na paṭikkositabbaṃ; anabhinanditvā appaṭikkositvā so [T 3.0142] evamassa vacanīyo – ‘imassa nu kho, āvuso, atthassa imāni vā byañjanāni etāni vā byañjanāni katamāni opāyikatarānī’ti? So ce evaṃ vadeyya – ‘imassa kho, āvuso, atthassa imāneva byañjanāni opayikatarāni, yāni ceva etānī’ti[V 3.0096]. So neva ussādetabbo na apasādetabbo; anussādetvā anapasādetvā sveva sādhukaṃ saññāpetabbo tesaññeva byañjanānaṃ nisantiyā.

180. Furthermore, Cunda, a fellow in the holy life might speak on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha. Therein, if it should occur to you: ‘This venerable one grasps the meaning correctly, but applies the phrasing wrongly,’ his words should neither be approved of nor rejected. Without approving or rejecting, he should be spoken to thus: ‘Friend, for this meaning, which phrasing is more suitable: this or that?’ If he should reply: ‘Friend, for this meaning, this very phrasing is more suitable,’ he should be neither extolled nor disparaged. Without extolling or disparaging him, he himself should be well instructed for the firm establishing of that very phrasing.

181. “Aparopi ce, cunda, sabrahmacārī saṅghe dhammaṃ bhāseyya. Tatra ce tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho āyasmā atthañceva sammā gaṇhāti byañjanāni [M 3.0107] ca sammā ropetī’ti. Tassa ‘sādhū’ti bhāsitaṃ abhinanditabbaṃ anumoditabbaṃ; tassa ‘sādhū’ti bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā so evamassa vacanīyo – ‘lābhā no āvuso, suladdhaṃ no āvuso, ye mayaṃ āyasmantaṃ tādisaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ passāma evaṃ atthupetaṃ byañjanupeta’nti.

181. Furthermore, Cunda, a fellow in the holy life might speak on the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha. Therein, if it should occur to you: ‘This venerable one grasps the meaning correctly and applies the phrasing correctly,’ his speech should be approved of and rejoiced in with the words, ‘Excellent!’ Having approved of and rejoiced in his speech, he should be spoken to thus: ‘It is a gain for us, friend, it is well-gained by us, that we see a venerable one such as yourself, a fellow in the holy life so endowed with meaning and phrasing.’

Paccayānuññātakāraṇaṃ

The Reason for the Allowance of Requisites

182. “Na vo ahaṃ, cunda, diṭṭhadhammikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ [P 3.0130] saṃvarāya dhammaṃ desemi. Na panāhaṃ, cunda, samparāyikānaṃyeva āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya dhammaṃ desemi. Diṭṭhadhammikānaṃ cevāhaṃ, cunda, āsavānaṃ saṃvarāya dhammaṃ desemi; samparāyikānañca āsavānaṃ paṭighātāya. Tasmātiha, cunda, yaṃ vo mayā cīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ, alaṃ vo taṃ – yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya, uṇhassa paṭighātāya, ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapa siriṃsapa (syā.) samphassānaṃ paṭighātāya, yāvadeva hirikopīnapaṭicchādanatthaṃ. Yo [T 3.0143] vo mayā piṇḍapāto anuññāto, alaṃ vo so yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya vihiṃsūparatiyā brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro ca cāti (bahūsu). Yaṃ vo mayā senāsanaṃ anuññātaṃ, alaṃ vo taṃ yāvadeva sītassa paṭighātāya, uṇhassa paṭighātāya, ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassānaṃ paṭighātāya, yāvadeva utuparissayavinodana paṭisallānārāmatthaṃ. Yo vo mayā gilānapaccayabhesajja parikkhāro anuññāto, alaṃ vo so yāvadeva uppannānaṃ veyyābādhikānaṃ vedanānaṃ paṭighātāya abyāpajjaparamatāya abyāpajjhaparamatāyāti (sī. syā. pī.), abyābajjhaparamatāya (?).

182. Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma merely for the restraint of taints pertaining only to the present life. Nor, Cunda, do I teach the Dhamma merely for the dispelling of taints pertaining only to the future life. Cunda, I teach the Dhamma for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life and for the dispelling of taints pertaining to the future life. Therefore, Cunda, the robe that I have allowed you is sufficient—just for warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and just for the purpose of covering the private parts. The alms-food that I have allowed you is sufficient—just for the maintenance and sustenance of this body, for the cessation of discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, with the thought: ‘Thus, I will dispel the old feeling and not allow a new feeling to arise. I will maintain myself, be blameless, and live in comfort.’ The lodging that I have allowed you is sufficient—just for warding off cold, for warding off heat, for warding off the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, and just for the purpose of dispelling the afflictions of the seasons and for delighting in seclusion. The medicinal requisites for the sick that I have allowed you are sufficient—just for warding off arisen feelings of affliction and for the supreme state of being unafflicted.

Sukhallikānuyogo

The Pursuit of Pleasure

183. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘sukhallikānuyogamanuyuttā samaṇā sakyaputtiyā viharantī’ti. Evaṃvādino vadamānā (syā.), cunda, aññatitthiyā [V 3.0097] paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘katamo so[M 3.0108], āvuso, sukhallikānuyogo? Sukhallikānuyogā hi bahū anekavihitā nānappakārakā’ti.

183. Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘The recluses who are sons of the Sakyan live devoted to the pursuit of pleasure.’ Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed in this way: ‘Friends, what is that pursuit of pleasure? For the pursuits of pleasure are many, of numerous kinds, and of various sorts.’

“Cattārome, cunda, sukhallikānuyogā hīnā gammā pothujjanikā anariyā anatthasaṃhitā na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattanti. Katame cattāro?

Cunda, these four pursuits of pleasure are base, of the village-dweller, of the ordinary person, ignoble, and unbeneficial; they do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, or to Nibbāna. What are the four?

“Idha, cunda, ekacco bālo pāṇe vadhitvā vadhitvā attānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti. Ayaṃ paṭhamo sukhallikānuyogo.

Here, Cunda, a certain foolish person, having repeatedly killed living beings, makes himself happy and gratified. This is the first pursuit of pleasure.

“Puna caparaṃ, cunda, idhekacco [T 3.0144][P 3.0131] adinnaṃ ādiyitvā ādiyitvā attānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti. Ayaṃ dutiyo sukhallikānuyogo.

Furthermore, Cunda, here a certain person, having repeatedly taken what is not given, makes himself happy and gratified. This is the second pursuit of pleasure.

“Puna caparaṃ, cunda, idhekacco musā bhaṇitvā bhaṇitvā attānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti. Ayaṃ tatiyo sukhallikānuyogo.

Furthermore, Cunda, here a certain person, having repeatedly spoken falsehood, makes himself happy and gratified. This is the third pursuit of pleasure.

“Puna caparaṃ, cunda, idhekacco pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti. Ayaṃ catuttho sukhallikānuyogo.

Furthermore, Cunda, here a certain person, provided and endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure, indulges in them. This is the fourth pursuit of pleasure.

“Ime kho, cunda, cattāro sukhallikānuyogā hīnā gammā pothujjanikā anariyā anatthasaṃhitā na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattanti.

These, Cunda, are the four pursuits of pleasure that are base, of the village-dweller, of the ordinary person, ignoble, and unbeneficial; they do not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, or to Nibbāna.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “ime cattāro sukhallikānuyoge anuyuttā samaṇā sakyaputtiyā viharantī’ti. Te vo te (sī. pī.) ‘māhevaṃ’ tissu vacanīyā. Na te vo sammā vadamānā vadeyyuṃ, abbhācikkheyyuṃ asatā abhūtena.

Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘The recluses who are sons of the Sakyan live devoted to these four pursuits of pleasure.’ They should be told by you: ‘Do not say so.’ They would not be speaking rightly of you; they would be slandering you with what is non-existent and untrue.

184. “Cattārome, cunda, sukhallikānuyogā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattanti. Katame cattāro?

184. Cunda, these four pursuits of pleasure lead exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna. What are the four?

“Idha[V 3.0098], cunda, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ paṭhamo sukhallikānuyogo.

Here, Cunda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This is the first pursuit of pleasure.

“Puna [M 3.0109] caparaṃ, cunda, bhikkhu vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ dutiyo sukhallikānuyogo.

Furthermore, Cunda, with the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is the second pursuit of pleasure.

“Puna caparaṃ, cunda, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā…pe… tatiyaṃ [T 3.0145] jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ tatiyo sukhallikānuyogo.

“Furthermore, Cunda, a bhikkhu, with the fading away of rapture… enters and abides in the third jhāna. This is the third devotion to pleasant feeling.”

“Puna caparaṃ, cunda, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā [P 3.0132] dukkhassa ca pahānā…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ catuttho sukhallikānuyogo.

“Furthermore, Cunda, a bhikkhu, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain… enters and abides in the fourth jhāna. This is the fourth devotion to pleasant feeling.”

“Ime kho, cunda, cattāro sukhallikānuyogā ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattanti.

“These, Cunda, are the four devotions to pleasant feeling that lead exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, and to Nibbāna.”

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – “ime cattāro sukhallikānuyoge anuyuttā samaṇā sakyaputtiyā viharantī’ti. Te vo ‘evaṃ’ tissu vacanīyā. Sammā te vo vadamānā vadeyyuṃ, na te vo abbhācikkheyyuṃ asatā abhūtena.

“Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘The recluses, sons of the Sakyan, live devoted to these four devotions to pleasant feeling.’ They should be told by you: ‘It is so.’ They would be speaking rightly of you; they would not be slandering you with what is non-existent and untrue.”

Sukhallikānuyogānisaṃso

The Benefits of Devotion to Pleasant Feeling

185. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ime panāvuso, cattāro sukhallikānuyoge anuyuttānaṃ viharataṃ kati phalāni katānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā’ti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘ime kho, āvuso, cattāro sukhallikānuyoge anuyuttānaṃ viharataṃ cattāri phalāni cattāro [V 3.0099] ānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā. Katame cattāro? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā sotāpanno hoti avinipātadhammo niyato sambodhiparāyaṇo. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ phalaṃ, paṭhamo ānisaṃso. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu tiṇṇaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā rāgadosamohānaṃ tanuttā sakadāgāmī hoti, sakideva imaṃ lokaṃ āgantvā dukkhassantaṃ [T 3.0146] karoti. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ phalaṃ, dutiyo ānisaṃso. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcannaṃ orambhāgiyānaṃ saṃyojanānaṃ parikkhayā opapātiko hoti, tattha parinibbāyī anāvattidhammo tasmā lokā. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ phalaṃ, tatiyo ānisaṃso. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ catutthaṃ phalaṃ catuttho ānisaṃso. Ime [M 3.0110] kho, āvuso, cattāro sukhallikānuyoge anuyuttānaṃ viharataṃ imāni cattāri phalāni, cattāro ānisaṃsā pāṭikaṅkhā”ti.

185. “It is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say: ‘Friends, for those who live devoted to these four devotions to pleasant feeling, what fruits and what benefits can be expected?’ Wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told: ‘Friends, for those who live devoted to these four devotions to pleasant feeling, four fruits and four benefits can be expected. What are the four? Here, friend, with the destruction of the three fetters, a bhikkhu becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to downfall, assured, and destined for awakening. This is the first fruit, the first benefit. Furthermore, friend, with the destruction of the three fetters and the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, a bhikkhu becomes a once-returner who, having returned to this world just once, makes an end of suffering. This is the second fruit, the second benefit. Furthermore, friend, with the destruction of the five lower fetters, a bhikkhu is spontaneously reborn, attains final Nibbāna there, and is not liable to return from that world. This is the third fruit, the third benefit. Furthermore, friend, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu, having realized for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enters and abides in the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom. This is the fourth fruit, the fourth benefit. These, friends, are the four fruits and four benefits that can be expected for those who live devoted to these four devotions to pleasant feeling.’”

Khīṇāsavaabhabbaṭhānaṃ

The Incapabilities of One Whose Taints Are Destroyed

186. “Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā [P 3.0133] paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘aṭṭhitadhammā samaṇā sakyaputtiyā viharantī’ti. Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sāvakānaṃ dhammā desitā paññattā yāvajīvaṃ anatikkamanīyā. Seyyathāpi, āvuso, indakhīlo vā ayokhīlo vā gambhīranemo sunikhāto acalo asampavedhī. Evameva kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena sāvakānaṃ dhammā desitā paññattā yāvajīvaṃ anatikkamanīyā. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto, abhabbo so nava ṭhānāni ajjhācarituṃ. Abhabbo, āvuso, khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sañcicca [T 3.0147] pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyituṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevituṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sampajānamusā bhāsituṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sannidhikārakaṃ kāme paribhuñjituṃ seyyathāpi pubbe āgārikabhūto; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu chandāgatiṃ gantuṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu dosāgatiṃ gantuṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu mohāgatiṃ gantuṃ; abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu bhayāgatiṃ gantuṃ. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu arahaṃ khīṇāsavo vusitavā katakaraṇīyo ohitabhāro anuppattasadattho parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojano sammadaññā vimutto, abhabbo so imāni nava ṭhānāni ajjhācaritu”nti.

186. “It is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say: ‘The recluses, sons of the Sakyan, live with an unstable doctrine.’ When they say this, Cunda, the wanderers of other sects should be told: ‘There are, friends, doctrines taught and laid down by the Blessed One—the knowing, the seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for his disciples, which are not to be transgressed for life. Just as, friends, an Indakhila pillar or an iron pillar, with a deep foundation, well-dug-in, is stable and unshakable, so too, friends, are the doctrines taught and laid down by the Blessed One—the knowing, the seeing, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for his disciples, which are not to be transgressed for life. A bhikkhu, friends, who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—such a bhikkhu is incapable of transgressing nine principles. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, friends, is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given, in the manner of theft. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of knowingly speaking a falsehood. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying stored-up sensual pleasures as he did formerly as a householder. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong course through desire. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong course through hatred. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong course through delusion. A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is incapable of following a wrong course through fear. A bhikkhu, friends, who is an Arahant, whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge—such a bhikkhu is incapable of transgressing these nine principles.’”

Pañhābyākaraṇaṃ

The Explanation of Questions

187. “Ṭhānaṃ [V 3.0100][P 3.0134] kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘atītaṃ kho addhānaṃ ārabbha samaṇo gotamo atīrakaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paññapeti, no ca kho anāgataṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha atīrakaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paññapeti, tayidaṃ kiṃsu tayidaṃ kathaṃsū’ti? Te ca aññatitthiyā [M 3.0111] paribbājakā aññavihitakena ñāṇadassanena aññavihitakaṃ ñāṇadassanaṃ paññapetabbaṃ maññanti yathariva bālā abyattā. Atītaṃ kho, cunda, addhānaṃ ārabbha tathāgatassa satānusāri ñāṇaṃ hoti; so yāvatakaṃ ākaṅkhati tāvatakaṃ anussarati. Anāgatañca kho addhānaṃ ārabbha tathāgatassa bodhijaṃ ñāṇaṃ uppajjati – ‘ayamantimā [T 3.0148] jāti, natthidāni punabbhavo’ti. ‘Atītaṃ cepi, cunda, hoti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, na taṃ tathāgato byākaroti. Atītaṃ cepi, cunda, hoti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, tampi tathāgato na byākaroti. Atītaṃ cepi cunda, hoti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇāya. Anāgataṃ cepi, cunda, hoti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, na taṃ tathāgato byākaroti…pe… tassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇāya. Paccuppannaṃ cepi, cunda, hoti abhūtaṃ atacchaṃ anatthasaṃhitaṃ, na taṃ tathāgato byākaroti. Paccuppannaṃ cepi, cunda, hoti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ [P 3.0135] anatthasaṃhitaṃ, tampi tathāgato na byākaroti. Paccuppannaṃ cepi, cunda, hoti bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ, tatra kālaññū tathāgato hoti tassa pañhassa veyyākaraṇāya.

187. “Cunda, this is a possible situation, that wanderers of other sects might say thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama proclaims boundless knowledge and vision concerning the past, but he does not proclaim boundless knowledge and vision concerning the future. What is this? For what reason is this?’ And those wanderers of other sects, being foolish and unskilled, think that a knowledge and vision of one kind should be declared by a knowledge and vision of another kind. Cunda, concerning the past, the Tathāgata has knowledge that follows upon memory; he recollects as much as he wishes. And concerning the future, the knowledge born of awakening arises in the Tathāgata: ‘This is the final birth; there is now no new existence.’ Cunda, if a past matter is unreal, untrue, and not connected with benefit, the Tathāgata does not explain it. Cunda, if a past matter is real, true, but not connected with benefit, the Tathāgata does not explain that either. Cunda, if a past matter is real, true, and connected with benefit, in that case the Tathāgata is a knower of the time for the explanation of that question. Cunda, if a future matter is unreal, untrue, and not connected with benefit, the Tathāgata does not explain it… for the explanation of that question. Cunda, if a present matter is unreal, untrue, and not connected with benefit, the Tathāgata does not explain it. Cunda, if a present matter is real, true, but not connected with benefit, the Tathāgata does not explain that either. Cunda, if a present matter is real, true, and connected with benefit, in that case the Tathāgata is a knower of the time for the explanation of that question.”

188. “Iti kho, cunda, atītānāgatapaccuppannesu dhammesu tathāgato kālavādī kālavādī saccavādī (syā.) bhūtavādī atthavādī dhammavādī vinayavādī, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccati. Yañca kho, cunda, sadevakassa lokassa samārakassa sabrahmakassa sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ viññātaṃ pattaṃ pariyesitaṃ anuvicaritaṃ manasā, sabbaṃ tathāgatena abhisambuddhaṃ, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccati. Yañca, cunda, rattiṃ tathāgato anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambujjhati, yañca rattiṃ anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyati, yaṃ etasmiṃ antare bhāsati [T 3.0149] lapati niddisati. Sabbaṃ taṃ tatheva hoti no aññathā, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccati. Yathāvādī, cunda, tathāgato tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī. Iti yathāvādī tathākārī, yathākārī tathāvādī, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccati. Sadevake loke, cunda, samārake sabrahmake sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiyā pajāya sadevamanussāya tathāgato abhibhū anabhibhūto aññadatthudaso vasavattī, tasmā ‘tathāgato’ti vuccati.

188. “Thus, Cunda, in regard to things past, future, and present, the Tathāgata is one who speaks at the proper time, one who speaks what is real, one who speaks on what is beneficial, one who speaks on the Dhamma, one who speaks on the discipline. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’ And, Cunda, whatever in this world with its devas, its Māra, its Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, and pondered by the mind—all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’ Cunda, on the night the Tathāgata fully awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and on the night he attains final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element without remainder, whatever he speaks, utters, and points out in that interval, all of that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’ Cunda, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he does; as he does, so he speaks. Thus, as he speaks, so he does; as he does, so he speaks. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’ Cunda, in the world with its devas, its Māra, its Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, one who sees with certainty, a wielder of power. Therefore, he is called ‘Tathāgata.’”

Abyākataṭṭhānaṃ

The Undeclared Points

189. “Ṭhānaṃ [M 3.0112][V 3.0101] kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘abyākataṃ kho, āvuso, bhagavatā [P 3.0136] – “hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’”nti.

189. “Cunda, this is a possible situation, that wanderers of other sects might say thus: ‘Friend, does a being exist after death? Is this alone true, and the other worthless?’ Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told this: ‘Friend, this has not been declared by the Blessed One: “A being exists after death; this alone is true, and the other is worthless.”’”

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kiṃ panāvuso, na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘etampi kho, āvuso, bhagavatā abyākataṃ – “na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’”nti.

“Cunda, this is a possible situation, that wanderers of other sects might say thus: ‘Friend, does a being not exist after death? Is this alone true, and the other worthless?’ Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told this: ‘Friend, this too has not been declared by the Blessed One: “A being does not exist after death; this alone is true, and the other is worthless.”’”

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kiṃ panāvuso, hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘abyākataṃ [T 3.0150] kho etaṃ, āvuso, bhagavatā – “hoti ca na ca hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’”nti.

“Cunda, this is a possible situation, that wanderers of other sects might say thus: ‘Friend, does a being both exist and not exist after death? Is this alone true, and the other worthless?’ Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told this: ‘Friend, this has not been declared by the Blessed One: “A being both exists and does not exist after death; this alone is true, and the other is worthless.”’”

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kiṃ panāvuso, neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘etampi kho, āvuso, bhagavatā abyākataṃ – “neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’”nti.

“Cunda, this is a possible situation, that wanderers of other sects might say thus: ‘Friend, does a being neither exist nor not exist after death? Is this alone true, and the other worthless?’ Cunda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told this: ‘Friend, this too has not been declared by the Blessed One: “A being neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, and the other is worthless.”’”

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kasmā panetaṃ, āvuso, samaṇena gotamena abyākata’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘na hetaṃ, āvuso, atthasaṃhitaṃ na dhammasaṃhitaṃ [V 3.0102] na ādibrahmacariyakaṃ na nibbidāya na virāgāya na nirodhāya na upasamāya na abhiññāya na sambodhāya na nibbānāya saṃvattati, tasmā taṃ bhagavatā abyākata’nti.

Indeed, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say thus: 'But why, friend, has this not been declared by the ascetic Gotama?' When wanderers of other sects speak thus, Cunda, they should be told: 'Because, friend, this is not connected with benefit, not connected with the Dhamma, not fundamental to the holy life, and does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna. That is why it has not been declared by the Blessed One.'

Byākataṭṭhānaṃ

The Declared Points

190. “Ṭhānaṃ [M 3.0113] kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kiṃ panāvuso, samaṇena gotamena byākata’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘idaṃ dukkhanti kho, āvuso, bhagavatā byākataṃ, ayaṃ dukkhasamudayoti kho, āvuso, bhagavatā byākataṃ, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhoti kho, āvuso, bhagavatā byākataṃ, ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadāti [T 3.0151] kho, āvuso, bhagavatā byākata’nti.

190. It is possible, Cunda, that wanderers of other sects might say thus: 'What, friend, has the ascetic Gotama declared?' When wanderers of other sects say this, Cunda, they should be told thus: '“This is suffering,” friend, has been declared by the Blessed One. “This is the origin of suffering,” friend, has been declared by the Blessed One. “This is the cessation of suffering,” friend, has been declared by the Blessed One. “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering,” friend, has been declared by the Blessed One.'

“Ṭhānaṃ [P 3.0137] kho panetaṃ, cunda, vijjati, yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘kasmā panetaṃ, āvuso, samaṇena gotamena byākata’nti? Evaṃvādino, cunda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘etañhi, āvuso, atthasaṃhitaṃ, etaṃ dhammasaṃhitaṃ, etaṃ ādibrahmacariyakaṃ ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya saṃvattati. Tasmā taṃ bhagavatā byākata’nti.

Indeed, Cunda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘But why, friend, has this been declared by the ascetic Gotama?’ When wanderers of other sects speak thus, Cunda, they should be told: ‘Because, friend, this is connected with benefit, this is connected with the Dhamma, this is fundamental to the holy life, and it leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, and to Nibbāna. That is why it has been declared by the Blessed One.’

Pubbantasahagatadiṭṭhinissayā

Grounds for Views Pertaining to the Past

191. “Yepi te, cunda, pubbantasahagatā diṭṭhinissayā, tepi vo mayā byākatā, yathā te byākātabbā. Yathā ca te na byākātabbā, kiṃ vo ahaṃ te tathā tattha (syā. ka.) byākarissāmi? Yepi te, cunda, aparantasahagatā diṭṭhinissayā, tepi vo mayā byākatā, yathā te byākātabbā. Yathā ca te na byākātabbā, kiṃ vo ahaṃ te tathā byākarissāmi? Katame ca te, cunda, pubbantasahagatā diṭṭhinissayā, ye vo mayā byākatā, yathā te byākātabbā. (Yathā ca te na byākātabbā, kiṃ vo ahaṃ te tathā byākarissāmi) (yathā ca te na byākātabbā) sabbattha? Santi kho, cunda, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Santi pana, cunda, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘asassato attā ca loko ca…pe… sassato ca asassato ca attā ca loko ca… neva sassato nāsassato attā ca loko ca… sayaṃkato [T 3.0152] attā ca loko ca… paraṃkato attā [V 3.0103] ca loko ca… sayaṃkato ca [M 3.0114] paraṃkato ca attā ca loko ca… asayaṃkāro [P 3.0138] aparaṃkāro adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Sassataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… asassataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… sassatañca asassatañca sukhadukkhaṃ… nevasassataṃ nāsassataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca sukhadukkhaṃ… asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti.

191. Cunda, those grounds for views connected with the past—I have declared them to you as they should be declared. And as they should not be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way? Cunda, those grounds for views connected with the future—I have declared them to you as they should be declared. And as they should not be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way? And what, Cunda, are those grounds for views connected with the past that I have declared to you as they should be declared? (And as they should not be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way?) There are, Cunda, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views: ‘The self and the world are eternal—this alone is true, all else is false.’ There are, Cunda, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views: ‘The self and the world are not eternal… both eternal and not eternal… neither eternal nor not eternal… self-made… made by another… both self-made and made by another… not self-made and not made by another, the self and the world have arisen without a cause—this alone is true, all else is false.’ ‘Pleasure and pain are eternal… not eternal… both eternal and not eternal… neither eternal nor not eternal… self-made… made by another… both self-made and made by another… not self-made and not made by another, pleasure and pain have arisen without a cause—this alone is true, all else is false.’

192. “Tatra, cunda, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘atthi nu kho idaṃ, āvuso, vuccati – “sassato attā ca loko cā”ti? Yañca kho te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Taṃ tesaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aññathāsaññinopi hettha, cunda, santeke sattā. Imāyapi kho ahaṃ, cunda, paññattiyā neva attanā samasamaṃ samanupassāmi kuto bhiyyo. Atha kho ahameva tattha bhiyyo yadidaṃ adhipaññatti.

192. Now, Cunda, as for those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of such views, who maintain: ‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, anything else is worthless,’ I go to them and say: ‘Is it true, friends, that you say: “The self and the world are eternal”?’ And that which they say—‘This alone is true, anything else is worthless’—that I do not approve of. Why is that? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who have different perceptions. In this designation, Cunda, I do not see one equal to myself, let alone a superior. Rather, I am indeed superior in that which is the higher designation.

193. “Tatra, cunda, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘asassato attā ca loko ca…pe… sassato ca asassato ca attā ca loko ca… nevasassato nāsassato attā [T 3.0153] ca loko ca… sayaṃkato attā ca loko ca… paraṃkato attā ca loko ca… sayaṃkato ca paraṃkato ca attā ca loko ca… asayaṃkāro aparaṃkāro adhiccasamuppanno attā ca loko ca… sassataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… asassataṃ [P 3.0139] sukhadukkhaṃ… sassatañca asassatañca sukhadukkhaṃ… nevasassataṃ nāsassataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… sayaṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… paraṃkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ… sayaṃkatañca paraṃkatañca sukhadukkhaṃ… asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkhaṃ, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘atthi nu kho idaṃ, āvuso, vuccati – “asayaṃkāraṃ aparaṃkāraṃ adhiccasamuppannaṃ sukhadukkha’”nti? Yañca kho te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Taṃ tesaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aññathāsaññinopi hettha, cunda, santeke sattā. Imāyapi kho ahaṃ, cunda, paññattiyā neva attanā samasamaṃ samanupassāmi kuto bhiyyo. Atha kho ahameva tattha bhiyyo yadidaṃ adhipaññatti. Ime kho te, cunda, pubbantasahagatā diṭṭhinissayā, ye vo mayā byākatā, yathā te byākātabbā[M 3.0115]. Yathā ca te na byākātabbā, kiṃ vo ahaṃ te tathā byākarissāmīti byākarissāmīti (sī. ka.)?

193. Cunda, among them, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘The self and the world are eternal; the self and the world are not eternal; the self and the world are both eternal and not eternal; the self and the world are neither eternal nor not eternal; the self and the world are self-made; the self and the world are made by another; the self and the world are both self-made and made by another; the self and the world are not self-made, not made by another, and have arisen without a cause; pleasure and pain are eternal; pleasure and pain are not eternal; pleasure and pain are both eternal and not eternal; pleasure and pain are neither eternal nor not eternal; pleasure and pain are self-made; pleasure and pain are made by another; pleasure and pain are both self-made and made by another; pleasure and pain are not self-made, not made by another, and have arisen without a cause; this alone is true, all else is worthless’—I approach them and speak thus: ‘Friends, is this statement indeed made: “Pleasure and pain are not self-made, not made by another, and have arisen without a cause”?’ And as to what they have said—‘This alone is true, all else is worthless’—I do not assent to that of theirs. For what reason? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive differently. In regard to this designation, Cunda, I do not see anyone equal to myself, how much less a superior one. Indeed, I myself am superior therein, that is, in this matter of higher designation. These, Cunda, are the foundations of views connected with the past, which have been declared by me to you as they should be declared. And as for how they should not be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way?

Aparantasahagatadiṭṭhinissayā

Foundations of Views Connected with the Future

194. “Katame [V 3.0104] ca te, cunda, aparantasahagatā diṭṭhinissayā, ye vo mayā byākatā, yathā te byākātabbā. (Yathā ca te na byākātabbā, kiṃ vo ahaṃ te tathā byākarissāmī) ( ) etthantare pāṭho sabbatthapi paripuṇṇo dissati? Santi, cunda, eke [T 3.0154] samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Santi pana, cunda, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘arūpī attā hoti…pe… rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti… nevarūpī nārūpī attā hoti… saññī [P 3.0140] attā hoti… asaññī attā hoti… nevasaññīnāsaññī attā hoti… attā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Tatra, cunda, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘atthi nu kho idaṃ, āvuso, vuccati – “rūpī attā hoti arogo paraṃ maraṇā’”ti? Yañca kho te evamāhaṃsu – ‘idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Taṃ tesaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aññathāsaññinopi hettha, cunda, santeke sattā. Imāyapi kho ahaṃ, cunda, paññattiyā neva attanā samasamaṃ samanupassāmi kuto bhiyyo. Atha kho ahameva tattha bhiyyo yadidaṃ adhipaññatti.

194. And what, Cunda, are those foundations of views connected with the future, which have been declared by me to you as they should be declared? And as for how they should not be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way? There are, Cunda, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘The self is material and permanent after death; this alone is true, all else is worthless.’ There are also, Cunda, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘The self is immaterial... the self is both material and immaterial... the self is neither material nor immaterial... the self is percipient... the self is non-percipient... the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient... the self is annihilated, perishes, and does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is worthless.’ Therein, Cunda, concerning those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘The self is material and permanent after death; this alone is true, all else is worthless’—I approach them and speak thus: ‘Friends, is this statement indeed made: “The self is material and permanent after death”?’ And as to what they have said—‘This alone is true, all else is worthless’—I do not assent to that of theirs. For what reason? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive differently. In regard to this designation, Cunda, I do not see anyone equal to myself, how much less a superior one. Indeed, I myself am superior therein, that is, in this matter of higher designation.

195. “Tatra, cunda, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘arūpī attā hoti…pe… rūpī ca arūpī ca attā hoti… nevarūpīnārūpī attā hoti… saññī attā hoti… asaññī attā hoti… nevasaññīnāsaññī [T 3.0155] attā hoti… attā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā, idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Tyāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadāmi – ‘atthi nu kho idaṃ, āvuso, vuccati – “attā ucchijjati vinassati na hoti paraṃ maraṇā’”ti? Yañca kho te, cunda, evamāhaṃsu – ‘idameva saccaṃ moghamañña’nti. Taṃ tesaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aññathāsaññinopi hettha, cunda, santeke sattā. Imāyapi kho ahaṃ, cunda, paññattiyā neva attanā [M 3.0116] samasamaṃ samanupassāmi, kuto bhiyyo. Atha kho ahameva tattha bhiyyo yadidaṃ adhipaññatti. Ime kho te, cunda, aparantasahagatā diṭṭhinissayā, ye vo mayā byākatā[P 3.0141], yathā te byākātabbā. Yathā ca te na byākātabbā, kiṃ vo ahaṃ te tathā byākarissāmīti byākarissāmīti (sī. ka.)?

195. Therein, Cunda, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘The self is immaterial... the self is both material and immaterial... the self is neither material nor immaterial... the self is percipient... the self is non-percipient... the self is neither percipient nor non-percipient... the self is annihilated, perishes, and does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is worthless’—I approach them and speak thus: ‘Friends, is this statement indeed made: “The self is annihilated, perishes, and does not exist after death”?’ And as to what they have said, Cunda—‘This alone is true, all else is worthless’—I do not assent to that of theirs. For what reason? Because, Cunda, there are some beings here who perceive differently. In regard to this designation, Cunda, I do not see anyone equal to myself, how much less a superior one. Indeed, I myself am superior therein, that is, in this matter of higher designation. These, Cunda, are the foundations of views connected with the future, which have been declared by me to you as they should be declared. And as for how they should not be declared, why should I declare them to you in that way?

196. “Imesañca, cunda, pubbantasahagatānaṃ diṭṭhinissayānaṃ imesañca aparantasahagatānaṃ diṭṭhinissayānaṃ [V 3.0105] pahānāya samatikkamāya evaṃ mayā cattāro satipaṭṭhānā desitā paññattā. Katame cattāro? Idha, cunda, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī…pe… citte cittānupassī… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Imesañca cunda, pubbantasahagatānaṃ diṭṭhinissayānaṃ imesañca aparantasahagatānaṃ diṭṭhinissayānaṃ [T 3.0156] pahānāya samatikkamāya. Evaṃ mayā ime cattāro satipaṭṭhānā desitā paññattā”ti.

196. For the abandoning and overcoming of these foundations of views connected with the past and these foundations of views connected with the future, Cunda, I have thus taught and established the four foundations of mindfulness. What are the four? Here, Cunda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. For the abandoning and overcoming of these foundations of views connected with the past and these foundations of views connected with the future, Cunda, I have thus taught and established these four foundations of mindfulness.

197. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmā upavāṇo bhagavato piṭṭhito ṭhito hoti bhagavantaṃ bījayamāno. Atha kho āyasmā upavāṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Pāsādiko vatāyaṃ, bhante, dhammapariyāyo; supāsādiko vatāyaṃ bhante, dhammapariyāyo, ko nāmāyaṃ bhante dhammapariyāyo”ti? “Tasmātiha tvaṃ, upavāṇa, imaṃ dhammapariyāyaṃ ‘pāsādiko’ tveva naṃ dhārehī”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamano āyasmā upavāṇo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandīti.

197. At that time, the Venerable Upavāṇa was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him. Then the Venerable Upavāṇa said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How inspiring is this exposition of the Dhamma, venerable sir! How exceedingly inspiring is this exposition of the Dhamma! What is the name of this exposition of the Dhamma, venerable sir?” “Therefore, Upavāṇa, you should remember this exposition of the Dhamma simply as ‘The Inspiring.’” This is what the Blessed One said. The Venerable Upavāṇa, delighted, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Pāsādikasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The sixth, the Pāsādika Sutta, is concluded.

7. Lakkhaṇasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Marks

Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni

The Thirty-Two Marks of a Great Man

198. Evaṃ [P 3.0142][M 3.0117][V 3.0106][T 3.0157] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti. “Bhaddante”ti bhadanteti (sī. syā. pī.) te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca –

198. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying: “Monks!” “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

199. “Dvattiṃsimāni, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni satta ratanāni bhavanti; seyyathidaṃ, cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchado vivaṭacchado (syā. ka.), vivattacchado (sī. pī.).

199. “Monks, there are these thirty-two marks of a Great Man, endowed with which a Great Man has only two destinies, no other. If he dwells in a household, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king, a king of righteousness, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has attained stability in his country, and is endowed with the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has over a thousand sons who are valiant, of heroic form, crushers of enemy armies. He dwells having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean, without rod, without weapon, by righteousness. But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One in the world, one who has the covering removed.”

200. “Katamāni ca tāni, bhikkhave, dvattiṃsa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa [P 3.0143] dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā? Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho [T 3.0158] loke vivaṭṭacchado.

200. “And what, monks, are those thirty-two marks of a Great Man, endowed with which a Great Man has only two destinies, no other? If he dwells in a household, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… and so on… But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One in the world, one who has the covering removed.”

“Idha, bhikkhave, mahāpuriso suppatiṭṭhitapādo hoti. Yampi, bhikkhave, mahāpuriso suppatiṭṭhitapādo hoti, idampi, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

“Monks, here the Great Man has level feet. That the Great Man has level feet, monks, this too is a mark of a Great Man.”

“Puna [V 3.0107] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa heṭṭhāpādatalesu cakkāni jātāni honti sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbākāraparipūrāni sabbākāraparipūrāni suvibhattantarāni (sī. pī.). Yampi[M 3.0118], bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa heṭṭhāpādatalesu cakkāni jātāni honti sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbākāraparipūrāni, idampi, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

“Furthermore, monks, on the soles of the Great Man's feet, wheels have arisen with a thousand spokes, with their rims and hubs, complete in all aspects. That on the soles of the Great Man's feet, wheels have arisen with a thousand spokes, with their rims and hubs, complete in all aspects, monks, this too is a mark of a Great Man.”

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mahāpuriso āyatapaṇhi hoti…pe… dīghaṅguli hoti… mudutalunahatthapādo hoti… jālahatthapādo hoti… ussaṅkhapādo hoti… eṇijaṅgho hoti… ṭhitakova anonamanto ubhohi pāṇitalehi jaṇṇukāni parimasati parimajjati… kosohitavatthaguyho hoti… suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hoti kañcanasannibhattaco… sukhumacchavi hoti, sukhumattā chaviyā rajojallaṃ kāye na upalimpati… ekekalomo [P 3.0144] hoti, ekekāni lomāni lomakūpesu jātāni… uddhaggalomo hoti, uddhaggāni lomāni jātāni nīlāni añjanavaṇṇāni kuṇḍalāvaṭṭāni kuṇḍalāvattāni (bahūsu) dakkhiṇāvaṭṭakajātāni dakkhiṇāvattakajātāni (sī. syā. pī.) … brahmujugatto hoti… sattussado hoti… sīhapubbaddhakāyo hoti… citantaraṃso pitantaraṃso (syā.) hoti… nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo hoti, yāvatakvassa kāyo tāvatakvassa byāmo yāvatakvassa byāmo tāvatakvassa kāyo… samavaṭṭakkhandho hoti… rasaggasaggī hoti… sīhahanu hoti… cattālīsadanto hoti [T 3.0159]… samadanto hoti… aviraḷadanto hoti… susukkadāṭho hoti… pahūtajivho hoti… brahmassaro hoti karavīkabhāṇī… abhinīlanetto hoti… gopakhumo hoti… uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā hoti, odātā mudutūlasannibhā. Yampi, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa uṇṇā bhamukantare jātā hoti, odātā mudutūlasannibhā, idampi, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

“Furthermore, monks, the Great Man has long heels… has long fingers and toes… has soft and tender hands and feet… has net-like hands and feet… has high-arched feet… has shanks like an Eṇī antelope… standing and without bending, he can touch and rub his knees with both his palms… has his male organ concealed in a sheath… has a golden complexion, his skin like burnished gold… has delicate skin, and because of the delicacy of his skin, no dust or dirt adheres to his body… has single body-hairs, with one hair growing in each pore… has body-hairs that turn upward; the hairs that have grown are dark blue, the color of collyrium, curling like rings, turning to the right… has a divinely straight body… has the seven convexities… has a chest like a lion… has the space between his shoulders filled out… has the proportions of a banyan tree: his arm-span is the same as his height, and his height is the same as his arm-span… has a perfectly rounded neck… has nerves for tasting that are supreme… has a jaw like a lion… has forty teeth… has even teeth… has teeth without gaps… has very white canine teeth… has a long and broad tongue… has a voice like Brahmā, that sounds like a Karavīka bird… has very dark blue eyes… has eyelashes like a heifer… an uṇṇā has grown between his eyebrows, white and soft like cotton down. That an uṇṇā has grown between the Great Man's eyebrows, white and soft like cotton down, monks, this too is a mark of a Great Man.”

“Puna [P 3.0145] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mahāpuriso uṇhīsasīso hoti. Yampi, bhikkhave, mahāpuriso uṇhīsasīso hoti, idampi, bhikkhave, mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ bhavati.

“Furthermore, monks, the Great Man has a head with a cranial protuberance. That the Great Man has a head with a cranial protuberance, monks, this too is a mark of a Great Man.”

“Imāni kho tāni, bhikkhave, dvattiṃsa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni, yehi samannāgatassa mahāpurisassa dveva gatiyo bhavanti anaññā. Sace [M 3.0119] agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchado.

“These, monks, are those thirty-two marks of a Great Man, endowed with which a Great Man has only two destinies, no other. If he dwells in a household, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… and so on… But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One in the world, one who has the covering removed.”
