“Imāni kho, bhikkhave, dvattiṃsa mahāpurisassa mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni bāhirakāpi isayo [V 3.0108] dhārenti, no ca kho te jānanti – ‘imassa kammassa kaṭattā idaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhatī’ti.

“Monks, these thirty-two marks of a Great Man are also maintained by seers outside the Dispensation, but they do not know: ‘It is due to the performance of this kamma that this mark is obtained.’”

(1) Suppatiṭṭhitapādatālakkhaṇaṃ

The Mark of Well-Placed Feet (1)

201. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno daḷhasamādāno ahosi kusalesu dhammesu, avatthitasamādāno kāyasucarite vacīsucarite manosucarite dānasaṃvibhāge sīlasamādāne uposathupavāse matteyyatāya petteyyatāya sāmaññatāya [T 3.0160] brahmaññatāya kule jeṭṭhāpacāyitāya aññataraññataresu ca adhikusalesu dhammesu[P 3.0146]. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā ussannattā vipulattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. So tattha aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhiggaṇhāti dibbena āyunā dibbena vaṇṇena dibbena sukhena dibbena yasena dibbena ādhipateyyena dibbehi rūpehi dibbehi saddehi dibbehi gandhehi dibbehi rasehi dibbehi phoṭṭhabbehi. So tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Suppatiṭṭhitapādo hoti. Samaṃ pādaṃ bhūmiyaṃ nikkhipati, samaṃ uddharati, samaṃ sabbāvantehi pādatalehi bhūmiṃ phusati.

201. “Monks, the Tathāgata knows a former birth, a former existence, a former abode. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was a human being, he was one who firmly undertook wholesome states, one whose undertaking was unwavering in good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct; in giving and sharing; in undertaking virtue; in observing the Uposatha; in reverence toward his mother and reverence toward his father; in reverence toward ascetics and reverence toward brahmins; in honoring the elders of the family; and in certain other exceedingly wholesome states. On account of that kamma having been done, having been accumulated, being abundant, and being extensive, with the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. There, he surpasses other devas in ten respects: in divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine glory, divine sovereignty, divine sights, divine sounds, divine scents, divine tastes, and divine tactile objects. Having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he obtains this mark of a great man: he has well-planted feet. He places his foot evenly on the ground, he lifts it evenly, and he touches the ground evenly with the entire sole of his foot.”

202. “So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni satta ratanāni bhavanti; seyyathidaṃ, cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ akhilamanimittamakaṇṭakaṃ iddhaṃ phītaṃ khemaṃ sivaṃ nirabbudaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati[M 3.0120]. Rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Akkhambhiyo avikkhambhiyo (sī. pī.) hoti kenaci manussabhūtena [T 3.0161] paccatthikena paccāmittena. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati. “Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchado. Buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Akkhambhiyo hoti abbhantarehi vā bāhirehi vā paccatthikehi paccāmittehi rāgena vā dosena vā mohena vā samaṇena vā [P 3.0147] brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

202. “Endowed with that mark, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning king, righteous, a king of righteousness, ruler of the four quarters, victorious, one who has attained stability in his country, and is endowed with the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has over a thousand sons who are valiant, of heroic form, and crushers of enemy armies. Having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean—making it free of thieves, free of enemies, and free of thorns; making it prosperous, flourishing, secure, safe, and free from calamity—he dwells there, ruling by righteousness, without rod or sword. Being a king, what does he obtain? He is unshakable by any human foe or enemy. This is what he obtains as a king. But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, with the covering removed. Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is unshakable by internal or external foes or enemies: by lust, hatred, or delusion; or by any ascetic or brahmin, by any deva, by Māra, or by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. This is what he obtains as a Buddha.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

203. Tatthetaṃ [V 3.0109] vuccati –

203. In this regard, it is said:

“Sacce ca dhamme ca dame ca saṃyame,

Soceyyasīlālayuposathesu ca;

Dāne ahiṃsāya asāhase rato,

Daḷhaṃ samādāya samattamācari samantamācari (syā. ka.).

“In truth and in Dhamma, in taming and in restraint, in purity, establishment in virtue, and Uposatha observances; delighting in giving, non-harming, and non-aggression, having undertaken it firmly, he practiced it completely.

“So tena kammena divaṃ samakkami apakkami (syā. ka.),

Sukhañca khiḍḍāratiyo ca anvabhi aṃnvabhi (ṭīkā);

Tato cavitvā punarāgato idha,

Samehi pādehi phusī vasundharaṃ.

“By that kamma, he went to heaven, and experienced happiness, play, and delight. Having passed away from there and returned here again, he touched the earth with even feet.

“Byākaṃsu veyyañjanikā samāgatā,

Samappatiṭṭhassa na hoti khambhanā;

Gihissa vā pabbajitassa vā puna pana (syā.),

Taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati tadatthajotakaṃ.

“The interpreters of marks, having gathered, declared: ‘For one with well-planted feet, there is no being shaken, whether for a householder or for one gone forth; that mark becomes an illuminator of that meaning.’

“Akkhambhiyo [T 3.0162] hoti agāramāvasaṃ,

Parābhibhū sattubhi nappamaddano;

Manussabhūtenidha hoti kenaci,

Akkhambhiyo tassa phalena kammuno.

“Dwelling in a house, he is unassailable, an overcomer of others, not crushed by foes; here, by any human being, he is unassailable, by the fruit of that kamma.

“Sace [M 3.0121] ca pabbajjamupeti tādiso,

Nekkhammachandābhirato vicakkhaṇo;

Aggo na so gacchati jātu khambhanaṃ,

Naruttamo esa hi tassa dhammatā”ti.

“And if such a discerning one goes forth, delighting in the desire for renunciation, he, the foremost, the best of men, never at all goes to a state of being shaken; for this is his nature.”

(2) Pādatalacakkalakkhaṇaṃ

(2) The Mark of Wheels on the Soles of the Feet

204. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto [V 3.0110] samāno bahujanassa [P 3.0148] sukhāvaho ahosi, ubbegauttāsabhayaṃ apanuditā, dhammikañca rakkhāvaraṇaguttiṃ saṃvidhātā, saparivārañca dānaṃ adāsi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā ussannattā vipulattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Heṭṭhāpādatalesu cakkāni jātāni honti sahassārāni sanemikāni sanābhikāni sabbākāraparipūrāni suvibhattantarāni.

204. “Monks, in a past birth, a past existence, a past abode, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, he brought happiness to many people, dispelled agitation, terror, and fear, arranged for righteous protection, defense, and security, and gave alms together with their requisites. As a result of that kamma having been done, accumulated, being abundant and extensive, with the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world... Having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he obtains this mark of a great man: On the soles of his feet, wheels appear, with a thousand spokes, with rims, with hubs, complete in all aspects, and with well-distinguished divisions.”

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāparivāro hoti; mahāssa honti parivārā brāhmaṇagahapatikā [T 3.0163] negamajānapadā gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati. Sace kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchado. Buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāparivāro hoti; mahāssa honti parivārā bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with this mark, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a king, a wheel-turning monarch... Being a king, what does he obtain? He has a great retinue; his great retinue consists of brahmins and householders, townsfolk and countryfolk, accountants and great ministers, army commanders, doorkeepers, ministers, and courtiers, tributary kings, vassals, and princes. This he obtains as a king. But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, with the covering removed. Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He has a great retinue; his great retinue consists of monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. This he obtains as a Buddha.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

205. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

205. Herein, this is said:

“Pure puratthā purimāsu jātisu,

Manussabhūto bahunaṃ sukhāvaho;

Ubbhegauttāsabhayāpanūdano,

Guttīsu rakkhāvaraṇesu ussuko.

“Formerly, in previous births, as a human being, he brought happiness to many; a dispeller of agitation, terror, and fear, zealous in matters of security, protection, and defense.

“So [M 3.0122][P 3.0149] tena kammena divaṃ samakkami,

Sukhañca khiḍḍāratiyo ca anvabhi;

Tato cavitvā punarāgato idha,

Cakkāni pādesu duvesu vindati.

“By that kamma, he went to heaven, and experienced happiness and playful delights; passing away from there, he came here again, and obtains wheels on both his feet.”

“Samantanemīni sahassarāni ca,

Byākaṃsu veyyañjanikā samāgatā;

Disvā [V 3.0111] kumāraṃ satapuññalakkhaṇaṃ,

Parivāravā hessati sattumaddano.

The interpreters of marks, having gathered, on seeing the prince with the marks of a hundred merits and the wheels with rims all around and a thousand spokes, declared: 'He will have a great retinue, a crusher of foes.'

Tathā hī cakkāni samantanemini,

Sace [T 3.0164] na pabbajjamupeti tādiso;

Vatteti cakkaṃ pathaviṃ pasāsati,

Tassānuyantādha tassānuyuttā idha (sī. pī.), tassānuyantā idha (syā. ka.) bhavanti khattiyā.

For he has wheels with rims all around; if such a one does not go forth into homelessness, he turns the wheel, ruling the earth, and here nobles become his followers.

“Mahāyasaṃ saṃparivārayanti naṃ,

Sace ca pabbajjamupeti tādiso;

Nekkhammachandābhirato vicakkhaṇo,

Devāmanussāsurasakkarakkhasā sattarakkhasā (ka.) sī. syāaṭṭhakathā oloketabbā.

They surround him, the one of great fame. And if such a one goes forth, delighting in the desire for renunciation, discerning, devas, humans, asuras, Sakka, and rakkhasas,

“Gandhabbanāgā vihagā catuppadā,

Anuttaraṃ devamanussapūjitaṃ;

Mahāyasaṃ saṃparivārayanti na”nti.

“Gandhabbas and nāgas, birds and four-footed creatures, surround him—the unsurpassed one, honored by gods and humans, the one of great fame.”

(3-5) Āyatapaṇhitāditilakkhaṇaṃ

The Three Characteristics Beginning with Long Heels

206. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato ahosi nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho lajjī dayāpanno, sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī vihāsi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā ussannattā vipulattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni tīṇi mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni [P 3.0150] paṭilabhati. Āyatapaṇhi ca hoti, dīghaṅguli ca brahmujugatto ca.

206. Monks, in a past birth, a past existence, a past dwelling, when the Tathāgata was formerly a human being, having abandoned the destruction of life, he abstained from it; laying aside the rod and the sword, he was conscientious and compassionate, dwelling sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. As a result of that kamma having been done, accumulated, increased, and extensively developed... having passed away from there and come to this state, he obtains these three marks of a great man: he has long heels, long fingers and toes, and a body as straight as Brahmā's.

“So [M 3.0123] tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Dīghāyuko hoti ciraṭṭhitiko, dīghamāyuṃ pāleti, na sakkā hoti antarā jīvitā voropetuṃ kenaci manussabhūtena paccatthikena paccāmittena[T 3.0165]. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Dīghāyuko hoti [V 3.0112] ciraṭṭhitiko, dīghamāyuṃ pāleti, na sakkā hoti antarā jīvitā voropetuṃ paccatthikehi paccāmittehi samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

Endowed with these marks, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch... As a king, what does he obtain? He is long-lived, long-enduring; he protects a long life, and it is not possible for any human adversary or enemy to deprive him of his life-faculty in the interim. This he obtains as a king... As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is long-lived, long-enduring; he protects a long life, and it is not possible for any adversary, enemy, ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone in the world to deprive him of his life-faculty in the interim. This he obtains as a Buddha.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

207. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

207. Therein, this is said:

“Māraṇavadhabhayattano maraṇavadhabhayattano (sī. pī. ka.), maraṇavadhabhayamattano (syā.) viditvā,

Paṭivirato paraṃ māraṇāyahosi;

Tena sucaritena saggamagamā tena so sucaritena saggamagamāsi (syā.),

Sukataphalavipākamanubhosi.

Knowing for himself the fear of killing and slaughter, he was one who refrained from killing others; by that good conduct, he went to the deva realm, experiencing the resultant fruit of his well-performed actions.

“Caviya punaridhāgato samāno,

Paṭilabhati idha tīṇi lakkhaṇāni;

Bhavati vipuladīghapāsaṇhiko,

Brahmāva suju subho sujātagatto.

Having passed away and come again to this world, he obtains here three characteristics: he becomes one with great, long heels, like Brahmā, very straight, beautiful, with a well-formed body.

“Subhujo susu susaṇṭhito sujāto,

Mudutalunaṅguliyassa honti;

Dīghā tībhi [P 3.0151] purisavaraggalakkhaṇehi,

Cirayapanāya cirayāpanāya (syā.) kumāramādisanti.

With beautiful arms, youthful, well-proportioned, and well-formed, his soft, tender fingers and toes are long; with these three foremost characteristics of a supreme man, the wise predict a long life for the boy.

“Bhavati yadi gihī ciraṃ yapeti,

Cirataraṃ pabbajati yadi tato hi;

Yāpayati [T 3.0166] ca vasiddhibhāvanāya,

Iti dīghāyukatāya taṃ nimitta”nti.

If he is a householder, he lives long; if he goes forth, he lives even longer than that; and he sustains his life through the development of mastery. Thus, that is the sign of long life.

(6) Sattussadatālakkhaṇaṃ

The Mark of Having Fullness of Flesh in Seven Places

208. “Yampi[M 3.0124], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno dātā ahosi paṇītānaṃ rasitānaṃ khādanīyānaṃ bhojanīyānaṃ sāyanīyānaṃ lehanīyānaṃ [V 3.0113] pānānaṃ. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati, sattussado hoti, sattassa ussadā honti; ubhosu hatthesu ussadā honti, ubhosu pādesu ussadā honti, ubhosu aṃsakūṭesu ussadā honti, khandhe ussado hoti.

208. Monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when the Tathāgata was previously a human being, he was a giver of exquisite and delicious hard foods, soft foods, savories, lickables, and drinks. Because that kamma was done… and so on… having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he obtains this mark of a great man: he has fullness of flesh in seven places. There is fullness of flesh in seven places: there is fullness of flesh on both hands, there is fullness of flesh on both feet, there is fullness of flesh on both shoulders, and there is fullness of flesh on the neck.

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Lābhī hoti paṇītānaṃ rasitānaṃ khādanīyānaṃ bhojanīyānaṃ sāyanīyānaṃ lehanīyānaṃ pānānaṃ. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Lābhī hoti paṇītānaṃ rasitānaṃ khādanīyānaṃ bhojanīyānaṃ sāyanīyānaṃ lehanīyānaṃ pānānaṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ [P 3.0152] bhagavā avoca.

Endowed with this mark, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… and so on… As a monarch, what does he obtain? He is a recipient of exquisite and delicious hard foods, soft foods, savories, lickables, and drinks. As a monarch, this is what he obtains. As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is a recipient of exquisite and delicious hard foods, soft foods, savories, lickables, and drinks. As a Buddha, this is what he obtains.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

209. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

209. Herein, it is said:

“Khajjabhojjamatha leyya sāyiyaṃ,

Uttamaggarasadāyako ahu;

Tena so sucaritena kammunā,

Nandane ciramabhippamodati.

A giver of hard and soft foods, of lickables and savories, of supreme and excellent taste he was. By that well-done kamma, he rejoices for long in the Nandana grove.

“Satta [T 3.0167] cussade idhādhigacchati,

Hatthapādamudutañca vindati;

Āhu byañjananimittakovidā,

Khajjabhojjarasalābhitāya naṃ.

Here he attains the seven areas of fullness and finds softness of hands and feet. Those skilled in signs and marks declare of him that it is for the obtaining of the taste of hard and soft foods.

“Yaṃ gihissapi na taṃ gihissāpi (syā.) tadatthajotakaṃ,

Pabbajjampi ca tadādhigacchati;

Khajjabhojjarasalābhiruttamaṃ,

Āhu sabbagihibandhanacchida”nti.

That which brings such a result even for a householder, he also attains upon going forth. They declare this to be the supreme gain of the taste of hard and soft foods for the one who cuts all household bonds.

(7-8) Karacaraṇamudujālatālakkhaṇāni

The Marks of Softness and Webbing of Hands and Feet

210. “Yampi[M 3.0125][V 3.0114], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ saṅgāhako ahosi – dānena peyyavajjena piyavācena (syā. ka.) atthacariyāya samānattatāya. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni [P 3.0153] paṭilabhati. Mudutalunahatthapādo ca hoti jālahatthapādo ca.

210. Monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when the Tathāgata was previously a human being, he was one who gathered the people with the four bases of sympathy: with giving, endearing speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. Because that kamma was done… and so on… having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, he obtains these two marks of a great man: he has soft and tender hands and feet, and he has webbed hands and feet.

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Susaṅgahitaparijano hoti, susaṅgahitāssa honti brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā [T 3.0168] gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Susaṅgahitaparijano hoti, susaṅgahitāssa honti bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a monarch, what does he obtain? He has a well-gathered retinue. His brahmins and householders, town and country folk, accountants and high officials, troops, doorkeepers, ministers, councillors, tributary kings, fief-holders, and princes are well-gathered. As a monarch, this is what he obtains… As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He has a well-gathered retinue. His monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas are well-gathered. As a Buddha, this is what he obtains.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

211. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

211. Herein, it is said:

“Dānampi catthacariyatañca dānampi ca atthacariyatampi ca (sī. pī.),

Piyavāditañca samānattatañca piyavadatañca samānachandatañca (sī. pī.);

Kariyacariyasusaṅgahaṃ bahūnaṃ,

Anavamatena guṇena yāti saggaṃ.

“Having practiced giving, beneficial conduct, pleasant speech, and impartiality, thereby bringing many to well-being, through such respected virtue one goes to heaven.

“Caviya punaridhāgato samāno,

Karacaraṇamudutañca jālino ca;

Atirucirasuvaggudassaneyyaṃ,

Paṭilabhati daharo susu kumāro.

“Having passed away and returned here again, as a very tender young boy he obtains softness of hands and feet and webbing, which are exceedingly pleasing, very smooth, and lovely to see.

“Bhavati [M 3.0126][P 3.0154] parijanassavo vidheyyo,

Mahimaṃ āvasito susaṅgahito;

Piyavadū [V 3.0115] hitasukhataṃ jigīsamāno jigiṃ samāno (sī. syā. pī.),

Abhirucitāni guṇāni ācarati.

“His retinue becomes obedient and compliant. Ruling this earth, he has a well-gathered following. Speaking pleasantly, striving for welfare and happiness, he practices pleasing virtues.

“Yadi ca jahati sabbakāmabhogaṃ,

Kathayati dhammakathaṃ jino janassa;

Vacanapaṭikarassābhippasannā[T 3.0169],

Sutvāna dhammānudhammamācarantī”ti.

“And if he should renounce all sensual enjoyments, then, having become a Victor, he teaches the Dhamma to the people. Those who heed his word, having heard the Dhamma, become exceedingly serene and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.”

(9-10) Ussaṅkhapādauddhaggalomatālakkhaṇāni

(9-10) The Marks of High-Set Ankles and Body-Hairs with Upward-Turning Tips

212. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno samāno bahuno janassa (sī. pī.) atthūpasaṃhitaṃ dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā ahosi, bahujanaṃ nidaṃsesi, pāṇīnaṃ hitasukhāvaho dhammayāgī. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Ussaṅkhapādo ca hoti, uddhaggalomo ca.

212. “Monks, it is because the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when he was a human being, spoke words connected with benefit and connected with the Dhamma, instructed many people, and was a giver of the gift of Dhamma, bringing welfare and happiness to beings. Due to that kamma having been done… having passed away from there and come to this state, he obtains these two marks of a great man: he has high-set ankles and has body-hairs with tips that turn upward.”

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato, sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Aggo ca hoti seṭṭho ca pāmokkho ca uttamo ca pavaro ca kāmabhogīnaṃ. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Aggo ca hoti seṭṭho ca pāmokkho ca uttamo ca pavaro ca sabbasattānaṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with these marks, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… Being a monarch, what does he obtain? He becomes the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent among enjoyers of sensual pleasures. As a monarch, this is what he obtains… Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He becomes the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent among all beings. As a Buddha, this is what he obtains.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

213. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

213. There, regarding this, it is said:

“Atthadhammasahitaṃ [P 3.0155] atthadhammasaṃhitaṃ (ka. sī. pī.), atthadhammupasaṃhitaṃ (ka.) pure giraṃ,

Erayaṃ bahujanaṃ nidaṃsayi;

Pāṇinaṃ hitasukhāvaho ahu,

Dhammayāgamayajī dhammayāgaṃ assaji (ka.) amaccharī.

“Formerly, uttering speech connected with benefit and the Dhamma, he instructed many people. He was a bringer of welfare and happiness to beings; being un-miserly, he gave the gift of the Dhamma.

“Tena [M 3.0127][V 3.0116] so sucaritena kammunā,

Suggatiṃ [T 3.0170] vajati tattha modati;

Lakkhaṇāni ca duve idhāgato,

Uttamappamukhatāya uttamasukhatāya (syā.), uttamapamukkhatāya (ka.) vindati.

“By that well-practiced kamma, he goes to a happy destination and rejoices there. Having come here, due to his supreme leadership, he obtains two marks.

“Ubbhamuppatitalomavā saso,

Pādagaṇṭhirahu sādhusaṇṭhitā;

Maṃsalohitācitā tacotthatā,

Uparicaraṇasobhanā uparijānusobhanā (syā.), upari ca pana sobhanā (sī. pī.) ahu.

“His body-hairs had tips that turned upward; his ankle bones were well-established, filled with flesh and blood, covered by skin; his feet were exceedingly beautiful.

“Gehamāvasati ce tathāvidho,

Aggataṃ vajati kāmabhoginaṃ;

Tena uttaritaro na vijjati,

Jambudīpamabhibhuyya iriyati.

“If such a one dwells in a house, he attains the foremost state among enjoyers of sensual pleasures. No one superior to him is found; having overcome Jambudīpa, he holds sway.

“Pabbajampi [P 3.0156] ca anomanikkamo,

Aggataṃ vajati sabbapāṇinaṃ;

Tena uttaritaro na vijjati,

Sabbalokamabhibhuyya viharatī”ti.

“And if, with noble effort, he goes forth, he attains the foremost state among all beings. No one superior to him is found; having overcome the entire world, he dwells.”

(11) Eṇijaṅghalakkhaṇaṃ

(11) The Mark of Shanks like an Antelope

214. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno sakkaccaṃ vācetā ahosi sippaṃ vā vijjaṃ vā caraṇaṃ vā kammaṃ vā – ‘kiṃ time khippaṃ vijāneyyuṃ, khippaṃ paṭipajjeyyuṃ, na ciraṃ kilisseyyu”nti. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno [T 3.0171] imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Eṇijaṅgho hoti.

214. “Monks, it is because the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when he was a human being, was a careful teacher of crafts, knowledge, conduct, or action, thinking: ‘How might these quickly understand, quickly practice, and not be weary for long?’ Due to that kamma having been done… having passed away from there and come to this state, he obtains this mark of a great man: he has shanks like an Eṇi antelope.”

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Yāni tāni rājārahāni rājaṅgāni rājūpabhogāni [V 3.0117] rājānucchavikāni tāni khippaṃ paṭilabhati. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Yāni [M 3.0128] tāni samaṇārahāni samaṇaṅgāni samaṇūpabhogāni samaṇānucchavikāni, tāni khippaṃ paṭilabhati. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with this mark, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… Being a monarch, what does he obtain? Whatever is worthy of a king, the constituents of royalty, the royal requisites, and things suitable for a king, those he quickly obtains. As a monarch, this is what he obtains… Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? Whatever is worthy of an ascetic, the constituents of asceticism, the ascetic's requisites, and things suitable for an ascetic, those he quickly obtains. As a Buddha, this is what he obtains.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

215. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

215. There, regarding this, it is said:

“Sippesu vijjācaraṇesu kammesu kammasu (sī. pī.),

Kathaṃ vijāneyyuṃ vijāneyya (sī. pī.), vijāneyyu (syā.) lahunti icchati;

Yadūpaghātāya [P 3.0157] na hoti kassaci,

Vāceti khippaṃ na ciraṃ kilissati.

“In crafts, knowledge, conduct, and actions, he desires, ‘How might they understand quickly?’ Whatever is not for the harm of anyone, he teaches quickly and does not cause them to be weary for long.

“Taṃ kammaṃ katvā kusalaṃ sukhudrayaṃ sukhindriyaṃ (ka.),

Jaṅghā manuññā labhate susaṇṭhitā;

Vaṭṭā sujātā anupubbamuggatā,

Uddhaggalomā sukhumattacotthatā.

“Having done that wholesome kamma that yields happiness, he obtains delightful, well-formed shanks—rounded, well-proportioned, gradually tapering upwards, with upward-turning hairs, covered by delicate skin.

“Eṇeyyajaṅghoti tamāhu puggalaṃ,

Sampattiyā khippamidhāhu khippamidāhu (?) lakkhaṇaṃ;

Gehānulomāni yadābhikaṅkhati,

Apabbajaṃ khippamidhādhigacchati khippamidādhigacchati (?).

“The wise call that person ‘one with shanks like an Eṇi deer’; they say this mark is a sign of swift attainment. When he desires things suitable for the household life, not having gone forth, he quickly attains them here.

“Sace [T 3.0172] ca pabbajjamupeti tādiso,

Nekkhammachandābhirato vicakkhaṇo;

Anucchavikassa yadānulomikaṃ,

Taṃ vindati khippamanomavikkamo nikkamo (sī. syā. pī.)”ti.

“And if such a discerning one, delighting in the desire for renunciation, goes forth, then, being of noble effort, he quickly finds whatever is suitable and appropriate for one who has gone forth.”

(12) Sukhumacchavilakkhaṇaṃ

(12) The Mark of Delicate Skin

216. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto [V 3.0118] samāno samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā upasaṅkamitvā paripucchitā ahosi – “kiṃ, bhante, kusalaṃ, kiṃ akusalaṃ, kiṃ sāvajjaṃ, kiṃ anavajjaṃ, kiṃ sevitabbaṃ, kiṃ na sevitabbaṃ, kiṃ me karīyamānaṃ dīgharattaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya assa, kiṃ vā pana me karīyamānaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya [M 3.0129] assā”ti. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Sukhumacchavi [P 3.0158] hoti, sukhumattā chaviyā rajojallaṃ kāye na upalimpati.

216. Monks, the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when he was previously a human being, approached a recluse or a brahmin and was one who inquired: ‘Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated? What should not be cultivated? What, being done by me, would lead to my long-term harm and suffering? Or what, being done by me, would lead to my long-term welfare and happiness?’ Because that kamma was performed by him… he, having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, obtains this mark of a great man: he has delicate skin, and because of the delicacy of his skin, dust and grime do not adhere to his body.

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāpañño hoti, nāssa hoti koci paññāya sadiso vā seṭṭho vā kāmabhogīnaṃ. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāpañño hoti puthupañño hāsapañño hāsupañño (sī. pī.) javanapañño tikkhapañño nibbedhikapañño, nāssa hoti koci paññāya sadiso vā seṭṭho vā sabbasattānaṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

Endowed with this mark, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a king, what does he obtain? He is of great wisdom; among those who enjoy sensual pleasures, there is no one equal or superior to him in wisdom. This is what he obtains as a king… As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is of great wisdom, broad wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, keen wisdom, and penetrative wisdom; among all beings, there is no one equal or superior to him in wisdom. This is what he obtains as a Buddha.’ The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

217. Tatthetaṃ [T 3.0173] vuccati –

217. In this regard, it is said:

“Pure puratthā purimāsu jātisu,

Aññātukāmo paripucchitā ahu;

Sussūsitā pabbajitaṃ upāsitā,

Atthantaro atthakathaṃ nisāmayi.

“In the past, long ago, in former births, desiring to know, he was one who asked questions; eager to listen, he attended on the renunciant; intent on the meaning, he carefully considered the discourse on the meaning.

“Paññāpaṭilābhagatena paññāpaṭilābhakatena (sī. pī.) ṭīkā oloketabbā kammunā,

Manussabhūto sukhumacchavī ahu;

Byākaṃsu uppādanimittakovidā,

Sukhumāni atthāni avecca dakkhiti.

“Through the kamma that is a cause for the attainment of wisdom, having become a human, he had delicate skin. The experts skilled in omens and signs declared: ‘He will see by penetrating subtle meanings.’

“Sace na pabbajjamupeti tādiso,

Vatteti cakkaṃ pathaviṃ pasāsati;

Atthānusiṭṭhīsu pariggahesu ca,

Na tena seyyo sadiso ca vijjati.

“If such a one does not go forth into the homeless life, he turns the wheel and rules the earth; in instructions on what is beneficial and in comprehensive grasp, none superior or equal to him is found.

“Sace [P 3.0159][V 3.0119] ca pabbajjamupeti tādiso,

Nekkhammachandābhirato vicakkhaṇo;

Paññāvisiṭṭhaṃ labhate anuttaraṃ,

Pappoti bodhiṃ varabhūrimedhaso”ti.

“And if such a one goes forth, delighting in the desire for renunciation and being discerning, he obtains unsurpassed, distinguished wisdom. A person of excellent, vast, and sagacious wisdom, he attains enlightenment.”

(13) Suvaṇṇavaṇṇalakkhaṇaṃ

The Mark of Golden Hue

218. “Yampi[M 3.0130], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno akkodhano ahosi anupāyāsabahulo, bahumpi vutto samāno nābhisajji na kuppi na byāpajji na [T 3.0174] patitthīyi, na kopañca dosañca appaccayañca pātvākāsi. Dātā ca ahosi sukhumānaṃ mudukānaṃ attharaṇānaṃ pāvuraṇānaṃ pāpuraṇānaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsikasukhumānaṃ koseyyasukhumānaṃ kambalasukhumānaṃ. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hoti kañcanasannibhattaco.

218. “Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when he was formerly a human being, was not given to anger and was not abounding in vexation. Even when spoken to at length, he did not take offense, did not become angry, did not become malicious, did not become resentful, and did not manifest anger, ill will, or discontent. And he was a giver of fine, soft spreads and coverings—fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool. Because that kamma was done and accumulated by him… he, having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, obtains this mark of a great man: he is of golden hue, his skin resembling gold.”

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Lābhī hoti sukhumānaṃ mudukānaṃ attharaṇānaṃ pāvuraṇānaṃ khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsikasukhumānaṃ koseyyasukhumānaṃ kambalasukhumānaṃ. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Lābhī hoti sukhumānaṃ mudukānaṃ attharaṇānaṃ pāvuraṇānaṃ khomasukhumānaṃ kappāsikasukhumānaṃ koseyyasukhumānaṃ kambalasukhumānaṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with that mark, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a monarch, what does he obtain? He is a recipient of fine, soft spreads and coverings—fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool. As a monarch, this is what he obtains… As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is a recipient of fine, soft spreads and coverings—fine linen, fine cotton, fine silk, and fine wool. As a Buddha, this is what he obtains.” The Blessed One spoke this matter.

219. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

219. In this regard, it is said:

“Akkodhañca adhiṭṭhahi adāsi adāsi ca (sī. pī.),

Dānañca vatthāni sukhumāni succhavīni;

Purimatarabhave [P 3.0160] ṭhito abhivissaji,

Mahimiva suro abhivassaṃ.

“He resolved upon non-anger and gave gifts; established in a former existence, he gave away fine cloths of goodly appearance, like a cloud raining heavily upon the earth.”

“Taṃ [V 3.0120] katvāna ito cuto dibbaṃ,

Upapajji upapajja (sī. pī.) sukataphalavipākamanubhutvā;

Kanakatanusannibho idhābhibhavati,

Suravarataroriva indo.

“Having done that, passing away from here, he arose in the divine realm. Experiencing the fruit and result of his good deeds, with a body resembling gold, he presides there, like Inda, most excellent among the devas.”

“Gehañcāvasati [T 3.0175][M 3.0131] naro apabbajja,

Micchaṃ mahatimahiṃ anusāsati pasāsati (syā.);

Pasayha sahidha sattaratanaṃ pasayha abhivasana-varataraṃ (sī. pī.),

Paṭilabhati vimala vipula (syā.), vipulaṃ (sī. pī.) sukhumacchaviṃ suciñca.

“If that man, desiring not to go forth, dwells in a house, he governs the great earth, having conquered it. Here he obtains the seven treasures, and a flawless, delicate, and pure complexion.”

“Lābhī acchādanavatthamokkhapāvuraṇānaṃ,

Bhavati yadi anāgāriyataṃ upeti;

Sahito suhita (syā.), sa hi (sī. pī.) purimakataphalaṃ anubhavati,

Na bhavati katassa panāso”ti.

“He becomes a recipient of spreads, excellent cloths, and cloaks, if he should go forth into the homeless life. For his own welfare, he experiences the fruit of deeds done previously; there is no perishing of what has been done.”

(14) Kosohitavatthaguyhalakkhaṇaṃ

The Mark of the Male Organ Being Concealed in a Sheath

220. Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno cirappanaṭṭhe sucirappavāsino ñātimitte suhajje sakhino samānetā ahosi. Mātarampi puttena samānetā ahosi, puttampi mātarā samānetā ahosi, pitarampi [P 3.0161] puttena samānetā ahosi, puttampi pitarā samānetā ahosi, bhātarampi bhātarā samānetā ahosi, bhātarampi bhaginiyā samānetā ahosi, bhaginimpi bhātarā samānetā ahosi, bhaginimpi bhaginiyā samānetā ahosi, samaṅgīkatvā samaggiṃ katvā (sī. syā. pī.) ca abbhanumoditā ahosi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati – kosohitavatthaguyho hoti.

220. Monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, the Tathāgata, when he was a human being, was one who united long-lost and long-separated relatives, friends, dear ones, and companions. He united mother with son, and son with mother; father with son, and son with father; brother with brother, brother with sister, sister with brother, and sister with sister. And having brought about harmony, he was one who expressed great approval. As a result of that action being done… he, having passed away from there and returned to this state of existence, obtains this mark of a great man: his male organ is concealed in a sheath.

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Pahūtaputto hoti, parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti [T 3.0176] sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno [V 3.0121] kiṃ labhati? Pahūtaputto hoti, anekasahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with that mark, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… What does he obtain as a monarch? He has many sons—indeed, for him there are over a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of others’ armies. As a monarch, he obtains this… What does he obtain as a Buddha? He has many sons—indeed, for him there are many thousands of sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of others’ armies. As a Buddha, he obtains this.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

221. Tatthetaṃ [M 3.0132] vuccati –

221. Therein, this is said:

“Pure puratthā purimāsu jātisu,

Cirappanaṭṭhe sucirappavāsino;

Ñātī suhajje sakhino samānayi,

Samaṅgikatvā anumoditā ahu.

“In the past, in former times, in previous births, he united relatives, dear ones, and companions who were long-lost and long-separated; having brought them into harmony, he caused them to rejoice.

“So tena sa tena (ka.) kammena divaṃ samakkami,

Sukhañca khiḍḍāratiyo ca anvabhi;

Tato cavitvā punarāgato idha,

Kosohitaṃ vindati vatthachādiyaṃ.

“By that deed, he went to heaven and experienced happiness and playful delights; having passed away from there and returned here again, he obtains the male organ concealed in a sheath.

“Pahūtaputto [P 3.0162] bhavatī tathāvidho,

Parosahassañca parosahassassa (sī. pī.) bhavanti atrajā;

Sūrā ca vīrā ca sūrā ca vīraṅgarūpā (ka.) amittatāpanā,

Gihissa pītiṃjananā piyaṃvadā.

“Such a one has many sons, and over a thousand offspring are born to him; they are brave and heroic, tormentors of enemies, bringing joy to the householder, and speakers of pleasant words.

“Bahūtarā pabbajitassa iriyato,

Bhavanti puttā vacanānusārino;

Gihissa vā pabbajitassa vā puna,

Taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ jāyati tadatthajotaka”nti.

“Even more numerous are the sons of one gone forth who conducts himself well, who are obedient to his word; whether for a householder or for one gone forth, that mark arises, illuminating that result.”

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The First Recitation Section is concluded.

(15-16) Parimaṇḍalaanonamajaṇṇuparimasanalakkhaṇāni

(15-16) The Characteristics of Being Perfectly Proportioned and of Touching the Knees Without Bending

222. “Yampi[T 3.0177][V 3.0122], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno mahājanasaṅgahaṃ mahājanasaṅgāhakaṃ (ka.) samekkhamāno samapekkhamāno (ka.) samaṃ jānāti sāmaṃ jānāti, purisaṃ jānāti purisavisesaṃ jānāti – ‘ayamidamarahati ayamidamarahatī’ti tattha tattha purisavisesakaro ahosi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ [M 3.0133] āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Nigrodha parimaṇḍalo ca hoti, ṭhitakoyeva ca anonamanto ubhohi pāṇitalehi jaṇṇukāni parimasati parimajjati.

222. “Monks, it is because the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when he was a human being, while considering how to support the great multitude, knew what was equitable and knew for himself, knew the person and knew the distinguished person—thinking, ‘This person is worthy of this; this person is worthy of that’—and thus in various instances acted for the benefit of distinguished persons. Because that kamma was done… he, having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, obtains these two marks of a great man. He is perfectly proportioned like a banyan tree, and while standing, without bending, he can touch and rub his knees with both palms.”

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati[P 3.0163]? Aḍḍho hoti mahaddhano mahābhogo pahūtajātarūparajato pahūtavittūpakaraṇo pahūtadhanadhañño paripuṇṇakosakoṭṭhāgāro. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati…pe… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Aḍḍho hoti mahaddhano mahābhogo. Tassimāni dhanāni honti, seyyathidaṃ, saddhādhanaṃ sīladhanaṃ hiridhanaṃ ottappadhanaṃ sutadhanaṃ cāgadhanaṃ paññādhanaṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with these marks, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a king, what does he obtain? He is affluent, of great wealth, of great possessions, with abundant gold and silver, with abundant wealth and property, with abundant riches and grain, and with full treasuries and storehouses. As a king, he obtains this… As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is affluent, of great wealth, of great possessions. These are his treasures, namely: the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom. As a Buddha, he obtains this.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

223. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

223. Therein, this is said:

“Tuliya paṭivicaya cintayitvā,

Mahājanasaṅgahanaṃ mahājanaṃ saṅgāhakaṃ (ka.) samekkhamāno;

Ayamidamarahati tattha tattha,

Purisavisesakaro pure ahosi.

“Having weighed, investigated, and considered, while observing how to support the great multitude, he determined in each case, ‘This person is worthy of this,’ and in the past, he acted for the benefit of distinguished persons.

“Mahiñca [T 3.0178] pana samā ca pana (syā.), sa hi ca pana (sī. pī.) ṭhito anonamanto,

Phusati karehi ubhohi jaṇṇukāni;

Mahiruhaparimaṇḍalo ahosi,

Sucaritakammavipākasesakena.

“Standing on the earth without bending, he touches both his knees with his hands; by the remaining result of his well-practiced kamma, he was proportioned like a banyan tree.

“Bahuvividhanimittalakkhaṇaññū,

Atinipuṇā manujā byākariṃsu;

Bahuvividhā [V 3.0123] gihīnaṃ arahāni,

Paṭilabhati daharo susu kumāro.

“Extremely subtle men, skilled in many and various signs and marks, prophesied: ‘This tender young boy obtains many and various things suitable for householders.’

“Idha [P 3.0164] ca mahīpatissa kāmabhogī,

Gihipatirūpakā bahū bhavanti;

Yadi ca jahati sabbakāmabhogaṃ,

Labhati anuttaraṃ uttamadhanagga”nti.

“‘And if he becomes a ruler of the earth here, there will be many sensual enjoyments suitable for a householder. But if he renounces all sensual enjoyment, he obtains the unsurpassed, supreme mass of treasure.’”

(17-19) Sīhapubbaddhakāyāditilakkhaṇaṃ

(17-19) The Three Characteristics Beginning with a Body like the Forepart of a Lion

224. “Yampi[M 3.0134], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno bahujanassa atthakāmo ahosi hitakāmo phāsukāmo yogakkhemakāmo – ‘kintime saddhāya vaḍḍheyyuṃ, sīlena vaḍḍheyyuṃ, sutena vaḍḍheyyuṃ sutena vaḍḍheyyuṃ, buddhiyā vaḍḍheyyuṃ (syā.), cāgena vaḍḍheyyuṃ, dhammena vaḍḍheyyuṃ, paññāya vaḍḍheyyuṃ, dhanadhaññena vaḍḍheyyuṃ, khettavatthunā vaḍḍheyyuṃ, dvipadacatuppadehi vaḍḍheyyuṃ, puttadārehi vaḍḍheyyuṃ, dāsakammakaraporisehi vaḍḍheyyuṃ, ñātīhi vaḍḍheyyuṃ, mittehi vaḍḍheyyuṃ, bandhavehi vaḍḍheyyu’nti. So tassa kammassa [T 3.0179] kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni tīṇi mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Sīhapubbaddhakāyo ca hoti citantaraṃso ca samavaṭṭakkhandho ca.

224. “Monks, it is because the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, when he was a human being, desired the welfare of many people, desired their benefit, their comfort, and their security from bondage—thinking, ‘How might these beings increase in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, Dhamma, wisdom, wealth and grain, fields and lands, bipeds and quadrupeds, sons and wives, servants, workers, and men, relatives, friends, and kinsmen?’ Because that kamma was done… he, having passed away from there and come to this state of existence, obtains these three marks of a great man: he has a body like the forepart of a lion, the space between his shoulders is filled out, and his trunk is evenly rounded.

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Aparihānadhammo [P 3.0165] hoti, na parihāyati dhanadhaññena khettavatthunā dvipadacatuppadehi puttadārehi dāsakammakaraporisehi ñātīhi mittehi bandhavehi, na parihāyati sabbasampattiyā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Aparihānadhammo hoti, na parihāyati saddhāya sīlena sutena cāgena paññāya, na parihāyati sabbasampattiyā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with these characteristics, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a king, what does he obtain? He is of a nature not to decline; he does not decline in wealth and grain, fields and lands, bipeds and quadrupeds, sons and wives, servants, workers, and men, relatives, friends, or kinsmen. He does not decline in any prosperity. As a king, he obtains this… As a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is of a nature not to decline; he does not decline in faith, virtue, learning, generosity, or wisdom. He does not decline in any prosperity. As a Buddha, he obtains this.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

225. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

225. Therein, this is said:

“Saddhāya sīlena sutena buddhiyā,

Cāgena dhammena bahūhi sādhuhi;

Dhanena [V 3.0124] dhaññena ca khettavatthunā,

Puttehi dārehi catuppadehi ca.

“Regarding faith, virtue, learning, and wisdom, generosity, Dhamma, and many excellent qualities; regarding wealth and grain, fields and lands, sons, wives, and quadrupeds;

“Ñātīhi mittehi ca bandhavehi ca,

Balena vaṇṇena sukhena cūbhayaṃ;

Kathaṃ na hāyeyyuṃ pareti icchati,

Atthassa middhī ca idaṃ samiddhañca (ka.), addhaṃ samiddhañca (syā.) panābhikaṅkhati.

“regarding relatives, friends, and kinsmen, strength, beauty, and happiness—in both; he wishes, ‘How might others not decline?’ and he longs for the success of their welfare.”

“Sa [M 3.0135] sīhapubbaddhasusaṇṭhito ahu,

Samavaṭṭakkhandho [T 3.0180] ca citantaraṃso;

Pubbe suciṇṇena katena kammunā,

Ahāniyaṃ pubbanimittamassa taṃ.

He had a torso as well-proportioned as the forepart of a lion, evenly rounded shoulders, and the space between his shoulders was filled out. Through kamma well-practiced and done in the past, that was for him a premonitory sign of non-decline.

“Gihīpi dhaññena dhanena vaḍḍhati,

Puttehi dārehi catuppadehi ca;

Akiñcano pabbajito anuttaraṃ,

Pappoti bodhiṃ asahānadhammata”nti sambodhimahānadhammatanti (syā. ka.) ṭīkā oloketabbā.

As a householder, he increases in grain and wealth, in sons, wives, and quadrupeds. As a renunciant with no possessions, he attains unsurpassed enlightenment, which is of a non-declining nature.

(20) Rasaggasaggitālakkhaṇaṃ

The Mark of Possessing the Supreme Faculty for Conveying Taste

226. “Yampi[P 3.0166], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno sattānaṃ aviheṭhakajātiko ahosi pāṇinā vā leḍḍunā vā daṇḍena vā satthena vā. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati, rasaggasaggī hoti, uddhaggāssa rasaharaṇīyo gīvāya jātā honti samābhivāhiniyo samavāharasaharaṇiyo (syā.).

226. Monks, when the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, having been a human being in the past, was of a nature not to harm beings with his hand, with a clod, with a stick, or with a weapon. He, on account of that kamma having been done and accumulated… having passed away from there and come to this human state, obtains this mark of a great man: he possesses the supreme faculty for conveying taste; taste-conveying channels that rise straight upwards arise in his neck, and they convey taste evenly.

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Appābādho hoti appātaṅko, samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Appābādho hoti appātaṅko samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā [V 3.0125] samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

He, being endowed with that mark, if he dwells in a house, becomes a wheel-turning monarch… Being a monarch, what does he obtain? He has few illnesses and few afflictions; he is endowed with a digestive faculty that digests evenly, being neither too cold nor too hot. Being a monarch, he obtains this… Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He has few illnesses and few afflictions; he is endowed with a digestive faculty that digests evenly, being neither too cold nor too hot, and which is moderate and suitable for striving. Being a Buddha, he obtains this.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

227. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

227. Regarding this, it is said:

“Na [T 3.0181] pāṇidaṇḍehi panātha leḍḍunā,

Satthena vā maraṇavadhena māraṇavadhena (ka.) vā pana;

Ubbādhanāya paritajjanāya vā,

Na heṭhayī janatamaheṭhako ahu.

He did not harm with hands or sticks, nor with a clod, nor with a weapon, nor by inciting others to kill; nor again by imprisonment or by banishment did he harm. He was one who did not harm the populace.

“Teneva [M 3.0136] so sugatimupecca modati,

Sukhapphalaṃ kariya sukhāni vindati;

Samojasā [P 3.0167] sampajjasā (sī. pī.), pāmuñjasā (syā.), sāmañca sā (ka.) rasaharaṇī susaṇṭhitā,

Idhāgato labhati rasaggasaggitaṃ.

On account of that kamma, having reached a good destination, he rejoices; by performing kamma that yields a pleasant fruit, he finds pleasures. His taste-conveying channels are well-established and function evenly. Having come here, he obtains the supreme faculty for conveying taste.

“Tenāhu naṃ atinipuṇā vicakkhaṇā,

Ayaṃ naro sukhabahulo bhavissati;

Gihissa vā pabbajitassa vā puna pana (syā.),

Taṃ lakkhaṇaṃ bhavati tadatthajotaka”nti.

Therefore, the very subtle and wise ones say of him: ‘This man will have much happiness.’ Again, whether for a householder or for one gone forth, that mark is an indicator of that result.

(21-22) Abhinīlanettagopakhumalakkhaṇāni

The Marks of Very Dark Eyes and Eyelashes Like a Bull’s

228. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno na ca visaṭaṃ, na ca visāci na ca visācitaṃ (sī. pī.), na ca visāvi (syā.), na ca pana viceyya pekkhitā, ujuṃ tathā pasaṭamujumano, piyacakkhunā bahujanaṃ udikkhitā ahosi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Abhinīlanetto ca [T 3.0182] hoti gopakhumo ca.

228. Monks, when the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, having been a human being in the past, was not one who looked at others in anger, nor one who looked askance in anger, nor one who stared fixedly in anger. Rather, he looked straight and with an open gaze; he had a straight mind and was one who looked upon the great populace with a loving eye. He, on account of that kamma having been done and accumulated… having passed away from there and come to this human state, obtains these two marks of a great man: he has very dark eyes and has eyelashes like a bull’s.

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato, sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Piyadassano hoti bahuno janassa, piyo hoti [V 3.0126] manāpo brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ negamajānapadānaṃ gaṇakamahāmattānaṃ [P 3.0168] anīkaṭṭhānaṃ dovārikānaṃ amaccānaṃ pārisajjānaṃ rājūnaṃ bhogiyānaṃ kumārānaṃ. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati…pe… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Piyadassano hoti bahuno janassa, piyo hoti manāpo bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ devānaṃ manussānaṃ asurānaṃ nāgānaṃ gandhabbānaṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

Endowed with these marks, if he dwells in a house, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… Being a monarch, what does he obtain? He is pleasant to see for many people; he is dear and beloved to brahmins and householders, town and country folk, accountants and great ministers, army commanders, doorkeepers, ministers, courtiers, kings, village headmen, and princes. Being a monarch, he obtains this… Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He is pleasant to see for many people; he is dear and beloved to monks, nuns, male lay followers, female lay followers, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. Being a Buddha, he obtains this.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

229. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

229. Regarding this, it is said:

“Na ca visaṭaṃ na ca visāci visācitaṃ (sī. pī.), visāvi (syā.), na ca pana viceyyapekkhitā;

Ujuṃ tathā pasaṭamujumano, piyacakkhunā bahujanaṃ udikkhitā.

He did not look with an angry, upturned gaze, nor with an angry, askance glance, nor with an angry, scrutinizing look; but straight and with a clear gaze, with a straight mind, he looked upon the great populace with a loving eye.

“Sugatīsu [M 3.0137] so phalavipākaṃ,

Anubhavati tattha modati;

Idha ca pana bhavati gopakhumo,

Abhinīlanettanayano sudassano.

In good destinations, he experiences the fruit and result of his kamma and rejoices there. But here, he has eyelashes like a bull’s and very dark eyes; he is beautiful to see.

“Abhiyogino ca nipuṇā,

Bahū pana nimittakovidā;

Sukhumanayanakusalā manujā,

Piyadassanoti [T 3.0183] abhiniddisanti naṃ.

Many subtle persons skilled in the science of marks, those expert in signs, and humans skilled in subtle observation, declare of him: ‘He is pleasant to see.’

“Piyadassano gihīpi santo ca,

Bhavati bahujanapiyāyito;

Yadi [P 3.0169] ca na bhavati gihī samaṇo hoti,

Piyo bahūnaṃ sokanāsano”ti.

Pleasant to see, even being a householder, he is beloved by many people. And if he is not a householder but becomes a recluse, he is dear to many, a dispeller of the sorrow of many.

(23) Uṇhīsasīsalakkhaṇaṃ

The Mark of a Head Like a Royal Turban

230. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno bahujanapubbaṅgamo ahosi kusalesu dhammesu bahujanapāmokkho kāyasucarite vacīsucarite [V 3.0127] manosucarite dānasaṃvibhāge sīlasamādāne uposathupavāse matteyyatāya petteyyatāya sāmaññatāya brahmaññatāya kule jeṭṭhāpacāyitāya aññataraññataresu ca adhikusalesu dhammesu. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati – uṇhīsasīso hoti.

230. Bhikkhus, in a former birth, a former state of being, a former abode, the Tathāgata, having previously been a human being, was a vanguard of many people in wholesome qualities, a leader among many—in good conduct of body, speech, and mind; in generosity and sharing; in undertaking the precepts; in observing the Uposatha; in dutifulness to mother; in dutifulness to father; in reverence to recluses; in reverence to brahmins; in honoring the elders of the family; and in various other superior wholesome qualities. Through the performance of that action… having passed away from there, on reappearing here, he obtains this mark of a great man: he has a head like a royal turban.

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāssa jano anvāyiko hoti, brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāssa jano anvāyiko hoti, bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ [T 3.0184] bhagavā avoca.

Endowed with this mark, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… What does he gain as a monarch? A great multitude follows him—brahmins and householders, townsmen and countryfolk, accountants and high officials, commanders of elephant and horse corps, doorkeepers, ministers, courtiers, kings, landowners, and princes. As a monarch, he gains this… What does he gain as a Buddha? A great multitude follows him—bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. As a Buddha, he gains this.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

231. Tatthetaṃ [M 3.0138] vuccati –

231. Herein, this is said:

“Pubbaṅgamo sucaritesu ahu,

Dhammesu dhammacariyābhirato;

Anvāyiko bahujanassa ahu,

Saggesu vedayittha puññaphalaṃ.

“Foremost in good conduct he was, greatly delighting in the practice of the Dhamma; he was one whom many people followed, and in the heavens experienced the fruit of that merit.

“Veditvā [P 3.0170] so sucaritassa phalaṃ,

Uṇhīsasīsattamidhajjhagamā;

Byākaṃsu byañjananimittadharā,

Pubbaṅgamo bahujanaṃ hessati.

“Having experienced the fruit of good conduct, he attained here the state of having a head like a royal turban. Experts in marks and signs declared: ‘He shall be a leader of many people.’

“Paṭibhogiyā manujesu idha,

Pubbeva tassa abhiharanti tadā;

Yadi khattiyo bhavati bhūmipati,

Paṭihārakaṃ bahujane labhati.

“Here among humans, even in his youth, attendants perform services for him. If he becomes a khattiya, a lord of the earth, he obtains many capable people to serve him.

“Atha [V 3.0128] cepi pabbajati so manujo,

Dhammesu hoti paguṇo visavī;

Tassānusāsaniguṇābhirato,

Anvāyiko bahujano bhavatī”ti.

“But if that person goes forth, he becomes proficient and masterful in the qualities of absorption. Delighting in the virtue of his instruction, many people become his followers.”

(24-25) Ekekalomatāuṇṇālakkhaṇāni

(24-25) The Marks of One Hair Per Pore and the Uṇṇā-tuft

232. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno musāvādaṃ pahāya musāvādā paṭivirato ahosi, saccavādī saccasandho theto paccayiko avisaṃvādako lokassa[T 3.0185]. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Ekekalomo ca hoti, uṇṇā ca bhamukantare jātā hoti odātā mudutūlasannibhā.

232. “Bhikkhus, in a former birth, a former state of being, a former abode, the Tathāgata, having previously been a human being, abandoned false speech and abstained from false speech. He was a speaker of truth, one who joins truth with truth, firm, reliable, and one who did not deceive the world. Due to the performance and accumulation of that kamma… having passed away from there, upon coming to this state, he obtains these two marks of a Great Man: he has one hair per pore, and an uṇṇā-tuft—white, soft, and like cotton-wool—grows between his eyebrows.”

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato, sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāssa jano upavattati, brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā [P 3.0171] gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā [M 3.0139] samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Mahāssa jano upavattati, bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a monarch, what does he gain? A great multitude follows his inclination: brahmins and householders, townsmen and countryfolk, accountants and high officials, commanders of elephant and horse corps, doorkeepers, ministers, courtiers, tributary kings, landowners, and princes. As a monarch, he gains this… As a Buddha, what does he gain? A great multitude follows his inclination: bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. As a Buddha, he gains this.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

233. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

233. Herein, this is said:

“Saccappaṭiñño purimāsu jātisu,

Advejjhavāco alikaṃ vivajjayi;

Na so visaṃvādayitāpi kassaci,

Bhūtena tacchena tathena bhāsayi tosayi (sī. pī.).

“In former births, he was true to his promise, of unequivocal speech, and he avoided falsehood; he was not one to deceive anyone, but spoke what was factual, true, and accurate.

“Setā susukkā mudutūlasannibhā,

Uṇṇā sujātā uṇṇāssa jātā (ka. sī.) bhamukantare ahu;

Na [V 3.0129] lomakūpesu duve ajāyisuṃ,

Ekekalomūpacitaṅgavā ahu.

“A white, exceedingly pure, soft uṇṇā-tuft, like cotton-wool, grew well between his eyebrows; two hairs did not grow in any hair-pore; he had a body endowed with single hairs in each pore.

“Taṃ lakkhaṇaññū bahavo samāgatā,

Byākaṃsu [T 3.0186] uppādanimittakovidā;

Uṇṇā ca lomā ca yathā susaṇṭhitā,

Upavattatī īdisakaṃ bahujjano.

“Many who knew the marks, experts in interpreting portents, assembled and declared: ‘As the uṇṇā-tuft and the single hairs are well-established, a great multitude follows such a one.’

“Gihimpi santaṃ upavattatī jano,

Bahu puratthāpakatena kammunā;

Akiñcanaṃ pabbajitaṃ anuttaraṃ,

Buddhampi santaṃ upavattati jano”ti.

“Because of kamma performed in the past, many people follow him, even as a householder. They follow him when he has gone forth, possessing nothing, and they follow him when he is the unsurpassed Buddha.”

(26-27) Cattālīsaaviraḷadantalakkhaṇāni

(26-27) The Marks of Forty Teeth and Close-set Teeth

234. “Yampi, bhikkhave tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato ahosi. Ito sutvā na amutra akkhātā imesaṃ bhedāya, amutra vā sutvā na imesaṃ akkhātā amūsaṃ bhedāya[M 3.0140], iti bhinnānaṃ vā sandhātā, sahitānaṃ [P 3.0172] vā anuppadātā, samaggārāmo samaggarato samagganandī samaggakaraṇiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā ahosi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Cattālīsadanto ca hoti aviraḷadanto ca.

234. “Bhikkhus, in a former birth, a former state of being, a former abode, the Tathāgata, having previously been a human being, abandoned divisive speech and abstained from divisive speech. Having heard something here, he would not repeat it elsewhere to cause division among those people; or having heard something elsewhere, he would not repeat it here to cause division among these people. Thus, he was a reconciler of those who were divided and a promoter of those who were united, delighting in concord, enjoying concord, rejoicing in concord, and speaking words that create concord. Due to the performance and accumulation of that kamma… having passed away from there, upon coming to this state, he obtains these two marks of a Great Man: he has forty teeth and his teeth are close-set.”

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Abhejjapariso hoti, abhejjāssa honti parisā, brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati [T 3.0187]… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Abhejjapariso hoti, abhejjāssa honti parisā, bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“Endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch… As a king, what does he gain? He has an unassailable retinue; his assembly is unassailable: brahmins and householders, townsmen and countryfolk, accountants and high officials, commanders of elephant and horse corps, doorkeepers, ministers, courtiers, tributary kings, landowners, and princes. As a king, he gains this… As a Buddha, what does he gain? He has an unassailable retinue; his assembly is unassailable: bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. As a Buddha, he gains this.” The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

235. Tatthetaṃ [V 3.0130] vuccati –

235. Herein, this is said:

“Vebhūtiyaṃ sahitabhedakāriṃ,

Bhedappavaḍḍhanavivādakāriṃ;

Kalahappavaḍḍhanaākiccakāriṃ,

Sahitānaṃ bhedajananiṃ na bhaṇi.

“In a former existence, he did not speak words that break up the united, that increase division and cause disputes, that increase quarrels and are an unwholesome undertaking, or that generate division among the united.

“Avivādavaḍḍhanakariṃ sugiraṃ,

Bhinnānusandhijananiṃ abhaṇi;

Kalahaṃ [P 3.0173] janassa panudī samaṅgī,

Sahitehi nandati pamodati ca.

“He spoke good words that promote non-dispute, that generate reconciliation among the divided. Being harmonious, he dispelled conflict among people, and he rejoiced and delighted with those in concord.

“Sugatīsu so phalavipākaṃ,

Anubhavati tattha modati;

Dantā idha honti aviraḷā sahitā,

Caturo dasassa mukhajā susaṇṭhitā.

“In good destinations he experiences the fruit and result of kamma, and there he delights. Here his teeth are close-set and well-joined; forty teeth, well-established, are born in his mouth.

“Yadi [M 3.0141] khattiyo bhavati bhūmipati,

Avibhediyāssa parisā bhavati;

Samaṇo ca hoti virajo vimalo,

Parisāssa hoti anugatā acalā”ti.

“If he is a khattiya, he becomes lord of the land, and his assembly becomes unbreakable. And if he is a samaṇa, dustless and stainless, his assembly becomes compliant and unwavering.”

(28-29) Pahūtajivhābrahmassaralakkhaṇāni

(28-29) The Marks of a Long and Broad Tongue and a Voice like Brahma's

236. “Yampi[T 3.0188], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno pharusaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato ahosi. Yā sā vācā nelā kaṇṇasukhā pemanīyā hadayaṅgamā porī bahujanakantā bahujanamanāpā, tathārūpiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā ahosi. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā upacitattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati. Pahūtajivho ca hoti brahmassaro ca karavīkabhāṇī.

236. “Bhikkhus, in a former birth, a former state of being, a former abode, the Tathāgata, having previously been a human being, abandoned harsh speech and was one who refrained from harsh speech. Whatever speech was faultless, pleasant to the ear, endearing, heart-touching, urbane, desired by many people, and pleasing to the minds of many people, he was one who spoke such words. Due to the performance and accumulation of that kamma… he, having passed away from there and come to this state, obtains these two marks of a Great Man: he has a long and broad tongue, and a voice like Brahma's, speaking sweetly like the Karavīka bird.”

“So [V 3.0131] tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Ādeyyavāco hoti, ādiyantissa vacanaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Ādeyyavāco [P 3.0174] hoti, ādiyantissa vacanaṃ bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“He, being endowed with those marks, if he dwells in a household, becomes a wheel-turning king... Being a king, what does he obtain? He becomes one whose words are to be heeded. His words are heeded by brahmins and householders, townsfolk and countryfolk, accountants and high officials, army commanders, gatekeepers, ministers, courtiers, kings, landed nobility, and princes. Being a king, he obtains this benefit... Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He becomes one whose words are to be heeded. His words are heeded by monks, nuns, male lay-followers, female lay-followers, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. Being a Buddha, he obtains this benefit.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

237. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

237. In that regard, this is said:

“Akkosabhaṇḍanavihesakāriṃ,

Ubbādhikaṃ ubbādhakaraṃ (syā.) bahujanappamaddanaṃ;

Abāḷhaṃ giraṃ so na bhaṇi pharusaṃ,

Madhuraṃ bhaṇi susaṃhitaṃ susahitaṃ (syā.) sakhilaṃ.

“He did not speak exceedingly harsh speech that causes abuse, quarreling, and vexation, that causes mental affliction, and is crushing to many people. He spoke words that were gentle, beneficial, and amiable.”

“Manaso [T 3.0189][M 3.0142] piyā hadayagāminiyo,

Vācā so erayati kaṇṇasukhā;

Vācāsuciṇṇaphalamanubhavi,

Saggesu vedayatha vedayati (?) ṭīkā oloketabbā puññaphalaṃ.

“He utters words that are dear to the mind, that go to the heart, and are pleasant to the ear. He experienced the fruit of well-practiced speech in the celestial realms; he experienced the fruit of merit.”

“Veditvā so sucaritassa phalaṃ,

Brahmassarattamidhamajjhagamā;

Jivhāssa hoti vipulā puthulā,

Ādeyyavākyavacano bhavati.

“Having experienced the fruit of good conduct, he attained here the state of having a voice like Brahma's. His tongue becomes broad and long; he becomes one whose words are to be heeded.”

“Gihinopi ijjhati yathā bhaṇato,

Atha ce pabbajati so manujo;

Ādiyantissa [P 3.0175] vacanaṃ janatā,

Bahuno bahuṃ subhaṇitaṃ bhaṇato”ti.

“Even as a householder, he prospers by speaking thus. And if that person goes forth, the people heed the words of him who speaks many well-spoken words to many.”

(30) Sīhahanulakkhaṇaṃ

(30) The Mark of the Lion's Jaw

238. “Yampi[V 3.0132], bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno samphappalāpaṃ pahāya samphappalāpā paṭivirato ahosi kālavādī bhūtavādī atthavādī dhammavādī vinayavādī, nidhānavatiṃ vācaṃ bhāsitā ahosi kālena sāpadesaṃ pariyantavatiṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ. So tassa kammassa kaṭattā…pe… so tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imaṃ mahāpurisalakkhaṇaṃ paṭilabhati, sīhahanu hoti.

238. “Monks, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, the Tathāgata, having been a human being, abandoned frivolous talk and was one who refrained from frivolous talk. He was a speaker in season, a speaker of fact, a speaker of benefit, a speaker of Dhamma, and a speaker of discipline. He was one who spoke, at the proper time, words worth treasuring, accompanied by reasons, with a limit, and connected with the goal. On account of that kamma having been done... he, having passed away from there and come to this state, obtains this mark of a great man: he has a jaw like a lion's.”

“So tena lakkhaṇena samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī…pe… rājā samāno kiṃ [T 3.0190] labhati? Appadhaṃsiyo hoti kenaci manussabhūtena paccatthikena paccāmittena. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati… buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Appadhaṃsiyo hoti abbhantarehi vā bāhirehi vā paccatthikehi paccāmittehi, rāgena vā dosena vā mohena vā samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā devena vā mārena vā brahmunā vā kenaci vā lokasmiṃ. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“He, being endowed with that mark, if he dwells in a household, becomes a wheel-turning king... Being a king, what does he obtain? He becomes unconquerable by any human being who is an adversary or an enemy. Being a king, he obtains this benefit... Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He becomes unconquerable by internal or external adversaries or enemies; by greed, hatred, or delusion; or by an ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. Being a Buddha, he obtains this benefit.” The Blessed One spoke on this matter.

239. Tatthetaṃ [M 3.0143] vuccati –

239. In that regard, this is said:

“Na samphappalāpaṃ na muddhataṃ buddhatanti (ka.),

Avikiṇṇavacanabyappatho ahosi;

Ahitamapi ca apanudi,

Hitamapi ca bahujanasukhañca abhaṇi.

“He did not speak frivolous or foolish talk; he was not one whose path of speech was scattered. He dispelled what was unbeneficial, and he spoke what was for the welfare and happiness of many people.”

“Taṃ [P 3.0176] katvā ito cuto divamupapajji,

Sukataphalavipākamanubhosi;

Caviya punaridhāgato samāno,

Dvidugamavaratarahanuttamalattha.

“Having done that kamma, passing away from here, he arose in the celestial realm. He experienced the resultant fruit of what was well-done. Having passed away from there and come here again, he obtained the supreme jaw, superior to that of the best of four-footed beings.”

“Rājā hoti suduppadhaṃsiyo,

Manujindo manujādhipati mahānubhāvo;

Tidivapuravarasamo [V 3.0133] bhavati,

Suravarataroriva indo.

“He becomes a king very difficult to overcome, a lord of men, a master of men, of great power. He becomes like Indra, superior to the devas, equal to the foremost of the Tāvatiṃsa gods.”

“Gandhabbāsurayakkharakkhasebhi surasakkarakkhasebhi (syā.),

Surehi na [T 3.0191] hi bhavati suppadhaṃsiyo;

Tathatto yadi bhavati tathāvidho,

Idha disā ca paṭidisā ca vidisā cā”ti.

“He is indeed not easily overcome by gandhabbas, asuras, yakkhas, rākkhasas, or by the devas. If one of such a nature, one who is true, exists here, he is not easily overcome in the cardinal directions, the directions above and below, or the intermediate directions.”

(31-32) Samadantasusukkadāṭhālakkhaṇāni

(31-32) The Marks of Even Teeth and Very White Canine Teeth

240. “Yampi, bhikkhave, tathāgato purimaṃ jātiṃ purimaṃ bhavaṃ purimaṃ niketaṃ pubbe manussabhūto samāno micchājīvaṃ pahāya sammāājīvena jīvikaṃ kappesi, tulākūṭa kaṃsakūṭa mānakūṭa ukkoṭana vañcana nikati sāciyoga chedana vadha bandhana viparāmosa ālopa sahasākārā sāhasākārā (sī. syā. pī.) paṭivirato ahosi. So tassa kammassa [P 3.0177] kaṭattā upacitattā ussannattā vipulattā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. So tattha aññe deve dasahi ṭhānehi adhigaṇhāti dibbena āyunā dibbena vaṇṇena dibbena sukhena dibbena yasena dibbena ādhipateyyena dibbehi rūpehi dibbehi saddehi dibbehi gandhehi dibbehi rasehi [M 3.0144] dibbehi phoṭṭhabbehi. So tato cuto itthattaṃ āgato samāno imāni dve mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭilabhati, samadanto ca hoti susukkadāṭho ca.

240. “Monks, when the Tathāgata, in a former birth, a former existence, a former abode, formerly being a human being, having abandoned wrong livelihood, maintained his life with right livelihood, refraining from false balances, false metal, false measures, bribery, deception, trickery, crooked practices, mutilation, killing, binding, robbery, plundering, and violent acts. Because that kamma was done, accumulated, abundant, and extensive, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. There, he surpasses the other devas in ten respects: in divine lifespan, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine glory, divine dominion, divine sights, divine sounds, divine smells, divine tastes, and divine tactile sensations. Deceasing from there and coming to this state, he obtains these two marks of a Great Man: he has even teeth and very white canine teeth.”

“So tehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasati, rājā hoti cakkavattī dhammiko dhammarājā cāturanto vijitāvī janapadatthāvariyappatto sattaratanasamannāgato. Tassimāni satta ratanāni bhavanti, seyyathidaṃ – cakkaratanaṃ hatthiratanaṃ assaratanaṃ maṇiratanaṃ itthiratanaṃ gahapatiratanaṃ pariṇāyakaratanameva sattamaṃ. Parosahassaṃ kho panassa puttā bhavanti sūrā vīraṅgarūpā parasenappamaddanā. So imaṃ pathaviṃ sāgarapariyantaṃ akhilamanimittamakaṇṭakaṃ [T 3.0192] iddhaṃ phītaṃ khemaṃ sivaṃ nirabbudaṃ adaṇḍena asatthena dhammena abhivijiya ajjhāvasati. Rājā samāno kiṃ labhati? Suciparivāro hoti sucissa honti parivārā brāhmaṇagahapatikā negamajānapadā gaṇakamahāmattā anīkaṭṭhā dovārikā amaccā pārisajjā rājāno bhogiyā kumārā. Rājā samāno idaṃ labhati.

“Endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, a righteous king of righteousness, ruler of the four quarters, a conqueror, who has attained stability in the country and who possesses the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has over a thousand sons who are brave, heroic in form, and crushers of foreign armies. He rules this earth bounded by the ocean—prosperous, flourishing, secure, peaceful, and untroubled, free of waste-land, danger, and thorns—having conquered it by righteousness, without rod or sword. Being a king, what does he obtain? He has a pure retinue. His retinue is pure, consisting of brahmins and householders, townsfolk and countryfolk, accountants and high officials, army commanders, gatekeepers, ministers, courtiers, vassal kings, landed nobility, and princes. Being a king, he obtains this benefit.”

“Sace [V 3.0134] kho pana agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajati, arahaṃ hoti sammāsambuddho loke vivaṭṭacchado. Buddho samāno kiṃ labhati? Suciparivāro hoti, sucissa honti parivārā, bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo upāsakā upāsikāyo devā manussā asurā nāgā gandhabbā. Buddho samāno idaṃ labhati”. Etamatthaṃ bhagavā avoca.

“But if he goes forth from the household life into homelessness, he becomes an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One in the world, one whose covering is removed. Being a Buddha, what does he obtain? He has a pure retinue. His retinue is pure: bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male and female lay followers, devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, and gandhabbas. Being a Buddha, this is what he obtains.’ The Blessed One spoke this meaning.

241. Tatthetaṃ vuccati –

241. Herein, this is said:

“Micchājīvañca avassaji samena vuttiṃ,

Sucinā so janayittha dhammikena;

Ahitamapi [P 3.0178] ca apanudi,

Hitamapi ca bahujanasukhañca acari.
