“He forsook wrong livelihood and generated a living that was balanced, pure, and righteous. He dispelled what was unbeneficial and practiced what was beneficial and for the happiness of many.”

“Sagge vedayati naro sukhapphalāni,

Karitvā nipuṇebhi vidūhi sabbhi;

Vaṇṇitāni tidivapuravarasamo,

Abhiramati ratikhiḍḍāsamaṅgī.

“Having done deeds praised by the skillful, wise, and virtuous, that man experiences the fruits of happiness in heaven. Like the foremost in the city of gods, he delights, endowed with pleasure and sport.”

“Laddhānaṃ [M 3.0145] mānusakaṃ bhavaṃ tato,

Cavitvāna sukataphalavipākaṃ;

Sesakena paṭilabhati lapanajaṃ,

Samamapi sucisusukkaṃ [T 3.0193] laddhāna manussakaṃ bhavaṃ tato caviya, puna sukataphalavipākasesakena; paṭilabhati lapanajaṃ samamapi, suci ca suvisuddhasusukkaṃ (syā.).

“Deceasing from there and obtaining a human existence by the remaining result of his well-done deeds, he obtains teeth that are even, pure, and very white.”

“Taṃ veyyañjanikā samāgatā bahavo,

Byākaṃsu nipuṇasammatā manujā;

Sucijanaparivāragaṇo bhavati,

Dijasamasukkasucisobhanadanto.

“Many sign-readers, men esteemed as skillful, having assembled, declared of him: ‘He will have a retinue of pure people; his teeth will be like a twice-born’s, even, white, pure, and beautiful.’”

“Rañño hoti bahujano,

Suciparivāro mahatiṃ mahiṃ anusāsato;

Pasayha [V 3.0135][P 3.0179] na ca janapadatudanaṃ,

Hitamapi ca bahujanasukhañca caranti.

“As a king ruling the great earth, he has a large populace and a pure retinue. He does not forcibly oppress the country, and his people practice for the welfare and happiness of the many.”

“Atha ce pabbajati bhavati vipāpo,

Samaṇo samitarajo vivaṭṭacchado;

Vigatadarathakilamatho,

Imamapi ca paramapi ca imampi ca parampi ca (pī.), paraṃpi paramaṃpi ca (syā.) passati lokaṃ.

“But if he goes forth, he becomes a recluse free from evil, his dust stilled, his covering removed. Free from distress and weariness, he sees this world and the next.”

“Tassovādakarā bahugihī ca pabbajitā ca,

Asuciṃ garahitaṃ dhunanti pāpaṃ;

Sa hi sucibhi parivuto bhavati,

Malakhilakalikilese panudehī”ti tassovādakarā bahugihī ca, pabbajitā ca asucivigarahita; panudipāpassa hi sucibhiparivuto, bhavati malakhilakakilese panudeti (syā.).

“Many householders and renunciants who follow his advice shake off what is impure, blameworthy, and evil. For he is surrounded by the pure, having dispelled the stains, barrenness, and all defilements.”

Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

The Blessed One said this. The bhikkhus, pleased, rejoiced at the Blessed One's words.

Lakkhaṇasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ sattamaṃ.

The seventh, the Discourse on the Marks, is concluded.

8. Siṅgālasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse to Siṅgāla

242. Evaṃ [M 3.0146][P 3.0180][V 3.0136][T 3.0194] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Tena kho pana samayena siṅgālako sigālako (sī.) gahapatiputto kālasseva uṭṭhāya rājagahā nikkhamitvā allavattho allakeso pañjaliko puthudisā puthuddisā (sī. syā. pī.) namassati – puratthimaṃ disaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pacchimaṃ disaṃ uttaraṃ disaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ disaṃ uparimaṃ disaṃ.

242. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place. Now at that time, the householder’s son Siṅgālaka, having arisen early in the morning and gone out from Rājagaha, with wet clothes and wet hair, and with hands clasped in reverence, was worshipping the various directions—the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the direction below, and the direction above.

243. Atha kho bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya rājagahaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Addasā kho bhagavā siṅgālakaṃ gahapatiputtaṃ kālasseva vuṭṭhāya rājagahā nikkhamitvā allavatthaṃ allakesaṃ pañjalikaṃ puthudisā namassantaṃ – puratthimaṃ disaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pacchimaṃ disaṃ uttaraṃ disaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ disaṃ uparimaṃ disaṃ. Disvā siṅgālakaṃ gahapatiputtaṃ etadavoca – “kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ, gahapatiputta, kālasseva uṭṭhāya rājagahā nikkhamitvā allavattho allakeso pañjaliko puthudisā [P 3.0181] namassasi – puratthimaṃ disaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pacchimaṃ disaṃ uttaraṃ disaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ disaṃ uparimaṃ disa”nti? “Pitā maṃ, bhante, kālaṃ karonto evaṃ avaca – ‘disā, tāta, namasseyyāsī’ti. So kho ahaṃ, bhante, pituvacanaṃ sakkaronto garuṃ karonto mānento pūjento kālasseva uṭṭhāya rājagahā nikkhamitvā allavattho allakeso pañjaliko puthudisā namassāmi – puratthimaṃ disaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ disaṃ pacchimaṃ disaṃ uttaraṃ disaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ disaṃ uparimaṃ [T 3.0195] disa”nti.

243. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One, having dressed and taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms-food. The Blessed One saw the householder’s son Siṅgālaka, who had arisen early in the morning, gone out from Rājagaha, and with wet clothes and wet hair, was worshipping the various directions with hands clasped in reverence—the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the direction below, and the direction above. Having seen him, the Blessed One said this to the householder’s son Siṅgālaka: “Why, householder’s son, having arisen early in the morning and gone out from Rājagaha, with wet clothes and wet hair, do you worship the various directions with hands clasped in reverence—the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the direction below, and the direction above?” “Venerable sir, my father, when he was dying, said this to me: ‘Dear son, you should worship the directions.’ Therefore, venerable sir, respecting, holding in high regard, esteeming, and venerating my father’s word, I arise early in the morning, go out from Rājagaha, and with wet clothes and wet hair, worship the various directions with hands clasped in reverence—the eastern direction, the southern direction, the western direction, the northern direction, the direction below, and the direction above.”

Cha disā

The Six Directions

244. “Na kho, gahapatiputta, ariyassa vinaye evaṃ cha disā chaddisā (sī. pī.) namassitabbā”ti. “Yathā kathaṃ pana, bhante, ariyassa vinaye cha disā chaddisā (sī. pī.) namassitabbā? Sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā tathā dhammaṃ desetu, yathā ariyassa vinaye cha disā chaddisā (sī. pī.) namassitabbā”ti.

244. “Householder’s son, in the discipline of the Noble One, the six directions should not be worshipped in this way.” “But how then, venerable sir, should the six directions be worshipped in the discipline of the Noble One? It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that the six directions are worshipped in the discipline of the Noble One.”

“Tena [V 3.0137] hi, gahapatiputta suṇohi sādhukaṃ manasikarohi bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho siṅgālako gahapatiputto bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca –

“In that case, householder’s son, listen and apply your mind well; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Siṅgālaka the householder’s son replied in assent to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:

“Yato [M 3.0147] kho, gahapatiputta, ariyasāvakassa cattāro kammakilesā pahīnā honti, catūhi ca ṭhānehi pāpakammaṃ na karoti, cha ca bhogānaṃ apāyamukhāni na sevati, so evaṃ cuddasa pāpakāpagato chaddisāpaṭicchādī paṭicchādī hoti (syā.) ubholokavijayāya paṭipanno hoti. Tassa ayañceva loko āraddho hoti paro ca loko. So kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati.

“When, householder’s son, a noble disciple’s four defilements of action are abandoned, he does not do evil action on four grounds, and he does not pursue the six channels for the dissipation of wealth, he, being thus free from the fourteen evils, is one who covers the six directions and is practicing for the conquest of both worlds. For him, this very world is undertaken, and the next world is also undertaken. With the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”

Cattārokammakilesā

The Four Defilements of Action

245. “Katamassa cattāro kammakilesā pahīnā honti? Pāṇātipāto kho, gahapatiputta, kammakileso, adinnādānaṃ kammakileso, kāmesumicchācāro kammakileso, musāvādo kammakileso. Imassa cattāro kammakilesā pahīnā hontī”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna idaṃ vatvā (sī. pī.) evamīdisesu ṭhānesu sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

245. “Which four defilements of action are abandoned by him? Householder's son, destruction of life is a defilement of action; taking what is not given is a defilement of action; misconduct in sensual pleasures is a defilement of action; false speech is a defilement of action. These four defilements of action are abandoned by him.’ This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-farer, the Teacher, further said this:

“Pāṇātipāto [P 3.0182] adinnādānaṃ, musāvādo ca vuccati;

Paradāragamanañceva, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā”ti.

“Destruction of life, taking what is not given, and what is called false speech, and also going to another’s wife—these the wise do not praise.”

Catuṭṭhānaṃ

The Four Grounds

246. “Katamehi catūhi ṭhānehi pāpakammaṃ na karoti? Chandāgatiṃ gacchanto [T 3.0196] pāpakammaṃ karoti, dosāgatiṃ gacchanto pāpakammaṃ karoti, mohāgatiṃ gacchanto pāpakammaṃ karoti, bhayāgatiṃ gacchanto pāpakammaṃ karoti. Yato kho, gahapatiputta, ariyasāvako neva chandāgatiṃ gacchati, na dosāgatiṃ gacchati, na mohāgatiṃ gacchati, na bhayāgatiṃ gacchati; imehi catūhi ṭhānehi pāpakammaṃ na karotī”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

246. “By which four bases does one not commit an evil action? Going by the wrong course of desire, one commits an evil action; going by the wrong course of hatred, one commits an evil action; going by the wrong course of delusion, one commits an evil action; going by the wrong course of fear, one commits an evil action. Since, son of a householder, a noble disciple does not go by the wrong course of desire, nor by the wrong course of hatred, nor by the wrong course of delusion, nor by the wrong course of fear, by these four bases he does not commit an evil action.’ This the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Well-farer, the Teacher, further said this:

“Chandā dosā bhayā mohā, yo dhammaṃ ativattati;

Nihīyati yaso tassa tassa yeso (bahūsu, vinayepi), kāḷapakkheva candimā.

“Whoever transgresses the Dhamma through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, their fame diminishes, like the moon in the waning fortnight.

“Chandā [V 3.0138] dosā bhayā mohā, yo dhammaṃ nātivattati;

Āpūrati yaso tassa tassa yeso (bahūsu, vinayepi), sukkapakkheva juṇhapakkheva (ka.) candimā”ti.

“Whoever does not transgress the Dhamma through desire, hatred, fear, or delusion, their fame increases, like the moon in the waxing fortnight.”

Cha apāyamukhāni

The Six Avenues for Dissipation

247. “Katamāni [M 3.0148] cha bhogānaṃ apāyamukhāni na sevati? Surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānānuyogo kho, gahapatiputta, bhogānaṃ apāyamukhaṃ, vikālavisikhācariyānuyogo bhogānaṃ apāyamukhaṃ, samajjābhicaraṇaṃ bhogānaṃ apāyamukhaṃ, jūtappamādaṭṭhānānuyogo bhogānaṃ apāyamukhaṃ, pāpamittānuyogo bhogānaṃ apāyamukhaṃ, ālasyānuyogo ālasānuyogo (sī. syā. pī.) bhogānaṃ apāyamukhaṃ.

247. “Which six avenues for the dissipation of wealth does one not pursue? Indulgence in intoxicants which are a cause of heedlessness, son of a householder, is an avenue for the dissipation of wealth. Roaming the streets at unseemly hours is an avenue for the dissipation of wealth. Frequenting shows and fairs is an avenue for the dissipation of wealth. Indulgence in gambling which is a cause of heedlessness is an avenue for the dissipation of wealth. Association with evil companions is an avenue for the dissipation of wealth. Devotion to idleness is an avenue for the dissipation of wealth.”

Surāmerayassa cha ādīnavā

The Six Drawbacks of Intoxicants

248. “Cha khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānānuyoge. Sandiṭṭhikā dhanajāni dhanañjāni (sī. pī.), kalahappavaḍḍhanī, rogānaṃ āyatanaṃ, akittisañjananī, kopīnanidaṃsanī[P 3.0183], paññāya dubbalikaraṇītveva chaṭṭhaṃ padaṃ bhavati. Ime kho, gahapatiputta, cha ādīnavā surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānānuyoge.

248. “Son of a householder, there are these six drawbacks in indulging in spirits, liquor, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness: immediate loss of wealth, an increase of quarrels, a breeding ground for disease, a cause of disrepute, indecent exposure, and the sixth point is the weakening of wisdom. These, son of a householder, are the six drawbacks in indulging in spirits, liquor, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness.”

Vikālacariyāya cha ādīnavā

The six drawbacks of roaming at unseemly hours.

249. “Cha [T 3.0197] khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā vikālavisikhācariyānuyoge. Attāpissa agutto arakkhito hoti, puttadāropissa agutto arakkhito hoti, sāpateyyaṃpissa aguttaṃ arakkhitaṃ hoti, saṅkiyo ca hoti pāpakesu ṭhānesu tesu tesu ṭhānesu (syā.), abhūtavacanañca tasmiṃ rūhati, bahūnañca dukkhadhammānaṃ purakkhato hoti. Ime kho, gahapatiputta, cha ādīnavā vikālavisikhācariyānuyoge.

249. “Son of a householder, there are these six drawbacks to indulging in wandering the streets at improper times. One's own self is unguarded and unprotected, one's wife and children are unguarded and unprotected, one's property is unguarded and unprotected, one is suspected of evil deeds, false speech is established concerning one, and one becomes a forerunner for many painful things. These, son of a householder, are the six drawbacks to indulging in wandering the streets at improper times.”

Samajjābhicaraṇassa cha ādīnavā

The six dangers of frequenting festivals.

250. “Cha khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā samajjābhicaraṇe. Kva kuvaṃ (ka. sī. pī.) naccaṃ, kva gītaṃ, kva vāditaṃ, kva akkhānaṃ, kva pāṇissaraṃ, kva kumbhathunanti. Ime kho, gahapatiputta, cha ādīnavā samajjābhicaraṇe.

250. “Son of a householder, there are these six drawbacks in frequenting festivals: 'Where is the dancing? Where is the singing? Where is the music? Where are the recitations? Where is the hand-clapping? Where is the pot-drumming?' These, son of a householder, are the six drawbacks in frequenting festivals.”

Jūtappamādassa cha ādīnavā

The six dangers of indulgence in gambling.

251. “Cha [M 3.0149][V 3.0139] khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā jūtappamādaṭṭhānānuyoge. Jayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, jino vittamanusocati, sandiṭṭhikā dhanajāni, sabhāgatassa sabhāye tassa (ka.) vacanaṃ na rūhati, mittāmaccānaṃ paribhūto hoti, āvāhavivāhakānaṃ apatthito hoti – ‘akkhadhutto ayaṃ purisapuggalo nālaṃ dārabharaṇāyā’ti. Ime kho, gahapatiputta, cha ādīnavā jūtappamādaṭṭhānānuyoge.

251. “Son of a householder, there are these six drawbacks in devoting oneself to gambling, which is a basis for heedlessness: the winner begets enmity, the loser grieves for his wealth, there is a visible loss of wealth, one's word is not accepted in an assembly, one is despised by friends and associates, and one is not sought after for marriage, with people saying, 'This gambler is not able to support a wife.' These, son of a householder, are the six drawbacks in devoting oneself to gambling, which is a basis for heedlessness.”

Pāpamittatāya cha ādīnavā

The six drawbacks of associating with bad friends.

252. “Cha khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā pāpamittānuyoge. Ye dhuttā, ye soṇḍā, ye pipāsā, ye nekatikā, ye vañcanikā, ye sāhasikā. Tyāssa mittā honti te sahāyā. Ime [P 3.0184] kho, gahapatiputta, cha ādīnavā pāpamittānuyoge.

252. “Son of a householder, there are these six drawbacks in associating with bad friends. Those who are gamblers, those who are drunkards, those who are tipplers, those who are deceivers, those who are cheats, and those who are violent. These are his friends; these are his companions. These, son of a householder, are the six drawbacks in associating with bad friends.”

Ālasyassa cha ādīnavā

The six drawbacks of laziness.

253. “Cha khome, gahapatiputta, ādīnavā ālasyānuyoge. Atisītanti [T 3.0198] kammaṃ na karoti, atiuṇhanti kammaṃ na karoti, atisāyanti kammaṃ na karoti, atipātoti kammaṃ na karoti, atichātosmīti kammaṃ na karoti, atidhātosmīti kammaṃ na karoti. Tassa evaṃ kiccāpadesabahulassa viharato anuppannā ceva bhogā nuppajjanti, uppannā ca bhogā parikkhayaṃ gacchanti. Ime kho, gahapatiputta, cha ādīnavā ālasyānuyoge”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

253. “Son of a householder, there are these six drawbacks in being addicted to laziness. 'It is too cold,' and one does not work. 'It is too hot,' and one does not work. 'It is too late,' and one does not work. 'It is too early,' and one does not work. 'I am too hungry,' and one does not work. 'I am too full,' and one does not work. For one living thus with many excuses concerning his duties, unarisen wealth does not arise, and arisen wealth goes to destruction. These, son of a householder, are the six drawbacks of being addicted to laziness.” The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-farer, the Teacher, further said this:

“Hoti pānasakhā nāma,

Hoti sammiyasammiyo;

Yo ca atthesu jātesu,

Sahāyo hoti so sakhā.

“There is one who is a drinking companion, there is one who is a friend only to your face; but he who is a companion when needs have arisen, he is a friend indeed.

“Ussūraseyyā [M 3.0150] paradārasevanā,

Verappasavo verappasaṅgo (sī. syā. pī.) ca anatthatā ca;

Pāpā [V 3.0140] ca mittā sukadariyatā ca,

Ete cha ṭhānā purisaṃ dhaṃsayanti.

“Sleeping late, consorting with others' wives, cultivating enmity, and harmfulness; bad friends, and extreme miserliness—these six things destroy a person.

“Pāpamitto pāpasakho,

Pāpaācāragocaro;

Asmā lokā paramhā ca,

Ubhayā dhaṃsate naro.

“A person with bad friends, bad companions, and with evil conduct and resort, declines from this world and from the next, from both.

“Akkhitthiyo vāruṇī naccagītaṃ,

Divā soppaṃ pāricariyā akāle;

Pāpā ca mittā sukadariyatā ca,

Ete cha ṭhānā purisaṃ dhaṃsayanti.

“Dice, women, liquor, dance and song, sleeping by day, roaming at improper times; bad friends, and extreme miserliness—these six things destroy a person.

“Akkhehi dibbanti suraṃ pivanti,

Yantitthiyo [T 3.0199] pāṇasamā paresaṃ;

Nihīnasevī [P 3.0185] na ca vuddhasevī vuddhisevī (syā.), buddhisevī (ka.),

Nihīyate kāḷapakkheva cando.

“They who gamble with dice and drink liquor, who go to the wives of others, dear to them as life; associating with the base and not with the wise, they decline like the moon in the waning fortnight.

“Yo vāruṇī addhano akiñcano,

Pipāso pivaṃ papāgato pipāsosi atthapāgato (syā.), pipāsopi samappapāgato (ka.);

Udakamiva iṇaṃ vigāhati,

Akulaṃ ākulaṃ (syā. ka.) kāhiti khippamattano.

“The man addicted to liquor, without wealth, without possessions, thirsty, goes to the tavern to drink; he plunges into debt as into water, and quickly brings ruin to his family.

“Na divā soppasīlena, rattimuṭṭhānadessinā rattinuṭṭhānadassinā (sī. pī.), rattinuṭṭhānasīlinā (?);

Niccaṃ mattena soṇḍena, sakkā āvasituṃ gharaṃ.

“By one accustomed to sleeping by day, by one who dislikes rising at night, by one who is always intoxicated and a drunkard, it is not possible to manage a household.

“Atisītaṃ atiuṇhaṃ, atisāyamidaṃ ahu;

Iti vissaṭṭhakammante, atthā accenti māṇave.

“‘It is too cold,’ ‘It is too hot,’ ‘It is too late in the day’—for the young men who, saying thus, leave their work undone, opportunities pass by.

“Yodha [M 3.0151][V 3.0141] sītañca uṇhañca, tiṇā bhiyyo na maññati;

Karaṃ purisakiccāni, so sukhaṃ sukhā (sabbattha) aṭṭhakathā oloketabbā na vihāyatī”ti.

“But he who regards cold and heat as no more than grass, doing the duties of a man, does not fall away from happiness.”

Mittapatirūpakā

Friends in Semblance

254. “Cattārome, gahapatiputta, amittā mittapatirūpakā veditabbā. Aññadatthuharo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo, vacīparamo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo, anuppiyabhāṇī amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo, apāyasahāyo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo.

254. “Son of a householder, these four who are not friends but are friends in semblance should be known. The one who only takes should be known as one who is not a friend but a friend in semblance; the one of lip-service should be known as one who is not a friend but a friend in semblance; the flatterer should be known as one who is not a friend but a friend in semblance; the companion in ruinous ways should be known as one who is not a friend but a friend in semblance.”

255. “Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi aññadatthuharo amitto [P 3.0186] mittapatirūpako veditabbo.

255. “Son of a householder, by four instances the one who only takes, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known.”

“Aññadatthuharo hoti, appena bahumicchati[T 3.0200];

Bhayassa kiccaṃ karoti, sevati atthakāraṇā.

“He is one who only takes; he desires much for little; he performs a duty out of fear; he associates for the sake of his own benefit.”

“Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi aññadatthuharo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo.

“Son of a householder, by these four instances the one who only takes, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known.”

256. “Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi vacīparamo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo. Atītena paṭisantharati paṭisandharati (ka.), anāgatena paṭisantharati, niratthakena saṅgaṇhāti, paccuppannesu kiccesu byasanaṃ dasseti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi vacīparamo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo.

256. “Son of a householder, by four instances the one of lip-service, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known. He makes friendly gestures concerning the past; he makes friendly gestures concerning the future; he tries to win favor with empty words; and when a present duty arises, he points to his own misfortune. Son of a householder, by these four instances the one of lip-service, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known.”

257. “Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi anuppiyabhāṇī amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo. Pāpakaṃpissa pāpakammaṃpissa (syā.) anujānāti, kalyāṇaṃpissa anujānāti, sammukhāssa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati, parammukhāssa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi anuppiyabhāṇī amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo.

257. “Son of a householder, by four instances the flatterer, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known. He consents to his friend's evil deeds; he consents to his friend's good deeds; he speaks his praise in his presence; he speaks his dispraise in his absence. Son of a householder, by these four instances the flatterer, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known.”

258. “Catūhi [M 3.0152] kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi apāyasahāyo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo[V 3.0142]. Surāmeraya majjappamādaṭṭhānānuyoge sahāyo hoti, vikāla visikhā cariyānuyoge sahāyo hoti, samajjābhicaraṇe sahāyo hoti, jūtappamādaṭṭhānānuyoge sahāyo hoti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi apāyasahāyo amitto mittapatirūpako veditabbo”ti.

258. “Son of a householder, by four instances the companion in ruinous ways, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known. He is a companion for indulging in spirits and liquor, which are a basis for heedlessness; he is a companion for roaming the streets at unseemly hours; he is a companion for frequenting fairs; and he is a companion for indulging in gambling, which is a basis for heedlessness. Son of a householder, by these four instances the companion in ruinous ways, who is not a friend but a friend in semblance, should be known.”

259. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

259. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Gone-One, the Teacher, then spoke this further:

“Aññadatthuharo [T 3.0201] mitto, yo ca mitto vacīparo vacīparamo (syā.);

Anuppiyañca yo āha, apāyesu ca yo sakhā.

“The friend who only takes, and the friend of lip-service; the one who is a flatterer, and the one who is a companion in ruinous ways.”

Ete amitte cattāro, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ paṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti.

“A wise person, having thus understood these four to be non-friends, should avoid them from afar, as one would a dangerous path.”

Suhadamitto

The Good-Hearted Friend

260. “Cattārome[P 3.0187], gahapatiputta, mittā suhadā veditabbā. Upakāro upakārako (syā.) mitto suhado veditabbo, samānasukhadukkho mitto suhado veditabbo, atthakkhāyī mitto suhado veditabbo, anukampako mitto suhado veditabbo.

260. “Son of a householder, these four are to be known as good-hearted friends. The helpful friend is to be known as a good-hearted friend; the one who is the same in happiness and suffering is to be known as a good-hearted friend; the one who speaks of what is beneficial is to be known as a good-hearted friend; the one who is compassionate is to be known as a good-hearted friend.”

261. “Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi upakāro mitto suhado veditabbo. Pamattaṃ rakkhati, pamattassa sāpateyyaṃ rakkhati, bhītassa saraṇaṃ hoti, uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu taddiguṇaṃ bhogaṃ anuppadeti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi upakāro mitto suhado veditabbo.

261. “Son of a householder, by four instances is the helpful friend, the good-hearted friend, to be known. He protects the heedless; he guards the property of the heedless; he is a refuge for the fearful; when duties and tasks arise, he provides double the wealth required. Son of a householder, by these four instances is the helpful friend, the good-hearted friend, to be known.”

262. “Catūhi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi samānasukhadukkho mitto suhado veditabbo. Guyhamassa ācikkhati, guyhamassa parigūhati, āpadāsu na vijahati, jīvitaṃpissa atthāya pariccattaṃ hoti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi samānasukhadukkho mitto suhado veditabbo.

262. “Son of a householder, by four instances is the friend who is the same in happiness and suffering, the good-hearted friend, to be known. He reveals his own secrets to his friend; he guards his friend's secrets; he does not abandon him in misfortune; his very life is given up for his friend's sake. Son of a householder, by these four instances is the friend who is the same in happiness and suffering, the good-hearted friend, to be known.”

263. “Catūhi [M 3.0153] kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi atthakkhāyī mitto suhado veditabbo. Pāpā nivāreti, kalyāṇe niveseti, assutaṃ sāveti, saggassa [T 3.0202] maggaṃ ācikkhati. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi atthakkhāyī mitto suhado veditabbo.

263. “Son of a householder, by four instances is the friend who speaks of what is beneficial, the good-hearted friend, to be known. He restrains one from evil; he establishes one in the good; he causes one to hear what has not been heard; he points out the path to a heavenly realm. Son of a householder, by these four instances is the friend who speaks of what is beneficial, the good-hearted friend, to be known.”

264. “Catūhi [V 3.0143] kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi anukampako mitto suhado veditabbo. Abhavenassa na nandati, bhavenassa nandati, avaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānaṃ nivāreti, vaṇṇaṃ bhaṇamānaṃ pasaṃsati. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, catūhi ṭhānehi anukampako mitto suhado veditabbo”ti.

264. “Son of a householder, by four instances is the compassionate, good-hearted friend, to be known. He does not delight in his friend's misfortune; he delights in his friend's prosperity; he restrains those who speak dispraise of his friend; he praises those who speak praise of his friend. Son of a householder, by these four instances is the compassionate, good-hearted friend, to be known.”

265. Idamavoca bhagavā, idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

265. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Gone-One, the Teacher, then spoke this further:

“Upakāro [P 3.0188] ca yo mitto, sukhe dukkhe sukhadukkho (syā. ka.) ca yo sakhā yo ca mitto sukhe dukkhe (sī. pī.);

Atthakkhāyī ca yo mitto, yo ca mittānukampako.

“The friend who is helpful,

the companion in happiness and suffering,

the friend who speaks of what is beneficial,

and the friend who is compassionate.”

“Etepi mitte cattāro, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Sakkaccaṃ payirupāseyya, mātā puttaṃ va orasaṃ;

Paṇḍito sīlasampanno, jalaṃ aggīva bhāsati.

“These four friends, a wise person, having thus known them,

should attend to them respectfully, as a mother to her own-born son.

A wise person endowed with virtue shines forth like a blazing fire.”

“Bhoge saṃharamānassa, bhamarasseva irīyato;

Bhogā sannicayaṃ yanti, vammikovupacīyati.

“For one who gathers wealth, like a bee gathering nectar,

wealth accumulates, just as an anthill grows.”

“Evaṃ bhoge samāhatvā samāharitvā (syā.), alamatto kule gihī;

Catudhā vibhaje bhoge, sa ve mittāni ganthati.

“A capable householder in a family, having thus collected wealth,

should divide that wealth into four parts; he indeed binds friends to himself.”

“Ekena bhoge bhuñjeyya, dvīhi kammaṃ payojaye;

Catutthañca nidhāpeyya, āpadāsu bhavissatī”ti.

“With one part, he should enjoy his wealth; with two, he should invest in his work;

and the fourth part he should set aside, for it will be needed in times of misfortune.”

Chaddisāpaṭicchādanakaṇḍaṃ

The Section on Covering the Six Directions

266. “Kathañca, gahapatiputta, ariyasāvako chaddisāpaṭicchādī hoti? Cha [T 3.0203] imā, gahapatiputta, disā veditabbā. Puratthimā disā mātāpitaro veditabbā, dakkhiṇā [P 3.0189] disā ācariyā veditabbā, pacchimā disā [M 3.0154] puttadārā veditabbā, uttarā disā mittāmaccā veditabbā, heṭṭhimā disā dāsakammakarā veditabbā, uparimā disā samaṇabrāhmaṇā veditabbā.

266. “And how, son of a householder, does a noble disciple cover the six directions? These six directions, son of a householder, should be known. Parents should be known as the eastern direction. Teachers should be known as the southern direction. Wife and children should be known as the western direction. Friends and companions should be known as the northern direction. Servants and workers should be known as the lower direction. Ascetics and brahmins should be known as the upper direction.”

267. “Pañcahi [V 3.0144] kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhātabbā – bhato ne nesaṃ (bahūsu) bharissāmi, kiccaṃ nesaṃ karissāmi, kulavaṃsaṃ ṭhapessāmi, dāyajjaṃ paṭipajjāmi, atha vā pana petānaṃ kālaṅkatānaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ anuppadassāmīti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi puttaṃ anukampanti. Pāpā nivārenti, kalyāṇe nivesenti, sippaṃ sikkhāpenti, patirūpena dārena saṃyojenti, samaye dāyajjaṃ niyyādenti niyyātenti (ka. sī.). Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi puttena puratthimā disā mātāpitaro paccupaṭṭhitā imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi puttaṃ anukampanti. Evamassa esā puratthimā disā paṭicchannā hoti khemā appaṭibhayā.

267. In five ways, son of a householder, a son should attend to his parents as the eastern direction: 'Having been supported, I will support them; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will prove myself worthy of the inheritance; and further, I will give offerings on behalf of the departed who have passed away.' Parents, attended to by their son in these five ways, show compassion to their son in five ways: they restrain him from evil, they establish him in what is good, they have him learn a craft, they join him with a suitable wife, and at the proper time they hand over the inheritance. Thus for him, this eastern direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.

268. “Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi antevāsinā dakkhiṇā disā ācariyā paccupaṭṭhātabbā – uṭṭhānena upaṭṭhānena sussusāya pāricariyāya sakkaccaṃ sippapaṭiggahaṇena sippaṃ paṭiggahaṇena (syā.), sippauggahaṇena (ka.). Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi antevāsinā dakkhiṇā disā ācariyā paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi [T 3.0204] ṭhānehi antevāsiṃ anukampanti – suvinītaṃ vinenti, suggahitaṃ gāhāpenti, sabbasippassutaṃ samakkhāyino bhavanti, mittāmaccesu paṭiyādenti paṭivedenti (syā.), disāsu parittāṇaṃ karonti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi antevāsinā [P 3.0190] dakkhiṇā disā ācariyā paccupaṭṭhitā imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi antevāsiṃ anukampanti. Evamassa esā dakkhiṇā disā paṭicchannā hoti khemā appaṭibhayā.

268. In five ways, son of a householder, a student should attend to his teachers as the southern direction: by rising, by waiting upon them, by eagerness to learn, by personal service, and by carefully grasping the craft. Teachers, attended to by their student in these five ways, show compassion to their student in five ways: they train him well, they make him learn it well, they instruct him thoroughly in every craft and branch of knowledge, they introduce him to their friends and companions, and they provide protection in all directions. Thus for him, this southern direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.

269. “Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhātabbā – sammānanāya anavamānanāya avimānanāya (syā. pī.) anaticariyāya issariyavossaggena alaṅkārānuppadānena. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi [M 3.0155] sāmikaṃ anukampati – susaṃvihitakammantā ca hoti, saṅgahitaparijanā susaṅgahitaparijanā (sī. syā. pī.) ca, anaticārinī ca, sambhatañca anurakkhati, dakkhā ca hoti analasā sabbakiccesu. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikena pacchimā disā bhariyā paccupaṭṭhitā imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi sāmikaṃ anukampati. Evamassa esā pacchimā disā paṭicchannā hoti khemā appaṭibhayā.

269. In five ways, son of a householder, a husband should attend to his wife as the western direction: by honoring her, by not disparaging her, by not being unfaithful, by handing over authority, and by providing her with adornments. The wife, thus attended to by her husband in these five ways, shows compassion to her husband in five ways: she manages her duties well, she is kind to the household, she is faithful, she safeguards his earnings, and she is skilled and diligent in all her tasks. Thus for him, this western direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.

270. “Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi kulaputtena uttarā disā mittāmaccā paccupaṭṭhātabbā – dānena peyyavajjena viyavajjena (syā. ka.) atthacariyāya samānattatāya avisaṃvādanatāya. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi kulaputtena uttarā disā mittāmaccā paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi [T 3.0205] ṭhānehi [V 3.0145] kulaputtaṃ anukampanti – pamattaṃ rakkhanti, pamattassa sāpateyyaṃ rakkhanti, bhītassa saraṇaṃ honti, āpadāsu na vijahanti, aparapajā cassa paṭipūjenti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi kulaputtena uttarā disā mittāmaccā paccupaṭṭhitā imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi kulaputtaṃ anukampanti. Evamassa esā uttarā disā paṭicchannā hoti khemā appaṭibhayā.

270. In five ways, son of a householder, a clansman should attend to his friends and companions as the northern direction: by generosity, by endearing speech, by acting for their welfare, by treating them as an equal, and by being reliable. Friends and companions, thus attended to by a clansman in these five ways, show compassion to him in five ways: they protect him when he is heedless, they guard his property when he is heedless, they are a refuge for him when he is afraid, they do not abandon him in misfortune, and they honor his descendants. Thus for him, this northern direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.

271. “Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi ayyirakena ayirakena (sī. syā. pī.) heṭṭhimā [P 3.0191] disā dāsakammakarā paccupaṭṭhātabbā – yathābalaṃ kammantasaṃvidhānena bhattavetanānuppadānena gilānupaṭṭhānena acchariyānaṃ rasānaṃ saṃvibhāgena samaye vossaggena. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi ayyirakena heṭṭhimā disā dāsakammakarā paccupaṭṭhitā pañcahi ṭhānehi ayyirakaṃ anukampanti – pubbuṭṭhāyino ca honti, pacchā nipātino ca, dinnādāyino ca, sukatakammakarā ca, kittivaṇṇaharā ca. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi ayyirakena heṭṭhimā disā dāsakammakarā paccupaṭṭhitā imehi pañcahi ṭhānehi ayyirakaṃ anukampanti. Evamassa esā heṭṭhimā disā paṭicchannā hoti khemā appaṭibhayā.

271. In five ways, son of a householder, a master should attend to his servants and workers as the lower direction: by assigning work according to their strength, by providing food and wages, by tending to them in sickness, by sharing special delicacies, and by granting leave at suitable times. Servants and workers, thus attended to by their master in these five ways, show compassion to him in five ways: they rise before him, they go to rest after him, they take only what is given, they perform their work well, and they spread his good reputation and praise. Thus for him, this lower direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.

272. “Pañcahi kho, gahapatiputta, ṭhānehi kulaputtena uparimā disā samaṇabrāhmaṇā paccupaṭṭhātabbā – mettena kāyakammena mettena vacīkammena mettena [M 3.0156] manokammena anāvaṭadvāratāya āmisānuppadānena. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi kulaputtena uparimā [T 3.0206] disā samaṇabrāhmaṇā paccupaṭṭhitā chahi ṭhānehi kulaputtaṃ anukampanti – pāpā nivārenti, kalyāṇe nivesenti, kalyāṇena manasā anukampanti, assutaṃ sāventi, sutaṃ pariyodāpenti, saggassa maggaṃ ācikkhanti. Imehi kho, gahapatiputta, pañcahi ṭhānehi kulaputtena uparimā disā samaṇabrāhmaṇā paccupaṭṭhitā imehi chahi ṭhānehi kulaputtaṃ anukampanti. Evamassa esā uparimā disā paṭicchannā hoti khemā appaṭibhayā”ti.

272. In five ways, son of a householder, a clansman should attend to ascetics and brahmins as the upper direction: with bodily action of loving-kindness, with verbal action of loving-kindness, with mental action of loving-kindness, by keeping an open door for them, and by providing material support. Ascetics and brahmins, thus attended to by a clansman in these five ways, show compassion to him in six ways: they restrain him from evil, they establish him in good, they care for him with a benevolent mind, they cause him to hear what he has not heard, they clarify what he has heard, and they point out the path to heaven. Thus for him, this upper direction is covered, secure, and free from fear.

273. Idamavoca bhagavā. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

273. The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then said further:

“Mātāpitā disā pubbā, ācariyā dakkhiṇā disā;

Puttadārā [P 3.0192] disā pacchā, mittāmaccā ca uttarā.

“Parents are the eastern direction, teachers are the southern direction; wife and children are the western direction, friends and companions the northern direction.

“Dāsakammakarā [V 3.0146] heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Etā disā namasseyya, alamatto kule gihī.

“Slaves and workers are the lower direction, ascetics and brahmins the upper; a householder in his family who is able should pay homage to these directions.

“Paṇḍito sīlasampanno, saṇho ca paṭibhānavā;

Nivātavutti atthaddho, tādiso labhate yasaṃ.

“Wise, virtuous, gentle, and quick-witted; humble, not arrogant—such a one attains glory.

“Uṭṭhānako analaso, āpadāsu na vedhati;

Acchinnavutti medhāvī, tādiso labhate yasaṃ.

“Energetic, not lazy, unshaken in misfortune, of unbroken conduct, wise—such a one attains glory.

“Saṅgāhako mittakaro, vadaññū vītamaccharo;

Netā vinetā anunetā, tādiso labhate yasaṃ.

“One who is supportive, a friend-maker, generous, free from stinginess; a guide, a trainer, a conciliator—such a one attains glory.

“Dānañca peyyavajjañca, atthacariyā ca yā idha;

Samānattatā ca dhammesu, tattha tattha yathārahaṃ;

Ete [T 3.0207] kho saṅgahā loke, rathassāṇīva yāyato.

“Giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality in matters, here and there as is fitting; these bonds of fellowship in the world are like the linchpin of a moving chariot.

“Ete ca saṅgahā nāssu, na mātā puttakāraṇā;

Labhetha mānaṃ pūjaṃ vā, pitā vā puttakāraṇā.

“If these bonds of fellowship did not exist, a mother would not receive honor or respect on account of her child, nor would a father on account of his child.

“Yasmā ca saṅgahā saṅgahe (ka.) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ icchitapāṭho ete, sammapekkhanti samavekkhanti (sī. pī. ka.) paṇḍitā;

Tasmā [P 3.0193] mahattaṃ papponti, pāsaṃsā ca bhavanti te”ti.

“And because the wise rightly regard these bonds of fellowship, they therefore attain greatness and become worthy of praise.”

274. Evaṃ [M 3.0157] vutte, siṅgālako gahapatiputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bhante! Abhikkantaṃ, bhante! Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya ‘cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantī’ti. Evamevaṃ bhagavatā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi dhammañca bhikkhusaṃghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhagavā dhāretu, ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti.

274. When this was said, the householder’s son Siṅgālaka said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what was overturned, reveal what was hidden, show the way to one who is lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness, thinking, ‘Those with eyes will see forms,’ so in the same way has the Blessed One made the Dhamma clear in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward, for as long as life lasts.”

Siṅgālasuttaṃ siṅgālovādasuttantaṃ (pī.) niṭṭhitaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Siṅgāla Sutta, the eighth, is concluded.

9. Āṭānāṭiyasuttaṃ

9. The Āṭānāṭiya Discourse

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro

First Recitation Section

275. Evaṃ [P 3.0194][M 3.0158][V 3.0147][T 3.0208] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate. Atha kho cattāro mahārājā mahārājāno (ka.) mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāya mahatiyā ca gandhabbasenāya mahatiyā ca kumbhaṇḍasenāya mahatiyā ca nāgasenāya catuddisaṃ rakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā catuddisaṃ gumbaṃ ṭhapetvā catuddisaṃ ovaraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṃ gijjhakūṭaṃ pabbataṃ obhāsetvā gijjhakūṭaṃ obhāsetvā (sī. syā. pī.) yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Tepi kho yakkhā appekacce bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu, appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

275. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, on Gijjhakūṭa, the Vulture Peak mountain. Then the Four Great Kings, with a great host of yakkhas, a great host of gandhabbas, a great host of kumbhaṇḍas, and a great host of nāgas, having established a guard in the four directions, having established a detachment in the four directions, and having established a barrier in the four directions, in the middle of the night, with a most pleasing appearance, illuminating the entire Gijjhakūṭa mountain, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Some of those yakkhas also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, after an exchange of courteous and amiable conversation, sat down to one side; some extended their joined hands in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence.

276. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho vessavaṇo mahārājā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “santi hi, bhante, uḷārā yakkhā bhagavato appasannā. Santi hi, bhante, uḷārā yakkhā bhagavato pasannā. Santi hi[P 3.0195], bhante, majjhimā yakkhā bhagavato appasannā. Santi hi, bhante, majjhimā yakkhā bhagavato pasannā. Santi hi, bhante, nīcā yakkhā bhagavato appasannā. Santi hi, bhante, nīcā yakkhā bhagavato pasannā. Yebhuyyena [T 3.0209] kho pana, bhante, yakkhā appasannāyeva bhagavato. Taṃ kissa hetu? Bhagavā hi, bhante, pāṇātipātā veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti, adinnādānā veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti, kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti, musāvādā veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti, surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti. Yebhuyyena kho pana, bhante, yakkhā appaṭiviratāyeva pāṇātipātā, appaṭiviratā adinnādānā, appaṭiviratā kāmesumicchācārā, appaṭiviratā musāvādā, appaṭiviratā surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā[V 3.0148]. Tesaṃ taṃ hoti appiyaṃ amanāpaṃ. Santi hi, bhante, bhagavato sāvakā araññavanapatthāni pantāni [M 3.0159] senāsanāni paṭisevanti appasaddāni appanigghosāni vijanavātāni manussarāhasseyyakāni manussarāhaseyyakāni (sī. syā. pī.) paṭisallānasāruppāni. Tattha santi uḷārā yakkhā nivāsino, ye imasmiṃ bhagavato pāvacane appasannā. Tesaṃ pasādāya uggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavā āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

276. Seated to one side, the Great King Vessavaṇa said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, there are eminent yakkhas who are not pleased with the Blessed One. There are eminent yakkhas who are pleased with the Blessed One. There are middling yakkhas who are not pleased with the Blessed One. There are middling yakkhas who are pleased with the Blessed One. There are lowly yakkhas who are not pleased with the Blessed One. There are lowly yakkhas who are pleased with the Blessed One. For the most part, venerable sir, the yakkhas are not pleased with the Blessed One. For what reason? Because, venerable sir, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for abstaining from the destruction of life, for abstaining from taking what is not given, for abstaining from sexual misconduct, for abstaining from false speech, and for abstaining from liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness. For the most part, venerable sir, the yakkhas do not abstain from the destruction of life, do not abstain from taking what is not given, do not abstain from sexual misconduct, do not abstain from false speech, and do not abstain from liquor, wine, and intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness. To them, that teaching is un-dear and displeasing. Venerable sir, there are disciples of the Blessed One who frequent remote forest and woodland abodes—secluded, with little sound, with little noise, free from the bustle of people, fit for secret human endeavors, suitable for solitary retreat. Therein dwell eminent yakkhas who are not pleased with this teaching of the Blessed One. For the sake of pleasing them, venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the security, safeguarding, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.” The Blessed One consented by way of silence.

Atha kho vessavaṇo mahārājā bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ abhāsi –

Then the Great King Vessavaṇa, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, at that time recited this Āṭānāṭiya protection:

277. “Vipassissa ca ime cakārā porāṇapotthakesu natthi namatthu, cakkhumantassa sirīmato.

277. Homage be to Vipassī, the one with vision, the glorious one.

Sikhissapi ca ime cakārā porāṇapotthakesu natthi namatthu, sabbabhūtānukampino.

And homage be to Sikhī, compassionate to all beings.

“Vessabhussa ca ime cakārā porāṇapotthakesu natthi namatthu, nhātakassa tapassino;

Namatthu [T 3.0210][P 3.0196] kakusandhassa, mārasenāpamaddino.

And homage be to Vessabhū, the one who has washed away defilements, the ascetic; Homage be to Kakusandha, the crusher of Māra’s army.

“Koṇāgamanassa namatthu, brāhmaṇassa vusīmato;

Kassapassa ca ime cakārā porāṇapotthakesu natthi namatthu, vippamuttassa sabbadhi.

Homage be to Koṇāgamana, the brāhmaṇa who has lived the holy life; And homage be to Kassapa, completely liberated in every way.

“Aṅgīrasassa namatthu, sakyaputtassa sirīmato;

Yo imaṃ dhammaṃ desesi dhammamadesesi (sī. syā. pī.), dhammaṃ deseti (?), sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ.

Homage be to Aṅgīrasa, the glorious son of the Sakyans, who taught this Dhamma, the dispeller of all suffering.

“Ye cāpi nibbutā loke, yathābhūtaṃ vipassisuṃ;

Te janā apisuṇātha apisuṇā (sī. syā. pī.), mahantā vītasāradā.

Those in the world who are extinguished, who have seen things as they truly are; those people are not slanderous, they are great, devoid of fear.

“Hitaṃ devamanussānaṃ, yaṃ namassanti gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

Gods and humans pay homage to Gotama, who is for the welfare of gods and humans, endowed with knowledge and conduct, great, and free from fear.

278. “Yato [V 3.0149] uggacchati sūriyo suriyo (sī. syā. pī.), ādicco maṇḍalī mahā.

278. From where the sun rises, the kinsman of Aditi, the great orb.

Yassa cuggacchamānassa, saṃvarīpi nirujjhati;

Yassa cuggate sūriye, ‘divaso’ti pavuccati.

And as it is rising, the night ceases; and when the sun has risen, it is called ‘day’.

“Rahadopi [M 3.0160] tattha gambhīro, samuddo saritodako;

Evaṃ taṃ tattha jānanti, ‘samuddo saritodako’.

There, too, is a deep lake, the ocean with flowing water; thus do people know it there as ‘the ocean with flowing water’.

“Ito [P 3.0197] ‘sā purimā disā’, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

‘From here, that is the eastern direction,’ so people declare it. It is the direction that the glorious Great King protects.

“Gandhabbānaṃ adhipati ādhipati (sī. syā. pī.) evamuparipi, ‘dhataraṭṭho’ti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, gandhabbehi purakkhato.

The lord of the gandhabbas, Dhataraṭṭha by name, delights in dance and song, attended by the gandhabbas.

“Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

He has many sons, so I have heard, all with the same name; ninety-one, named Inda, of great strength.

Te [T 3.0211] cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they too, having seen the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun, pay homage from afar to the great one, free from fear.

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O highest of men. With wisdom you look upon all. Even non-humans pay homage to you. This we have heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.

“‘Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ’.

‘Pay homage to Gotama the Conqueror.’ ‘We pay homage to Gotama the Conqueror; we pay homage to Gotama the Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct.’

279. “Yena petā pavuccanti, pisuṇā piṭṭhimaṃsikā.

279. The direction by which are led the departed, slanderers, backbiters,

Pāṇātipātino luddā luddhā (pī. ka.), corā nekatikā janā.

“Killers of living beings, hunters, thieves, and people of cruel deeds.”

“Ito [V 3.0150][P 3.0198] ‘sā dakkhiṇā disā’, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

‘From here, that is the southern direction,’ so people declare it. It is the direction that the glorious Great King protects.

“Kumbhaṇḍānaṃ adhipati, ‘virūḷho’ iti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, kumbhaṇḍehi purakkhato.

The lord of the kumbhaṇḍas, Virūḷha by name, delights in dance and song, attended by the kumbhaṇḍas.

“Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

He has many sons, so I have heard, all with the same name; ninety-one, named Inda, of great strength.

Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they too, having seen the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun, pay homage from afar to the great one, free from fear.

“Namo [M 3.0161] te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O highest of men. With wisdom you look upon all. Even non-humans pay homage to you. This we have heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.

“‘Jinaṃ [T 3.0212] vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ’.

‘Pay homage to Gotama the Conqueror.’ ‘We pay homage to Gotama the Conqueror; we pay homage to Gotama the Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct.’

280. “Yattha coggacchati sūriyo, ādicco maṇḍalī mahā.

280. The direction where the sun sets, the kinsman of Aditi, the great orb.

Yassa coggacchamānassa, divasopi nirujjhati;

Yassa coggate sūriye, ‘saṃvarī’ti pavuccati.

And as it is setting, the day ceases; and when the sun has set, it is called ‘night’.

“Rahadopi tattha gambhīro, samuddo saritodako;

Evaṃ taṃ tattha jānanti, ‘samuddo saritodako’.

There, too, is a deep lake, the ocean with flowing water; thus do people know it there as ‘the ocean with flowing water’.

“Ito ‘sā pacchimā disā’, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ [P 3.0199] disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

‘From here, that is the western direction,’ so people declare it. It is the direction that the glorious Great King protects.

“Nāgānañca [V 3.0151] adhipati, ‘virūpakkho’ti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, nāgeheva purakkhato.

The lord of the nāgas, Virūpakkha by name, delights in dance and song, attended by the nāgas.

“Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

He has many sons, so I have heard, all with the same name; ninety-one, named Inda, of great strength.

Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they too, having seen the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun, pay homage from afar to the great one, free from fear.

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O highest of men. With wisdom you look upon all. Even non-humans pay homage to you. This we have heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.

“‘Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ’.

‘Pay homage to Gotama the Conqueror.’ ‘We pay homage to Gotama the Conqueror; we pay homage to Gotama the Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct.’

281. “Yena [T 3.0213] uttarakuruvho uttarakurū rammā (sī. syā. pī.), mahāneru sudassano.

281. The direction where Uttarakuru lies, and the great, beautiful Mount Neru.

Manussā tattha jāyanti, amamā apariggahā.

Humans are born there without possessiveness, without possessions.

“Na [M 3.0162] te bījaṃ pavapanti, napi nīyanti naṅgalā;

Akaṭṭhapākimaṃ sāliṃ, paribhuñjanti mānusā.

They do not sow seed, nor are plows brought forth; humans there consume Sāli rice that ripens without cultivation.

“Akaṇaṃ athusaṃ suddhaṃ, sugandhaṃ taṇḍulapphalaṃ;

Tuṇḍikīre [P 3.0200] pacitvāna, tato bhuñjanti bhojanaṃ.

Without broken grains, without husk, pure, and fragrant is the rice-fruit. Having cooked it in a pot, they then eat their meal.

“Gāviṃ ekakhuraṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ;

Pasuṃ ekakhuraṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

Making a cow into a swift vehicle, they travel in every direction; making a beast into a swift vehicle, they travel in every direction.

“Itthiṃ vā vāhanaṃ itthī-vāhanaṃ (sī. pī.), itthīṃ vāhanaṃ (syā.) katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ;

Purisaṃ vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

Making a woman into a vehicle, they travel in every direction; making a man into a vehicle, they travel in every direction.

“Kumāriṃ [V 3.0152] vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ;

Kumāraṃ vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

Making a young woman into a vehicle, they travel in every direction; making a young man into a vehicle, they travel in every direction.

“Te yāne abhiruhitvā,

Sabbā disā anupariyāyanti anupariyanti (syā.);

Pacārā tassa rājino.

Having mounted those vehicles, the attendants of that king travel around to all directions.

“Hatthiyānaṃ assayānaṃ, dibbaṃ yānaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ;

Pāsādā sivikā ceva, mahārājassa yasassino.

Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and divine vehicles are at his service; palaces and palanquins, too, for that glorious great king.

“Tassa ca nagarā ahu,

Antalikkhe sumāpitā;

Āṭānāṭā kusināṭā parakusināṭā,

Nāṭasuriyā nāṭapuriyā (sī. pī.), nāṭapariyā (syā.) parakusiṭanāṭā.

And for him there were cities, well-fashioned in the sky: Āṭānāṭā, Kusināṭā, Parakusināṭā, Nāṭasuriyā, and Parakusiṭanāṭā.

“Uttarena [P 3.0201] kasivanto kapivanto (sī. syā. pī),

Janoghamaparena ca;

Navanavutiyo ambaraambaravatiyo,

Āḷakamandā nāma rājadhānī.

To the north is Kasivanta, and to the west, Janogha; also Navanavutiyo, Ambara-ambaravatiyo, and the royal capital named Āḷakamandā.

“Kuverassa [T 3.0214] kho pana, mārisa, mahārājassa visāṇā nāma rājadhānī;

Tasmā kuvero mahārājā, ‘vessavaṇo’ti pavuccati.

Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the great king Kuvera has a royal capital named Visāṇā; therefore, the great king Kuvera is called Vessavaṇa.

“Paccesanto [M 3.0163] pakāsenti, tatolā tattalā tatotalā;

Ojasi tejasi tatojasī, sūro rājā ariṭṭho nemi.

Those who question individually and make things known are: Tatolā, Tattalā, Tatotalā, Ojasi, Tejasi, Tatojasī, Sūro, Rājā, Ariṭṭho, and Nemi.

“Rahadopi tattha dharaṇī nāma, yato meghā pavassanti;

Vassā yato patāyanti, sabhāpi tattha sālavatī bhagalavatī (sī. syā. pī.) nāma.

There, too, is a lake named Dharaṇī, from which the clouds rain down, from which the showers issue forth. There, too, is the assembly hall named Sālavatī.

“Yattha [V 3.0153] yakkhā payirupāsanti, tattha niccaphalā rukkhā;

Nānā dijagaṇā yutā, mayūrakoñcābhirudā;

Kokilādīhi vagguhi.

Where the yakkhas assemble, there are trees perpetually in fruit, frequented by various flocks of birds, resounding with the calls of peacocks and herons, and with the sweet sounds of cuckoos and other birds.

“Jīvañjīvakasaddettha, atho oṭṭhavacittakā;

Kukkuṭakā [P 3.0202] kukutthakā (sī. pī.) kuḷīrakā, vane pokkharasātakā.

Here is the sound of the Jīvañjīvaka bird, and also the Oṭṭhavacittakā birds. There are jungle fowl and golden-colored crabs, and in the forest, the Pokkharasātaka birds.

“Sukasāḷikasaddettha, daṇḍamāṇavakāni ca;

Sobhati sabbakālaṃ sā, kuveranaḷinī sadā.

Here are the sounds of parrots and mynas, and the Daṇḍamāṇavaka birds. That lotus pond of Kuvera, Dharaṇī, is beautiful at all times.

“Ito ‘sā uttarā disā’, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

‘From here, that is the northern direction,’ thus do people declare it. It is the direction which that glorious great king protects.

“Yakkhānañca adhipati, ‘kuvero’ iti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, yakkheheva purakkhato.

The lord of the yakkhas, Kuvera by name, delights in dance and song, surrounded by yakkhas.

“Puttāpi [T 3.0215] tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

His sons are also many, and I have heard they have one name. They are eighty and ten and one, named Inda, of great strength.

“Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And those sons, too, having seen the Buddha, the kinsman of the Sun, pay homage from afar to the great one who is free from fear.

“Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men; homage to you, O supreme among men. You regard all with wholesome wisdom. Even non-humans pay homage to you. This we have heard repeatedly; therefore, we speak thus.

“‘Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotama’”nti.

‘Pay homage to the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We pay homage to the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We pay homage to Gotama, the Buddha endowed with knowledge and conduct.’

“Ayaṃ [P 3.0203][V 3.0154] kho sā, mārisa, āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāya.

This, Venerable Sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the security, guarding, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, male lay devotees, and female lay devotees.

282. “Yassa [M 3.0164] kassaci, mārisa, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā upāsakassa vā upāsikāya vā ayaṃ āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā suggahitā bhavissati samattā pariyāputā pariyāpuṭā (ka.). Taṃ ce amanusso yakkho vā yakkhinī vā yakkhapotako vā yakkhapotikā vā yakkhamahāmatto vā yakkhapārisajjo vā yakkhapacāro vā, gandhabbo vā gandhabbī vā gandhabbapotako vā gandhabbapotikā vā gandhabbamahāmatto vā gandhabbapārisajjo vā gandhabbapacāro vā, kumbhaṇḍo vā kumbhaṇḍī vā kumbhaṇḍapotako vā kumbhaṇḍapotikā vā kumbhaṇḍamahāmatto vā kumbhaṇḍapārisajjo vā kumbhaṇḍapacāro vā, nāgo vā nāgī vā nāgapotako vā nāgapotikā [T 3.0216] vā nāgamahāmatto vā nāgapārisajjo vā nāgapacāro vā, paduṭṭhacitto bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā upāsakaṃ vā upāsikaṃ vā gacchantaṃ vā anugaccheyya, ṭhitaṃ vā upatiṭṭheyya, nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya, nipannaṃ vā upanipajjeyya. Na me so, mārisa, amanusso labheyya gāmesu vā nigamesu vā sakkāraṃ vā garukāraṃ vā. Na me so, mārisa, amanusso labheyya āḷakamandāya nāma rājadhāniyā vatthuṃ vā vāsaṃ vā. Na me so, mārisa, amanusso labheyya yakkhānaṃ samitiṃ gantuṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā anāvayhampi naṃ kareyyuṃ avivayhaṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā attāhipi paripuṇṇāhi paribhāsāhi paribhāseyyuṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā rittaṃpissa pattaṃ sīse nikkujjeyyuṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā sattadhāpissa muddhaṃ phāleyyuṃ.

282. Venerable Sir, for any monk, nun, male lay devotee, or female lay devotee for whom this Āṭānāṭiya protection will be well-grasped, fully learned, and repeatedly recited: should any non-human—a male or female yakkha, a young male or female yakkha, a yakkha minister, a yakkha councilor, or a yakkha attendant; or a male or female gandhabba, a young male or female gandhabba, a gandhabba minister, a gandhabba councilor, or a gandhabba attendant; or a male or female kumbhaṇḍa, a young male or female kumbhaṇḍa, a kumbhaṇḍa minister, a kumbhaṇḍa councilor, or a kumbhaṇḍa attendant; or a male or female nāga, a young male or female nāga, a nāga minister, a nāga councilor, or a nāga attendant—with a mind of ill-will, follow a monk, nun, male lay devotee, or female lay devotee who is walking, or stand near one who is standing, or sit near one who is sitting, or lie down near one who is lying down; then, Venerable Sir, that non-human would not receive honor or respect in villages or towns. Venerable Sir, that non-human would not obtain a place or a dwelling in the royal city named Āḷakamandā. Venerable Sir, that non-human would not be able to go to the assembly of the yakkhas. Moreover, Venerable Sir, the non-humans would make him unfit for marriage, neither giving in marriage nor taking in marriage. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the non-humans would revile him with full and complete insults. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the non-humans would overturn an empty bowl on his head. Furthermore, Venerable Sir, the non-humans would split his head into seven pieces.

“Santi hi, mārisa, amanussā caṇḍā ruddhā ruddā (sī. pī.) rabhasā, te neva mahārājānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti. Te kho te, mārisa, amanussā mahārājānaṃ [P 3.0204] avaruddhā nāma vuccanti. Seyyathāpi, mārisa, rañño māgadhassa vijite mahācorā. Te neva rañño māgadhassa ādiyanti, na rañño māgadhassa purisakānaṃ ādiyanti, na rañño māgadhassa purisakānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti. Te kho te, mārisa, mahācorā rañño māgadhassa avaruddhā nāma vuccanti. Evameva kho, mārisa, santi amanussā caṇḍā ruddhā rabhasā, te neva mahārājānaṃ [T 3.0217] ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti. Te [M 3.0165] kho te, mārisa, amanussā mahārājānaṃ avaruddhā nāma vuccanti. Yo hi koci, mārisa, amanusso yakkho vā yakkhinī vā…pe… gandhabbo vā gandhabbī vā [V 3.0155]… kumbhaṇḍo vā kumbhaṇḍī vā… nāgo vā nāgī vā nāgapotako vā nāgapotikā vā nāgamahāmatto vā nāgapārisajjo vā nāgapacāro vā paduṭṭhacitto bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā upāsakaṃ vā upāsikaṃ vā gacchantaṃ vā anugaccheyya, ṭhitaṃ vā upatiṭṭheyya, nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya, nipannaṃ vā upanipajjeyya. Imesaṃ yakkhānaṃ mahāyakkhānaṃ senāpatīnaṃ mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikkanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ – ‘ayaṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ yakkho āvisati, ayaṃ yakkho heṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho viheṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho hiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho vihiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho na muñcatī’ti.

Venerable Sir, there are non-humans who are fierce, cruel, and violent. They do not heed the Great Kings, nor the officers of the Great Kings, nor the officers of the officers of the Great Kings. These non-humans, Venerable Sir, are called the rebels of the Great Kings. Just as, Venerable Sir, in the realm of the king of Magadha there are great bandits who do not heed the king of Magadha, nor the officers of the king of Magadha, nor the officers of the officers of the king of Magadha. These great bandits, Venerable Sir, are called the rebels of the king of Magadha. In the very same way, Venerable Sir, there are non-humans who are fierce, cruel, and violent. They do not heed the Great Kings, nor the officers of the Great Kings, nor the officers of the officers of the Great Kings. These non-humans, Venerable Sir, are called the rebels of the Great Kings. If any non-human, Venerable Sir—a male or female yakkha… a male or female gandhabba… a male or female kumbhaṇḍa… a male or female nāga, a young male or female nāga, a nāga minister, a nāga councilor, or a nāga attendant—with a mind of ill-will, should follow a monk, nun, male lay devotee, or female lay devotee who is walking, or stand near one who is standing, or sit near one who is sitting, or lie down near one who is lying down, then these yakkhas, these great yakkhas, these generals, these great generals should be informed, cried out to, and proclaimed to: ‘This yakkha is seizing! This yakkha is possessing! This yakkha is oppressing! This yakkha is greatly oppressing! This yakkha is harming! This yakkha is greatly harming! This yakkha does not release!’

283. “Katamesaṃ yakkhānaṃ mahāyakkhānaṃ senāpatīnaṃ mahāsenāpatīnaṃ?

283. Who are these yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals?

“Indo somo varuṇo ca, bhāradvājo pajāpati;

Candano kāmaseṭṭho ca, kinnughaṇḍu nighaṇḍu ca.

Inda, Soma, and Varuṇa, Bhāradvāja and Pajāpati; Candana, Kāmaseṭṭha, Kinnughaṇḍu, and Nighaṇḍu.

“Panādo [T 3.0218] opamañño ca, devasūto ca mātali;

Cittaseno ca gandhabbo, naḷo rājā janesabho janosabho (syā.).

Panāda and Opamañña, Mātali the deva’s messenger, Cittasena the gandhabba, King Naḷa, and Janesabha.

“Sātāgiro hemavato, puṇṇako karatiyo guḷo;

Sivako [P 3.0205] mucalindo ca, vessāmitto yugandharo.

Sātāgira of Hemavata, Puṇṇaka, Karatiya, Guḷa, Sivaka, and Mucalinda, Vessāmitta, and Yugandhara.

“Gopālo supparodho ca suppagedho ca (sī. syā. pī.), hiri netti hirī nettī (sī. pī.) ca mandiyo;

Pañcālacaṇḍo āḷavako, pajjunno sumano sumukho;

Dadhimukho maṇi māṇivaro maṇi mānicaro (syā. pī.) dīgho, atho serīsako saha.

Gopāla and Supparodha, Hiri, Netti, and Mandiya, Pañcālacaṇḍa, Āḷavaka, Pajjunna, Sumana, Sumukha, Dadhimukha, Maṇi, Māṇi, Vara, and Dīgha, and with them, Serīsaka as well.

“Imesaṃ yakkhānaṃ mahāyakkhānaṃ senāpatīnaṃ mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikkanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ – ‘ayaṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ yakkho āvisati, ayaṃ yakkho heṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho viheṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho hiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho vihiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho na muñcatī’ti.

These yakkhas, great yakkhas, generals, and great generals should be informed, cried out to, and proclaimed to: ‘This yakkha is seizing! This yakkha is possessing! This yakkha is oppressing! This yakkha is greatly oppressing! This yakkha is harming! This yakkha is greatly harming! This yakkha does not release!’

“Ayaṃ [M 3.0166] kho sā, mārisa, āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāya. Handa ca dāni mayaṃ, mārisa, gacchāma [V 3.0156] bahukiccā mayaṃ bahukaraṇīyā”ti. “Yassadāni tumhe mahārājāno kālaṃ maññathā”ti.

“Venerable Sir, this is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, for their security, for their non-harming, and for their comfortable dwelling. And now, Venerable Sir, let us depart; we have many duties, we have much to do.” “Great Kings, you may now do as you deem the time is right.”

284. Atha kho cattāro mahārājā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Tepi kho yakkhā uṭṭhāyāsanā appekacce bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu[P 3.0206]. Appekacce [T 3.0219] yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce tuṇhībhūtā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsūti.

284. Then the four great kings rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and vanished right there. Those yakkhas, too, rose from their seats. Some paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, and vanished right there. Some exchanged courteous and memorable greetings with the Blessed One, and after concluding their talk, they vanished right there. Some raised their joined palms in reverence toward the Blessed One and vanished right there. Some announced their name and clan and vanished right there. Some remained silent and vanished right there.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The first recitation section is concluded.

Dutiyabhāṇavāro

The Second Recitation Section

285. Atha kho bhagavā tassā rattiyā accayena bhikkhū āmantesi – “imaṃ, bhikkhave, rattiṃ cattāro mahārājā mahatiyā ca yakkhasenāya mahatiyā ca gandhabbasenāya mahatiyā ca kumbhaṇḍasenāya mahatiyā ca nāgasenāya catuddisaṃ rakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā catuddisaṃ gumbaṃ ṭhapetvā catuddisaṃ ovaraṇaṃ ṭhapetvā abhikkantāya rattiyā abhikkantavaṇṇā kevalakappaṃ gijjhakūṭaṃ pabbataṃ obhāsetvā yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Tepi kho, bhikkhave, yakkhā appekacce maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce mayā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce yenāhaṃ tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce nāmagottaṃ sāvetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Appekacce tuṇhībhūtā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu.

285. Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, last night the Four Great Kings, with their great army of yakkhas, great army of gandhabbas, great army of kumbhaṇḍas, and great army of nāgas, having set a guard in the four directions, having set troops in the four directions, having set an enclosure in the four directions, when the night was far advanced, having a beautiful radiance, illuminating the entire Vulture Peak mountain, approached where I was. Having approached, they paid homage to me and sat to one side. Those yakkhas, too, monks, some paid homage to me and sat to one side. Some exchanged courteous and memorable greetings with me, and after concluding their talk, sat to one side. Some raised their joined palms in reverence toward me and sat to one side. Some announced their name and clan and sat to one side. Some remained silent and sat to one side.

286. “Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho, bhikkhave, vessavaṇo mahārājā maṃ etadavoca – ‘santi hi, bhante, uḷārā yakkhā bhagavato appasannā…pe… santi hi[M 3.0167], bhante nīcā [T 3.0220] yakkhā bhagavato pasannā. Yebhuyyena kho pana, bhante, yakkhā appasannāyeva bhagavato. Taṃ kissa hetu? Bhagavā hi, bhante, pāṇātipātā veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti… surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā [V 3.0157] veramaṇiyā dhammaṃ deseti. Yebhuyyena kho pana, bhante, yakkhā appaṭiviratāyeva pāṇātipātā… appaṭiviratā surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā. Tesaṃ taṃ hoti appiyaṃ amanāpaṃ. Santi hi, bhante, bhagavato sāvakā araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevanti appasaddāni appanigghosāni vijanavātāni manussarāhasseyyakāni paṭisallānasāruppāni. Tattha santi uḷārā yakkhā nivāsino, ye imasmiṃ bhagavato pāvacane appasannā, tesaṃ pasādāya uggaṇhātu, bhante, bhagavā āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāyā’ti. Adhivāsesiṃ kho ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vessavaṇo mahārājā me adhivāsanaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ abhāsi –

286. “Having sat to one side, monks, the great king Vessavaṇa said this to me: ‘Venerable sir, there are powerful yakkhas who are not pleased with the Blessed One… Venerable sir, there are lowly yakkhas who are pleased with the Blessed One. But for the most part, venerable sir, the yakkhas are not pleased with the Blessed One. What is the reason for that? Because, venerable sir, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for abstaining from the destruction of life… teaches the Dhamma for abstaining from intoxicants, liquor, and distilled spirits which are the basis for heedlessness. But for the most part, venerable sir, the yakkhas do not abstain from the destruction of life… do not abstain from intoxicants, liquor, and distilled spirits which are the basis for heedlessness. To them, that is un-dear and disagreeable. Venerable sir, there are disciples of the Blessed One who frequent forest and woodland tracts, remote lodgings that are quiet, with little noise, free from the presence of people, suitable for privacy, and fit for seclusion. There dwell powerful yakkhas who are not pleased with this teaching of the Blessed One. For the sake of their confidence, venerable sir, let the Blessed One learn the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, for their security, for their non-harming, and for their comfortable dwelling.’ I consented, monks, by remaining silent. Then, monks, the great king Vessavaṇa, knowing my consent, on that occasion recited this Āṭānāṭiya protection:

287. ‘Vipassissa ca namatthu, cakkhumantassa sirīmato.

287. “Homage to Vipassī, possessed of vision, the glorious one.

Sikhissapi ca namatthu, sabbabhūtānukampino.

Homage also to Sikhī, compassionate to all beings.

‘Vessabhussa ca namatthu, nhātakassa tapassino;

Namatthu kakusandhassa, mārasenāpamaddino.

“Homage to Vessabhū, the purified one, the ascetic; Homage to Kakusandha, the crusher of Māra’s army.

‘Koṇāgamanassa namatthu, brāhmaṇassa vusīmato;

Kassapassa ca namatthu, vippamuttassa sabbadhi.

“Homage to Koṇāgamana, the brahmin who has lived the holy life; Homage to Kassapa, who is liberated in every way.

‘Aṅgīrasassa namatthu, sakyaputtassa sirīmato;

Yo imaṃ dhammaṃ desesi, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ.

“Homage to Aṅgīrasa, the glorious Sakyan son; Who taught this Dhamma, which removes all suffering.

‘Ye cāpi nibbutā loke, yathābhūtaṃ vipassisuṃ;

Te janā apisuṇātha, mahantā vītasāradā.

“And those who are extinguished in the world, who saw things as they truly are—those people are not slanderous, they are great, free from fear.

‘Hitaṃ devamanussānaṃ, yaṃ namassanti gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

“They pay homage to Gotama, who is for the welfare of gods and humans, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the great one, free from fear.

288. ‘Yato [V 3.0158] uggacchati sūriyo, ādicco maṇḍalī mahā.

288. “Whence the sun rises, the son of Aditi, with its great orb.

Yassa cuggacchamānassa, saṃvarīpi nirujjhati;

Yassa cuggate sūriye, “divaso”ti pavuccati.

“And as it is rising, the night ceases; and when the sun has risen, it is called ‘day’.

‘Rahadopi [M 3.0168] tattha gambhīro, samuddo saritodako;

Evaṃ taṃ tattha jānanti, “samuddo saritodako”.

“There, a deep lake is an ocean with flowing water; thus they know it there: ‘an ocean with flowing water’.

‘Ito “sā purimā disā”, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

“‘From here, that is the eastern direction,’ thus do people call it; the direction which that glorious great king protects.

‘Gandhabbānaṃ adhipati, “dhataraṭṭho”ti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, gandhabbehi purakkhato.

The lord of the gandhabbas, Dhataraṭṭha by name; he delights in dance and song, surrounded by gandhabbas.

‘Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

He has many sons, all of one name, so I have heard; ninety-one, named Inda, of great strength.

‘Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they, seeing the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun, pay homage from afar to the great one, free from fear.

‘Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tassā evaṃ vademase.

‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man; you look upon all with skill. Even non-humans pay homage to you. This we have heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.

“Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ”.

‘Pay homage to the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We pay homage to the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, accomplished in knowledge and conduct.’

289. ‘Yena petā pavuccanti, pisuṇā piṭṭhimaṃsikā.

289. The direction to which are banished the departed, slanderers, and backbiters,

Pāṇātipātino luddā, corā nekatikā janā.

destroyers of life, the cruel, thieves, and deceitful people.

‘Ito [V 3.0159] “sā dakkhiṇā disā”, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

From here, people declare, ‘That is the southern direction,’ the direction which that glorious great king governs.

‘Kumbhaṇḍānaṃ adhipati, “virūḷho” iti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, kumbhaṇḍehi purakkhato.

Lord of the Kumbhaṇḍas, Virūḷha by name; he delights in dance and song, surrounded by Kumbhaṇḍas.

‘Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

He has many sons, I have heard, all of one name; ninety-one, mighty ones named Inda.

‘Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they, seeing the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, pay homage from afar to him, the great one, free from fear.

‘Namo [M 3.0169] te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man; you contemplate with skill, and even non-humans revere you. This we have heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.

“Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ”.

‘Worship the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We worship the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We worship the Buddha Gotama, endowed with knowledge and conduct.’

290. ‘Yattha coggacchati sūriyo, ādicco maṇḍalī mahā.

290. The direction where the sun, the great radiant orb, sets.

Yassa coggacchamānassa, divasopi nirujjhati;

Yassa coggate sūriye, “saṃvarī”ti pavuccati.

And when it is setting, the day ceases; and when the sun has set, it is called ‘night’.

‘Rahadopi tattha gambhīro, samuddo saritodako;

Evaṃ taṃ tattha jānanti, samuddo saritodako.

There is a deep lake there, an ocean fed by rivers; thus they know it there: ‘an ocean fed by rivers’.

‘Ito “sā pacchimā disā”, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

From here, people declare, ‘That is the western direction,’ the direction which that glorious great king protects.

‘Nāgānañca [V 3.0160] adhipati, “virūpakkho”ti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, nāgeheva purakkhato.

Lord of the Nāgas, Virūpakkha by name; he delights in dance and song, surrounded by Nāgas.

‘Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.
