He has many sons, I have heard, all of one name; ninety-one, of great strength, named Inda.

‘Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they, seeing the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, pay homage from afar to the great one, who is free from fear.

‘Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

‘Homage to you, O thoroughbred of men, homage to you, O supreme man. You see with wisdom. Even non-humans pay homage to you. This we have heard repeatedly, therefore we speak thus.

“Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ”.

‘Pay homage to the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We pay homage to the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We pay homage to the Buddha Gotama, endowed with knowledge and conduct.’

291. ‘Yena uttarakuruvho, mahāneru sudassano.

291. The direction wherein lies Uttarakuru, and the beautiful Great Neru.

Manussā tattha jāyanti, amamā apariggahā.

Humans are born there, without possessiveness, without possessions.

‘Na [M 3.0170] te bījaṃ pavapanti, nāpi nīyanti naṅgalā;

Akaṭṭhapākimaṃ sāliṃ, paribhuñjanti mānusā.

They do not sow seed, nor are ploughs led forth; humans there enjoy rice that ripens without cultivation.

‘Akaṇaṃ athusaṃ suddhaṃ, sugandhaṃ taṇḍulapphalaṃ;

Tuṇḍikīre pacitvāna, tato bhuñjanti bhojanaṃ.

Without broken grains, without husk, pure, and fragrant is the rice-grain fruit; having cooked it in a pot, they then eat their meal.

‘Gāviṃ ekakhuraṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ;

Pasuṃ ekakhuraṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

Making a cow into a mount like a horse, they travel to every direction; making a beast into a mount like a horse, they travel to every direction.

‘Itthiṃ vā vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ;

Purisaṃ vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

Making a woman a vehicle, they travel to every direction; making a man a vehicle, they travel to every direction.

‘Kumāriṃ [V 3.0161] vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ;

Kumāraṃ vāhanaṃ katvā, anuyanti disodisaṃ.

Making a maiden a vehicle, they travel to every direction; making a youth a vehicle, they travel to every direction.

‘Te yāne abhiruhitvā,

Sabbā disā anupariyāyanti;

Pacārā tassa rājino.

The attendants of that king, having mounted those vehicles, travel around to all directions.

‘Hatthiyānaṃ assayānaṃ,

Dibbaṃ yānaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ;

Pāsādā sivikā ceva,

Mahārājassa yasassino.

Elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, and divine vehicles are at hand; palaces and palanquins as well, for the glorious great king.

‘Tassa ca nagarā ahu,

Antalikkhe sumāpitā;

Āṭānāṭā kusināṭā parakusināṭā,

Nāṭasuriyā parakusiṭanāṭā.

And for him there were cities, well-fashioned in the sky: Āṭānāṭā, Kusināṭā, Parakusināṭā, Nāṭasuriyā, and Parakusiṭanāṭā.

‘Uttarena kasivanto,

Janoghamaparena ca;

Navanavutiyo ambaraambaravatiyo,

Āḷakamandā nāma rājadhānī.

To the north is Kasivanta, and to the west, Janogha; also Navanavutiyo, Ambara-ambaravatiyo, and the royal capital named Āḷakamandā.

‘Kuverassa kho pana, mārisa, mahārājassa visāṇā nāma rājadhānī;

Tasmā kuvero mahārājā, “vessavaṇo”ti pavuccati.

Indeed, good sir, for the great king Kuvera, the royal capital is named Visāṇā. Therefore, the great king Kuvera is called Vessavaṇa.

‘Paccesanto [M 3.0171] pakāsenti, tatolā tattalā tatotalā;

Ojasi tejasi tatojasī, sūro rājā ariṭṭho nemi.

His intelligence-gatherers who report are renowned: Tatolā, Tattalā, Tatotalā, Ojasī, Tejasī, Tatojasī, Sūro, Rājā, Ariṭṭho, and Nemi.

‘Rahadopi tattha dharaṇī nāma, yato meghā pavassanti;

Vassā yato patāyanti, sabhāpi tattha sālavatī nāma.

There is also a lake there named Dharaṇī, from which the clouds rain, and from which the waters spread forth. There is also a hall there named Sālavatī.

‘Yattha [V 3.0162] yakkhā payirupāsanti, tattha niccaphalā rukkhā;

Nānā dijagaṇā yutā, mayūrakoñcābhirudā;

Kokilādīhi vagguhi.

Where yakkhas assemble, there are trees ever-fruitful, filled with flocks of various birds, resounding with peacocks and herons, and with the pleasant voices of cuckoos and others.

‘Jīvañjīvakasaddettha, atho oṭṭhavacittakā;

Kukkuṭakā kuḷīrakā, vane pokkharasātakā.

Here is the sound of Jīvajīvaka birds, and also Oṭṭhavacittaka birds; there are wild fowl and crabs, and in the forest, Pokkharasātaka birds.

‘Sukasāḷika saddettha, daṇḍamāṇavakāni ca;

Sobhati sabbakālaṃ sā, kuveranaḷinī sadā.

Here are the calls of parrots and mynas, and also the Daṇḍamāṇavaka birds. That lotus-lake of Kuvera is always beautiful at all times.

‘Ito “sā uttarā disā”, iti naṃ ācikkhatī jano;

Yaṃ disaṃ abhipāleti, mahārājā yasassi so.

From here, people declare, ‘That is the northern direction,’ the direction which that glorious great king protects.

‘Yakkhānañca adhipati, “kuvero” iti nāmaso;

Ramatī naccagītehi, yakkheheva purakkhato.

The lord of the yakkhas, Kuvera by name, delights in dance and song, attended only by yakkhas.

‘Puttāpi tassa bahavo, ekanāmāti me sutaṃ;

Asīti dasa eko ca, indanāmā mahabbalā.

He has many sons, so I have heard, all of one name. They are eighty, ten, and one—named Inda, of great strength.

‘Te cāpi buddhaṃ disvāna, buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunaṃ;

Dūratova namassanti, mahantaṃ vītasāradaṃ.

And they, seeing the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, pay homage from afar to the great one who is free from fear.

‘Namo te purisājañña, namo te purisuttama;

Kusalena samekkhasi, amanussāpi taṃ vandanti;

Sutaṃ netaṃ abhiṇhaso, tasmā evaṃ vademase.

Homage to you, O noble man, homage to you, supreme among men! You contemplate with skill; even non-humans revere you. This we have repeatedly heard, therefore, thus we speak.

“Jinaṃ vandatha gotamaṃ, jinaṃ vandāma gotamaṃ;

Vijjācaraṇasampannaṃ, buddhaṃ vandāma gotama”nti.

‘Revere the Victor, Gotama.’ ‘We revere the Victor, Gotama. Endowed with knowledge and conduct, we revere the Buddha, Gotama.’”

292. ‘Ayaṃ kho sā, mārisa[T 3.0221], āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ [V 3.0163] upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāya. Yassa kassaci, mārisa, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā upāsakassa vā upāsikāya [M 3.0172] vā ayaṃ āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā suggahitā bhavissati samattā pariyāputā taṃ ce amanusso yakkho vā yakkhinī vā…pe… gandhabbo vā gandhabbī vā…pe… kumbhaṇḍo vā kumbhaṇḍī vā…pe… nāgo vā nāgī vā nāgapotako vā nāgapotikā vā nāgamahāmatto vā nāgapārisajjo vā nāgapacāro vā, paduṭṭhacitto bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā upāsakaṃ vā upāsikaṃ vā gacchantaṃ vā anugaccheyya, ṭhitaṃ vā upatiṭṭheyya, nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya, nipannaṃ vā upanipajjeyya. Na me so, mārisa, amanusso labheyya gāmesu vā nigamesu vā sakkāraṃ vā garukāraṃ vā. Na me so, mārisa, amanusso labheyya āḷakamandāya nāma rājadhāniyā vatthuṃ vā vāsaṃ vā. Na me so, mārisa, amanusso labheyya yakkhānaṃ samitiṃ gantuṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā anāvayhampi naṃ kareyyuṃ avivayhaṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā attāhi paripuṇṇāhi paribhāsāhi paribhāseyyuṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā rittaṃpissa pattaṃ sīse nikkujjeyyuṃ. Apissu naṃ, mārisa, amanussā sattadhāpissa muddhaṃ phāleyyuṃ. Santi hi, mārisa, amanussā caṇḍā ruddhā rabhasā, te neva mahārājānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti. Te kho te, mārisa, amanussā mahārājānaṃ avaruddhā nāma vuccanti. Seyyathāpi, mārisa, rañño māgadhassa vijite mahācorā. Te neva rañño māgadhassa ādiyanti, na rañño māgadhassa purisakānaṃ ādiyanti, na rañño māgadhassa purisakānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti. Te kho te, mārisa, mahācorā rañño māgadhassa avaruddhā nāma vuccanti. Evameva kho, mārisa, santi amanussā caṇḍā ruddhā rabhasā, te neva mahārājānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti, na mahārājānaṃ purisakānaṃ purisakānaṃ ādiyanti. Te kho te, mārisa, amanussā mahārājānaṃ avaruddhā nāma vuccanti. Yo hi koci, mārisa, amanusso yakkho vā yakkhinī vā…pe… gandhabbo vā gandhabbī vā…pe… kumbhaṇḍo vā kumbhaṇḍī vā…pe… nāgo vā nāgī vā…pe… paduṭṭhacitto bhikkhuṃ vā bhikkhuniṃ vā upāsakaṃ vā upāsikaṃ vā gacchantaṃ vā upagaccheyya, ṭhitaṃ vā upatiṭṭheyya, nisinnaṃ vā upanisīdeyya, nipannaṃ vā upanipajjeyya. Imesaṃ yakkhānaṃ mahāyakkhānaṃ senāpatīnaṃ mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikkanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ – ‘ayaṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ yakkho āvisati, ayaṃ yakkho [M 3.0173] heṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho viheṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho hiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho vihiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho na muñcatī’ti.

292. This, dear sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Whoever, dear sir—whether monk, nun, layman, or laywoman—has properly grasped, mastered, and learned this Āṭānāṭiya protection, if any non-human being—a male yakkha or female yakkhinī... a male gandhabba or female gandhabbī... a male kumbhaṇḍa or female kumbhaṇḍī... a male nāga or female nāgī, a young nāga male or female, a nāga minister, a nāga attendant, or a nāga follower—with a malevolent mind should follow a monk, nun, layman, or laywoman who is walking, or stand near one who is standing, or sit near one who is sitting, or lie near one who is lying down—then, dear sir, that non-human being will not receive honor or respect in villages or towns. That non-human being, dear sir, will not find a place to dwell or reside in the royal city named Āḷakamandā. That non-human being, dear sir, will not be allowed to attend the assemblies of yakkhas. Moreover, dear sir, the non-human beings would make them unfit for marriage. Moreover, dear sir, the non-human beings will rebuke them with full reproaches. Moreover, dear sir, the non-human beings will overturn an empty bowl upon their head. Moreover, dear sir, the non-human beings will split their head into seven pieces. For there are, dear sir, fierce, harsh, and violent non-human beings who pay no heed to the great kings, nor to the officers of the great kings, nor to the officers of their officers. These, dear sir, are called the rebels against the great kings. Just as, dear sir, in the realm of the Magadhan king, there are great bandits who pay no heed to the king, nor to the officers of the Magadhan king, nor to the officers of their officers. These, dear sir, are called the rebels against the Magadhan king. In the same way, dear sir, there are fierce, harsh, and violent non-human beings who pay no heed to the great kings, nor to the officers of the great kings, nor to the officers of their officers. These, dear sir, are called the rebels against the great kings. If any non-human being—whether a male yakkha or female yakkhinī... a male gandhabba or female gandhabbī... a male kumbhaṇḍa or female kumbhaṇḍī... a male nāga or female nāgī...—with a malevolent mind should approach a monk, nun, layman, or laywoman who is walking, or stand near one who is standing, or sit near one who is sitting, or lie near one who is lying down—they must be reported to, cried out to, and proclaimed to these yakkhas, great yakkhas, commanders, and great commanders: ‘This yakkha seizes, this yakkha possesses, this yakkha harasses, this yakkha torments, this yakkha harms, this yakkha injures, this yakkha does not release!’

293. ‘Katamesaṃ [V 3.0164] yakkhānaṃ mahāyakkhānaṃ senāpatīnaṃ mahāsenāpatīnaṃ?

293. To which yakkhas, great yakkhas, commanders, and great commanders?

‘Indo somo varuṇo ca, bhāradvājo pajāpati;

Candano kāmaseṭṭho ca, kinnughaṇḍu nighaṇḍu ca.

Inda, Soma, and Varuṇa, Bhāradvāja and Pajāpati; Candana and Kāmaseṭṭha, Kinnughaṇḍu and Nighaṇḍu.

‘Panādo opamañño ca, devasūto ca mātali;

Cittaseno ca gandhabbo, naḷo rājā janesabho.

Panāda and Opamañña, Mātali the messenger of the devas; Cittasena the gandhabba, King Naḷa, and Janesabha.

‘Sātāgiro hevamato, puṇṇako karatiyo guḷo;

Sivako mucalindo ca, vessāmitto yugandharo.

Sātāgira, Hemavata, Puṇṇaka, Karatiya, Guḷa; Sivaka and Mucalinda, Vessāmitta and Yugandhara.

‘Gopālo supparodho ca, hiri netti ca mandiyo;

Pañcālacaṇḍo āḷavako, pajjunno sumano sumukho;

Dadhimukho maṇi māṇivaro dīgho, atho serīsako saha.

Gopāla and Supparodha, Hiri, Netti, and Mandiya; Pañcālacaṇḍa, Āḷavaka, Pajjunna, Sumana, Sumukha; Dadhimukha, Maṇi, Māṇivara, and Dīgha; and also Serīsaka with them.

‘Imesaṃ yakkhānaṃ mahāyakkhānaṃ senāpatīnaṃ mahāsenāpatīnaṃ ujjhāpetabbaṃ vikkanditabbaṃ viravitabbaṃ – “ayaṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ yakkho āvisati, ayaṃ yakkho heṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho viheṭheti, ayaṃ yakkho hiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho vihiṃsati, ayaṃ yakkho na muñcatī”ti. Ayaṃ kho, mārisa, āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāya. Handa ca dāni mayaṃ, mārisa, gacchāma, bahukiccā mayaṃ bahukaraṇīyā’”ti. “‘Yassa dāni tumhe mahārājāno kālaṃ maññathā’”ti.

To these yakkhas, great yakkhas, commanders, and great commanders, it must be reported, cried out, and proclaimed: ‘This yakkha seizes, this yakkha possesses, this yakkha harasses, this yakkha greatly harasses, this yakkha harms, this yakkha greatly harms, this yakkha does not release!’ This, dear sir, is the Āṭānāṭiya protection for the guarding, protection, non-harming, and comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. And now, dear sir, we shall go; we have many duties, much to do.’ ‘Now, great kings, you may do as you think it is time for.’”

294. “Atha kho, bhikkhave, cattāro mahārājā uṭṭhāyāsanā maṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Tepi kho, bhikkhave, yakkhā uṭṭhāyāsanā appekacce maṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce mayā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu, sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce yenāhaṃ tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce nāmagottaṃ [M 3.0174] sāvetvā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu. Appekacce tuṇhībhūtā tatthevantaradhāyiṃsu.

294. Then, monks, the Four Great Kings rose from their seats, paid homage to me, circumambulated me respectfully, and vanished right there. Those yakkhas too, monks, rose from their seats: some paid homage to me, circumambulated me respectfully, and vanished right there; some exchanged joyful greetings with me, and having concluded the pleasant and memorable conversation, vanished right there; some raised their joined palms toward me and vanished right there; some announced their name and clan and vanished right there; and some, having become silent, vanished right there.

295. “Uggaṇhātha[V 3.0165], bhikkhave, āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ. Pariyāpuṇātha, bhikkhave, āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ. Dhāretha, bhikkhave, āṭānāṭiyaṃ rakkhaṃ. Atthasaṃhitā atthasaṃhitāyaṃ (syā.), bhikkhave, āṭānāṭiyā rakkhā bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ guttiyā rakkhāya avihiṃsāya phāsuvihārāyā”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā. Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

295. “Take up, monks, the Āṭānāṭiya protection. Master, monks, the Āṭānāṭiya protection. Bear in mind, monks, the Āṭānāṭiya protection. The Āṭānāṭiya protection, monks, is connected with welfare; it is for the security, for the protection, for the non-harming, and for the comfortable dwelling of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.” This the Blessed One said. Delighted, those monks rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.

Āṭānāṭiyasuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ navamaṃ.

The Āṭānāṭiya Sutta, the ninth, is concluded.

10. Saṅgītisuttaṃ

10. The Saṅgīti Sutta

296. Evaṃ [P 3.0207][M 3.0175][V 3.0166][T 3.0222] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā mallesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi yena pāvā nāma mallānaṃ nagaraṃ tadavasari. Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā pāvāyaṃ viharati cundassa kammāraputtassa ambavane.

296. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a great Saṅgha of monks, with five hundred monks, arrived at the city of the Mallas named Pāvā. There the Blessed One was dwelling in Pāvā, in the mango grove of Cunda the smith's son.

Ubbhatakanavasandhāgāraṃ

The New Assembly Hall named Ubbhataka

297. Tena kho pana samayena pāveyyakānaṃ mallānaṃ ubbhatakaṃ nāma navaṃ sandhāgāraṃ santhāgāraṃ (sī. pī.), saṇṭhāgāraṃ (syā. kaṃ.) acirakāritaṃ hoti anajjhāvuṭṭhaṃ anajjhāvutthaṃ (sī. syā. pī. ka.) samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtena. Assosuṃ kho pāveyyakā mallā – “bhagavā kira mallesu cārikaṃ caramāno mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi pāvaṃ anuppatto pāvāyaṃ viharati cundassa kammāraputtassa ambavane”ti. Atha kho pāveyyakā mallā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho pāveyyakā mallā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “idha, bhante, pāveyyakānaṃ mallānaṃ ubbhatakaṃ nāma navaṃ sandhāgāraṃ acirakāritaṃ hoti anajjhāvuṭṭhaṃ samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtena. Tañca [P 3.0208] kho, bhante, bhagavā paṭhamaṃ paribhuñjatu, bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ paribhuttaṃ pacchā pāveyyakā mallā paribhuñjissanti. Tadassa pāveyyakānaṃ mallānaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi kho bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

297. At that time, the Mallas of Pāvā had a new, recently built assembly hall named Ubbhataka, which had not yet been dwelt in by any recluse, brahmin, or any human being. The Mallas of Pāvā heard: “The Blessed One, it is said, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a great Saṅgha of monks, with five hundred monks, has arrived at Pāvā and is dwelling in the mango grove of Cunda the smith's son.” Then the Mallas of Pāvā approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Mallas of Pāvā said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, there is here a new, recently built assembly hall of the Mallas of Pāvā named Ubbhataka, which has not yet been dwelt in by any recluse, brahmin, or any human being. May the Blessed One, Venerable Sir, be the first to use it. After it has been used by the Blessed One, the Mallas of Pāvā will use it afterwards. That will be for the long-term welfare and happiness of the Mallas of Pāvā.” The Blessed One consented by means of silence.

298. Atha kho pāveyyakā mallā [T 3.0223] bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena sandhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā sabbasanthariṃ sabbasanthariṃ santhataṃ (ka.) sandhāgāraṃ santharitvā bhagavato āsanāni paññāpetvā udakamaṇikaṃ patiṭṭhapetvā telapadīpaṃ āropetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ [V 3.0167] aṭṭhaṃsu. Ekamantaṃ ṭhitā kho te pāveyyakā mallā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “sabbasantharisanthataṃ sabbasanthariṃ santhataṃ (sī. pī. ka.), bhante, sandhāgāraṃ, bhagavato āsanāni [M 3.0176] paññattāni, udakamaṇiko patiṭṭhāpito, telapadīpo āropito. Yassadāni, bhante, bhagavā kālaṃ maññatī”ti.

298. Then the Mallas of Pāvā, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and approached the assembly hall. Having approached, they spread the assembly hall completely with coverings, prepared seats for the Blessed One, set up a water pot, and placed an oil lamp. Then they approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, those Mallas of Pāvā said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, the assembly hall is completely spread with coverings, seats for the Blessed One have been prepared, a water pot has been set up, and an oil lamp has been placed. Now, Venerable Sir, it is for the Blessed One to do as he deems fit.”

299. Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena sandhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā pāde pakkhāletvā sandhāgāraṃ pavisitvā majjhimaṃ thambhaṃ nissāya puratthābhimukho nisīdi. Bhikkhusaṅghopi kho pāde pakkhāletvā sandhāgāraṃ pavisitvā pacchimaṃ bhittiṃ nissāya puratthābhimukho [P 3.0209] nisīdi bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvā. Pāveyyakāpi kho mallā pāde pakkhāletvā sandhāgāraṃ pavisitvā puratthimaṃ bhittiṃ nissāya pacchimābhimukhā nisīdiṃsu bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvā. Atha kho bhagavā pāveyyake malle bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṃsetvā uyyojesi – “abhikkantā kho, vāseṭṭhā, ratti. Yassadāni tumhe kālaṃ maññathā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho pāveyyakā mallā bhagavato paṭissutvā [T 3.0224] uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu.

299. Then the Blessed One, having put on his lower robe and taken his bowl and outer robe, approached the assembly hall together with the Saṅgha of monks. Having approached, he washed his feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down facing east, leaning against the central pillar. The Saṅgha of monks also washed their feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down facing east, leaning against the western wall, with the Blessed One before them. The Mallas of Pāvā also washed their feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down facing west, leaning against the eastern wall, with the Blessed One before them. Then the Blessed One, for a great part of the night, instructed, established, roused, and gladdened the Mallas of Pāvā with a talk on the Dhamma, and then dismissed them, saying: “Vāseṭṭhas, the night is far advanced. Now is the time for that which you deem fit.” “So be it, Venerable Sir,” the Mallas of Pāvā replied to the Blessed One, and rising from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and departed.

300. Atha kho bhagavā acirapakkantesu pāveyyakesu mallesu tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ bhikkhusaṃghaṃ anuviloketvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi – “vigatathinamiddho vigatathīnamiddho (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) kho, sāriputta, bhikkhusaṅgho. Paṭibhātu taṃ, sāriputta, bhikkhūnaṃ dhammīkathā. Piṭṭhi me āgilāyati. Tamahaṃ āyamissāmī”ti āyameyyāmīti (syā. kaṃ.). “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā sāriputto bhagavato paccassosi. Atha kho bhagavā catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi pāde pādaṃ accādhāya, sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā.

300. Then, not long after the Mallas of Pāvā had departed, the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent Saṅgha of monks, addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: “Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of monks is free from sloth and torpor. Let a talk on the Dhamma occur to you, Sāriputta, for the monks. My back is tired; I shall stretch it.” “So be it, Venerable Sir,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having folded his outer robe in four, lay down on his right side in the lion's posture, placing one foot slightly over the other, mindful and fully aware, establishing in his mind the perception of rising.

Bhinnanigaṇṭhavatthu

The Story of the Schism of the Nigaṇṭhas

301. Tena kho pana samayena nigaṇṭho nāṭaputto pāvāyaṃ [P 3.0210] adhunākālaṅkato hoti. Tassa kālaṅkiriyāya bhinnā nigaṇṭhā dvedhikajātā ddheḷhakajātā (syā. kaṃ.) bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ [M 3.0177] mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharanti vicaranti (syā. kaṃ.) – “na tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāsi, ahaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānāmi, kiṃ tvaṃ imaṃ dhammavinayaṃ ājānissasi! Micchāpaṭipanno tvamasi, ahamasmi sammāpaṭipanno. Sahitaṃ me, asahitaṃ te. Purevacanīyaṃ pacchā avaca, pacchāvacanīyaṃ pure avaca. Adhiciṇṇaṃ te viparāvattaṃ, āropito te vādo, niggahito tvamasi, cara vādappamokkhāya, nibbeṭhehi vā sace pahosī”ti. Vadhoyeva kho maññe nigaṇṭhesu [V 3.0168] nāṭaputtiyesu vattati. Yepi yepi te (sī. pī.) nigaṇṭhassa nāṭaputtassa sāvakā gihī odātavasanā[T 3.0225], tepi nigaṇṭhesu nāṭaputtiyesu nibbinnarūpā virattarūpā paṭivānarūpā, yathā taṃ durakkhāte dhammavinaye duppavedite aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite bhinnathūpe appaṭisaraṇe.

301. Now at that time, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta had recently passed away at Pāvā. Due to his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas became divided, forming two factions, becoming quarrelsome, contentious, and falling into dispute, and they dwelt piercing one another with verbal spears: ‘You do not know this Dhamma and Vinaya; I know this Dhamma and Vinaya. How could you know this Dhamma and Vinaya? You are one of wrong practice; I am one of right practice. My words are coherent; yours are incoherent. What should have been said before, you said after; what should have been said after, you said before. Your long-practiced view is overturned. Your doctrine is censured. You are defeated. Go, practice for release from this argument, or disentangle it if you can!’ It seems that only slaughter prevailed among the Nigaṇṭhas, the followers of Nāṭaputta. Even those lay disciples of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta who wear white clothes were disgusted with, disaffected from, and reproachful of the Nigaṇṭhas, followers of Nāṭaputta, just as one would be towards a Dhamma and Vinaya that is badly proclaimed, badly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, not declared by a Perfectly Enlightened One, with a shattered stūpa and without a refuge.

302. Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi – “nigaṇṭho, āvuso, nāṭaputto pāvāyaṃ adhunākālaṅkato, tassa kālaṅkiriyāya bhinnā nigaṇṭhā dvedhikajātā…pe… bhinnathūpe appaṭisaraṇe”. “Evañhetaṃ, āvuso, hoti durakkhāte dhammavinaye duppavedite aniyyānike anupasamasaṃvattanike asammāsambuddhappavedite. Ayaṃ [P 3.0211] kho panāvuso amhākaṃ asmākaṃ (pī.) bhagavatā bhagavato (ka. sī.) dhammo svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

302. Then the venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: ‘Friends, the Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta has recently passed away at Pāvā. Due to his passing, the Nigaṇṭhas have become divided, forming two factions… with a shattered stūpa and without a refuge.’ ‘So it is, friends, in a Dhamma and Vinaya that is badly proclaimed, badly expounded, not leading out, not conducive to peace, and not declared by a Perfectly Enlightened One. But this Dhamma of ours, friends, has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One, well-expounded, leading out, conducive to peace, and declared by a Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant in unison, without disputing, so that this holy life might be long-lasting and endure for a long time. That would be for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans.’

“Katamo cāvuso, amhākaṃ bhagavatā bhagavato (ka. sī.) dhammo svākkhāto suppavedito niyyāniko upasamasaṃvattaniko sammāsambuddhappavedito; yattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ?

‘And which, friends, is the Dhamma well-proclaimed by our Blessed One, well-expounded, leading out, conducive to peace, and declared by a Perfectly Enlightened One, wherein all should chant in unison, without disputing, so that this holy life might be long-lasting and endure for a long time, for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans?

Ekakaṃ

The Ones

303. “Atthi [M 3.0178] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena eko dhammo sammadakkhāto. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ[T 3.0226], tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katamo eko dhammo? Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Sabbe sattā saṅkhāraṭṭhitikā. Ayaṃ kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena eko dhammo sammadakkhāto. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ[P 3.0212], yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

303. Friends, there is one Dhamma well-proclaimed by that Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together and not dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and endure for a long time. That would be for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans. What is that one Dhamma? All beings are sustained by nutriment; all beings are sustained by formations. This, friends, is that one Dhamma well-proclaimed by that Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together and not dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and endure for a long time. That would be for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans.

Dukaṃ

The Pairs

304. “Atthi [V 3.0169] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dve dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame dve dve dhammo (syā. kaṃ.) evamuparipi?

304. Friends, there are two Dhammas well-proclaimed by that Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together and not dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and endure for a long time. That would be for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans. What are the two?

“Nāmañca rūpañca.

Name and form.

“Avijjā ca bhavataṇhā ca.

Ignorance and craving for existence.

“Bhavadiṭṭhi ca vibhavadiṭṭhi ca.

The view of eternalism and the view of annihilationism.

“Ahirikañca ahirīkañca (katthaci) anottappañca.

Lack of moral shame and lack of moral dread.

“Hirī ca ottappañca.

Moral shame and moral dread.

“Dovacassatā ca pāpamittatā ca.

Being difficult to admonish and having bad friends.

“Sovacassatā ca kalyāṇamittatā ca.

Being easy to admonish and having good friends.

“Āpattikusalatā ca āpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā ca.

Skill in what constitutes an offense and skill in rehabilitation from an offense.

“Samāpattikusalatā ca samāpattivuṭṭhānakusalatā ca.

Skill in meditative attainments and skill in emerging from meditative attainments.

“Dhātukusalatā [M 3.0179] ca manasikārakusalatā ca.

Skill in the elements and skill in attention.

“Āyatanakusalatā ca paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā ca.

Skill in the sense bases and skill in dependent origination.

“Ṭhānakusalatā ca aṭṭhānakusalatā ca.

Skill in what is possible and skill in what is impossible.

“Ajjavañca [P 3.0213][V 3.0170] lajjavañca.

Uprightness and modesty.

“Khanti ca soraccañca.

Patience and delight in goodness.

“Sākhalyañca paṭisanthāro ca.

Gentle courtesy and hospitality.

“Avihiṃsā ca soceyyañca.

Non-harming and purity.

“Muṭṭhassaccañca asampajaññañca.

Lapsed mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension.

“Sati ca sampajaññañca[T 3.0227].

Mindfulness and clear comprehension.

“Indriyesu aguttadvāratā ca bhojane amattaññutā ca.

Having unguarded sense faculties and lack of moderation in eating.

“Indriyesu guttadvāratā ca bhojane mattaññutā ca.

Guarding the sense faculties and moderation in eating.

“Paṭisaṅkhānabalañca paṭisandhānabalañca (syā.) bhāvanābalañca.

The power of reflection and the power of development.

“Satibalañca samādhibalañca.

The power of mindfulness and the power of concentration.

“Samatho ca vipassanā ca.

Tranquility and insight.

“Samathanimittañca paggahanimittañca.

The sign of tranquility and the sign of exertion.

“Paggaho ca avikkhepo ca.

Exertion and non-distraction.

“Sīlavipatti ca diṭṭhivipatti ca.

Corruption of virtue and corruption of view.

“Sīlasampadā ca diṭṭhisampadā ca.

Accomplishment in virtue and accomplishment in view.

“Sīlavisuddhi [V 3.0171][P 3.0214] ca diṭṭhivisuddhi ca.

Purification of virtue and purification of view.

“Diṭṭhivisuddhi kho pana yathā diṭṭhissa ca padhānaṃ.

Purification of view, and the striving of one who has seen thus.

“Saṃvego ca saṃvejanīyesu ṭhānesu saṃviggassa ca yoniso padhānaṃ.

A sense of urgency regarding grounds for urgency, and the wise striving of one who is stirred.

“Asantuṭṭhitā ca kusalesu dhammesu appaṭivānitā ca padhānasmiṃ.

Non-contentment with wholesome qualities and unremittingness in striving.

“Vijjā [M 3.0180] ca vimutti ca.

True knowledge and liberation.

“Khayeñāṇaṃ anuppādeñāṇaṃ.

Knowledge of destruction and knowledge of non-arising.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dve dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

Friends, these two dhammas have been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, all should chant together in unison, without dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and endure for a long time. This would be for the welfare and happiness of the multitude, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.

Tikaṃ

The Triads

305. “Atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena tayo dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame tayo?

305. Friends, there are three dhammas that have been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, all should chant together in unison... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. What are the three?

“Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho akusalamūlaṃ, doso akusalamūlaṃ, moho akusalamūlaṃ.

Three unwholesome roots: greed is an unwholesome root, hatred is an unwholesome root, and delusion is an unwholesome root.

“Tīṇi kusalamūlāni – alobho kusalamūlaṃ, adoso kusalamūlaṃ, amoho kusalamūlaṃ.

Three wholesome roots: non-greed is a wholesome root, non-hatred is a wholesome root, and non-delusion is a wholesome root.

“Tīṇi duccaritāni – kāyaduccaritaṃ, vacīduccaritaṃ, manoduccaritaṃ.

Three kinds of misconduct: bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct.

“Tīṇi [V 3.0172][P 3.0215] sucaritāni – kāyasucaritaṃ, vacīsucaritaṃ[T 3.0228], manosucaritaṃ.

Three kinds of good conduct: bodily good conduct, verbal good conduct, and mental good conduct.

“Tayo akusalavitakkā – kāmavitakko, byāpādavitakko, vihiṃsāvitakko.

Three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, thought of ill will, and thought of harming.

“Tayo kusalavitakkā – nekkhammavitakko, abyāpādavitakko, avihiṃsāvitakko.

Three wholesome thoughts: thought of renunciation, thought of non-ill will, and thought of non-harming.

“Tayo akusalasaṅkappā – kāmasaṅkappo, byāpādasaṅkappo, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo.

Three unwholesome intentions: sensual intention, intention of ill will, and intention of harming.

“Tayo kusalasaṅkappā – nekkhammasaṅkappo, abyāpādasaṅkappo, avihiṃsāsaṅkappo.

Three wholesome intentions: intention of renunciation, intention of non-ill will, and intention of non-harming.

“Tisso [M 3.0181] akusalasaññā – kāmasaññā, byāpādasaññā, vihiṃsāsaññā.

Three unwholesome perceptions: sensual perception, perception of ill will, and perception of harming.

“Tisso kusalasaññā – nekkhammasaññā, abyāpādasaññā, avihiṃsāsaññā.

Three wholesome perceptions: perception of renunciation, perception of non-ill will, and perception of non-harming.

“Tisso akusaladhātuyo – kāmadhātu, byāpādadhātu, vihiṃsādhātu.

Three unwholesome elements: the element of sensuality, the element of ill will, and the element of harming.

“Tisso kusaladhātuyo – nekkhammadhātu, abyāpādadhātu, avihiṃsādhātu.

Three wholesome elements: the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, and the element of non-harming.

“Aparāpi tisso dhātuyo – kāmadhātu, rūpadhātu, arūpadhātu.

Three further elements: the sense-sphere element, the form-sphere element, and the formless-sphere element.

“Aparāpi tisso dhātuyo – rūpadhātu, arūpadhātu, nirodhadhātu.

Three further elements: the form-sphere element, the formless-sphere element, and the element of cessation.

“Aparāpi tisso dhātuyo – hīnadhātu, majjhimadhātu, paṇītadhātu.

Three further elements: the inferior element, the middling element, and the sublime element.

“Tisso [P 3.0216] taṇhā – kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā.

Three cravings: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.

“Aparāpi tisso taṇhā – kāmataṇhā, rūpataṇhā, arūpataṇhā.

Three further cravings: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.

“Aparāpi tisso taṇhā – rūpataṇhā, arūpataṇhā, nirodhataṇhā.

Three further cravings: craving for form, craving for the formless, and craving for cessation.

“Tīṇi [V 3.0173] saṃyojanāni – sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāso.

Three fetters: identity view, doubt, and grasping at precepts and vows.

“Tayo āsavā – kāmāsavo, bhavāsavo, avijjāsavo.

Three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance.

“Tayo bhavā – kāmabhavo, rūpabhavo, arūpabhavo.

Three kinds of existence: sensual existence, form existence, and formless existence.

“Tisso esanā – kāmesanā, bhavesanā, brahmacariyesanā.

Three searches: the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for a holy life based on wrong view.

“Tisso vidhā – seyyohamasmīti vidhā, sadisohamasmīti vidhā, hīnohamasmīti vidhā.

Three kinds of conceit: the conceit ‘I am superior,’ the conceit ‘I am equal,’ and the conceit ‘I am inferior.’

“Tayo addhā – atīto addhā, anāgato addhā, paccuppanno [T 3.0229] addhā.

Three times: past time, future time, and present time.

“Tayo antā – sakkāyo anto, sakkāyasamudayo anto, sakkāyanirodho anto.

Three extremes: the existing body, the origin of the existing body, and the cessation of the existing body.

“Tisso vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā.

Three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

“Tisso dukkhatā – dukkhadukkhatā, saṅkhāradukkhatā, vipariṇāmadukkhatā.

Three kinds of suffering: suffering as pain, suffering due to formations, and suffering due to change.

“Tayo [P 3.0217] rāsī [M 3.0182] – micchattaniyato rāsi, sammattaniyato rāsi, aniyato rāsi.

Three groups: the group fixed in wrongness, the group fixed in rightness, and the unfixed group.

“Tayo tamā tisso kaṅkhā (bahūsu) aṭṭhakathā oloketabbā – atītaṃ vā addhānaṃ ārabbha kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, anāgataṃ vā addhānaṃ ārabbha kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, etarahi vā paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati.

Three kinds of doubt: with regard to the past, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident; with regard to the future, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident; with regard to the present, one doubts, is uncertain, is not resolved, and is not confident.

“Tīṇi tathāgatassa arakkheyyāni – parisuddhakāyasamācāro āvuso tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa kāyaduccaritaṃ, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya – ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti. Parisuddhavacīsamācāro āvuso, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa vacīduccaritaṃ, yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya – ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti. Parisuddhamanosamācāro, āvuso, tathāgato, natthi tathāgatassa manoduccaritaṃ yaṃ tathāgato rakkheyya – ‘mā me idaṃ paro aññāsī’ti.

Three things the Tathāgata has no need to guard: Friends, the Tathāgata is of purified bodily conduct; there is no bodily misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May no one else know this of me.’ Friends, the Tathāgata is of purified verbal conduct; there is no verbal misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May no one else know this of me.’ Friends, the Tathāgata is of purified mental conduct; there is no mental misconduct of the Tathāgata that he would need to guard, thinking, ‘May no one else know this of me.’

“Tayo [V 3.0174] kiñcanā – rāgo kiñcanaṃ, doso kiñcanaṃ, moho kiñcanaṃ.

Three impediments: greed, hatred, and delusion.

“Tayo aggī – rāgaggi, dosaggi, mohaggi.

Three fires: the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.

“Aparepi tayo aggī – āhuneyyaggi, gahapataggi, dakkhiṇeyyaggi.

Three further fires: the fire of those worthy of offerings, the fire of the householder, and the fire of those worthy of donations.

“Tividhena rūpasaṅgaho – sanidassanasappaṭighaṃ rūpaṃ sanidassanasappaṭigharūpaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) evamitaradvayepi, anidassanasappaṭighaṃ rūpaṃ, anidassanaappaṭighaṃ rūpaṃ.

A threefold classification of material form: visible and resistant material form, invisible and resistant material form, and invisible and non-resistant material form.

“Tayo saṅkhārā – puññābhisaṅkhāro, apuññābhisaṅkhāro[T 3.0230], āneñjābhisaṅkhāro.

Three volitional formations: meritorious volitional formation, demeritorious volitional formation, and imperturbable volitional formation.

“Tayo [P 3.0218] puggalā – sekkho puggalo, asekkho puggalo, nevasekkhonāsekkho puggalo.

Three kinds of persons: the person in training, the person beyond training, and the person who is neither in training nor beyond training.

“Tayo therā – jātithero, dhammathero, sammutithero sammatithero (syā. kaṃ.).

Three kinds of elders: an elder by birth, an elder by Dhamma, and an elder by convention.

“Tīṇi puññakiriyavatthūni – dānamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, sīlamayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu, bhāvanāmayaṃ puññakiriyavatthu.

Three grounds for meritorious action: the ground for meritorious action consisting of giving, the ground for meritorious action consisting of moral virtue, and the ground for meritorious action consisting of mental development.

“Tīṇi codanāvatthūni – diṭṭhena, sutena, parisaṅkāya.

Three grounds for admonition: based on what was seen, based on what was heard, and based on suspicion.

“Tisso [M 3.0183] kāmūpapattiyo kāmuppattiyo (sī.), kāmupapattiyo (syā. pī. ka.) – santāvuso sattā paccupaṭṭhitakāmā, te paccupaṭṭhitesu kāmesu vasaṃ vattenti, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā kāmūpapatti. Santāvuso, sattā nimmitakāmā, te nimminitvā nimminitvā kāmesu vasaṃ vattenti, seyyathāpi devā nimmānaratī. Ayaṃ dutiyā kāmūpapatti. Santāvuso sattā paranimmitakāmā, te paranimmitesu kāmesu vasaṃ vattenti, seyyathāpi devā paranimmitavasavattī. Ayaṃ tatiyā kāmūpapatti.

Three kinds of attainment of sensual pleasures: Friends, there are beings for whom sensual pleasures are readily available, and they wield power over these readily available sensual pleasures. Such are human beings, some devas, and some beings in states of deprivation. This is the first kind of attainment of sensual pleasures. Friends, there are beings who create sensual pleasures, and having created them again and again, they wield power over those sensual pleasures. Such are the devas who delight in creation. This is the second kind of attainment of sensual pleasures. Friends, there are beings who wield power over sensual pleasures created by others. Such are the devas who wield power over the creations of others. This is the third kind of attainment of sensual pleasures.

“Tisso sukhūpapattiyo sukhupapattiyo (syā. pī. ka.) – santāvuso sattā sattā sukhaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) uppādetvā uppādetvā sukhaṃ viharanti, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā sukhūpapatti. Santāvuso, sattā sukhena abhisannā parisannā paripūrā paripphuṭā. Te kadāci karahaci udānaṃ udānenti – ‘aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha’nti[V 3.0175], seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ dutiyā sukhūpapatti. Santāvuso, sattā sukhena abhisannā parisannā paripūrā paripphuṭā. Te santaṃyeva tusitā santusitā (syā. kaṃ.) sukhaṃ [P 3.0219] cittasukhaṃ (syā. ka.) paṭisaṃvedenti, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ tatiyā sukhūpapatti[T 3.0231].

Three kinds of attainment of happiness: Friends, there are beings who, having repeatedly generated happiness, dwell happily; such are the devas of Brahmā's retinue. This is the first attainment of happiness. Friends, there are beings who are drenched, steeped, filled, and suffused with happiness. At certain times, they utter the inspired utterance: 'Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!'; such are the devas of Streaming Radiance. This is the second attainment of happiness. Friends, there are beings who are drenched, steeped, filled, and suffused with happiness. They, being satisfied, experience a sublime and peaceful happiness; such are the devas of Refulgent Glory. This is the third attainment of happiness.

“Tisso paññā – sekkhā paññā, asekkhā paññā, nevasekkhānāsekkhā paññā.

Three kinds of wisdom: the wisdom of one in training, the wisdom of one beyond training, and the wisdom of one who is neither in training nor beyond training.

“Aparāpi tisso paññā – cintāmayā paññā, sutamayā paññā, bhāvanāmayā paññā.

Three other kinds of wisdom: wisdom consisting of thought, wisdom consisting of learning, and wisdom consisting of mental development.

“Tīṇāvudhāni – sutāvudhaṃ, pavivekāvudhaṃ, paññāvudhaṃ.

Three weapons: the weapon of learning, the weapon of seclusion, and the weapon of wisdom.

“Tīṇindriyāni – anaññātaññassāmītindriyaṃ, aññindriyaṃ, aññātāvindriyaṃ.

Three faculties: the faculty of the thought 'I shall come to know the unknown,' the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has final knowledge.

“Tīṇi cakkhūni – maṃsacakkhu, dibbacakkhu, paññācakkhu.

Three eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom.

“Tisso sikkhā – adhisīlasikkhā, adhicittasikkhā, adhipaññāsikkhā.

Three trainings: the training in higher moral virtue, the training in higher concentration, and the training in higher wisdom.

“Tisso bhāvanā – kāyabhāvanā, cittabhāvanā, paññābhāvanā.

Three kinds of development: development of the body, development of the mind, and development of wisdom.

“Tīṇi [M 3.0184] anuttariyāni – dassanānuttariyaṃ, paṭipadānuttariyaṃ, vimuttānuttariyaṃ.

Three unsurpassed things: unsurpassed vision, unsurpassed practice, and unsurpassed liberation.

“Tayo samādhī – savitakkasavicāro samādhi, avitakkavicāramatto samādhi, avitakkaavicāro samādhi.

Three kinds of concentration: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought, with sustained thought only; and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought.

“Aparepi tayo samādhī – suññato samādhi, animitto samādhi, appaṇihito samādhi.

Furthermore, there are three other concentrations: the emptiness concentration, the signless concentration, and the undirected concentration.

“Tīṇi soceyyāni – kāyasoceyyaṃ, vacīsoceyyaṃ, manosoceyyaṃ.

Three purities: purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.

“Tīṇi [P 3.0220] moneyyāni – kāyamoneyyaṃ, vacīmoneyyaṃ, manomoneyyaṃ.

Three forms of sagehood: sagehood in body, sagehood in speech, and sagehood in mind.

“Tīṇi [V 3.0176] kosallāni – āyakosallaṃ, apāyakosallaṃ, upāyakosallaṃ.

Three skills: skill in progress, skill in decline, and skill in the means thereto.

“Tayo madā – ārogyamado, yobbanamado, jīvitamado.

Three intoxications: intoxication with health, intoxication with youth, and intoxication with life.

“Tīṇi ādhipateyyāni – attādhipateyyaṃ, lokādhipateyyaṃ, dhammādhipateyyaṃ.

Three sovereignties: sovereignty of self, sovereignty of the world, and sovereignty of the Dhamma.

“Tīṇi kathāvatthūni – atītaṃ vā addhānaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ katheyya – ‘evaṃ ahosi atītamaddhāna’nti; anāgataṃ vā addhānaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ katheyya – ‘evaṃ bhavissati anāgatamaddhāna’nti; etarahi vā paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ ārabbha kathaṃ katheyya – ‘evaṃ hoti etarahi paccuppannaṃ addhāna’nti.

Three grounds for talk: one might speak with reference to the past, saying, ‘Thus it was in the past’; or one might speak with reference to the future, saying, ‘Thus it will be in the future’; or one might speak with reference to the present, saying, ‘Thus it is now in the present.’

“Tisso vijjā [T 3.0232] – pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ vijjā, sattānaṃ cutūpapāteñāṇaṃ vijjā, āsavānaṃ khayeñāṇaṃ vijjā.

Three true knowledges: the knowledge of recollecting previous lives, the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.

“Tayo vihārā – dibbo vihāro, brahmā vihāro, ariyo vihāro.

Three abidings: the divine abiding, the sublime abiding, and the noble abiding.

“Tīṇi pāṭihāriyāni – iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ, ādesanāpāṭihāriyaṃ, anusāsanīpāṭihāriyaṃ.

Three miracles: the miracle of psychic power, the miracle of telepathy, and the miracle of instruction.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena tayo dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

Friends, these are the three things that have been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who is the knowing one, the seeing one, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together... for the good, for the welfare, and for the happiness of gods and humans.

Catukkaṃ

The Section on Fours

306. “Atthi [M 3.0185][P 3.0221] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ, na vivaditabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame cattāro?

306. Friends, there are four things that have been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who is the knowing one, the seeing one, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together and not dispute... for the good, for the welfare, and for the happiness of gods and humans. What are the four?

“Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno [V 3.0177] satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Vedanāsu vedanānupassī…pe… citte cittānupassī…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ.

Four foundations of mindfulness. Here, friends, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—having removed covetousness and displeasure with regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—having removed covetousness and displeasure with regard to the world.

“Cattāro sammappadhānā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ [T 3.0233] paggaṇhāti padahati. Anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati.

Four right strivings. Here, friends, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of evil, unwholesome states that have not yet arisen. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of evil, unwholesome states that have arisen. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of wholesome states that have not yet arisen. He generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-fading, increase, expansion, development, and culmination of wholesome states that have arisen.

“Cattāro iddhipādā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Cittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ [P 3.0222] iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Vīmaṃsāsamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti.

There are four bases of spiritual power. Here, friends, a monk develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to desire and the formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to mind and the formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to energy and the formations of striving. He develops the basis of spiritual power that is endowed with concentration due to investigation and the formations of striving.

“Cattāri jhānāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ paṭhamajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ dutiyajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca [M 3.0186] kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ tatiyajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) upasampajja viharati.

There are four jhānas. Here, friends, a monk—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states—enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. With the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimously, mindful and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body—that of which the noble ones declare, ‘Equanimous and mindful, he dwells in pleasure’—and so he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

307. “Catasso samādhibhāvanā. Atthāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā [T 3.0234] diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati. Atthāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati. Atthāvuso samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satisampajaññāya saṃvattati. Atthāvuso samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati.

307. There are four developments of concentration. Friends, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to a pleasant abiding in the present life. Friends, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the attainment of knowledge and vision. Friends, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to mindfulness and clear comprehension. Friends, there is a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the destruction of the taints.

“Katamā [V 3.0178] cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ…pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ, āvuso[P 3.0223], samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārāya saṃvattati.

And which, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to a pleasant abiding in the present life? Here, friends, a monk—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states... enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna. This, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to a pleasant abiding in the present life.

“Katamā cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu ālokasaññaṃ manasi karoti, divāsaññaṃ adhiṭṭhāti yathā divā tathā rattiṃ, yathā rattiṃ tathā divā. Iti vivaṭena cetasā apariyonaddhena sappabhāsaṃ cittaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ, āvuso samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā ñāṇadassanapaṭilābhāya saṃvattati.

And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the acquisition of knowledge and vision? Here, friends, a monk attends to the perception of light; he establishes the perception of daytime: ‘As by day, so by night; as by night, so by day.’ Thus, with a mind that is open and unconfined, he develops a luminous mind. This, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the acquisition of knowledge and vision.

“Katamā cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satisampajaññāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno viditā vedanā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Viditā saññā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Viditā vitakkā uppajjanti, viditā upaṭṭhahanti, viditā abbhatthaṃ gacchanti. Ayaṃ, āvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā satisampajaññāya saṃvattati.

And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to mindfulness and clear comprehension? Here, friends, for a monk, feelings arise known, are present known, and cease known. Perceptions arise known, are present known, and cease known. Thoughts arise known, are present known, and cease known. This, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to mindfulness and clear comprehension.

“Katamā [T 3.0235][M 3.0187] cāvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassī viharati. Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo. Iti vedanā…pe… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo. Ayaṃ, āvuso, samādhibhāvanā bhāvitā bahulīkatā āsavānaṃ khayāya saṃvattati.

And what, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the destruction of the taints? Here, friends, a monk dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates of clinging: ‘Such is form, such its arising, such its passing away. Such is feeling… such is perception… such are formations… such is consciousness, such its arising, such its passing away.’ This, friends, is the development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the destruction of the taints.

308. “Catasso [V 3.0179] appamaññā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati. Tathā dutiyaṃ. Tathā tatiyaṃ. Tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho [P 3.0224] tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena abyāpajjhena (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) pharitvā viharati. Karuṇāsahagatena cetasā…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā…pe… upekkhāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati. Tathā dutiyaṃ. Tathā tatiyaṃ. Tathā catutthaṃ. Iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati.

308. There are four boundless states. Here, friends, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, sublime, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will. With a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with appreciative joy… with a mind imbued with equanimity, he dwells pervading one direction; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, sublime, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will. These are the four boundless states.

“Cattāro āruppā. arūpā (syā. kaṃ. pī.) Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ [T 3.0236] upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati.

There are four immaterial attainments. Here, friends, a monk, by completely surmounting perceptions of form, by the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, by not attending to perceptions of diversity, perceiving ‘space is infinite,’ enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. By completely surmounting the base of infinite space, perceiving ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. By completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, perceiving ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and dwells in the base of nothingness. By completely surmounting the base of nothingness, he enters and dwells in the base of neither perception nor non-perception. These are the four immaterial attainments.

“Cattāri apassenāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti.

There are four reliances. Here, friends, a monk uses one thing after reflection, endures one thing after reflection, avoids one thing after reflection, and dispels one thing after reflection. These are the four reliances.

309. “Cattāro [M 3.0188] ariyavaṃsā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena cīvarena, itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca cīvarahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca cīvaraṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca cīvaraṃ agadhito agathito (sī. pī.) amucchito anajjhāpanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati; tāya ca pana itarītaracīvarasantuṭṭhiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso [P 3.0225] – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

309. “There are four noble lineages. Here, friends, a monk is content with any kind of robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe. He does not, on account of a robe, engage in improper and unsuitable searching. If he does not obtain a robe, he is not distressed; and when he has obtained a robe, he uses it without being greedy, infatuated, or attached, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. And by means of that contentment with any kind of robe, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Whichever monk is skilled, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful therein—this, friends, is called a monk who is established in the ancient, foremost noble lineage.”

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca piṇḍapātahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ agadhito amucchito anajjhāpanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati; tāya ca pana itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā [V 3.0180] nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato[T 3.0237], ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is content with any kind of almsfood, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood. He does not, on account of almsfood, engage in improper and unsuitable searching. If he does not obtain almsfood, he is not distressed; and when he has obtained almsfood, he uses it without being greedy, infatuated, or attached, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. And by means of that contentment with any kind of almsfood, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Whichever monk is skilled, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful therein—this, friends, is called a monk who is established in the ancient, foremost noble lineage.”

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarena senāsanena, itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca senāsanahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati; aladdhā ca senāsanaṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca senāsanaṃ agadhito amucchito anajjhāpanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjati; tāya ca pana itarītarasenāsanasantuṭṭhiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato, ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is content with any kind of lodging, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of lodging. He does not, on account of lodging, engage in improper and unsuitable searching. If he does not obtain lodging, he is not distressed; and when he has obtained lodging, he uses it without being greedy, infatuated, or attached, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. And by means of that contentment with any kind of lodging, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Whichever monk is skilled, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful therein—this, friends, is called a monk who is established in the ancient, foremost noble lineage.”

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu pahānārāmo hoti pahānarato, bhāvanārāmo hoti bhāvanārato; tāya ca pana pahānārāmatāya pahānaratiyā bhāvanārāmatāya bhāvanāratiyā nevattānukkaṃseti na paraṃ vambheti. Yo hi tattha dakkho analaso sampajāno paṭissato ayaṃ vuccatāvuso – ‘bhikkhu porāṇe aggaññe ariyavaṃse ṭhito’.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk delights in abandoning and is devoted to abandoning; he delights in development and is devoted to development. And because of this delight in abandoning and devotion to abandoning, and this delight in development and devotion to development, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. Whichever monk is skilled, not lazy, clearly comprehending, and mindful therein—this, friends, is called a monk who is established in the ancient, foremost noble lineage.”

310. “Cattāri [M 3.0189] padhānāni. Saṃvarapadhānaṃ pahānapadhānaṃ bhāvanāpadhānaṃ bhāvanāppadhānaṃ (syā.) anurakkhaṇāpadhānaṃ anurakkhanāppadhānaṃ (syā.). Katamañcāvuso, saṃvarapadhānaṃ? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ [P 3.0226] viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati, rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena [T 3.0238] phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati, rakkhati manindriyaṃ, manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Idaṃ vuccatāvuso, saṃvarapadhānaṃ.

310. “There are four strivings: the striving of restraint, the striving of abandoning, the striving of development, and the striving of preservation. And what, friends, is the striving of restraint? Here, friends, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, does not grasp at its signs or features. In consequence of which, were he to dwell with the eye-faculty unrestrained, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him; therefore, he practices for its restraint, he guards the eye-faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the eye-faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having felt a tactile object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or features. In consequence of which, were he to dwell with the mind-faculty unrestrained, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might assail him; therefore, he practices for its restraint, he guards the mind-faculty, he undertakes the restraint of the mind-faculty. This, friends, is called the striving of restraint.”

“Katamañcāvuso, pahānapadhānaṃ? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantiṃ karoti byantī karoti (syā. kaṃ.) anabhāvaṃ gameti. Uppannaṃ byāpādavitakkaṃ…pe… uppannaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ… uppannuppanne pāpake akusale dhamme nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantiṃ karoti anabhāvaṃ gameti. Idaṃ vuccatāvuso, pahānapadhānaṃ.

“And what, friends, is the striving of abandoning? Here, friends, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, causes it to go to non-existence. He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will… an arisen thought of cruelty… any arisen evil unwholesome states; he abandons them, dispels them, brings them to an end, causes them to go to non-existence. This, friends, is called the striving of abandoning.”

“Katamañcāvuso[V 3.0181], bhāvanāpadhānaṃ? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… vīriyasambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… pītisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… passaddhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… samādhisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti… upekkhāsambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Idaṃ vuccatāvuso, bhāvanāpadhānaṃ.

“And what, friends, is the striving of development? Here, friends, a monk develops the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, culminating in relinquishment. He develops the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena… he develops the enlightenment factor of energy… he develops the enlightenment factor of rapture… he develops the enlightenment factor of tranquility… he develops the enlightenment factor of concentration… he develops the enlightenment factor of equanimity, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, culminating in relinquishment. This, friends, is called the striving of development.”

“Katamañcāvuso, anurakkhaṇāpadhānaṃ? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu uppannaṃ bhadrakaṃ bhaddakaṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.) samādhinimittaṃ anurakkhati – aṭṭhikasaññaṃ, puḷuvakasaññaṃ puḷavakasaññaṃ (sī. pī.), vinīlakasaññaṃ, vicchiddakasaññaṃ, uddhumātakasaññaṃ. Idaṃ vuccatāvuso, anurakkhaṇāpadhānaṃ.

“And what, friends, is the striving of preservation? Here, friends, a monk preserves a good sign for concentration that has arisen—the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-eaten corpse, the perception of a discolored corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a bloated corpse. This, friends, is called the striving of preservation.”

“Cattāri [T 3.0239] ñāṇāni – dhamme ñāṇaṃ, anvaye ñāṇaṃ, pariye paricce (sī. ka.), paricchede (syā. pī. ka.) ṭīkā oloketabbā ñāṇaṃ, sammutiyā ñāṇaṃ sammatiñāṇaṃ (syā. kaṃ.).

“There are four knowledges: knowledge in the Dhamma, knowledge in what follows, knowledge in comprehending others' minds, and knowledge in convention.”

“Aparānipi [M 3.0190][P 3.0227] cattāri ñāṇāni – dukkhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhasamudaye ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhe ñāṇaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminiyā paṭipadāya ñāṇaṃ.

“There are another four knowledges: knowledge in suffering, knowledge in the origin of suffering, knowledge in the cessation of suffering, and knowledge in the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”

311. “Cattāri sotāpattiyaṅgāni – sappurisasaṃsevo, saddhammassavanaṃ, yonisomanasikāro, dhammānudhammappaṭipatti.

311. “There are four factors of stream-entry: association with true persons, hearing the true Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma.”

“Cattāri sotāpannassa aṅgāni. Idhāvuso, ariyasāvako buddhe aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho, bhagavā’ti. Dhamme aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti – ‘svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo sandiṭṭhiko akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko opanayiko (syā. kaṃ.) paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī’ti. Saṅghe aveccappasādena samannāgato hoti – ‘suppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho ujuppaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho ñāyappaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho sāmīcippaṭipanno bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho yadidaṃ cattāri purisayugāni aṭṭha purisapuggalā, esa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho āhuneyyo pāhuneyyo dakkhiṇeyyo añjalikaraṇīyo anuttaraṃ puññakkhettaṃ lokassā’ti. Ariyakantehi sīlehi samannāgato hoti akhaṇḍehi acchiddehi asabalehi akammāsehi bhujissehi viññuppasatthehi aparāmaṭṭhehi samādhisaṃvattanikehi.

There are four qualities of a stream-enterer. Here, friends, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘Indeed, the Blessed One is an Arahant, perfectly self-enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.’ He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally experienced by the wise.’ He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One's disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ He possesses virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, unpierced, unspotted, unblotched, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, conducive to concentration.

“Cattāri [T 3.0240][V 3.0182] sāmaññaphalāni – sotāpattiphalaṃ, sakadāgāmiphalaṃ, anāgāmiphalaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ.

There are four fruits of recluseship: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship.

“Catasso [P 3.0228] dhātuyo – pathavīdhātu, āpodhātu, tejodhātu, vāyodhātu.

There are four elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.

“Cattāro āhārā – kabaḷīkāro āhāro oḷāriko vā sukhumo vā, phasso dutiyo, manosañcetanā tatiyā, viññāṇaṃ catutthaṃ.

There are four nutriments: physical food, whether coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth.

“Catasso viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Rūpūpāyaṃ vā, āvuso, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭhati rūpārammaṇaṃ rūpāramaṇaṃ (?) rūpappatiṭṭhaṃ nandūpasecanaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjati; vedanūpāyaṃ [M 3.0191] vā āvuso…pe… saññūpāyaṃ vā, āvuso…pe… saṅkhārūpāyaṃ vā, āvuso, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭhati saṅkhārārammaṇaṃ saṅkhārappatiṭṭhaṃ nandūpasecanaṃ vuddhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ āpajjati.

There are four stations of consciousness. When, friends, consciousness, while standing, stands with form as its support, with form as its object, established upon form, sprinkled with delight, it attains growth, increase, and expansion. When, friends, with feeling as its support… when, friends, with perception as its support… when, friends, consciousness, while standing, stands with formations as its support, with formations as its object, established upon formations, sprinkled with delight, it attains growth, increase, and expansion.

“Cattāri agatigamanāni – chandāgatiṃ gacchati, dosāgati gacchati, mohāgatiṃ gacchati, bhayāgatiṃ gacchati.

There are four wrong courses: one goes the wrong course through desire, one goes the wrong course through hatred, one goes the wrong course through delusion, one goes the wrong course through fear.

“Cattāro taṇhuppādā – cīvarahetu vā, āvuso, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati; piṇḍapātahetu vā, āvuso, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati; senāsanahetu vā, āvuso, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati; itibhavābhavahetu vā, āvuso, bhikkhuno taṇhā uppajjamānā uppajjati.

There are four arisings of craving. Friends, for a bhikkhu, craving, while arising, arises on account of robes; friends, for a bhikkhu, craving, while arising, arises on account of almsfood; friends, for a bhikkhu, craving, while arising, arises on account of lodgings; friends, for a bhikkhu, craving, while arising, arises on account of this or that state of being.

“Catasso [T 3.0241] paṭipadā – dukkhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā, dukkhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā, sukhā paṭipadā dandhābhiññā, sukhā paṭipadā khippābhiññā.

There are four ways of practice: painful practice with slow direct knowledge, painful practice with quick direct knowledge, pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge, and pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.

“Aparāpi [P 3.0229] catasso paṭipadā – akkhamā paṭipadā, khamā paṭipadā, damā paṭipadā, samā paṭipadā.

Furthermore, there are four ways of practice: the unenduring practice, the enduring practice, the disciplined practice, and the tranquil practice.

“Cattāri [V 3.0183] dhammapadāni – anabhijjhā dhammapadaṃ, abyāpādo dhammapadaṃ, sammāsati dhammapadaṃ, sammāsamādhi dhammapadaṃ.

There are four Dhamma-principles: non-covetousness is a Dhamma-principle, non-ill will is a Dhamma-principle, right mindfulness is a Dhamma-principle, and right concentration is a Dhamma-principle.

“Cattāri dhammasamādānāni – atthāvuso, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhañceva āyatiñca dukkhavipākaṃ. Atthāvuso, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannadukkhaṃ āyatiṃ sukhavipākaṃ. Atthāvuso, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhaṃ āyatiṃ dukkhavipākaṃ. Atthāvuso, dhammasamādānaṃ paccuppannasukhañceva āyatiñca sukhavipākaṃ.

There are four undertakings of Dhamma. Friends, there is an undertaking of Dhamma that is painful in the present and has a painful result in the future. Friends, there is an undertaking of Dhamma that is painful in the present but has a pleasant result in the future. Friends, there is an undertaking of Dhamma that is pleasant in the present but has a painful result in the future. Friends, there is an undertaking of Dhamma that is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future.

“Cattāro dhammakkhandhā – sīlakkhandho, samādhikkhandho, paññākkhandho, vimuttikkhandho.

There are four aggregates of Dhamma: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, and the aggregate of liberation.

“Cattāri balāni – vīriyabalaṃ, satibalaṃ, samādhibalaṃ, paññābalaṃ.

There are four powers: the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

“Cattāri adhiṭṭhānāni – paññādhiṭṭhānaṃ, saccādhiṭṭhānaṃ, cāgādhiṭṭhānaṃ, upasamādhiṭṭhānaṃ.

There are four determinations: the determination of wisdom, the determination of truth, the determination of relinquishment, and the determination of peace.

312. “Cattāri [M 3.0192] pañhabyākaraṇāni – cattāro pañhābyākaraṇā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ekaṃsabyākaraṇīyo pañho, paṭipucchābyākaraṇīyo pañho, vibhajjabyākaraṇīyo pañho, ṭhapanīyo pañho.

312. There are four ways of answering questions: a question to be answered categorically, a question to be answered by questioning in return, a question to be answered analytically, and a question to be set aside.

“Cattāri [T 3.0242][P 3.0230] kammāni – atthāvuso, kammaṃ kaṇhaṃ kaṇhavipākaṃ; atthāvuso, kammaṃ sukkaṃ sukkavipākaṃ; atthāvuso, kammaṃ kaṇhasukkaṃ kaṇhasukkavipākaṃ; atthāvuso, kammaṃ akaṇhaasukkaṃ akaṇhaasukkavipākaṃ kammakkhayāya saṃvattati.

There are four kinds of kamma.
