Friends, there is dark kamma with a dark result; there is bright kamma with a bright result; there is dark and bright kamma with a dark and bright result; and there is kamma that is neither dark nor bright with a neither-dark-nor-bright result, which conduces to the destruction of kamma.

“Cattāro sacchikaraṇīyā dhammā – pubbenivāso satiyā sacchikaraṇīyo; sattānaṃ cutūpapāto cakkhunā sacchikaraṇīyo; aṭṭha vimokkhā kāyena sacchikaraṇīyā; āsavānaṃ khayo paññāya sacchikaraṇīyo.

There are four dhammas to be realized: previous existences are to be realized by means of mindfulness; the passing away and rebirth of beings are to be realized by means of the divine eye; the eight liberations are to be realized by means of the body; and the destruction of the taints is to be realized by means of wisdom.

“Cattāro oghā – kāmogho, bhavogho, diṭṭhogho, avijjogho.

There are four floods: the flood of sensuality, the flood of becoming, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.

“Cattāro yogā – kāmayogo, bhavayogo, diṭṭhiyogo, avijjāyogo.

There are four yokes: the yoke of sensuality, the yoke of becoming, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.

“Cattāro [V 3.0184] visaññogā – kāmayogavisaññogo, bhavayogavisaññogo, diṭṭhiyogavisaññogo, avijjāyogavisaññogo.

There are four disjoinings from the yokes: disjoining from the yoke of sensuality, disjoining from the yoke of becoming, disjoining from the yoke of views, and disjoining from the yoke of ignorance.

“Cattāro ganthā – abhijjhā kāyagantho, byāpādo kāyagantho, sīlabbataparāmāso kāyagantho, idaṃsaccābhiniveso kāyagantho.

There are four bodily knots: the bodily knot of covetousness, the bodily knot of ill will, the bodily knot of clinging to rules and observances, and the bodily knot of dogmatic insistence that 'this alone is true'.

“Cattāri upādānāni – kāmupādānaṃ kāmūpādānaṃ (sī. pī.) evamitaresupi, diṭṭhupādānaṃ, sīlabbatupādānaṃ, attavādupādānaṃ.

There are four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.

“Catasso yoniyo – aṇḍajayoni, jalābujayoni, saṃsedajayoni, opapātikayoni.

There are four modes of birth: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously arisen.

“Catasso [T 3.0243][P 3.0231] gabbhāvakkantiyo. Idhāvuso, ekacco asampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, asampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ paṭhamā gabbhāvakkanti. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, idhekacco [M 3.0193] sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, asampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ dutiyā gabbhāvakkanti. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, sampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, asampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ tatiyā gabbhāvakkanti. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, idhekacco sampajāno mātukucchiṃ okkamati, sampajāno mātukucchismiṃ ṭhāti, sampajāno mātukucchimhā nikkhamati, ayaṃ catutthā gabbhāvakkanti.

There are four descents into a womb. Here, friends, a certain person descends into the mother’s womb without clear comprehension, remains in the mother’s womb without clear comprehension, and emerges from the mother’s womb without clear comprehension. This is the first descent into a womb. Furthermore, friends, here a certain person descends into the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, but remains in the mother’s womb without clear comprehension, and emerges from the mother’s womb without clear comprehension. This is the second descent into a womb. Furthermore, friends, here a certain person descends into the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, remains in the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, but emerges from the mother’s womb without clear comprehension. This is the third descent into a womb. Furthermore, friends, here a certain person descends into the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, remains in the mother’s womb with clear comprehension, and emerges from the mother’s womb with clear comprehension. This is the fourth descent into a womb.

“Cattāro attabhāvapaṭilābhā. Atthāvuso, attabhāvapaṭilābho, yasmiṃ attabhāvapaṭilābhe attasañcetanāyeva kamati, no parasañcetanā. Atthāvuso, attabhāvapaṭilābho, yasmiṃ attabhāvapaṭilābhe parasañcetanāyeva kamati, no attasañcetanā. Atthāvuso, attabhāvapaṭilābho, yasmiṃ attabhāvapaṭilābhe attasañcetanā ceva kamati parasañcetanā ca. Atthāvuso, attabhāvapaṭilābho, yasmiṃ attabhāvapaṭilābhe neva attasañcetanā kamati, no parasañcetanā.

There are four acquisitions of individual existence. Friends, there is an acquisition of individual existence in which one's own volition is effective, but not another's volition. Friends, there is an acquisition of individual existence in which another's volition is effective, but not one's own volition. Friends, there is an acquisition of individual existence in which both one's own volition and another's volition are effective. Friends, there is an acquisition of individual existence in which neither one's own volition nor another's volition is effective.

313. “Catasso dakkhiṇāvisuddhiyo. Atthāvuso, dakkhiṇā dāyakato visujjhati no paṭiggāhakato. Atthāvuso, dakkhiṇā paṭiggāhakato [T 3.0244] visujjhati no dāyakato. Atthāvuso, dakkhiṇā neva dāyakato visujjhati no [P 3.0232] paṭiggāhakato. Atthāvuso, dakkhiṇā dāyakato ceva visujjhati paṭiggāhakato ca.

313. There are four purifications of an offering. Friends, there is an offering that is purified on the part of the giver, but not on the part of the recipient. Friends, there is an offering that is purified on the part of the recipient, but not on the part of the giver. Friends, there is an offering that is purified neither on the part of the giver nor on the part of the recipient. Friends, there is an offering that is purified on the part of both the giver and the recipient.

“Cattāri [V 3.0185] saṅgahavatthūni – dānaṃ, peyyavajjaṃ piyavajjaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.), atthacariyā, samānattatā.

There are four grounds for fellowship: generosity, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.

“Cattāro anariyavohārā – musāvādo, pisuṇāvācā, pharusāvācā, samphappalāpo.

There are four ignoble forms of speech: false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.

“Cattāro ariyavohārā – musāvādā veramaṇī veramaṇi (ka.), pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī, pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī, samphappalāpā veramaṇī.

There are four noble forms of speech: abstinence from false speech, abstinence from divisive speech, abstinence from harsh speech, and abstinence from idle chatter.

“Aparepi cattāro anariyavohārā – adiṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditā, assute sutavāditā, amute mutavāditā, aviññāte viññātavāditā.

Furthermore, there are four other ignoble forms of speech: in regard to the unseen, stating it has been seen; in regard to the unheard, stating it has been heard; in regard to the unsensed, stating it has been sensed; in regard to the uncognized, stating it has been cognized.

“Aparepi [M 3.0194] cattāro ariyavohārā – adiṭṭhe adiṭṭhavāditā, assute assutavāditā, amute amutavāditā, aviññāte aviññātavāditā.

Furthermore, there are four other noble forms of speech: in regard to the unseen, stating it has not been seen; in regard to the unheard, stating it has not been heard; in regard to the unsensed, stating it has not been sensed; in regard to the uncognized, stating it has not been cognized.

“Aparepi cattāro anariyavohārā – diṭṭhe adiṭṭhavāditā, sute assutavāditā, mute amutavāditā, viññāte aviññātavāditā.

Furthermore, there are four other ignoble forms of speech: in regard to the seen, stating it has not been seen; in regard to the heard, stating it has not been heard; in regard to the sensed, stating it has not been sensed; in regard to the cognized, stating it has not been cognized.

“Aparepi cattāro ariyavohārā – diṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditā, sute sutavāditā, mute mutavāditā, viññāte viññātavāditā.

Furthermore, there are four other noble forms of speech: in regard to the seen, stating it has been seen; in regard to the heard, stating it has been heard; in regard to the sensed, stating it has been sensed; in regard to the cognized, stating it has been cognized.

314. “Cattāro puggalā. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo attantapo hoti attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo parantapo [T 3.0245] hoti paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo attantapo ca hoti attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto, parantapo ca paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo neva attantapo hoti na attaparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto na parantapo na paraparitāpanānuyogamanuyutto. So anattantapo aparantapo [P 3.0233] diṭṭheva dhamme nicchāto nibbuto sītībhūto sītibhūto (ka.) sukhappaṭisaṃvedī brahmabhūtena attanā viharati.

314. There are four persons. Here, friends, a certain person is a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment. Here, friends, a certain person is a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, friends, a certain person is both a self-tormentor, devoted to the practice of self-torment, and a tormentor of others, devoted to the practice of tormenting others. Here, friends, a certain person is neither a self-tormentor, not devoted to the practice of self-torment, nor a tormentor of others, not devoted to the practice of tormenting others. He, being neither a self-tormentor nor a tormentor of others, in this very life is without craving, extinguished, cooled, and experiences bliss, abiding with a self that has become sublime.

“Aparepi cattāro puggalā. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo attahitāya paṭipanno hoti no parahitāya. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo parahitāya paṭipanno hoti no attahitāya. Idhāvuso[V 3.0186], ekacco puggalo neva attahitāya paṭipanno hoti no parahitāya. Idhāvuso, ekacco puggalo attahitāya ceva paṭipanno hoti parahitāya ca.

Furthermore, there are four other persons. Here, friends, a certain person is one who practices for his own welfare, but not for the welfare of others. Here, friends, a certain person is one who practices for the welfare of others, but not for his own welfare. Here, friends, a certain person is one who practices neither for his own welfare nor for the welfare of others. Here, friends, a certain person is one who practices for his own welfare as well as for the welfare of others.

“Aparepi cattāro puggalā – tamo tamaparāyano, tamo jotiparāyano, joti tamaparāyano, joti jotiparāyano.

Furthermore, there are four other persons: the one in darkness bound for darkness, the one in darkness bound for light, the one in light bound for darkness, and the one in light bound for light.

“Aparepi cattāro puggalā – samaṇamacalo, samaṇapadumo, samaṇapuṇḍarīko, samaṇesu samaṇasukhumālo.

Furthermore, there are four other persons: the unshakable ascetic, the red lotus ascetic, the white lotus ascetic, and the refined ascetic among ascetics.

“Ime [M 3.0195] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cattāro dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

Friends, these four dhammas have been well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together... for the good, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The first recitation section is concluded.

Pañcakaṃ

The Fives

315. “Atthi [T 3.0246] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena pañca dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame pañca?

315. Friends, there are indeed five dhammas well-proclaimed by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant in unison… for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. What are the five?

“Pañcakkhandhā. Rūpakkhandho vedanākkhandho saññākkhandho saṅkhārakkhandho viññāṇakkhandho.

The five aggregates: the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness.

“Pañcupādānakkhandhā. Rūpupādānakkhandho rūpūpādānakkhandho (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) evamitaresupi vedanupādānakkhandho [P 3.0234] saññupādānakkhandho saṅkhārupādānakkhandho viññāṇupādānakkhandho.

The five aggregates of clinging: the aggregate of form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of formations subject to clinging, the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging.

“Pañca kāmaguṇā. Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasañhitā rajanīyā[V 3.0187], sotaviññeyyā saddā… ghānaviññeyyā gandhā… jivhāviññeyyā rasā… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasañhitā rajanīyā.

The five cords of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear… odors cognizable by the nose… flavors cognizable by the tongue… tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing.

“Pañca gatiyo – nirayo, tiracchānayoni, pettivisayo, manussā, devā.

There are five destinations: hell, the animal realm, the sphere of petas, human beings, and devas.

“Pañca macchariyāni – āvāsamacchariyaṃ, kulamacchariyaṃ, lābhamacchariyaṃ, vaṇṇamacchariyaṃ, dhammamacchariyaṃ.

There are five kinds of stinginess: stinginess regarding dwellings, stinginess regarding families, stinginess regarding gains, stinginess regarding appearance, and stinginess regarding the Dhamma.

“Pañca nīvaraṇāni – kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ, uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇaṃ, vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ.

There are five hindrances: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.

“Pañca orambhāgiyāni saññojanāni – sakkāyadiṭṭhi, vicikicchā, sīlabbataparāmāso, kāmacchando, byāpādo.

There are five lower fetters: identity view, doubt, clinging to rites and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will.

“Pañca [T 3.0247][M 3.0196] uddhambhāgiyāni saññojanāni – rūparāgo, arūparāgo, māno, uddhaccaṃ, avijjā.

There are five higher fetters: lust for form, lust for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.

“Pañca [P 3.0235] sikkhāpadāni – pāṇātipātā veramaṇī, adinnādānā veramaṇī, kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī, musāvādā veramaṇī, surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā veramaṇī.

There are five training precepts: abstinence from the destruction of life, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from sexual misconduct, abstinence from false speech, and abstinence from distilled and fermented intoxicants which are the basis for heedlessness.

316. “Pañca abhabbaṭṭhānāni. Abhabbo, āvuso, khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sañcicca pāṇaṃ jīvitā voropetuṃ. Abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyituṃ ādātuṃ (syā. kaṃ. pī.). Abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevituṃ. Abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sampajānamusā bhāsituṃ. Abhabbo khīṇāsavo bhikkhu sannidhikārakaṃ kāme paribhuñjituṃ, seyyathāpi pubbe āgārikabhūto.

316. There are five impossibilities. Friends, a monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of intentionally depriving a living being of life. A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of taking what is not given, amounting to theft. A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse. A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of knowingly speaking a falsehood. A monk whose taints are destroyed is incapable of enjoying stored-up sensual pleasures as he did formerly when a householder.

“Pañca byasanāni – ñātibyasanaṃ, bhogabyasanaṃ, rogabyasanaṃ, sīlabyasanaṃ, diṭṭhibyasanaṃ. Nāvuso, sattā ñātibyasanahetu vā bhogabyasanahetu vā rogabyasanahetu vā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti. Sīlabyasanahetu vā, āvuso, sattā diṭṭhibyasanahetu [V 3.0188] vā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjanti.

There are five calamities: the calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, the calamity of illness, the calamity of virtue, and the calamity of view. Friends, beings are not reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, in hell, after the breakup of the body, after death, on account of the calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, or the calamity of illness. But, friends, beings are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, in hell, after the breakup of the body, after death, on account of the calamity of virtue or the calamity of view.

“Pañca sampadā – ñātisampadā, bhogasampadā, ārogyasampadā, sīlasampadā, diṭṭhisampadā. Nāvuso, sattā ñātisampadāhetu vā bhogasampadāhetu vā ārogyasampadāhetu vā kāyassa bhedā [T 3.0248] paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti. Sīlasampadāhetu vā, āvuso, sattā diṭṭhisampadāhetu vā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjanti.

There are five accomplishments: accomplishment in relatives, accomplishment in wealth, accomplishment in health, accomplishment in virtue, and accomplishment in view. Friends, beings are not reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death, on account of an accomplishment in relatives, an accomplishment in wealth, or an accomplishment in health. But, friends, beings are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, after the breakup of the body, after death, on account of an accomplishment in virtue or an accomplishment in view.

“Pañca ādīnavā dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā. Idhāvuso[P 3.0236], dussīlo sīlavipanno pamādādhikaraṇaṃ mahatiṃ bhogajāniṃ nigacchati, ayaṃ paṭhamo ādīnavo dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, dussīlassa sīlavipannassa pāpako kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, ayaṃ dutiyo ādīnavo dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, dussīlo sīlavipanno [M 3.0197] yaññadeva parisaṃ upasaṅkamati yadi khattiyaparisaṃ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṃ yadi gahapatiparisaṃ yadi samaṇaparisaṃ, avisārado upasaṅkamati maṅkubhūto, ayaṃ tatiyo ādīnavo dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, dussīlo sīlavipanno sammūḷho kālaṃ karoti, ayaṃ catuttho ādīnavo dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, dussīlo sīlavipanno kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati, ayaṃ pañcamo ādīnavo dussīlassa sīlavipattiyā.

There are five drawbacks for one who is immoral, due to failure in virtue. Here, friends, an immoral person who has failed in virtue, on account of heedlessness, incurs a great loss of wealth. This is the first drawback for one who is immoral, due to failure in virtue. Furthermore, friends, a bad reputation spreads about an immoral person who has failed in virtue. This is the second drawback for one who is immoral, due to failure in virtue. Furthermore, friends, whatever assembly an immoral person who has failed in virtue approaches—be it an assembly of nobles, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—he approaches it timidly and crestfallen. This is the third drawback for one who is immoral, due to failure in virtue. Furthermore, friends, an immoral person who has failed in virtue dies confused. This is the fourth drawback for one who is immoral, due to failure in virtue. Furthermore, friends, an immoral person who has failed in virtue, after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a downfall, in hell. This is the fifth drawback for one who is immoral, due to failure in virtue.

“Pañca ānisaṃsā sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Idhāvuso, sīlavā sīlasampanno appamādādhikaraṇaṃ mahantaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ adhigacchati, ayaṃ paṭhamo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, sīlavato sīlasampannassa kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchati, ayaṃ dutiyo [T 3.0249] ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, sīlavā sīlasampanno yaññadeva parisaṃ upasaṅkamati yadi khattiyaparisaṃ yadi brāhmaṇaparisaṃ yadi gahapatiparisaṃ yadi samaṇaparisaṃ, visārado upasaṅkamati amaṅkubhūto, ayaṃ tatiyo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, sīlavā sīlasampanno asammūḷho kālaṃ karoti, ayaṃ catuttho ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, sīlavā sīlasampanno kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati, ayaṃ pañcamo ānisaṃso sīlavato sīlasampadāya.

There are five benefits for one who is virtuous, due to accomplishment in virtue. Here, friends, a virtuous person who is accomplished in virtue, on account of heedfulness, acquires a great mass of wealth. This is the first benefit for one who is virtuous, due to accomplishment in virtue. Furthermore, friends, a good reputation spreads about a virtuous person who is accomplished in virtue. This is the second benefit for one who is virtuous, due to accomplishment in virtue. Furthermore, friends, whatever assembly a virtuous person who is accomplished in virtue approaches—be it an assembly of nobles, an assembly of brahmins, an assembly of householders, or an assembly of ascetics—he approaches it confidently and not crestfallen. This is the third benefit for one who is virtuous, due to accomplishment in virtue. Furthermore, friends, a virtuous person who is accomplished in virtue dies unconfused. This is the fourth benefit for one who is virtuous, due to accomplishment in virtue. Furthermore, friends, a virtuous person who is accomplished in virtue, after the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This is the fifth benefit for one who is virtuous, due to accomplishment in virtue.

“Codakena[V 3.0189], āvuso, bhikkhunā paraṃ codetukāmena pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā paro codetabbo. Kālena vakkhāmi no akālena, bhūtena vakkhāmi no abhūtena, saṇhena vakkhāmi no pharusena, atthasaṃhitena [P 3.0237] vakkhāmi no anatthasaṃhitena, mettacittena mettācittena (katthaci) vakkhāmi no dosantarenāti. Codakena, āvuso, bhikkhunā paraṃ codetukāmena ime pañca dhamme ajjhattaṃ upaṭṭhapetvā paro codetabbo.

Friends, a monk who wishes to admonish another should establish five qualities within himself before admonishing another: ‘I will speak at the right time, not at the wrong time; I will speak with what is true, not with what is untrue; I will speak gently, not harshly; I will speak with what is beneficial, not with what is unbeneficial; I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner aversion.’ Friends, a monk who wishes to admonish another should establish these five qualities within himself before admonishing another.

317. “Pañca [M 3.0198] padhāniyaṅgāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saddho hoti, saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato, lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti. Appābādho hoti appātaṅko, samavepākiniyā [T 3.0250] gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya. Asaṭho hoti amāyāvī, yathābhūtaṃ attānaṃ āvikattā satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu. Āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. Paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammādukkhakkhayagāminiyā.

317. There are five factors for striving. Here, friends, a bhikkhu is faithful; he has faith in the Tathāgata's enlightenment: ‘Thus is the Blessed One an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Fortunate One, a Knower of the World, an Unsurpassed Trainer of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, an Enlightened One, a Blessed One.’ He is without illness, without affliction, endowed with a digestive power that is well-balanced, neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and suitable for striving. He is not deceitful or fraudulent; he reveals himself as he truly is to the Teacher, or to the wise, or to his companions in the holy life. He dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the burden in wholesome states. He is wise, endowed with wisdom that comprehends arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.

318. “Pañca suddhāvāsā – avihā, atappā, sudassā, sudassī, akaniṭṭhā.

318. There are five Pure Abodes: Avihā, Atappā, Sudassā, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭhā.

“Pañca anāgāmino – antarāparinibbāyī, upahaccaparinibbāyī, asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī, uddhaṃsotoakaniṭṭhagāmī.

There are five kinds of non-returners: one who attains parinibbāna in the interval, one who attains parinibbāna after passing the middle of the lifespan, one who attains parinibbāna without exertion, one who attains parinibbāna with exertion, and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.

319. “Pañca cetokhilā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari kaṅkhati [P 3.0238] vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya, yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya, ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhilo. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu dhamme kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… saṅghe kaṅkhati vicikicchati… sikkhāya kaṅkhati vicikicchati… sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu [T 3.0251] sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya, yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya, ayaṃ pañcamo cetokhilo.

319. There are five barrennesses of mind. Here, friends, a bhikkhu doubts and is uncertain about the Teacher, is not resolved, and is not confident. Friends, for whichever bhikkhu doubts and is uncertain about the Teacher, is not resolved, and is not confident, his mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion. For one whose mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion, this is the first barrenness of mind. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu doubts and is uncertain about the Dhamma… doubts and is uncertain about the Saṅgha… doubts and is uncertain about the training… is angry with his companions in the holy life, is displeased, has a mind that is hurt, and has become barren. Friends, for whichever bhikkhu is angry with his companions in the holy life, is displeased, has a mind that is hurt, and has become barren, his mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion. For one whose mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion, this is the fifth barrenness of mind.

320. “Pañca [V 3.0190] cetasovinibandhā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāmesu avītarāgo hoti avigatacchando avigatapemo avigatapipāso avigatapariḷāho [M 3.0199] avigatataṇho. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu kāmesu avītarāgo hoti avigatacchando avigatapemo avigatapipāso avigatapariḷāho avigatataṇho, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Ayaṃ paṭhamo cetaso vinibandho. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kāye avītarāgo hoti…pe… rūpe avītarāgo hoti…pe… puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu yāvadatthaṃ udarāvadehakaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhaṃ passasukhaṃ middhasukhaṃ anuyutto viharati…pe… puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu [P 3.0239] aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati – ‘imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā’ti. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati – ‘imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā’ti, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya [T 3.0252] padhānāya. Ayaṃ pañcamo cetaso vinibandho.

320. There are five bonds of the mind. Here, friends, a bhikkhu is not free from passion for sensual pleasures; his desire has not departed, his affection has not departed, his thirst has not departed, his torment has not departed, his craving has not departed. Friends, for whichever bhikkhu is not free from passion for sensual pleasures, whose desire has not departed, whose affection has not departed, whose thirst has not departed, whose torment has not departed, whose craving has not departed, his mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion. For one whose mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion, this is the first bond of the mind. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is not free from passion for the body… is not free from passion for form… Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, having eaten to his belly's fill, dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining on his side, and the pleasure of drowsiness… Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu practices the holy life aspiring to some group of devas, thinking: ‘By this virtue or observance or austerity or holy life, I will become a deva or one of the devas.’ Friends, for whichever bhikkhu practices the holy life aspiring to some group of devas, thinking: ‘By this virtue or observance or austerity or holy life, I will become a deva or one of the devas,’ his mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion. For one whose mind does not incline toward ardency, dedication, perseverance, and exertion, this is the fifth bond of the mind.

“Pañcindriyāni – cakkhundriyaṃ, sotindriyaṃ, ghānindriyaṃ, jivhindriyaṃ, kāyindriyaṃ.

There are five faculties: the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty.

“Aparānipi pañcindriyāni – sukhindriyaṃ, dukkhindriyaṃ, somanassindriyaṃ, domanassindriyaṃ, upekkhindriyaṃ.

There are another five faculties: the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of gladness, the faculty of sadness, and the faculty of equanimity.

“Aparānipi pañcindriyāni – saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ.

There are another five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.

321. “Pañca nissaraṇiyā nissāraṇīyā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) ṭīkā oloketabbā dhātuyo. Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāme manasikaroto kāmesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Nekkhammaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto nekkhamme cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ [P 3.0240] subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ kāmehi. Ye ca kāmapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā vighātapariḷāhā (syā. kaṃ.), mutto so tehi, na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

321. There are five elements of escape. Here, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to sensual pleasures, his mind does not leap forward into sensual pleasures, does not become serene, does not become established, and is not liberated. But when he attends to renunciation, his mind leaps forward into renunciation, becomes serene, becomes established, and is liberated. His mind is thus well-gone, well-developed, well-risen, well-liberated, and disjoined from sensual pleasures. And whatever taints, distresses, and torments arise on account of sensual pleasures, he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling. This is declared as the escape from sensual pleasures.

“Puna [M 3.0200] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno byāpādaṃ manasikaroto byāpāde cittaṃ na pakkhandati na [V 3.0191] pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Abyāpādaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto abyāpāde cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ byāpādena. Ye ca byāpādapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi, na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ byāpādassa [T 3.0253] nissaraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to ill will, his mind does not leap forward into ill will, does not become serene, is not established, and is not liberated. But when he attends to non-ill will, his mind leaps forward into non-ill will, becomes serene, is established, and is liberated. His mind is thus well-gone, well-developed, well-risen, well-liberated, and disjoined from ill will. And whatever taints, distresses, and torments arise on account of ill will, he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling. This is declared as the escape from ill will.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno vihesaṃ manasikaroto vihesāya cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Avihesaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto avihesāya cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ vihesāya. Ye ca vihesāpaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi, na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ vihesāya nissaraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to vexation, his mind does not enter into vexation, does not become serene, is not established, and is not released. But when he attends to non-vexation, his mind enters into non-vexation, becomes serene, is established, and is released. That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-risen, well-freed from vexation, and disassociated from vexation. And whatever taints, distress, and torments arise on account of vexation, he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from vexation.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno rūpe manasikaroto rūpesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Arūpaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto arūpe cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ rūpehi. Ye ca rūpapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi, na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to form, his mind does not enter into forms, does not become serene, is not established, and is not released. But when he attends to the immaterial, his mind enters into the immaterial, becomes serene, is established, and is released. That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-risen, well-freed from forms, and disassociated from forms. And whatever taints, distress, and torments arise on account of form, he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from forms.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno sakkāyaṃ manasikaroto sakkāye cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Sakkāyanirodhaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto sakkāyanirodhe cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ sakkāyena. Ye ca sakkāyapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so [P 3.0241] tehi, na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ sakkāyassa nissaraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to embodied identity, his mind does not enter into embodied identity, does not become serene, is not established, and is not released. But when he attends to the cessation of embodied identity, his mind enters into the cessation of embodied identity, becomes serene, is established, and is released. That mind of his is well-gone, well-developed, well-risen, well-freed from embodied identity, and disassociated from embodied identity. And whatever taints, distress, and torments arise on account of embodied identity, he is freed from them; he does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from embodied identity.

322. “Pañca [T 3.0254] vimuttāyatanāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī[M 3.0201]. Tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthapaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthapaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

322. There are five grounds for liberation. Here, friends, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or a fellow practitioner worthy of respect does. In whatever way, friends, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or a fellow practitioner worthy of respect does, in that same way he comes to experience the meaning and the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, gladness is born. For one who is gladdened, rapture is born. For one of rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the first ground for liberation.

“Puna [V 3.0192] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, api ca kho yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti…pe… api ca kho yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti…pe… api ca kho yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati…pe… [P 3.0242] api ca khvassa aññataraṃ samādhinimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ paññāya. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhuno aññataraṃ samādhinimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ paññāya tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthapaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthapaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti[P 3.0243], sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor does a respected fellow practitioner... but he teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard and learned it... or he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard and learned it... or he reflects on, considers, and mentally examines the Dhamma as he has heard and learned it... or a certain sign of concentration has been well-grasped by him, well-attended to, well-considered, and well-penetrated with wisdom. In whatever way, friends, a certain sign of concentration has been well-grasped by the bhikkhu, well-attended to, well-considered, and well-penetrated with wisdom, in that same way he comes to experience the meaning and the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, gladness is born. For one who is gladdened, rapture is born. For one of rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the fifth ground for liberation.

“Pañca [T 3.0255] vimuttiparipācanīyā saññā – aniccasaññā, anicce dukkhasaññā, dukkhe anattasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā.

There are five perceptions conducive to the ripening of liberation: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, and the perception of dispassion.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena pañca dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ saṅgitiyapañcakaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ (syā. kaṃ.).

These, friends, are the five principles well expounded by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, all should chant together... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans.

Chakkaṃ

The Sixes

323. “Atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cha dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame cha?

323. Friends, there are six principles well-expounded by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, all should chant together... for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. What are the six?

“Cha ajjhattikāni [M 3.0202] āyatanāni – cakkhāyatanaṃ, sotāyatanaṃ, ghānāyatanaṃ, jivhāyatanaṃ, kāyāyatanaṃ, manāyatanaṃ.

Six internal sense bases: the eye-base, the ear-base, the nose-base, the tongue-base, the body-base, and the mind-base.

“Cha bāhirāni āyatanāni – rūpāyatanaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ, gandhāyatanaṃ, rasāyatanaṃ, phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ, dhammāyatanaṃ.

Six external sense bases: the form-base, the sound-base, the odor-base, the taste-base, the tangible-object-base, and the mind-object-base.

“Cha [V 3.0193] viññāṇakāyā – cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, sotaviññāṇaṃ, ghānaviññāṇaṃ, jivhāviññāṇaṃ, kāyaviññāṇaṃ, manoviññāṇaṃ.

Six groups of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.

“Cha phassakāyā – cakkhusamphasso, sotasamphasso, ghānasamphasso, jivhāsamphasso, kāyasamphasso, manosamphasso.

Six groups of contact: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.

“Cha vedanākāyā – cakkhusamphassajā vedanā, sotasamphassajā [P 3.0244] vedanā, ghānasamphassajā vedanā, jivhāsamphassajā vedanā, kāyasamphassajā vedanā, manosamphassajā vedanā.

Six groups of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, and feeling born of mind-contact.

“Cha saññākāyā – rūpasaññā, saddasaññā, gandhasaññā, rasasaññā, phoṭṭhabbasaññā, dhammasaññā.

Six groups of perception: perception of form, perception of sound, perception of odor, perception of taste, perception of tangible objects, and perception of mind-objects.

“Cha sañcetanākāyā – rūpasañcetanā, saddasañcetanā, gandhasañcetanā, rasasañcetanā, phoṭṭhabbasañcetanā, dhammasañcetanā.

Six groups of volition: volition regarding form, volition regarding sound, volition regarding odor, volition regarding taste, volition regarding tangible objects, and volition regarding mind-objects.

“Cha [T 3.0256] taṇhākāyā – rūpataṇhā, saddataṇhā, gandhataṇhā, rasataṇhā, phoṭṭhabbataṇhā, dhammataṇhā.

Six groups of craving: craving for form, craving for sound, craving for odor, craving for taste, craving for tangible objects, and craving for mind-objects.

324. “Cha agāravā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso; dhamme agāravo viharati appatisso; saṅghe agāravo viharati appatisso; sikkhāya agāravo viharati appatisso; appamāde agāravo viharati appatisso; paṭisanthāre paṭisandhāre (ka.) agāravo viharati appatisso.

324. Six kinds of disrespect. Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells without respect and without deference for the Teacher; he dwells without respect and without deference for the Dhamma; he dwells without respect and without deference for the Saṅgha; he dwells without respect and without deference for the training; he dwells without respect and without deference for diligence; he dwells without respect and without deference for hospitality.

“Cha gāravā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari sagāravo viharati sappatisso; dhamme sagāravo viharati sappatisso; saṅghe sagāravo viharati sappatisso; sikkhāya sagāravo viharati sappatisso; appamāde sagāravo viharati sappatisso; paṭisanthāre sagāravo viharati sappatisso.

Six kinds of respect. Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with respect and with deference for the Teacher; he dwells with respect and with deference for the Dhamma; he dwells with respect and with deference for the Saṅgha; he dwells with respect and with deference for the training; he dwells with respect and with deference for diligence; he dwells with respect and with deference for hospitality.

“Cha somanassūpavicārā[M 3.0203]. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicarati; sotena [V 3.0194] saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā. Manasā dhammaṃ viññāya somanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ dhammaṃ upavicarati.

Six investigations accompanied by joy. Having seen a form with the eye, one investigates a form that is a basis for joy; having heard a sound with the ear... having smelled an odor with the nose... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having touched a tangible object with the body... having cognized a mind-object with the mind, one investigates a mind-object that is a basis for joy.

“Cha [T 3.0257][P 3.0245] domanassūpavicārā. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā domanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ rūpaṃ upavicarati…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya domanassaṭṭhāniyaṃ dhammaṃ upavicarati.

Six investigations accompanied by displeasure. Having seen a form with the eye, one investigates a form that is a basis for displeasure... having cognized a mind-object with the mind, one investigates a mind-object that is a basis for displeasure.

“Cha upekkhūpavicārā. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ upekkhāṭhāniyaṃ (ka.) rūpaṃ upavicarati…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ dhammaṃ upavicarati.

Six investigations accompanied by equanimity. Having seen a form with the eye, one investigates a form that is a basis for equanimity... having cognized a mind-object with the mind, one investigates a mind-object that is a basis for equanimity.

“Cha sāraṇīyā dhammā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi āvī (ka. sī. pī. ka.) ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Six states to be remembered. Here, friends, a bhikkhu's bodily action accompanied by loving-kindness is established towards his fellow monastics, both openly and in private. This dhamma is also one to be remembered, creating affection, creating respect, and conducing to cohesion, non-dispute, harmony, and unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu's verbal action accompanied by loving-kindness is established towards his fellow monastics, both openly and in private. This dhamma is also one to be remembered... conducing to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno mettaṃ manokammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu's mental action accompanied by loving-kindness is established towards his fellow monastics, both openly and in private. This dhamma is also one to be remembered... conducing to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu ye te lābhā dhammikā dhammaladdhā antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampi, tathārūpehi lābhehi appaṭivibhattabhogī hoti sīlavantehi sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogī. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, whatever gains a bhikkhu has that are righteous and righteously obtained, even down to the contents of his alms-bowl, he is one who enjoys them without division, sharing them in common with his virtuous fellow monastics. This dhamma is also one to be remembered... conducing to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni, tathārūpesu sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato viharati [P 3.0246] sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, with regard to those virtues that are unbroken, unflawed, unspotted, unblemished, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and conducive to concentration, a bhikkhu dwells in commonality of virtue with his fellow monastics, both openly and in private. This dhamma is also one to be remembered... conducing to unity.

“Puna [M 3.0204] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tathārūpāya [T 3.0258] diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhisāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva [V 3.0195] raho ca. Ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, with regard to that view that is noble and emancipating, which leads one who acts accordingly to the complete destruction of suffering, a bhikkhu dwells in commonality of view with his fellow monastics, both openly and in private. This dhamma is also one to be remembered, creating affection, creating respect, and conducing to cohesion, non-dispute, harmony, and unity.

325. Cha vivādamūlāni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti upanāhī. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu kodhano hoti upanāhī, so sattharipi agāravo viharati appatisso, dhammepi agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghepi agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāyapi na paripūrakārī paripūrīkārī (syā. kaṃ.) hoti. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso, dhamme agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghe agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāya na paripūrakārī, so saṅghe vivādaṃ janeti. Yo hoti vivādo bahujanaahitāya bahujanaasukhāya anatthāya ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe, āvuso, vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā samanupasseyyātha. Tatra tumhe, āvuso, tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānāya vāyameyyātha. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe, āvuso, vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā na samanupasseyyātha. Tatra tumhe, āvuso, tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavāya paṭipajjeyyātha. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānaṃ hoti. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavo hoti.

325. Six roots of disputes. Here, friends, a bhikkhu is wrathful and bears a grudge. That bhikkhu, friends, who is wrathful and bears a grudge dwells without reverence or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training. That bhikkhu, friends, who dwells without reverence or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training, creates disputes in the Saṅgha. That dispute is for the harm and unhappiness of many people, for the non-benefit, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. If you, friends, perceive such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then you, friends, should strive for the abandoning of that same evil root of dispute. If you, friends, do not perceive such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then you, friends, should practice for the non-arising in the future of that same evil root of dispute. Thus there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute. Thus there is its non-arising in the future.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu makkhī hoti paḷāsī…pe… issukī hoti maccharī…pe… saṭho hoti māyāvī… pāpiccho hoti micchādiṭṭhī… sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī [T 3.0259][P 3.0247] hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī…pe… yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu sandiṭṭhiparāmāsī hoti ādhānaggāhī duppaṭinissaggī, so sattharipi agāravo viharati appatisso, dhammepi agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghepi agāravo viharati appatisso, sikkhāyapi na paripūrakārī hoti. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso, dhamme agāravo viharati appatisso, saṅghe agāravo viharati appatisso[M 3.0205], sikkhāya na paripūrakārī, so saṅghe vivādaṃ janeti. Yo hoti vivādo bahujanaahitāya bahujanaasukhāya anatthāya ahitāya dukkhāya devamanussānaṃ. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe, āvuso, vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā samanupasseyyātha. Tatra tumhe, āvuso, tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānāya vāyameyyātha. Evarūpaṃ ce tumhe, āvuso, vivādamūlaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā na samanupasseyyātha. Tatra tumhe, āvuso, tasseva pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavāya paṭipajjeyyātha. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa pahānaṃ hoti. Evametassa pāpakassa vivādamūlassa āyatiṃ anavassavo hoti.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is disparaging and rivalrous… is envious and stingy… is crafty and deceitful… has evil desires… clings to his own views, holds to them tenaciously, and relinquishes them with difficulty. That bhikkhu, friends, who clings to his own views, holds to them tenaciously, and relinquishes them with difficulty, dwells without reverence or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training. That bhikkhu, friends, who dwells without reverence or deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and does not fulfill the training, creates disputes in the Saṅgha. That dispute is for the harm and unhappiness of many people, for the non-benefit, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. If you, friends, perceive such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then you, friends, should strive for the abandoning of that same evil root of dispute. If you, friends, do not perceive such a root of dispute either internally or externally, then you, friends, should practice for the non-recurrence in the future of that same evil root of dispute. Thus there is the abandoning of this evil root of dispute. Thus there is its non-recurrence in the future.

“Cha dhātuyo [V 3.0196] – pathavīdhātu, āpodhātu, tejodhātu, vāyodhātu, ākāsadhātu, viññāṇadhātu.

There are six elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

326. “Cha nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘mettā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā [P 3.0248] yānīkatā vatthukatā [T 3.0260] anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, atha ca pana me byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So ‘mā hevaṃ’, tissa vacanīyo, ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso, yaṃ mettāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya. Atha ca panassa byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa, yadidaṃ mettā cetovimuttī’ti.

326. There are six elements that lead to escape. Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, practiced it frequently, made it a vehicle, made it a foundation, established it, become familiar with it, and undertaken it well. And yet, ill will still overcomes my mind and remains.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say so, venerable sir. Do not speak thus. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus. It is impossible, friends, it cannot be, that when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, practiced frequently, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, become familiar with, and undertaken well, ill will would still overcome his mind and remain. That situation does not exist. For this, friends, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness.’

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘karuṇā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Atha ca pana me vihesā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti, so ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ āvuso, anavakāso, yaṃ karuṇāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya [M 3.0206] anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya, atha ca panassa vihesā cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, vihesāya, yadidaṃ karuṇā cetovimuttī’ti.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through compassion, practiced it frequently, made it a vehicle, made it a foundation, established it, become familiar with it, and undertaken it well. And yet, cruelty still overcomes my mind and remains.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say so, venerable sir. Do not speak thus. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus. It is impossible, friends, it cannot be, that when the liberation of mind through compassion has been developed, practiced frequently, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, become familiar with, and undertaken well, cruelty would still overcome his mind and remain. That situation does not exist. For this, friends, is the escape from cruelty, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion.’

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘muditā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Atha ca pana me [T 3.0261] arati cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti, so ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo “māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso, yaṃ muditāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya [P 3.0249] anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya, atha ca panassa arati cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, aratiyā, yadidaṃ muditā cetovimuttī’ti.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy, practiced it frequently, made it a vehicle, made it a foundation, established it, become familiar with it, and undertaken it well. And yet, discontent still overcomes my mind and remains.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say so, venerable sir. Do not speak thus. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus. It is impossible, friends, it cannot be, that when the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy has been developed, practiced frequently, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, become familiar with, and undertaken well, discontent would still overcome his mind and remain. That situation does not exist. For this, friends, is the escape from discontent, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy.’

“Idha [V 3.0197] panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘upekkhā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Atha ca pana me rāgo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso, yaṃ upekkhāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya, atha ca panassa rāgo cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, rāgassa, yadidaṃ upekkhā cetovimuttī’ti.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through equanimity, practiced it frequently, made it a vehicle, made it a foundation, established it, become familiar with it, and undertaken it well. And yet, lust still overcomes my mind and remains.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say so, venerable sir. Do not speak thus. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak thus. It is impossible, friends, it cannot be, that when the liberation of mind through equanimity has been developed, practiced frequently, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, become familiar with, and undertaken well, lust would still overcome his mind and remain. That situation does not exist. For this, friends, is the escape from lust, namely, the liberation of mind through equanimity.’

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘animittā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Atha ca pana me nimittānusāri viññāṇaṃ hotī’ti. So ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa [T 3.0262] vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso, yaṃ animittāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya, atha ca panassa nimittānusāri [M 3.0207] viññāṇaṃ bhavissati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, sabbanimittānaṃ, yadidaṃ animittā cetovimuttī’ti.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the signless liberation of mind, cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, repeatedly practiced it, and well undertaken it. Yet, my consciousness still follows after signs.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say so, venerable sir. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say such a thing. It is impossible, friends, it cannot be that when the signless liberation of mind has been developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, repeatedly practiced, and well undertaken, his consciousness would still follow after signs. That situation does not exist. For this, friends, is the escape from all signs: that is, the signless liberation of mind.’

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘asmīti kho me vigataṃ vighātaṃ (sī. pī.), vigate (syā. ka.), ayamahamasmīti na samanupassāmi, atha ca pana me vicikicchākathaṅkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na hi sādhu [P 3.0250] bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso, yaṃ asmīti vigate vighāte (sī. pī.) ayamahamasmīti asamanupassato, atha ca panassa vicikicchākathaṅkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, vicikicchākathaṅkathāsallassa, yadidaṃ asmimānasamugghāto’ti.

Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: 'The thought ‘I am’ has vanished for me, and I do not perceive ‘I am this.’ Yet, the dart of doubt and perplexity still overwhelms my mind and persists.' He should be told: 'Do not say so, venerable sir. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say such a thing. It is impossible, friends, it cannot be that when the thought ‘I am’ has vanished and one does not perceive ‘I am this,’ the dart of doubt and perplexity would overwhelm his mind and persist. That situation does not exist. For this, friends, is the escape from the dart of doubt and perplexity: that is, the uprooting of the conceit ‘I am.’'

327. “Cha anuttariyāni – dassanānuttariyaṃ, savanānuttariyaṃ, lābhānuttariyaṃ, sikkhānuttariyaṃ, pāricariyānuttariyaṃ, anussatānuttariyaṃ.

327. Six unsurpassed things: unsurpassed seeing, unsurpassed hearing, unsurpassed gain, unsurpassed training, unsurpassed service, and unsurpassed recollection.

“Cha anussatiṭṭhānāni [V 3.0198] – buddhānussati, dhammānussati, saṅghānussati, sīlānussati, cāgānussati, devatānussati.

Six grounds for recollection: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the deities.

328. “Cha [T 3.0263] satatavihārā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako upekkhako ca (syā. ka.) viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno.

328. Six constant abidings. Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither gladdened nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear... and so on... Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither gladdened nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending.

329. “Chaḷābhijātiyo. Idhāvuso, ekacco kaṇhābhijātiko [P 3.0251] samāno kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati. Idha panāvuso, ekacco kaṇhābhijātiko samāno sukkaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati. Idha panāvuso, ekacco kaṇhābhijātiko samāno akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ nibbānaṃ abhijāyati. Idha panāvuso, ekacco sukkābhijātiko samāno sukkaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati. Idha panāvuso, ekacco sukkābhijātiko samāno kaṇhaṃ dhammaṃ abhijāyati. Idha panāvuso, ekacco sukkābhijātiko samāno [M 3.0208] akaṇhaṃ asukkaṃ nibbānaṃ abhijāyati.

329. Six kinds of birth. Here, friends, a certain person of dark birth gives rise to a dark state. Here, friends, a certain person of dark birth gives rise to a bright state. Here, friends, a certain person of dark birth gives rise to the neither-dark-nor-bright Nibbāna. Here, friends, a certain person of bright birth gives rise to a bright state. Here, friends, a certain person of bright birth gives rise to a dark state. Here, friends, a certain person of bright birth gives rise to the neither-dark-nor-bright Nibbāna.

“Cha nibbedhabhāgiyā saññā nibbedhabhāgiyasaññā (syā. kaṃ.) – aniccasaññā anicce, dukkhasaññā dukkhe, anattasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā, nirodhasaññā.

Six perceptions conducive to penetration: the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in the impermanent, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena cha dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

These, friends, are the six principles well proclaimed by the Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein, all should chant together... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans.

Sattakaṃ

The Chapter of Sevens

330. “Atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā [T 3.0264] sammāsambuddhena satta dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame satta?

330. There are, friends, seven qualities well proclaimed by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant in unison... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans. What are the seven?

“Satta [V 3.0199] ariyadhanāni – saddhādhanaṃ, sīladhanaṃ, hiridhanaṃ, ottappadhanaṃ, sutadhanaṃ, cāgadhanaṃ, paññādhanaṃ.

The seven noble treasures: the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom.

“Satta bojjhaṅgā – satisambojjhaṅgo, dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo[P 3.0252], vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pītisambojjhaṅgo, passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, samādhisambojjhaṅgo, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo.

The seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

“Satta samādhiparikkhārā – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati.

The seven requisites for concentration: Right View, Right Intention, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, and Right Mindfulness.

“Satta asaddhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu assaddho hoti, ahiriko hoti, anottappī hoti, appassuto hoti, kusīto hoti, muṭṭhassati hoti, duppañño hoti.

The seven ignoble qualities: Here, friends, a bhikkhu is without faith, without moral shame, without moral dread, has little learning, is lazy, is unmindful, and is unwise.

“Satta saddhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu saddho hoti, hirimā hoti, ottappī hoti, bahussuto hoti, āraddhavīriyo hoti, upaṭṭhitassati hoti, paññavā hoti.

The seven noble qualities: Here, friends, a bhikkhu has faith, has moral shame, has moral dread, is learned, has aroused energy, has established mindfulness, and is wise.

“Satta sappurisadhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu dhammaññū ca hoti atthaññū ca attaññū ca mattaññū ca kālaññū ca parisaññū ca puggalaññū ca.

The seven qualities of a true person: Here, friends, a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma, knows the meaning, knows himself, knows the right measure, knows the right time, knows the assembly, and knows individuals.

331. “Satta [M 3.0209] niddasavatthūni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sikkhāsamādāne tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca sikkhāsamādāne avigatapemo. Dhammanisantiyā [T 3.0265] tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca dhammanisantiyā avigatapemo. Icchāvinaye tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca icchāvinaye avigatapemo. Paṭisallāne tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca paṭisallāne avigatapemo. Vīriyārambhe tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca vīriyārambhe avigatapemo. Satinepakke tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca satinepakke avigatapemo[P 3.0253]. Diṭṭhipaṭivedhe tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca diṭṭhipaṭivedhe avigatapemo.

331. Seven grounds for commendation: Here, friends, a bhikkhu has a strong desire for undertaking the training, and in the future has undiminished affection for undertaking the training. He has a strong desire for investigating the Dhamma, and in the future has undiminished affection for investigating the Dhamma. He has a strong desire for the removal of craving, and in the future has undiminished affection for the removal of craving. He has a strong desire for seclusion, and in the future has undiminished affection for seclusion. He has a strong desire for arousing energy, and in the future has undiminished affection for arousing energy. He has a strong desire for mindfulness and prudence, and in the future has undiminished affection for mindfulness and prudence. He has a strong desire for the penetration of right view, and in the future has undiminished affection for the penetration of right view.

“Satta saññā – aniccasaññā, anattasaññā, asubhasaññā, ādīnavasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā, nirodhasaññā.

Seven perceptions: the perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of foulness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation.

“Satta [V 3.0200] balāni – saddhābalaṃ, vīriyabalaṃ, hiribalaṃ, ottappabalaṃ, satibalaṃ, samādhibalaṃ, paññābalaṃ.

Seven powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

332. “Satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo. Santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

332. Seven stations of consciousness. There are, friends, beings diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation. This is the first station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings diverse in body but unified in perception, such as the devas of Brahmā’s retinue who are first reborn there. This is the second station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings unified in body but diverse in perception, such as the devas of Streaming Radiance. This is the third station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catutthī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings unified in body and unified in perception, such as the devas of Refulgent Glory. This is the fourth station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti [T 3.0266] ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ pañcamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the dimension of infinite space. This is the fifth station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ chaṭṭhī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso[M 3.0210], sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ sattamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely transcending the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ have reached the dimension of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness.

“Satta puggalā dakkhiṇeyyā – ubhatobhāgavimutto[P 3.0254], paññāvimutto, kāyasakkhi, diṭṭhippatto, saddhāvimutto, dhammānusārī, saddhānusārī.

Seven persons worthy of offerings: one liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one who has attained the view, one liberated by faith, a Dhamma-follower, and a faith-follower.

“Satta anusayā – kāmarāgānusayo, paṭighānusayo, diṭṭhānusayo, vicikicchānusayo, mānānusayo, bhavarāgānusayo, avijjānusayo.

Seven latent tendencies: the latent tendency of sensual lust, the latent tendency of aversion, the latent tendency of views, the latent tendency of doubt, the latent tendency of conceit, the latent tendency of craving for existence, and the latent tendency of ignorance.

“Satta [V 3.0201] saññojanāni – anunayasaññojanaṃ kāmasaññojanaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), paṭighasaññojanaṃ, diṭṭhisaññojanaṃ, vicikicchāsaññojanaṃ, mānasaññojanaṃ, bhavarāgasaññojanaṃ, avijjāsaññojanaṃ.

Seven fetters: the fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of craving for existence, and the fetter of ignorance.

“Satta adhikaraṇasamathā – uppannuppannānaṃ adhikaraṇānaṃ samathāya vūpasamāya sammukhāvinayo dātabbo, sativinayo dātabbo, amūḷhavinayo dātabbo, paṭiññāya kāretabbaṃ, yebhuyyasikā, tassapāpiyasikā, tiṇavatthārako.

Seven principles for settling disputes: For the settling and pacification of disputes that have arisen, the procedure of being in the presence should be employed, the procedure of mindfulness should be employed, the procedure for one who is no longer confused should be employed, an act should be carried out on admission, a decision by majority, a verdict of misconduct, and the covering over with grass.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena satta dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

These, friends, are the seven qualities well proclaimed by the Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant in unison... for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans.

Dutiyabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The second recitation section is concluded.

Aṭṭhakaṃ

The Eights

333. “Atthi [T 3.0267] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena aṭṭha dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame aṭṭha?

333. Friends, there are eight qualities well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; therein, all should recite in unison… for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans. What are these eight?

“Aṭṭha micchattā – micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchākammanto, micchāājīvo, micchāvāyāmo micchāsati, micchāsamādhi.

Eight wrong states: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.

“Aṭṭha [M 3.0211][P 3.0255] sammattā – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi.

Eight right states: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

“Aṭṭha puggalā dakkhiṇeyyā – sotāpanno, sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno; sakadāgāmī, sakadāgāmiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno; anāgāmī, anāgāmiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno; arahā, arahattaphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipanno.

Eight individuals worthy of offerings: the stream-enterer, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; the once-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; the non-returner, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning; and the arahant, one practicing for the realization of the fruit of arahantship.

334. “Aṭṭha [V 3.0202] kusītavatthūni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kammaṃ kho me kātabbaṃ bhavissati, kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa kāyo kilamissati, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu.

334. Eight grounds for laziness. Here, friends, a bhikkhu has some work to do. He thinks: ‘I will have to do some work, and doing it will tire my body. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy for attaining the unattained, for gaining the ungained, for realizing the unrealized. This is the first ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kataṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ, kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa [T 3.0268] kāyo kilanto, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati…pe… idaṃ dutiyaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has done some work. He thinks: ‘I have done some work, and my body is tired from doing it. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the second ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gantabbo hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilamissati, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ tatiyaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has a journey to make. He thinks: ‘I will have to make a journey, and traveling will tire my body. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the third ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gato hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilanto, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ catutthaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has made a journey. He thinks: ‘I have made a journey, and my body is tired from traveling. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the fourth ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto na labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya [P 3.0256] caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo kilanto akammañño, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ pañcamaṃ kusītavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while walking for alms in a village or town, does not obtain enough coarse or fine food to fill his belly. He thinks: ‘While walking for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain enough coarse or fine food to fill my belly. My body is tired and unfit for work. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the fifth ground for laziness.

“Puna [M 3.0212] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo garuko akammañño, māsācitaṃ maññe[T 3.0269], handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ kusītavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while walking for alms in a village or town, obtains enough coarse or fine food to fill his belly. He thinks: ‘While walking for alms in a village or town, I obtained enough coarse or fine food to fill my belly. My body is heavy and unfit for work; it feels like it is filled with wet beans.
