Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the sixth ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno uppanno hoti appamattako ābādho. Tassa evaṃ hoti [V 3.0203] – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho; atthi kappo nipajjituṃ, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ sattamaṃ kusītavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a minor illness has arisen in a bhikkhu. He thinks: ‘This minor illness has arisen in me; it is suitable to lie down. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the seventh ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gilānā vuṭṭhito gilānavuṭṭhito (saddanīti) a. ni. 6.16 nakulapitusuttaṭīkā passitabbā hoti aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gilānā vuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā, tassa me kāyo dubbalo akammañño, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti! So nipajjati na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recovered from an illness, having recently recovered from his affliction. He thinks: ‘I have recovered from an illness, having recently recovered from my affliction. My body is weak and unfit for work. Now, let me lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized. This is the eighth ground for laziness.

335. “Aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kammaṃ kho me kātabbaṃ bhavissati, kammaṃ kho pana me karontena na sukaraṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya, asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāyā’ti! So vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā, anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

335. “Eight grounds for arousing energy. Here, friends, a bhikkhu has some work to do. He thinks: ‘I will have to do some work. While doing the work, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Now, let me arouse energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized.’ So he arouses energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized. This is the first ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ [P 3.0257] kataṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ, kammaṃ kho panāhaṃ karonto nāsakkhiṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… so [T 3.0270] vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ dutiyaṃ ārambhavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has done some work. He thinks: ‘I have done some work, but while doing it, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Now, let me arouse energy…’ So he arouses energy… This is the second ground for arousing energy.

“Puna [M 3.0213] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gantabbo hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantena na sukaraṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ. Handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… so vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ tatiyaṃ ārambhavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has a journey to make. He thinks: ‘I will have to make a journey, and while traveling, it will not be easy for me to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Now, let me arouse energy…’ So he arouses energy… This is the third ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gato hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ, maggaṃ kho panāhaṃ gacchanto nāsakkhiṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasi kātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… so vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ catutthaṃ ārambhavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has made a journey. He thinks: ‘I have made a journey. While traveling, I was unable to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Now, let me arouse energy…’ So he arouses energy… This is the fourth ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto na labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ[V 3.0204]. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo lahuko kammañño, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… so vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ pañcamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while walking for alms in a village or town, does not obtain enough coarse or fine food to fill his belly. He thinks: ‘While walking for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain enough coarse or fine food to fill my belly. My body is light and fit for work. Now, let me arouse energy…’ So he arouses energy… This is the fifth ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo balavā kammañño, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… so vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ ārambhavatthu[T 3.0271].

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while walking for alms in a village or town, obtains enough coarse or fine food to fill his belly. He thinks: ‘While walking for alms in a village or town, I obtained enough coarse or fine food to fill my belly. My body is strong and fit for work. Now, let me arouse energy…’ So he arouses energy… This is the sixth ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno uppanno hoti appamattako ābādho. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati yaṃ me ābādho pavaḍḍheyya, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… so vīriyaṃ ārabhati… idaṃ [P 3.0258] sattamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a minor illness has arisen in a bhikkhu. He thinks: ‘This minor illness has arisen in me. There is a possibility that my illness might worsen. Now, let me arouse energy…’ So he arouses energy… This is the seventh ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gilānā vuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati yaṃ me ābādho paccudāvatteyya, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāyā”ti! So vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā [M 3.0214] anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recovered from an illness, having recently recovered from his affliction. He thinks: ‘I have recovered from an illness, having recently recovered from my affliction. There is a possibility that my illness might return. Now, let me arouse energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized!’ So he arouses energy for attaining the unattained, for achieving the unachieved, for realizing the unrealized. This is the eighth ground for arousing energy.

336. “Aṭṭha dānavatthūni. Āsajja dānaṃ deti, bhayā dānaṃ deti, ‘adāsi me’ti dānaṃ deti, ‘dassati me’ti dānaṃ deti, ‘sāhu dāna’nti dānaṃ deti, ‘ahaṃ pacāmi, ime na pacanti, nārahāmi pacanto apacantānaṃ dānaṃ na dātu’nti dānaṃ deti, ‘idaṃ me dānaṃ dadato kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggacchatī’ti dānaṃ deti. Cittālaṅkāra-cittaparikkhāratthaṃ dānaṃ deti.

336. There are eight grounds for giving. One gives a gift upon being approached. One gives a gift out of fear. One gives a gift thinking, ‘He gave to me.’ One gives a gift thinking, ‘He will give to me.’ One gives a gift thinking, ‘Giving is good.’ One gives a gift thinking, ‘I cook, but these others do not cook; it is not proper for me, who cooks, not to give to those who do not cook.’ One gives a gift thinking, ‘By giving this gift, a good report of my fame will spread.’ One gives a gift for the adornment and equipment of the mind.

337. “Aṭṭha dānūpapattiyo. Idhāvuso, ekacco dānaṃ deti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ yānaṃ mālāgandhavilepanaṃ seyyāvasathapadīpeyyaṃ. So yaṃ deti taṃ paccāsīsati paccāsiṃsati (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). So passati [T 3.0272] khattiyamahāsālaṃ vā brāhmaṇamahāsālaṃ vā gahapatimahāsālaṃ vā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitaṃ samaṅgībhūtaṃ paricārayamānaṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa [V 3.0205] bhedā paraṃ maraṇā khattiyamahāsālānaṃ vā brāhmaṇamahāsālānaṃ vā gahapatimahāsālānaṃ vā sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti! So taṃ cittaṃ dahati, taṃ cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, taṃ cittaṃ bhāveti, tassa taṃ cittaṃ hīne vimuttaṃ uttari abhāvitaṃ tatrūpapattiyā saṃvattati[P 3.0259]. Tañca kho sīlavato vadāmi no dussīlassa. Ijjhatāvuso, sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā.

337. There are eight kinds of rebirth resulting from giving. Here, friends, a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin: food, drink, clothing, a vehicle, garlands, scents, and ointments, a bed, a dwelling, and a lamp. What he gives, he hopes for in return. He sees wealthy nobles, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders furnished and endowed with, and enjoying, the five strands of sensual pleasure. To him, this thought occurs: ‘Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of wealthy nobles, wealthy brahmins, or wealthy householders!’ He establishes that thought, resolves upon that thought, and develops that thought. That thought of his, being inclined towards the inferior and not developed for what is higher, conduces to rebirth there. And this, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is unvirtuous. Friends, the aspiration of the virtuous succeeds on account of its purity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, idhekacco dānaṃ deti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā annaṃ pānaṃ…pe… seyyāvasathapadīpeyyaṃ. So yaṃ deti taṃ paccāsīsati. Tassa sutaṃ hoti – ‘cātumahārājikā cātummahārājikā (sī. syā. pī.) devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā”ti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā cātumahārājikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”nti! So taṃ cittaṃ dahati, taṃ cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, taṃ cittaṃ bhāveti, tassa taṃ cittaṃ hīne vimuttaṃ uttari abhāvitaṃ tatrūpapattiyā saṃvattati. Tañca kho sīlavato vadāmi no dussīlassa. Ijjhatāvuso, sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā.

Furthermore, friends, here a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin: food, drink… a bed, a dwelling, and a lamp. What he gives, he hopes for in return. He has heard: ‘The devas of the realm of the Four Great Kings are long-lived, beautiful, and have abundant happiness.’ To him, this thought occurs: ‘Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of the devas of the realm of the Four Great Kings!’ He establishes that thought, resolves upon that thought, and develops that thought. That thought of his, being inclined towards the inferior and not developed for what is higher, conduces to rebirth there. And this, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is unvirtuous. Friends, the aspiration of the virtuous succeeds on account of its purity.

“Puna [M 3.0215] caparaṃ, āvuso, idhekacco dānaṃ deti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā annaṃ pānaṃ…pe… seyyāvasathapadīpeyyaṃ. So yaṃ deti taṃ paccāsīsati. Tassa sutaṃ hoti – ‘tāvatiṃsā devā…pe… yāmā devā…pe… tusitā devā [T 3.0273] …pe… nimmānaratī devā…pe… paranimmitavasavattī devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā’ti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā paranimmitavasavattīnaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya”nti! So taṃ cittaṃ dahati, taṃ cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, taṃ cittaṃ bhāveti, tassa taṃ cittaṃ hīne vimuttaṃ uttari abhāvitaṃ tatrūpapattiyā saṃvattati. Tañca kho sīlavato vadāmi no dussīlassa. Ijjhatāvuso, sīlavato cetopaṇidhi visuddhattā.

Furthermore, friends, here a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin: food, drink… a bed, a dwelling, and a lamp. What he gives, he hopes for in return. He has heard: ‘The Tāvatiṃsa devas… the Yāma devas… the Tusita devas… the Nimmānaratī devas… the Paranimmitavasavattī devas are long-lived, beautiful, and have abundant happiness.’ To him, this thought occurs: ‘Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavattī devas!’ He establishes that thought, resolves upon that thought, and develops that thought. That thought of his, being inclined towards the inferior and not developed for what is higher, conduces to rebirth there. And this, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is unvirtuous. Friends, the aspiration of the virtuous succeeds on account of its purity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, idhekacco dānaṃ deti samaṇassa vā brāhmaṇassa vā annaṃ pānaṃ vatthaṃ yānaṃ mālāgandhavilepanaṃ seyyāvasathapadīpeyyaṃ. So yaṃ deti taṃ paccāsīsati. Tassa sutaṃ hoti – ‘brahmakāyikā devā dīghāyukā vaṇṇavanto sukhabahulā’ti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘aho vatāhaṃ kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā brahmakāyikānaṃ devānaṃ sahabyataṃ upapajjeyya’nti! So taṃ cittaṃ dahati, taṃ cittaṃ adhiṭṭhāti, taṃ cittaṃ bhāveti, tassa taṃ cittaṃ hīne vimuttaṃ uttari abhāvitaṃ tatrūpapattiyā saṃvattati. Tañca kho sīlavato [P 3.0260] vadāmi no dussīlassa; vītarāgassa no sarāgassa. Ijjhatāvuso, sīlavato cetopaṇidhi vītarāgattā.

Furthermore, friends, here a certain person gives a gift to a recluse or a brahmin: food, drink, clothing, a vehicle, garlands, scents, and ointments, a bed, a dwelling, and a lamp. What he gives, he hopes for in return. He has heard: ‘The devas of the Brahmā world are long-lived, beautiful, and have abundant happiness.’ To him, this thought occurs: ‘Oh, that on the dissolution of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of the devas of the Brahmā world!’ He establishes that thought, resolves upon that thought, and develops that thought. That thought of his, being inclined towards the inferior and not developed for what is higher, conduces to rebirth there. And this, I say, is for one who is virtuous, not for one who is unvirtuous; for one free from passion, not for one with passion. Friends, the aspiration of the virtuous succeeds on account of freedom from passion.

“Aṭṭha [V 3.0206] parisā – khattiyaparisā, brāhmaṇaparisā, gahapatiparisā, samaṇaparisā, cātumahārājikaparisā, tāvatiṃsaparisā, māraparisā, brahmaparisā[T 3.0274].

Eight assemblies: the assembly of nobles, the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of recluses, the assembly of the devas of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the assembly of Māra, and the assembly of Brahmā.

“Aṭṭha lokadhammā – lābho ca, alābho ca, yaso ca, ayaso ca, nindā ca, pasaṃsā ca, sukhañca, dukkhañca.

Eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disgrace, censure and praise, pleasure and pain.

338. “Aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni. Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

338. There are eight spheres of mastery. Perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms, limited, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the first sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ [M 3.0216] rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti – evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms, immeasurable, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the second sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms, limited, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the third sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ catutthaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms, immeasurable, of good and bad color. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the fourth sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma umāpupphaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ. Evameva evamevaṃ (ka.) ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni [P 3.0261] nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—blue, of blue color, with a blue appearance, and a blue radiance. Just as a flax flower is blue, of blue color, with a blue appearance, and a blue radiance, or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is blue, of blue color, with a blue appearance, and a blue radiance; even so, not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—blue, of blue color, with a blue appearance, and a blue radiance. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the fifth sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma kaṇikārapupphaṃ [T 3.0275] kaṇṇikārapupphaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ [V 3.0207] pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ. Evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—yellow, of yellow color, with a yellow appearance, and a yellow radiance. Just as a kaṇikāra flower is yellow, of yellow color, with a yellow appearance, and a yellow radiance, or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, of yellow color, with a yellow appearance, and a yellow radiance; even so, not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—yellow, of yellow color, with a yellow appearance, and a yellow radiance. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the sixth sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma bandhujīvakapupphaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ. Evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko [M 3.0217] bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ sattamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—red, of red color, with a red appearance, and a red radiance. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, with a red appearance, and a red radiance, or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is red, of red color, with a red appearance, and a red radiance; even so, not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—red, of red color, with a red appearance, and a red radiance. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the seventh sphere of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma osadhitārakā odātā odātavaṇṇā odātanidassanā odātanibhāsā, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ odātaṃ odātavaṇṇaṃ odātanidassanaṃ odātanibhāsaṃ. Evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni[T 3.0276], ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—white, of white color, with a white appearance, and a white radiance. Just as the morning star is white, of white color, with a white appearance, and a white radiance, or just as a Benares cloth, smoothed on both sides, is white, of white color, with a white appearance, and a white radiance; even so, not perceiving form internally, a certain person sees external forms—white, of white color, with a white appearance, and a white radiance. He is one who perceives thus: ‘Having mastered them, I know, I see.’ This is the eighth sphere of mastery.

339. “Aṭṭha vimokkhā. Rūpī rūpāni passati. Ayaṃ paṭhamo vimokkho.

339. There are eight liberations. Possessed of form, one sees forms. This is the first liberation.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā [P 3.0262] rūpāni passati. Ayaṃ dutiyo vimokkho.

Not perceiving form internally, one sees external forms. This is the second liberation.

“Subhanteva adhimutto hoti. Ayaṃ tatiyo vimokkho.

One is intent only on the beautiful. This is the third liberation.

“Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ catuttho vimokkho.

With the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. This is the fourth liberation.

“Sabbaso [V 3.0208] ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ pañcamo vimokkho.

By completely transcending the sphere of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness. This is the fifth liberation.

“Sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho vimokkho.

Having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, one attains and abides in the sphere of nothingness, aware that 'There is nothing whatsoever.' This is the sixth liberation.

“Sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ sattamo vimokkho.

Having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, one attains and abides in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the seventh liberation.

“Sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayita nirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo vimokkho.

Having completely transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the eighth liberation.

“Ime [M 3.0218] kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena aṭṭha dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

These, friends, are the eight qualities well-expounded by that Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. All should recite them together… for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.

Navakaṃ

The Section of Nines

340. “Atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā [T 3.0277] sammāsambuddhena nava dhammā sammadakkhātā; tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame nava?

340. There are, friends, nine qualities well-expounded by that Blessed One—the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. All should recite them together… for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. What are the nine?

“Nava āghātavatthūni. ‘Anatthaṃ me acarī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati; ‘anatthaṃ me caratī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati; ‘anatthaṃ me carissatī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati; ‘piyassa me manāpassa anatthaṃ acarī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… anatthaṃ caratīti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… anatthaṃ carissatīti āghātaṃ bandhati; ‘appiyassa me amanāpassa atthaṃ acarī’ti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… atthaṃ caratīti āghātaṃ bandhati…pe… atthaṃ carissatīti āghātaṃ bandhati.

Nine grounds for resentment. One harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He has done me harm.’ One harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He is doing me harm.’ One harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He will do me harm.’ One harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He has done harm to a person dear and beloved to me.’… ‘He is doing harm to a person dear and beloved to me.’… ‘He will do harm to a person dear and beloved to me.’ One harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He has benefited a person not dear and unloved by me.’… ‘He is benefiting a person not dear and unloved by me.’… ‘He will benefit a person not dear and unloved by me.’

“Nava āghātapaṭivinayā. ‘Anatthaṃ me acari acarīti (syā. ka.) evaṃ “carati carissati” padesupi, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti[V 3.0209]; ‘anatthaṃ me [P 3.0263] carati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘anatthaṃ me carissati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘piyassa me manāpassa anatthaṃ acari…pe… anatthaṃ carati…pe… anatthaṃ carissati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti; ‘appiyassa me amanāpassa atthaṃ acari…pe… atthaṃ carati…pe… atthaṃ carissati, taṃ kutettha labbhā’ti āghātaṃ paṭivineti.

Nine removals of resentment. One removes resentment, thinking: ‘He has done me harm—but how could it have been otherwise?’ One removes resentment, thinking: ‘He is doing me harm—but how could it be otherwise?’ One removes resentment, thinking: ‘He will do me harm—but how could it be otherwise?’ One removes resentment, thinking: ‘He has done harm to a person dear and beloved to me… is doing harm… will do harm—but how could it have been otherwise?’ One removes resentment, thinking: ‘He has benefited a person not dear and unloved by me… is benefiting… will benefit—but how could it have been otherwise?’

341. “Nava sattāvāsā. Santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamo sattāvāso.

341. Nine abodes of beings. There are, friends, beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as human beings, some gods, and some beings in the states of deprivation. This is the first abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyo sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings with diverse bodies and unified perception, such as the devas of Brahmā’s company who are first reborn. This is the second abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyo [T 3.0278] sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhassara devas. This is the third abode of beings.

“Santāvuso[M 3.0219], sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catuttho sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings with unified bodies and unified perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas. This is the fourth abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā asaññino appaṭisaṃvedino, seyyathāpi devā asaññasattā asaññisattā (syā. kaṃ.). Ayaṃ pañcamo sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings who are non-percipient and non-experiencing, such as the non-percipient gods. This is the fifth abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings who, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, have reached the sphere of infinite space, aware that 'Space is infinite.' This is the sixth abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ sattamo sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite space, have reached the sphere of infinite consciousness, aware that 'Consciousness is infinite.' This is the seventh abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcāññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, have reached the sphere of nothingness, aware that 'There is nothing whatsoever.' This is the eighth abode of beings.

“Santāvuso[V 3.0210], sattā sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma samatikkamma santametaṃ paṇītametanti (syā. kaṃ.) nevasaññānāsaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ navamo sattāvāso.

There are, friends, beings who, having completely transcended the sphere of nothingness, have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is the ninth abode of beings.

342. “Nava akkhaṇā asamayā brahmacariyavāsāya. Idhāvuso[P 3.0264], tathāgato ca loke uppanno hoti arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca desiyati opasamiko parinibbāniko sambodhagāmī sugatappavedito. Ayañca puggalo nirayaṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ paṭhamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

342. Nine inopportune moments, unseasonable for living the holy life. Here, friends, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is taught—conducive to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to awakening, proclaimed by the Sugata. But this person has been reborn in hell. This is the first inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, tathāgato ca loke uppanno hoti arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca desiyati opasamiko parinibbāniko sambodhagāmī sugatappavedito. Ayañca puggalo [T 3.0279] tiracchānayoniṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ dutiyo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore, friends, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Dhamma is taught—conducive to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to awakening, proclaimed by the Sugata. But this person has been reborn in the animal realm. This is the second inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… pettivisayaṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ tatiyo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person is reborn in the realm of spirits. This is the third inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna [M 3.0220] caparaṃ…pe… asurakāyaṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ catuttho akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person is reborn in the host of asuras. This is the fourth inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… aññataraṃ dīghāyukaṃ devanikāyaṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ pañcamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person is reborn in a certain long-lived host of gods. This is the fifth inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… paccantimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti milakkhesu milakkhakesu (syā. kaṃ.) milakkhūsu (ka.) aviññātāresu, yattha natthi gati bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person is reborn in the border regions among barbarians who are uncomprehending, where there is no access for bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, laymen, or laywomen. This is the sixth inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… majjhimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti. So ca hoti micchādiṭṭhiko viparītadassano – ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ sukaṭa dukkaṭānaṃ (sī. pī.) kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paro loko, natthi [P 3.0265] mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ [V 3.0211] parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. Ayaṃ sattamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person is reborn in the middle countries, but he holds wrong view and has a perverted perspective: ‘There is no result in what is given, no result in what is sacrificed, no result in what is offered; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone and well-practiced, who, having realized this world and the next for themselves by direct knowledge, make it known.’ This is the seventh inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… majjhimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti. So ca hoti duppañño jaḷo eḷamūgo, nappaṭibalo subhāsitadubbhāsitānamatthamaññātuṃ. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person is reborn in the middle countries, but he is unwise, dull, and a deaf-mute, unable to understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken. This is the eighth inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, tathāgato ca loke na katthaci nakāro na dissati uppanno hoti arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca na desiyati opasamiko parinibbāniko sambodhagāmī sugatappavedito. Ayañca puggalo majjhimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti, so ca hoti paññavā ajaḷo aneḷamūgo, paṭibalo subhāsita-dubbhāsitānamatthamaññātuṃ. Ayaṃ navamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore, friends, a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, has not arisen in the world, and the Dhamma is not taught that is conducive to peace, leading to Nibbāna, leading to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Well-Gone One. And this person is reborn in the middle countries, and he is wise, not dull, not a deaf-mute, and is able to understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and ill-spoken. This is the ninth inopportune moment, unseasonable for living the holy life.

343. “Nava anupubbavihārā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja [T 3.0280] viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā…pe… dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā…pe… tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sukhassa ca pahānā [M 3.0221] …pe… catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā…pe… ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma [P 3.0266] ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati.

343. “There are nine successive abidings. Here, friends, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought… he enters and abides in the second jhāna. With the fading away of rapture… he enters and abides in the third jhāna. With the abandoning of pleasure… he enters and abides in the fourth jhāna. With the complete transcendence of perceptions of form… he enters and abides in the base of the infinity of space. With the complete transcendence of the base of the infinity of space, perceiving ‘consciousness is infinite,’ he enters and abides in the base of the infinity of consciousness. With the complete transcendence of the base of the infinity of consciousness, perceiving ‘there is nothing,’ he enters and abides in the base of nothingness. With the complete transcendence of the base of nothingness, he enters and abides in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. With the complete transcendence of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters and abides in the cessation of perception and feeling.

344. “Nava anupubbanirodhā. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa kāmasaññā niruddhā hoti. Dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā niruddhā honti. Tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa pīti niruddhā hoti. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa assāsapassāssā niruddhā honti. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ [T 3.0281] samāpannassa rūpasaññā niruddhā hoti. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākāsānañcāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti. Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa viññāṇañcāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ [V 3.0212] samāpannassa ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti. Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca niruddhā honti.

344. “There are nine successive cessations. For one who has attained the first jhāna, perception of sensuality has ceased. For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought have ceased. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, in-breathing and out-breathing have ceased. For one who has attained the base of the infinity of space, perception of form has ceased. For one who has attained the base of the infinity of consciousness, the perception of the base of the infinity of space has ceased. For one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of the infinity of consciousness has ceased. For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has ceased. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena nava dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ.

“These, friends, are the nine qualities well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together… for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans.”

Dasakaṃ

The Tens

345. “Atthi kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dasa dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ…pe… atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussānaṃ. Katame dasa?

345. “Friends, there are ten qualities well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Therein, all should chant together… for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans. What are the ten?

“Dasa nāthakaraṇā dhammā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti. Pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu [M 3.0222] sīlavā [P 3.0267] hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati, ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Ten qualities that make a refuge. Here, friends, a monk is virtuous. He dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, endowed with good conduct and suitable resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, he undertakes and trains in the training rules. Friends, that a monk is virtuous, dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, endowed with good conduct and suitable resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and trains by undertaking the training rules—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo. Ye [T 3.0282] te dhammā ādikalyāṇā majjhekalyāṇā pariyosānakalyāṇā sātthā sabyañjanā sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ abhivadanti, tathārūpāssa dhammā bahussutā honti dhatā (ka. sī. syā. kaṃ.) dhātā vacasā paricitā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā, yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu bahussuto hoti…pe… diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is very learned, a retainer of what has been heard, one who has accumulated what has been heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings have been much heard by him, retained, practiced verbally, reflected upon mentally, and well penetrated by wisdom. Friends, that a monk is very learned... and well penetrated by wisdom—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto hoti kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto hoti kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards good friends. Friends, that a monk has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards good friends—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu suvaco hoti sovacassakaraṇehi dhammehi samannāgato khamo [V 3.0213] padakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu suvaco hoti…pe… padakkhiṇaggāhī anusāsaniṃ. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is easy to admonish, possesses qualities that make him easy to admonish, is patient, and respectfully accepts instruction. Friends, that a monk is easy to admonish... and respectfully accepts instruction—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ uccāvacāni kiṃkaraṇīyāni, tattha dakkho hoti analaso tatrupāyāya vīmaṃsāya samannāgato, alaṃ kātuṃ alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu yāni tāni sabrahmacārīnaṃ…pe… alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, regarding the various duties, high and low, for his companions in the holy life, a monk is skilled, not lazy, endowed with investigation into the means thereto, capable of doing them, and capable of arranging for them to be done. Friends, that a monk, regarding the various duties for his companions in the holy life... is capable of arranging for them to be done—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu dhammakāmo hoti piyasamudāhāro, abhidhamme abhivinaye uḷārapāmojjo uḷārapāmujjo (sī. pī.), oḷārapāmojjo (syā. kaṃ.). Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu dhammakāmo hoti…pe… uḷārapāmojjo uḷārapāmujjo (sī. pī.), oḷārapāmojjo (syā. kaṃ.). Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, one who speaks in a pleasing manner, and has great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya. Friends, that a monk is a lover of the Dhamma... and has great joy—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna [M 3.0223] caparaṃ, āvuso[P 3.0268], bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti itarītarehi cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārehi[T 3.0283]. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu santuṭṭho hoti…pe… parikkhārehi. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive. Friends, that a monk is content... with requisites—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo viharati…pe… anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is resolute, firm in his striving, and does not throw off the burden in regard to wholesome states. Friends, that a monk dwells with aroused energy... and does not throw off the burden in regard to wholesome states—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu satimā hoti paramena satinepakkena samannāgato cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu satimā hoti…pe… saritā anussaritā. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

“Furthermore, friends, a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and discernment, able to remember and recollect what was done and said long ago. Friends, that a monk is mindful... able to remember and recollect—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu paññavā hoti, udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammādukkhakkhayagāminiyā. Yaṃpāvuso, bhikkhu paññavā hoti…pe… sammādukkhakkhayagāminiyā. Ayampi dhammo nāthakaraṇo.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is wise, endowed with wisdom concerning arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. Friends, that a bhikkhu is wise, endowed with wisdom concerning arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering—this too is a quality that makes a refuge.

346. Dasa kasiṇāyatanāni. Pathavīkasiṇameko sañjānāti, uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ [V 3.0214] appamāṇaṃ. Āpokasiṇameko sañjānāti…pe… tejokasiṇameko sañjānāti… vāyokasiṇameko sañjānāti… nīlakasiṇameko sañjānāti… pītakasiṇameko sañjānāti… [T 3.0284] lohitakasiṇameko sañjānāti… odātakasiṇameko sañjānāti… ākāsakasiṇameko sañjānāti… viññāṇakasiṇameko sañjānāti, uddhaṃ adho tiriyaṃ advayaṃ appamāṇaṃ.

346. The ten kasiṇa-bases. One perceives the earth-kasiṇa: above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable. One perceives the water-kasiṇa... one perceives the fire-kasiṇa... one perceives the wind-kasiṇa... one perceives the blue-kasiṇa... one perceives the yellow-kasiṇa... one perceives the red-kasiṇa... one perceives the white-kasiṇa... one perceives the space-kasiṇa... one perceives the consciousness-kasiṇa: above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable.

347. “Dasa [P 3.0269] akusalakammapathā – pāṇātipāto, adinnādānaṃ, kāmesumicchācāro, musāvādo, pisuṇā vācā, pharusā vācā, samphappalāpo, abhijjhā, byāpādo, micchādiṭṭhi.

347. The ten unwholesome courses of action: destroying life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slanderous speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view.

“Dasa [M 3.0224] kusalakammapathā – pāṇātipātā veramaṇī, adinnādānā veramaṇī, kāmesumicchācārā veramaṇī, musāvādā veramaṇī, pisuṇāya vācāya veramaṇī, pharusāya vācāya veramaṇī, samphappalāpā veramaṇī, anabhijjhā, abyāpādo, sammādiṭṭhi.

The ten wholesome courses of action: abstaining from destroying life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from slanderous speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from frivolous chatter, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view.

348. “Dasa ariyavāsā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti, chaḷaṅgasamannāgato, ekārakkho, caturāpasseno, paṇunnapaccekasacco, samavayasaṭṭhesano, anāvilasaṅkappo, passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro, suvimuttacitto, suvimuttapañño.

348. The ten noble dwellings. Here, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports, has dispelled individual truths, has stilled his quest, has untroubled intentions, has tranquil bodily formation, is well-liberated in mind, and is well-liberated in wisdom.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thinamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcaṅgavippahīno hoti.

And how, friends, has a bhikkhu abandoned five factors? Here, friends, for a bhikkhu, sensual desire is abandoned, ill will is abandoned, sloth and torpor are abandoned, restlessness and remorse are abandoned, and doubt is abandoned. In this way, friends, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ [T 3.0285] sutvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chaḷaṅgasamannāgato hoti.

And how, friends, is a bhikkhu endowed with six factors? Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither gladdened nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear... Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is neither gladdened nor saddened, but dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is endowed with six factors.

“Kathañcāvuso[V 3.0215], bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satārakkhena cetasā samannāgato hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu ekārakkho hoti[P 3.0270].

And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have a single guard? Here, friends, a bhikkhu is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has a single guard.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu saṅkhāyekaṃ paṭisevati, saṅkhāyekaṃ adhivāseti, saṅkhāyekaṃ parivajjeti, saṅkhāyekaṃ vinodeti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu caturāpasseno hoti.

And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have four supports? Here, friends, a bhikkhu, after reflection, makes use of one thing; after reflection, endures one thing; after reflection, avoids one thing; and after reflection, dispels one thing. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has four supports.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu paṇunnapaccekasacco hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno yāni tāni puthusamaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ puthupaccekasaccāni, sabbāni tāni nunnāni honti paṇunnāni cattāni vantāni muttāni pahīnāni paṭinissaṭṭhāni. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu paṇunnapaccekasacco hoti.

And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one who has dispelled the individual truths? Here, friends, for a bhikkhu, whatever many individual truths of the many ascetics and brahmins there are, all of them have been removed, completely removed, given up, relinquished, released, abandoned, and cast off. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one who has dispelled the individual truths.

“Kathañcāvuso[M 3.0225], bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmesanā pahīnā hoti, bhavesanā pahīnā hoti, brahmacariyesanā paṭippassaddhā. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu samavayasaṭṭhesano hoti.

And how, friends, is a bhikkhu one whose quests have been allayed? Here, friends, for a bhikkhu, the quest for sensual pleasures is abandoned, the quest for existence is abandoned, and the quest for the holy life is pacified. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is one whose quests have been allayed.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāmasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, byāpādasaṅkappo pahīno hoti, vihiṃsāsaṅkappo pahīno hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu anāvilasaṅkappo hoti.

And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have untroubled intentions? Here, friends, for a bhikkhu, sensual intention is abandoned, the intention of ill will is abandoned, and the intention of harming is abandoned. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has untroubled intentions.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti[T 3.0286]? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu passaddhakāyasaṅkhāro hoti.

And how, friends, does a bhikkhu have tranquil bodily formation? Here, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and sorrow, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu has tranquil bodily formation.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttacitto hoti.

And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-liberated in mind? Here, friends, a bhikkhu’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, and his mind is liberated from delusion. It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-liberated in mind.

“Kathañcāvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu ‘rāgo me pahīno ucchinnamūlo [V 3.0216] tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato [P 3.0271] āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. ‘Doso me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. ‘Moho me pahīno ucchinnamūlo tālāvatthukato anabhāvaṃkato āyatiṃ anuppādadhammo’ti pajānāti. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, bhikkhu suvimuttapañño hoti.

And how, friends, is a bhikkhu well-liberated in wisdom? Here, friends, a bhikkhu understands thus: ‘My lust is abandoned, its root has been cut off, it has been made like a palm stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and is of a nature not to arise in the future.’ He understands thus: ‘My hatred is abandoned...’ He understands thus: ‘My delusion is abandoned, its root has been cut off, it has been made like a palm stump, brought to a state of non-existence, and is of a nature not to arise in the future.’ It is in this way, friends, that a bhikkhu is well-liberated in wisdom.

“Dasa asekkhā dhammā – asekkhā sammādiṭṭhi, asekkho sammāsaṅkappo, asekkhā sammāvācā, asekkho sammākammanto, asekkho sammāājīvo, asekkho sammāvāyāmo, asekkhā sammāsati, asekkho sammāsamādhi, asekkhaṃ sammāñāṇaṃ, asekkhā sammāvimutti.

The ten qualities of one beyond training: the right view of one beyond training, the right intention of one beyond training, the right speech of one beyond training, the right action of one beyond training, the right livelihood of one beyond training, the right effort of one beyond training, the right mindfulness of one beyond training, the right concentration of one beyond training, the right knowledge of one beyond training, and the right liberation of one beyond training.

“Ime kho, āvuso, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena dasa dhammā sammadakkhātā. Tattha sabbeheva saṅgāyitabbaṃ na [M 3.0226] vivaditabbaṃ, yathayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ addhaniyaṃ assa [T 3.0287] ciraṭṭhitikaṃ, tadassa bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya lokānukampāya atthāya hitāya sukhāya devamanussāna”nti.

These, friends, are the ten qualities well-proclaimed by that Blessed One who is the Knowing One, the Seeing One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. Herein, all should chant in unison, without dispute, so that this holy life may be long-lasting and endure for a long time. This would be for the benefit of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the good, benefit, and happiness of devas and humans.

349. Atha kho bhagavā uṭṭhahitvā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi – ‘sādhu sādhu, sāriputta, sādhu kho tvaṃ, sāriputta, bhikkhūnaṃ saṅgītipariyāyaṃ abhāsī’ti. Idamavocāyasmā sāriputto, samanuñño satthā ahosi. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti.

349. Then the Blessed One arose and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: 'Good, good, Sāriputta! It is good, Sāriputta, that you have delivered the discourse on communal recitation to the bhikkhus.' The Venerable Sāriputta spoke thus, and the Teacher was approving. Those bhikkhus, being delighted, rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Sāriputta.

Saṅgītisuttaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Discourse on Communal Recitation, the tenth, is concluded.

11. Dasuttarasuttaṃ

11. The Dasuttara Sutta

350. Evaṃ [P 3.0272][M 3.0227][V 3.0217][T 3.0288] me sutaṃ – ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā campāyaṃ viharati gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi. Tatra kho āyasmā sāriputto bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso bhikkhave”ti! “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato sāriputtassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā sāriputto etadavoca –

350. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond, together with a great community of monks, with five hundred monks. There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: 'Friends, monks!' 'Friend,' those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Dasuttaraṃ pavakkhāmi, dhammaṃ nibbānapattiyā;

Dukkhassantakiriyāya, sabbaganthappamocanaṃ”.

I shall declare the Dasuttara Dhamma, which releases from all fetters, for the attainment of Nibbāna, for making an end of suffering.

Eko dhammo

One Dhamma

351. “Eko, āvuso, dhammo bahukāro, eko dhammo bhāvetabbo, eko dhammo pariññeyyo, eko dhammo pahātabbo, eko dhammo hānabhāgiyo, eko dhammo visesabhāgiyo, eko dhammo duppaṭivijjho, eko dhammo uppādetabbo, eko dhammo abhiññeyyo, eko dhammo sacchikātabbo.

351. Friends, one Dhamma is of great benefit, one Dhamma is to be developed, one Dhamma is to be fully understood, one Dhamma is to be abandoned, one Dhamma partakes of decline, one Dhamma partakes of distinction, one Dhamma is difficult to penetrate, one Dhamma is to be aroused, one Dhamma is to be directly known, one Dhamma is to be realized.

(Ka) “katamo eko dhammo bahukāro? Appamādo kusalesu dhammesu. Ayaṃ eko dhammo bahukāro.

(a) Which one Dhamma is of great benefit? Heedfulness in wholesome qualities. This one Dhamma is of great benefit.

(Kha) “katamo eko dhammo bhāvetabbo? Kāyagatāsati sātasahagatā. Ayaṃ eko dhammo bhāvetabbo.

(b) Which one Dhamma is to be developed? Mindfulness directed to the body, accompanied by pleasure. This one Dhamma is to be developed.

(Ga) “katamo [V 3.0218] eko dhammo pariññeyyo? Phasso sāsavo upādāniyo. Ayaṃ eko dhammo pariññeyyo.

(c) Which one Dhamma is to be fully understood? Contact that is tainted and a basis for clinging. This one Dhamma is to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katamo [T 3.0289][P 3.0273] eko dhammo pahātabbo? Asmimāno. Ayaṃ eko dhammo pahātabbo.

(d) Which one Dhamma is to be abandoned? The conceit 'I am.' This one Dhamma is to be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katamo eko dhammo hānabhāgiyo? Ayoniso manasikāro. Ayaṃ eko dhammo hānabhāgiyo.

(e) Which one Dhamma partakes of decline? Unwise attention. This one Dhamma partakes of decline.

(Ca) “katamo eko dhammo visesabhāgiyo? Yoniso manasikāro. Ayaṃ eko dhammo visesabhāgiyo.

(f) Which one Dhamma partakes of distinction? Wise attention. This one Dhamma partakes of distinction.

(Cha) “katamo [M 3.0228] eko dhammo duppaṭivijjho? Ānantariko cetosamādhi. Ayaṃ eko dhammo duppaṭivijjho.

(g) Which one Dhamma is difficult to penetrate? The immediate concentration of mind. This one Dhamma is difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katamo eko dhammo uppādetabbo? Akuppaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Ayaṃ eko dhammo uppādetabbo.

(h) Which one Dhamma is to be aroused? Unshakable knowledge. This one Dhamma is to be aroused.

(Jha) “katamo eko dhammo abhiññeyyo? Sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā. Ayaṃ eko dhammo abhiññeyyo.

(i) Which one Dhamma is to be directly known? All beings are sustained by nutriment. This one Dhamma is to be directly known.

(Ña) “katamo eko dhammo sacchikātabbo? Akuppā cetovimutti. Ayaṃ eko dhammo sacchikātabbo.

(j) Which one Dhamma is to be realized? The unshakable liberation of mind. This one Dhamma is to be realized.

“Iti ime dasa dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these ten Dhammas are real, actual, true, not otherwise, and unalterable; they have been perfectly and fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Dve dhammā

Two Dhammas

352. “Dve dhammā bahukārā, dve dhammā bhāvetabbā, dve dhammā pariññeyyā, dve dhammā pahātabbā[V 3.0219], dve dhammā hānabhāgiyā, dve dhammā visesabhāgiyā, dve dhammā duppaṭivijjhā, dve dhammā uppādetabbā, dve dhammā abhiññeyyā, dve dhammā [T 3.0290] sacchikātabbā.

352. Two Dhammas are of great benefit, two Dhammas are to be developed, two Dhammas are to be fully understood, two Dhammas are to be abandoned, two Dhammas partake of decline, two Dhammas partake of distinction, two Dhammas are difficult to penetrate, two Dhammas are to be aroused, two Dhammas are to be directly known, two Dhammas are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame dve dhammā bahukārā? Sati ca sampajaññañca. Ime dve dhammā bahukārā.

(a) What two Dhammas are of great benefit? Mindfulness and clear comprehension. These two Dhammas are of great benefit.

(Kha) “katame dve dhammā bhāvetabbā? Samatho ca vipassanā ca. Ime dve dhammā bhāvetabbā.

(b) What two Dhammas are to be developed? Serenity and insight. These two Dhammas are to be developed.

(Ga) “katame dve dhammā pariññeyyā? Nāmañca rūpañca. Ime dve dhammā pariññeyyā.

(c) What two Dhammas are to be fully understood? Mentality and materiality. These two Dhammas are to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katame [P 3.0274] dve dhammā pahātabbā? Avijjā ca bhavataṇhā ca. Ime dve dhammā pahātabbā.

(d) What two Dhammas are to be abandoned? Ignorance and craving for existence. These two Dhammas are to be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katame dve dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Dovacassatā ca pāpamittatā ca. Ime dve dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

(e) What two Dhammas partake of decline? Being difficult to admonish and having bad friends. These two Dhammas partake of decline.

(Ca) “katame dve dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Sovacassatā ca kalyāṇamittatā ca. Ime dve dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

(f) What two Dhammas partake of distinction? Being easy to admonish and having good friends. These two Dhammas partake of distinction.

(Cha) “katame [M 3.0229] dve dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Yo ca hetu yo ca paccayo sattānaṃ saṃkilesāya, yo ca hetu yo ca paccayo sattānaṃ visuddhiyā. Ime dve dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

(g) What two Dhammas are difficult to penetrate? The cause and condition for the defilement of beings, and the cause and condition for the purification of beings. These two Dhammas are difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame dve dhammā uppādetabbā? Dve ñāṇāni – khaye ñāṇaṃ, anuppāde ñāṇaṃ. Ime dve dhammā uppādetabbā.

(h) What two Dhammas are to be aroused? Two kinds of knowledge: the knowledge of destruction and the knowledge of non-arising. These two Dhammas are to be aroused.

(Jha) “katame dve dhammā abhiññeyyā? Dve dhātuyo – saṅkhatā ca dhātu asaṅkhatā ca dhātu. Ime dve dhammā abhiññeyyā.

(i) What two Dhammas are to be directly known? Two elements: the conditioned element and the unconditioned element. These two Dhammas are to be directly known.

(Ña) “katame [T 3.0291] dve dhammā sacchikātabbā? Vijjā ca vimutti ca. Ime dve dhammā sacchikātabbā.

(j) What two Dhammas are to be realized? True knowledge and liberation. These two Dhammas are to be realized.

“Iti [V 3.0220] ime vīsati dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these twenty Dhammas are real, actual, true, not otherwise, and unalterable; they have been perfectly and fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Tayo dhammā

Three Dhammas

353. “Tayo dhammā bahukārā, tayo dhammā bhāvetabbā…pe… tayo dhammā sacchikātabbā.

353. Three Dhammas are of great benefit, three Dhammas are to be developed… and so on… three Dhammas are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame tayo dhammā bahukārā? Sappurisasaṃsevo, saddhammassavanaṃ, dhammānudhammappaṭipatti. Ime tayo dhammā bahukārā.

(a) What three Dhammas are of great benefit? Associating with true persons, listening to the true Dhamma, and practicing in accordance with the Dhamma. These three Dhammas are of great benefit.

(Kha) “katame tayo dhammā bhāvetabbā? Tayo samādhī – savitakko savicāro samādhi, avitakko vicāramatto samādhi, avitakko avicāro samādhi. Ime tayo dhammā bhāvetabbā.

(b) What three Dhammas are to be developed? Three kinds of concentration: concentration with applied thought and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought, with only sustained thought; and concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought. These three Dhammas are to be developed.

(Ga) “katame [P 3.0275] tayo dhammā pariññeyyā? Tisso vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Ime tayo dhammā pariññeyyā.

What three states are to be fully understood? Three kinds of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These three states are to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katame tayo dhammā pahātabbā? Tisso taṇhā – kāmataṇhā, bhavataṇhā, vibhavataṇhā. Ime tayo dhammā pahātabbā.

What three states are to be abandoned? Three kinds of craving: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. These three states are to be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katame tayo dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Tīṇi akusalamūlāni – lobho [T 3.0292] akusalamūlaṃ, doso akusalamūlaṃ, moho akusalamūlaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

What three states partake of decline? Three unwholesome roots: greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root. These three states partake of decline.

(Ca) “katame [M 3.0230] tayo dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Tīṇi kusalamūlāni – alobho kusalamūlaṃ, adoso kusalamūlaṃ, amoho kusalamūlaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

What three states partake of distinction? Three wholesome roots: non-greed as a wholesome root, non-hatred as a wholesome root, and non-delusion as a wholesome root. These three states partake of distinction.

(Cha) “katame tayo dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Tisso nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo – kāmānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ nekkhammaṃ, rūpānametaṃ nissaraṇaṃ yadidaṃ arūpaṃ, yaṃ kho pana kiñci bhūtaṃ saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ, nirodho tassa nissaraṇaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

What three states are difficult to penetrate? Three elements of escape. The escape from sensual pleasures is this: renunciation. The escape from form is this: the formless. The escape from whatever has come to be, is conditioned and dependently arisen, is its cessation. These three states are difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame [V 3.0221] tayo dhammā uppādetabbā? Tīṇi ñāṇāni – atītaṃse ñāṇaṃ, anāgataṃse ñāṇaṃ, paccuppannaṃse ñāṇaṃ. Ime tayo dhammā uppādetabbā.

What three states are to be brought into being? Three kinds of knowledge: knowledge concerning the past, knowledge concerning the future, and knowledge concerning the present. These three states are to be brought into being.

(Jha) “katame tayo dhammā abhiññeyyā? Tisso dhātuyo – kāmadhātu, rūpadhātu, arūpadhātu. Ime tayo dhammā abhiññeyyā.

What three states are to be directly known? Three elements: the sense-sphere element, the form-sphere element, and the formless-sphere element. These three states are to be directly known.

(Ña) “katame tayo dhammā sacchikātabbā? Tisso vijjā – pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇaṃ vijjā, sattānaṃ cutūpapāte ñāṇaṃ vijjā, āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ vijjā. Ime tayo dhammā sacchikātabbā.

What three states are to be realized? Three kinds of true knowledge: the true knowledge of recollecting past lives, the true knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings, and the true knowledge of the destruction of the taints. These three states are to be realized.

“Iti [P 3.0276] ime tiṃsa dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these thirty states are actual, factual, thus, unfalsified, unalterable, and have been perfectly, fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Cattāro dhammā

The Fours

354. “Cattāro [T 3.0293] dhammā bahukārā, cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā…pe… cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā.

354. Four states are of great service, four states are to be developed... four states are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame cattāro dhammā bahukārā? Cattāri cakkāni – patirūpadesavāso, sappurisūpanissayo sappurisupassayo (syā. kaṃ.), attasammāpaṇidhi, pubbe ca katapuññatā. Ime cattāro dhammā bahukārā.

Which four states are of great service? The four wheels: residing in a suitable place, associating with good persons, establishing oneself rightly, and having previously made merit. These four states are of great service.

(Kha) “katame cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Vedanāsu…pe… citte… dhammesu [M 3.0231] dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā bhāvetabbā.

Which four states are to be developed? The four establishments of mindfulness. Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. These four states are to be developed.

(Ga) “katame cattāro dhammā pariññeyyā? Cattāro āhārā – kabaḷīkāro kavaḷīkāro (syā. kaṃ.) āhāro oḷāriko [V 3.0222] vā sukhumo vā, phasso dutiyo, manosañcetanā tatiyā, viññāṇaṃ catutthaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā pariññeyyā.

Which four states are to be fully understood? The four nutriments: edible food, whether gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These four states are to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katame cattāro dhammā pahātabbā? Cattāro oghā [T 3.0294] – kāmogho, bhavogho, diṭṭhogho, avijjogho. Ime cattāro dhammā pahātabbā.

Which four states are to be abandoned? The four floods: the flood of sensuality, the flood of becoming, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance. These four states are to be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katame cattāro dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Cattāro yogā – kāmayogo, bhavayogo, diṭṭhiyogo, avijjāyogo. Ime cattāro dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

Which four states partake of decline? The four yokes: the yoke of sensuality, the yoke of becoming, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance. These four states partake of decline.

(Ca) “katame cattāro dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Cattāro visaññogā – kāmayogavisaṃyogo, bhavayogavisaṃyogo, diṭṭhiyogavisaṃyogo, avijjāyogavisaṃyogo. Ime cattāro dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

Which four states partake of distinction? The four disjunctions: disjunction from the yoke of sensuality, disjunction from the yoke of becoming, disjunction from the yoke of views, and disjunction from the yoke of ignorance. These four states partake of distinction.

(Cha) “katame [P 3.0277] cattāro dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Cattāro samādhī – hānabhāgiyo samādhi, ṭhitibhāgiyo samādhi, visesabhāgiyo samādhi, nibbedhabhāgiyo samādhi. Ime cattāro dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

Which four states are difficult to penetrate? The four concentrations: concentration partaking of decline, concentration partaking of stability, concentration partaking of distinction, and concentration partaking of penetration. These four states are difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame cattāro dhammā uppādetabbā? Cattāri ñāṇāni – dhamme ñāṇaṃ, anvaye ñāṇaṃ, pariye ñāṇaṃ, sammutiyā ñāṇaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā uppādetabbā.

Which four states are to be produced? The four knowledges: knowledge in the cause, knowledge in the consequence, knowledge of the minds of others, and knowledge in convention. These four states are to be produced.

(Jha) “katame cattāro dhammā abhiññeyyā? Cattāri ariyasaccāni – dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhasamudayaṃ dukkhasamudayo (syā. kaṃ.) ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhaṃ dukkhanirodho (syā. kaṃ.) ariyasaccaṃ, dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā ariyasaccaṃ. Ime cattāro dhammā abhiññeyyā.

Which four states are to be directly known? The four noble truths: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. These four states are to be directly known.

(Ña) “katame cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā? Cattāri sāmaññaphalāni – sotāpattiphalaṃ, sakadāgāmiphalaṃ, anāgāmiphalaṃ, arahattaphalaṃ[T 3.0295]. Ime cattāro dhammā sacchikātabbā.

Which four states are to be realized? The four fruits of recluseship: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arahantship. These four states are to be realized.

“Iti [M 3.0232] ime cattārīsadhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these forty states are actual, factual, thus, unfalsified, unalterable, and have been perfectly, fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Pañca dhammā

The Fives

355. “Pañca [V 3.0223] dhammā bahukārā…pe… pañca dhammā sacchikātabbā.

355. Five states are of great benefit… five states are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame pañca dhammā bahukārā? Pañca padhāniyaṅgāni – idhāvuso, bhikkhu saddho hoti, saddahati tathāgatassa bodhiṃ – ‘itipi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā’ti. Appābādho hoti appātaṅko samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā samannāgato nātisītāya nāccuṇhāya majjhimāya padhānakkhamāya. Asaṭho hoti amāyāvī yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvīkattā satthari vā viññūsu vā sabrahmacārīsu. Āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. Paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato ariyāya nibbedhikāya sammā dukkhakkhayagāminiyā. Ime pañca dhammā bahukārā.

(Ka) “What are the five qualities that are of great benefit? The five factors for striving: Here, friends, a bhikkhu has faith; he has confidence in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘For this reason, the Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, a Well-Gone One, a Knower of the world, an Unsurpassed Trainer of persons to be tamed, a Teacher of gods and humans, an Enlightened One, a Blessed One.’ He has few illnesses, few afflictions, and is endowed with a digestive power that is even, not too cold and not too hot, moderate, and suitable for striving. He is not deceitful or devious, but reveals himself as he truly is to the Teacher, or to the wise, or to his fellow practitioners of the holy life. He dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities and for the undertaking of wholesome qualities; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, not shirking the burden in regard to wholesome qualities. He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering. These five qualities are of great benefit.”

(Kha) “katame [T 3.0296] pañca dhammā bhāvetabbā? Pañcaṅgiko sammāsamādhi – pītipharaṇatā, sukhapharaṇatā, cetopharaṇatā[P 3.0278], ālokapharaṇatā, paccavekkhaṇanimittaṃ paccavekkhaṇānimittaṃ (syā. kaṃ.). Ime pañca dhammā bhāvetabbā.

(Kha) “What are the five qualities that are to be developed? The five-factored right concentration: the state of being pervaded by rapture, the state of being pervaded by pleasure, the state of being pervaded by the knowledge of others' minds, the state of being pervaded by the divine eye knowledge, and the sign for reviewing. These are the five qualities that are to be developed.”

(Ga) “katame pañca dhammā pariññeyyā? Pañcupādānakkhandhā seyyathīdaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) – rūpupādānakkhandho, vedanupādānakkhandho, saññupādānakkhandho, saṅkhārupādānakkhandho viññāṇupādānakkhandho. Ime pañca dhammā pariññeyyā.

(Ga) “What are the five qualities that are to be fully understood? The five aggregates of clinging: the form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the formations aggregate of clinging, and the consciousness aggregate of clinging. These are the five qualities that are to be fully understood.”

(Gha) “katame pañca dhammā pahātabbā? Pañca nīvaraṇāni – kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, byāpādanīvaraṇaṃ, thinamiddhanīvaraṇaṃ, uddhaccakukuccanīvaraṇaṃ, vicikicchānīvaraṇaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā pahātabbā.

(Gha) “What are the five qualities that are to be abandoned? The five hindrances: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt. These are the five qualities that are to be abandoned.”

(Ṅa) “katame pañca dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Pañca cetokhilā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati. Yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu satthari kaṅkhati vicikicchati nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, tassa [M 3.0233] cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya[V 3.0224]. Ayaṃ paṭhamo cetokhilo. Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu dhamme kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… saṅghe kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… sikkhāya kaṅkhati vicikicchati…pe… sabrahmacārīsu kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto, yo so, āvuso, bhikkhu sabrahmacārīsu [T 3.0297] kupito hoti anattamano āhatacitto khilajāto, tassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Yassa cittaṃ na namati ātappāya anuyogāya sātaccāya padhānāya. Ayaṃ pañcamo cetokhilo. Ime pañca dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

(Ṅa) “What are the five qualities that partake of decline? The five mental barrennesses: Here, friends, a bhikkhu doubts the Teacher, is uncertain, is not inclined, and is not confident. That bhikkhu, friends, who doubts the Teacher, is uncertain, is not inclined, and is not confident, his mind does not incline towards ardent effort, towards repeated exertion, towards persistent effort, towards striving. The mind of one whose mind does not incline towards ardent effort, towards repeated exertion, towards persistent effort, towards striving—this is the first mental barrenness. Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu doubts the Dhamma, is uncertain… he doubts the Saṅgha… he doubts the training… he is angry with his fellow practitioners of the holy life, displeased, with a mind that wants to harm, a mind that has become barren. That bhikkhu, friends, who is angry with his fellow practitioners of the holy life, displeased, with a mind that wants to harm, a mind that has become barren, his mind does not incline towards ardent effort, towards repeated exertion, towards persistent effort, towards striving. The mind of one whose mind does not incline towards ardent effort, towards repeated exertion, towards persistent effort, towards striving—this is the fifth mental barrenness. These are the five qualities that partake of decline.”

(Ca) “katame pañca dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Pañcindriyāni – saddhindriyaṃ, vīriyindriyaṃ, satindriyaṃ, samādhindriyaṃ, paññindriyaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

(Ca) “What are the five qualities that partake of distinction? The five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom. These are the five qualities that partake of distinction.”

(Cha) “katame pañca dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Pañca nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo – idhāvuso, bhikkhuno kāme manasikaroto kāmesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Nekkhammaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto nekkhamme cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ kāmehi. Ye ca kāmapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ kāmānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

(Cha) “What are the five qualities that are difficult to penetrate? The five elements of escape: Here, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to sensual pleasures, his mind does not enter into, does not become clear about, does not stand firm in, and is not inclined towards sensual pleasures. But when he attends to renunciation, his mind enters into, becomes clear about, stands firm in, and is inclined towards renunciation. That mind of his is well-directed, well-developed, well-risen from, well-liberated from, and disjoined from sensual pleasures. And those taints, mental weariness, and mental fevers that arise on account of sensual pleasures—he is liberated from them. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from sensual pleasures.”

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno byāpādaṃ manasikaroto byāpāde cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Abyāpādaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto abyāpāde cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ byāpādena.
