Ye ca byāpādapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na [T 3.0298] so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ byāpādassa nissaraṇaṃ.

“Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to ill will, his mind does not enter into, does not become clear about, does not stand firm in, and is not inclined towards ill will. But when he attends to non-ill will, his mind enters into, becomes clear about, stands firm in, and is inclined towards non-ill will. That mind of his is well-directed, well-developed, well-risen from, well-liberated from, and disjoined from ill will. And those taints, mental weariness, and mental fevers that arise on account of ill will—he is liberated from them. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from ill will.”

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno vihesaṃ manasikaroto vihesāya cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Avihesaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto avihesāya cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati[M 3.0234]. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ vihesāya. Ye ca vihesāpaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ vihesāya nissaraṇaṃ.

“Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to harming, his mind does not enter into, does not become clear about, does not stand firm in, and is not inclined towards harming. But when he attends to harmlessness, his mind enters into, becomes clear about, stands firm in, and is inclined towards harmlessness. That mind of his is well-directed, well-developed, well-risen from, well-liberated from, and disjoined from harming. And those taints, mental weariness, and mental fevers that arise on account of harming—he is liberated from them. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from harming.”

“Puna [V 3.0225] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno rūpe manasikaroto rūpesu cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Arūpaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto arūpe cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ rūpehi. Ye ca rūpapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ rūpānaṃ nissaraṇaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to forms, his mind does not enter, does not become serene, does not become established, and is not released in regard to forms. But when he attends to the formless, his mind enters, becomes serene, becomes established, and is released in regard to the formless. His mind is thus well-perfected, well-developed, well-risen from, well-released from, and disjoined from forms. And he is freed from the taints, vexations, and fevers that arise conditioned by forms. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from forms.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno sakkāyaṃ manasikaroto sakkāye cittaṃ na pakkhandati na pasīdati na santiṭṭhati na vimuccati. Sakkāyanirodhaṃ kho panassa manasikaroto sakkāyanirodhe cittaṃ pakkhandati pasīdati santiṭṭhati vimuccati. Tassa taṃ cittaṃ sugataṃ subhāvitaṃ suvuṭṭhitaṃ suvimuttaṃ visaṃyuttaṃ sakkāyena. Ye ca sakkāyapaccayā uppajjanti āsavā vighātā pariḷāhā, mutto so tehi. Na so taṃ vedanaṃ vedeti. Idamakkhātaṃ sakkāyassa nissaraṇaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā [T 3.0299] duppaṭivijjhā.

Furthermore, friends, when a bhikkhu attends to embodied identity, his mind does not enter, does not become serene, does not become established, and is not released in regard to embodied identity. But when he attends to the cessation of embodied identity, his mind enters, becomes serene, becomes established, and is released in regard to the cessation of embodied identity. His mind is thus well-perfected, well-developed, well-risen from, well-released from, and disjoined from embodied identity. And he is freed from the taints, vexations, and fevers that arise conditioned by embodied identity. He does not experience that feeling. This is declared to be the escape from embodied identity. These five qualities are difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame pañca dhammā uppādetabbā? Pañca ñāṇiko sammāsamādhi – ‘ayaṃ samādhi paccuppannasukho ceva āyatiñca sukhavipāko’ti paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ayaṃ samādhi ariyo nirāmiso’ti paccattaññeva [P 3.0279] ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ayaṃ samādhi akāpurisasevito’ti paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘Ayaṃ samādhi santo paṇīto paṭippassaddhaladdho ekodibhāvādhigato, na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāritagato’ti na ca sasaṅkhāraniggayha vāritavatoti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavārivāvato (ka.), na sasaṅkhāraniggayhavāriyādhigato (?) paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. ‘So kho panāhaṃ imaṃ samādhiṃ satova samāpajjāmi sato vuṭṭhahāmī’ti paccattaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ uppajjati. Ime pañca dhammā uppādetabbā.

What are the five things that are to be brought into being? Right concentration is endowed with five kinds of knowledge: ‘This concentration is pleasant in the present and has a pleasant result in the future’—thus, knowledge arises in oneself. ‘This concentration is noble and unworldly’—thus, knowledge arises in oneself. ‘This concentration is resorted to by superior persons’—thus, knowledge arises in oneself. ‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, obtained through tranquility, attained through unification, and not achieved by means of forceful suppression and restraint’—thus, knowledge arises in oneself. ‘Indeed, I enter this concentration mindfully and emerge from it mindfully’—thus, knowledge arises in oneself. These are the five things that are to be brought into being.

(Jha) “katame pañca dhammā abhiññeyyā? Pañca vimuttāyatanāni – idhāvuso, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī. Yathā [M 3.0235] yathā, āvuso, bhikkhuno satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, tathā tathā so bhikkhu (syā. kaṃ.) tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

What are the five things to be known by direct knowledge? The five grounds for liberation. Here, friends, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or a respected fellow in the holy life does. In whatever way, friends, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, or a respected fellow in the holy life does, in that way, in that Dhamma, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma. For him, who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the first ground for liberation.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, api ca kho yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ [T 3.0300] vitthārena paresaṃ deseti yathā [V 3.0226] yathā, āvuso, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti. Tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhu, nor does a respected fellow in the holy life. But rather, the bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has learned it. In whatever way, friends, the bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has learned it, in that way, in that Dhamma, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma. For him, who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the second ground for liberation.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti. Api ca kho, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhu, nor does a respected fellow in the holy life, nor does the bhikkhu teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has learned it. But rather, he recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it and as he has learned it. In whatever way, friends, the bhikkhu recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it and as he has learned it, in that way, in that Dhamma, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma. For him, who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the third ground for liberation.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti. Api ca kho, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati. Yathā yathā[M 3.0236], āvuso[T 3.0301], bhikkhu yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammapaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammapaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ catutthaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ.

Furthermore, friends, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhu, nor does a respected fellow in the holy life; nor does the bhikkhu teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has learned it, nor does he recite it in detail. But rather, he mentally considers, examines, and contemplates the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has learned it. In whatever way, friends, the bhikkhu mentally considers, examines, and contemplates the Dhamma as he has heard it and as he has learned it, in that way, in that Dhamma, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma. For him, who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the fourth ground for liberation.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno na heva kho satthā dhammaṃ deseti, aññataro vā garuṭṭhāniyo sabrahmacārī, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena paresaṃ deseti, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ vitthārena sajjhāyaṃ karoti, nāpi yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ cetasā anuvitakketi anuvicāreti manasānupekkhati; api ca khvassa aññataraṃ samādhinimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ paññāya. Yathā yathā, āvuso, bhikkhuno aññataraṃ samādhinimittaṃ suggahitaṃ hoti sumanasikataṃ sūpadhāritaṃ suppaṭividdhaṃ [V 3.0227] paññāya tathā tathā so tasmiṃ dhamme atthappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammappaṭisaṃvedī ca. Tassa atthappaṭisaṃvedino dhammappaṭisaṃvedino pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ vimuttāyatanaṃ. Ime pañca dhammā abhiññeyyā.

Furthermore, friends, the Teacher does not teach the Dhamma to the bhikkhu, nor does a respected fellow in the holy life; nor does the bhikkhu teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it and as he has learned it, nor does he recite it in detail, nor does he mentally consider, examine, and contemplate it. But a certain sign of concentration is well grasped by him, well attended to in the mind, well retained, and well penetrated with wisdom. In whatever way, friends, a certain sign of concentration is well grasped by the bhikkhu, well attended to in the mind, well retained, and well penetrated with wisdom, in that way, in that Dhamma, he becomes one who experiences the meaning and one who experiences the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the mental body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil mental body, he feels happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This is the fifth ground for liberation. These are the five things to be known by direct knowledge.

(Ña) “katame pañca dhammā sacchikātabbā? Pañca dhammakkhandhā – sīlakkhandho[T 3.0302], samādhikkhandho, paññākkhandho, vimuttikkhandho, vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandho. Ime pañca dhammā sacchikātabbā.

What five dhammas are to be realized? The five aggregates of Dhamma: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. These five dhammas are to be realized.

“Iti ime paññāsa dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these fifty dhammas are real, actual, unerring, unfalsified, not otherwise, and have been rightly and fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Cha dhammā

Six Dhammas

356. “Cha dhammā bahukārā…pe… cha dhammā sacchikātabbā.

356. Six dhammas are very helpful... six dhammas are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame cha dhammā bahukārā? Cha sāraṇīyā dhammā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhuno mettaṃ kāyakammaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ [P 3.0280] hoti sabrahmacārīsu āvi ceva raho [M 3.0237] ca, ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

What six dhammas are very helpful? The six states to be remembered. Here, friends, a bhikkhu maintains a bodily action of loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners, both openly and in private. This dhamma, too, is a state to be remembered, endearing, inspiring respect, and is conducive to cohesion, non-dispute, concord, and unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno mettaṃ vacīkammaṃ…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu maintains a verbal action of loving-kindness... it is conducive to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno mettaṃ manokammaṃ…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu maintains a mental action of loving-kindness... it is conducive to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu ye te lābhā dhammikā dhammaladdhā antamaso pattapariyāpannamattampi, tathārūpehi lābhehi appaṭivibhattabhogī hoti sīlavantehi sabrahmacārīhi sādhāraṇabhogī, ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo…pe… ekībhāvāya [T 3.0303] saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, whatever gains a bhikkhu has that are righteous, obtained righteously, even down to the contents of his alms-bowl, with such gains he is one who partakes without apportionment, who partakes in common with his virtuous fellow practitioners. This dhamma, too, is a state to be remembered... it is conducive to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu, yāni tāni sīlāni akhaṇḍāni acchiddāni asabalāni akammāsāni bhujissāni viññuppasatthāni aparāmaṭṭhāni samādhisaṃvattanikāni, tathārūpesu [V 3.0228] sīlesu sīlasāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca, ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo…pe… ekībhāvāya saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells in commonality of virtue with his fellow practitioners, both openly and in private, in regard to those virtues that are unbroken, flawless, spotless, unblotched, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, and conducive to concentration. This dhamma, too, is a state to be remembered... it is conducive to unity.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu yāyaṃ diṭṭhi ariyā niyyānikā niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāya, tathārūpāya diṭṭhiyā diṭṭhi sāmaññagato viharati sabrahmacārīhi āvi ceva raho ca, ayampi dhammo sāraṇīyo piyakaraṇo garukaraṇo, saṅgahāya avivādāya sāmaggiyā ekībhāvāya saṃvattati. Ime cha dhammā bahukārā.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells in commonality of view with his fellow practitioners, both openly and in private, in regard to that view which is noble, leading out, which leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering. This dhamma, too, is a state to be remembered, endearing, inspiring respect, and is conducive to cohesion, non-dispute, concord, and unity. These six dhammas are very helpful.

(Kha) “katame cha dhammā bhāvetabbā? Cha anussatiṭṭhānāni – buddhānussati, dhammānussati, saṅghānussati, sīlānussati, cāgānussati, devatānussati. Ime cha dhammā bhāvetabbā.

What six dhammas are to be developed? The six bases of recollection: recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the devas. These six dhammas are to be developed.

(Ga) “katame cha dhammā pariññeyyā? Cha ajjhattikāni āyatanāni – cakkhāyatanaṃ, sotāyatanaṃ, ghānāyatanaṃ, jivhāyatanaṃ, kāyāyatanaṃ, manāyatanaṃ. Ime cha dhammā pariññeyyā.

What six dhammas are to be fully understood? The six internal sense bases: the eye sense base, the ear sense base, the nose sense base, the tongue sense base, the body sense base, and the mind sense base. These six dhammas are to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katame cha dhammā pahātabbā? Cha taṇhākāyā – rūpataṇhā, saddataṇhā, gandhataṇhā, rasataṇhā, phoṭṭhabbataṇhā, dhammataṇhā. Ime cha dhammā pahātabbā.

What six dhammas are to be abandoned? The six bodies of craving: craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for smells, craving for tastes, craving for tactile objects, and craving for mental objects. These six dhammas are to be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katame [T 3.0304][M 3.0238] cha dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Cha agāravā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari agāravo viharati appatisso. Dhamme…pe… saṅghe… sikkhāya… appamāde… paṭisanthāre agāravo viharati appatisso. Ime cha dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

What six dhammas partake of decline? Six kinds of disrespect. Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with disrespect and without deference toward the Teacher, toward the Dhamma... toward the Sangha... toward the training... toward diligence... and toward hospitality. These six dhammas partake of decline.

(Ca) “katame cha dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Cha gāravā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthari sagāravo viharati sappatisso dhamme…pe… saṅghe… sikkhāya… appamāde… paṭisanthāre sagāravo viharati sappatisso. Ime cha dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

What six dhammas partake of distinction? Six kinds of respect. Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with respect and with deference toward the Teacher, toward the Dhamma... toward the Sangha... toward the training... toward diligence... and toward hospitality. These six dhammas partake of distinction.

(Cha) “katame cha dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Cha nissaraṇiyā dhātuyo – idhāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘mettā hi kho me, cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā, atha ca pana me byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi. Na hi [V 3.0229] sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ āvuso anavakāso yaṃ mettāya cetovimuttiyā bhāvitāya bahulīkatāya yānīkatāya vatthukatāya anuṭṭhitāya paricitāya susamāraddhāya. Atha ca panassa byāpādo cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassatīti, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, byāpādassa, yadidaṃ mettācetovimuttī’ti.

(Cha) "What six dhammas are hard to penetrate? The six elements of escape. Here, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through loving-kindness, cultivated it, made it my vehicle, made it my basis, established it, practiced it, and well-undertaken it, and yet ill will still obsesses my mind.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say that, venerable sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, for the Blessed One would not say such a thing. It is impossible, friends, it cannot happen that when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed, cultivated, made one’s vehicle, made one's basis, established, practiced, and well-undertaken, ill will would still obsess the mind. That is not possible. For this, friends, is the escape from ill will, namely, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness.’"

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘karuṇā [T 3.0305] hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā. Atha ca pana me vihesā cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo, ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, vihesāya, yadidaṃ karuṇācetovimuttī’ti.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through compassion, cultivated it, made it my vehicle, made it my basis, established it, practiced it, and well-undertaken it, and yet harmfulness still obsesses my mind.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say that, venerable sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One… For this, friends, is the escape from harmfulness, namely, the liberation of mind through compassion.’"

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘muditā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā…pe… atha ca pana me arati cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso aratiyā, yadidaṃ muditācetovimuttī’ti.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy… and yet discontent still obsesses my mind.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say that, venerable sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One… For this, friends, is the escape from discontent, namely, the liberation of mind through sympathetic joy.’"

“Idha [M 3.0239] panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘upekkhā hi kho me cetovimutti [T 3.0306] bhāvitā…pe… atha ca pana me rāgo cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, rāgassa yadidaṃ upekkhācetovimuttī’ti.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the liberation of mind through equanimity… and yet lust still obsesses my mind.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say that, venerable sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One… For this, friends, is the escape from lust, namely, the liberation of mind through equanimity.’"

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘animittā hi kho me cetovimutti bhāvitā…pe… atha ca pana me nimittānusāri viññāṇaṃ hotī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca…pe… nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, sabbanimittānaṃ yadidaṃ animittā cetovimuttī’ti.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘I have developed the signless liberation of mind… and yet my consciousness still follows after signs.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say that, venerable sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One… For this, friends, is the escape from all signs, namely, the signless liberation of mind.’"

“Idha panāvuso, bhikkhu evaṃ vadeyya – ‘asmīti kho me vigataṃ, ayamahamasmīti na [T 3.0307] samanupassāmi, atha ca pana me vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī’ti. So – ‘mā hevaṃ’ tissa vacanīyo ‘māyasmā evaṃ avaca, mā bhagavantaṃ abbhācikkhi, na [V 3.0230] hi sādhu bhagavato abbhakkhānaṃ, na hi bhagavā evaṃ vadeyya. Aṭṭhānametaṃ, āvuso, anavakāso yaṃ asmīti vigate ayamahamasmīti asamanupassato. Atha ca panassa vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallaṃ cittaṃ pariyādāya ṭhassati, netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Nissaraṇaṃ hetaṃ, āvuso, vicikicchākathaṃkathāsallassa, yadidaṃ asmimānasamugghāṭo’ti. Ime cha dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

“Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu might say: ‘The conceit “I am” has been eliminated in me, and I do not perceive “I am this.” Yet, the dart of doubt and perplexity still obsesses my mind.’ He should be told: ‘Do not say that, venerable sir! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not say such a thing. It is impossible, friends, it cannot happen that when the conceit “I am” has been eliminated and one does not perceive “I am this,” the dart of doubt and perplexity would still obsess one’s mind—that is not possible. For this, friends, is the escape from the dart of doubt and perplexity, namely, the uprooting of the conceit “I am.”’ These six dhammas are hard to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame [P 3.0281] cha dhammā uppādetabbā? Cha satatavihārā. Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya neva sumano hoti na dummano, upekkhako viharati sato sampajāno. Ime cha dhammā uppādetabbā.

(Ja) "What six dhammas are to be developed? The six constant abidings. Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is neither gladdened nor displeased, but abides equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having felt a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither gladdened nor displeased, but abides equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending. These six dhammas are to be developed."

(Jha) “katame cha dhammā abhiññeyyā? Cha anuttariyāni – dassanānuttariyaṃ, savanānuttariyaṃ, lābhānuttariyaṃ, sikkhānuttariyaṃ, pāricariyānuttariyaṃ, anussatānuttariyaṃ. Ime cha dhammā abhiññeyyā.

(Jha) "What six dhammas are to be directly known? The six unsurpassed states: the unsurpassed seeing, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed gain, the unsurpassed training, the unsurpassed service, and the unsurpassed recollection. These six dhammas are to be directly known."

(Ña) “katame cha dhammā sacchikātabbā? Cha abhiññā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu anekavihitaṃ iddhividhaṃ paccanubhoti – ekopi hutvā bahudhā hoti[T 3.0308], bahudhāpi hutvā eko hoti. Āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvaṃ. Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati seyyathāpi ākāse[M 3.0240]. Pathaviyāpi ummujjanimujjaṃ karoti seyyathāpi udake. Udakepi abhijjamāne gacchati seyyathāpi pathaviyaṃ. Ākāsepi pallaṅkena kamati seyyathāpi pakkhī sakuṇo. Imepi candimasūriye evaṃmahiddhike evaṃmahānubhāve pāṇinā parāmasati parimajjati. Yāva brahmalokāpi kāyena vasaṃ vatteti.

(Ña) "What six dhammas are to be realized? The six higher knowledges. Here, friends, a bhikkhu experiences various kinds of psychic power: being one, he becomes many; being many, he becomes one. He appears and vanishes. He goes unhindered through a wall, a rampart, or a mountain as if through space. He dives into and emerges from the earth as if it were water. He walks on water without breaking through as if on earth. He travels cross-legged in the sky like a winged bird. He touches and strokes with his hand these moon and sun, so mighty and powerful. He exercises mastery with his body even as far as the Brahmā world."

“Dibbāya sotadhātuyā visuddhāya atikkantamānusikāya ubho sadde suṇāti dibbe ca mānuse ca, ye dūre santike ca.

“With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near.”

“Parasattānaṃ [V 3.0231] parapuggalānaṃ cetasā ceto paricca pajānāti jānāti (syā. kaṃ.), sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti pajānāti [T 3.0309] …pe… avimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ avimuttaṃ cittanti pajānāti.

“He knows the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with his own mind. He knows a mind with lust as a mind with lust… and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind.”

“So anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati, seyyathidaṃ ekampi jātiṃ…pe… iti sākāraṃ sauddesaṃ anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati.

“He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth… Thus with their aspects and details he recollects his manifold past lives.”

“Dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena satte passati cavamāne upapajjamāne hīne paṇīte suvaṇṇe dubbaṇṇe sugate duggate yathākammūpage satte pajānāti [T 3.0310]…pe…

With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he knows beings as they fare according to their kamma…

“Āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharati. Ime cha dhammā sacchikātabbā.

Through the destruction of the taints, in this very life he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, and entering upon them, abides in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. These six dhammas are to be realized.

“Iti ime saṭṭhi dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these sixty dhammas are actual, real, unerring, unperverted, and not otherwise, rightly and fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Satta dhammā

The Seven Dhammas

357. “Satta [P 3.0282] dhammā bahukārā…pe… satta dhammā sacchikātabbā.

357. Seven dhammas are of great service... seven dhammas are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame satta dhammā bahukārā? Satta ariyadhanāni – saddhādhanaṃ, sīladhanaṃ, hiridhanaṃ, ottappadhanaṃ, sutadhanaṃ, cāgadhanaṃ, paññādhanaṃ. Ime satta dhammā bahukārā.

(A) What seven dhammas are of great service? The seven noble treasures: the treasure of faith, the treasure of virtue, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of moral dread, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom. These seven dhammas are of great service.

(Kha) “katame [M 3.0241] satta dhammā bhāvetabbā? Satta sambojjhaṅgā – satisambojjhaṅgo, dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo, vīriyasambojjhaṅgo, pītisambojjhaṅgo, passaddhisambojjhaṅgo, samādhisambojjhaṅgo, upekkhāsambojjhaṅgo[T 3.0311]. Ime satta dhammā bhāvetabbā.

(B) What seven dhammas are to be developed? The seven factors of enlightenment: the mindfulness factor of enlightenment, the investigation of phenomena factor of enlightenment, the energy factor of enlightenment, the rapture factor of enlightenment, the tranquility factor of enlightenment, the concentration factor of enlightenment, and the equanimity factor of enlightenment. These seven dhammas are to be developed.

(Ga) “katame satta dhammā pariññeyyā? Satta viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo – santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamā viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

(C) What seven dhammas are to be fully understood? The seven stations of consciousness: There are, friends, beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation. This is the first station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso[V 3.0232], sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings with diverse bodies and unified perception, such as the devas of Brahmā’s retinue who are first arisen. This is the second station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyā viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the devas of Streaming Radiance. This is the third station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catutthī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings with unified bodies and unified perception, such as the devas of Refulgent Glory. This is the fourth station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā…pe… ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ pañcamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely surmounting perceptions of form... perceiving, ‘Space is infinite,’ have reached the base of the infinity of space. This is the fifth station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ chaṭṭhī viññāṇaṭṭhiti.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely surmounting the base of the infinity of space, perceiving, ‘Consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the base of the infinity of consciousness. This is the sixth station of consciousness.

“Santāvuso, sattā sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanūpagā. Ayaṃ sattamī viññāṇaṭṭhiti. Ime satta dhammā pariññeyyā.

There are, friends, beings who, by completely surmounting the base of the infinity of consciousness, perceiving, ‘There is nothing,’ have reached the base of nothingness. This is the seventh station of consciousness. These seven dhammas are to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katame satta dhammā pahātabbā? Sattānusayā – kāmarāgānusayo, paṭighānusayo, diṭṭhānusayo, vicikicchānusayo, mānānusayo, bhavarāgānusayo[T 3.0312], avijjānusayo. Ime satta dhammā pahātabbā.

(D) What seven dhammas are to be abandoned? The seven underlying tendencies: the underlying tendency to sensual desire, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to craving for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. These seven dhammas are to be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katame satta dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Satta asaddhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu assaddho hoti, ahiriko hoti, anottappī hoti, appassuto [M 3.0242] hoti, kusīto hoti, muṭṭhassati hoti, duppañño hoti. Ime satta dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

(E) What seven dhammas are conducive to decline? The seven unwholesome dhammas: Here, friends, a bhikkhu is faithless, shameless, unscrupulous, of little learning, lazy, of lapsed mindfulness, and unwise. These seven dhammas are conducive to decline.

(Ca) “katame satta dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Satta saddhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu saddho hoti, hirimā hiriko (syā. kaṃ.) hoti, ottappī hoti, bahussuto hoti, āraddhavīriyo hoti, upaṭṭhitassati hoti, paññavā hoti. Ime satta dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

(F) What seven dhammas are conducive to distinction? The seven wholesome dhammas: Here, friends, a bhikkhu is faithful, conscientious, scrupulous, learned, with energy aroused, with mindfulness established, and wise. These seven dhammas are conducive to distinction.

(Cha) “katame [V 3.0233][P 3.0283] satta dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Satta sappurisadhammā – idhāvuso, bhikkhu dhammaññū ca hoti atthaññū ca attaññū ca mattaññū ca kālaññū ca parisaññū ca puggalaññū ca. Ime satta dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

(G) What seven dhammas are difficult to penetrate? The seven dhammas of a true person: Here, friends, a bhikkhu is a knower of the Dhamma, a knower of the meaning, a knower of himself, a knower of moderation, a knower of the proper time, a knower of the assembly, and a knower of individuals. These seven dhammas are difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame satta dhammā uppādetabbā? Satta saññā – aniccasaññā, anattasaññā, asubhasaññā, ādīnavasaññā, pahānasaññā, virāgasaññā, nirodhasaññā. Ime satta dhammā uppādetabbā.

(H) What seven dhammas are to be brought into being? The seven perceptions: the perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of foulness, the perception of danger, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation. These seven dhammas are to be brought into being.

(Jha) “katame satta dhammā abhiññeyyā? Satta niddasavatthūni – idhāvuso, bhikkhu sikkhāsamādāne tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca sikkhāsamādāne avigatapemo. Dhammanisantiyā tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca [T 3.0313] dhammanisantiyā avigatapemo. Icchāvinaye tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca icchāvinaye avigatapemo. Paṭisallāne tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca paṭisallāne avigatapemo. Vīriyāramme tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca vīriyāramme avigatapemo. Satinepakke tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca satinepakke avigatapemo. Diṭṭhipaṭivedhe tibbacchando hoti, āyatiñca diṭṭhipaṭivedhe avigatapemo. Ime satta dhammā abhiññeyyā.

(I) What seven dhammas are to be known by direct knowledge? The seven grounds for instruction: Here, friends, a bhikkhu has a strong desire for undertaking the training, and in the future his love for undertaking the training is not lost. He has a strong desire for reflection on the Dhamma, and in the future his love for reflection on the Dhamma is not lost. He has a strong desire for the removal of craving, and in the future his love for the removal of craving is not lost. He has a strong desire for seclusion, and in the future his love for seclusion is not lost. He has a strong desire for arousing energy, and in the future his love for arousing energy is not lost. He has a strong desire for mindfulness and prudence, and in the future his love for mindfulness and prudence is not lost. He has a strong desire for the penetration of views, and in the future his love for the penetration of views is not lost. These seven dhammas are to be known by direct knowledge.

(Ña) “katame satta dhammā sacchikātabbā? Satta khīṇāsavabalāni – idhāvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno aniccato sabbe saṅkhārā yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhā honti. Yaṃpāvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno aniccato sabbe saṅkhārā yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhā honti, idampi khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno balaṃ hoti, yaṃ balaṃ āgamma khīṇāsavo bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayaṃ paṭijānāti – ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti.

(J) What seven dhammas are to be realized? The seven powers of one whose taints are destroyed: Here, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, all formations are well seen with right wisdom as they actually are: as impermanent. That, friends, which for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed is that all formations are well seen with right wisdom as they actually are, as impermanent, this is a power of the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed. Relying on this power, the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed professes the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’

“Puna [M 3.0243] caparaṃ, āvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhā honti. Yaṃpāvuso…pe… ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti.

Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures are well seen with right wisdom as they actually are: as comparable to a pit of glowing embers. That, friends… ‘My taints are destroyed.’

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno vivekaninnaṃ cittaṃ hoti vivekapoṇaṃ vivekapabbhāraṃ vivekaṭṭhaṃ nekkhammābhirataṃ byantībhūtaṃ sabbaso āsavaṭṭhāniyehi [T 3.0314] dhammehi. Yaṃpāvuso…pe… ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti.

Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, his mind is inclined to seclusion, sloping towards seclusion, tending towards seclusion, established in seclusion, delighting in renunciation, and is rid of all things that are a basis for the taints. For which reason, friends... he knows distinctly, 'My taints are destroyed.'

“Puna [V 3.0234] caparaṃ, āvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno cattāro satipaṭṭhānā bhāvitā honti subhāvitā[P 3.0284]. Yaṃpāvuso…pe… ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti.

Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four establishments of mindfulness are developed and well developed. For which reason, friends... he knows distinctly, 'My taints are destroyed.'

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno pañcindriyāni bhāvitāni honti subhāvitāni. Yaṃpāvuso…pe… ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti.

Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the five faculties are developed and well developed. For which reason, friends... he knows distinctly, 'My taints are destroyed.'

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno satta bojjhaṅgā bhāvitā honti subhāvitā. Yaṃpāvuso…pe… ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti.

Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the seven factors of enlightenment are cultivated and well cultivated. For which reason, friends... he knows distinctly, 'My taints are destroyed.'

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo bhāvito hoti subhāvito. Yaṃpāvuso, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko [T 3.0315] maggo bhāvito hoti subhāvito, idampi khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno balaṃ hoti, yaṃ balaṃ āgamma khīṇāsavo bhikkhu āsavānaṃ khayaṃ paṭijānāti – ‘khīṇā me āsavā’ti. Ime satta dhammā sacchikātabbā.

Furthermore, friends, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the Noble Eightfold Path is developed and well developed. And friends, because the Noble Eightfold Path is developed and well developed for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, this too is a strength of the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by relying on which strength the bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed knows distinctly the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’ These seven phenomena are to be realized.

“Itime sattati dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these seventy phenomena are real, true, thus, not unreal, not otherwise, and are perfectly awakened to by the Tathāgata.

Paṭhamabhāṇavāro niṭṭhito.

The first recitation portion is concluded.

Aṭṭha dhammā

Eight Phenomena

358. “Aṭṭha dhammā bahukārā…pe… aṭṭha dhammā sacchikātabbā.

358. Eight phenomena are of great help... eight phenomena are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame aṭṭha dhammā bahukārā? Aṭṭha hetū aṭṭha paccayā ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya [M 3.0244] vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattanti. Katame aṭṭha? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu satthāraṃ satthāraṃ vā (syā. ka.) upanissāya viharati aññataraṃ vā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ, yatthassa tibbaṃ hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti pemañca gāravo [V 3.0235] ca. Ayaṃ paṭhamo hetu paṭhamo paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya[P 3.0285]. Paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

What are the eight phenomena that are of great help? There are eight causes, eight conditions that conduce to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained. What eight? Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence on the Teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in a position of respect, towards whom he has established a strong sense of moral shame and moral dread, as well as affection and reverence. This is the first cause, the first condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Taṃ kho pana satthāraṃ upanissāya viharati aññataraṃ vā garuṭṭhāniyaṃ sabrahmacāriṃ[T 3.0316], yatthassa tibbaṃ hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ hoti pemañca gāravo ca. Te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhati – ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ? Imassa ko attho’ti? Tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttānī anuttānikatañca uttāniṃ (ka.) karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Ayaṃ dutiyo hetu dutiyo paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya, vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

Dwelling in dependence on that Teacher or on a certain fellow practitioner in a position of respect, towards whom he has established a strong sense of moral shame and moral dread, as well as affection and reverence, he approaches them from time to time to question and inquire: ‘Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones then reveal to him what is unrevealed, make clear what is not yet clear, and dispel his doubt concerning various matters that are grounds for doubt. This is the second cause, the second condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Taṃ kho pana dhammaṃ sutvā dvayena vūpakāsena sampādeti – kāyavūpakāsena ca cittavūpakāsena ca. Ayaṃ tatiyo hetu tatiyo paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

Having heard that Dhamma, he accomplishes a twofold seclusion: seclusion of body and seclusion of mind. This is the third cause, the third condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu sīlavā hoti, pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuto viharati ācāragocarasampanno, aṇumattesu vajjesu bhayadassāvī samādāya sikkhati sikkhāpadesu. Ayaṃ catuttho hetu catuttho paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha restraint, is endowed with right conduct and resort, and sees danger in the slightest faults. He trains by undertaking the training rules. This is the fourth cause, the fourth condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu bahussuto hoti sutadharo sutasannicayo. Ye te dhammā ādikalyāṇā majjhekalyāṇā pariyosānakalyāṇā sātthā sabyañjanā kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ abhivadanti, tathārūpāssa dhammā bahussutā honti dhātā [T 3.0317] vacasā [M 3.0245] paricitā manasānupekkhitā diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhā. Ayaṃ pañcamo hetu pañcamo paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has heard much, retains what he has heard, and accumulates what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the holy life that is utterly complete and pure—such teachings have been much heard by him, retained, practiced verbally, examined mentally, and well penetrated by view. This is the fifth cause, the fifth condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu āraddhavīriyo viharati akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānāya, kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ upasampadāya, thāmavā daḷhaparakkamo anikkhittadhuro kusalesu dhammesu. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho [P 3.0286][V 3.0236] hetu chaṭṭho paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome phenomena and for the attainment of wholesome phenomena; he is strong, steadfast in exertion, and does not throw off the burden in regard to wholesome phenomena. This is the sixth cause, the sixth condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu satimā hoti paramena satinepakkena samannāgato. Cirakatampi cirabhāsitampi saritā anussaritā. Ayaṃ sattamo hetu sattamo paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and discretion, able to remember and recollect what was done and said long ago. This is the seventh cause, the seventh condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu, udayabbayānupassī viharati – ‘iti rūpaṃ iti rūpassa samudayo iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā iti vedanāya samudayo iti vedanāya atthaṅgamo; iti saññā iti saññāya samudayo iti saññāya atthaṅgamo; iti saṅkhārā iti saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo iti saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo; iti viññāṇaṃ iti viññāṇassa samudayo iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo hetu aṭṭhamo paccayo ādibrahmacariyikāya [T 3.0318] paññāya appaṭiladdhāya paṭilābhāya, paṭiladdhāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā saṃvattati. Ime aṭṭha dhammā bahukārā.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating arising and passing away in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the passing away of perception; such are formations, such is the origin of formations, such is the passing away of formations; such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ This is the eighth cause, the eighth condition that conduces to the gaining of wisdom that is fundamental to the holy life—wisdom not yet gained—and for the increase, abundance, development, and fulfillment of wisdom already gained. These eight qualities are of great help.

(Kha) “katame aṭṭha dhammā bhāvetabbā? Ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi. Ime aṭṭha dhammā bhāvetabbā.

What eight qualities should be developed? The Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. These eight qualities should be developed.

(Ga) “katame aṭṭha dhammā pariññeyyā? Aṭṭha lokadhammā – lābho ca, alābho ca, yaso ca, ayaso ca, nindā ca, pasaṃsā ca, sukhañca, dukkhañca. Ime aṭṭha dhammā pariññeyyā.

What eight qualities are to be fully understood? The eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, censure and praise, pleasure and pain. These eight qualities are to be fully understood.

(Gha) “katame [M 3.0246] aṭṭha dhammā pahātabbā? Aṭṭha micchattā [P 3.0287] – micchādiṭṭhi, micchāsaṅkappo, micchāvācā, micchākammanto, micchāājīvo, micchāvāyāmo, micchāsati, micchāsamādhi. Ime aṭṭha dhammā pahātabbā.

What eight qualities should be abandoned? The eight wrongnesses: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration. These eight qualities should be abandoned.

(Ṅa) “katame aṭṭha dhammā hānabhāgiyā? Aṭṭha kusītavatthūni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kammaṃ kho me kātabbaṃ bhavissati, kammaṃ kho pana [V 3.0237] me karontassa kāyo kilamissati, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu.

What are the eight qualities that partake of decline? The eight grounds for laziness. Here, friends, a bhikkhu has work to do, and it occurs to him: ‘I will have work to do, and while doing it, my body will become tired. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized. This is the first ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kataṃ hoti[T 3.0319]. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ, kammaṃ kho pana me karontassa kāyo kilanto, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhati…pe… idaṃ dutiyaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has done work. It occurs to him: ‘I have done work, and while doing it, my body became tired. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the second ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gantabbo hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilamissati, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhati…pe… idaṃ tatiyaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has a journey to make. It occurs to him: ‘I will have a journey to make, and while traveling, my body will become tired. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the third ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gato hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantassa kāyo kilanto, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati, na vīriyaṃ ārabhati…pe… idaṃ catutthaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has made a journey. It occurs to him: ‘I have made a journey, and while traveling, my body became tired. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down and does not arouse energy… This is the fourth ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto na labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ, tassa me kāyo kilanto akammañño, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti…pe… idaṃ pañcamaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while walking for alms in a village or town, does not obtain his fill of coarse or fine food. It occurs to him: ‘While walking for alms in a village or town, I did not obtain my fill of coarse or fine food. My body is tired and unfit for work. Suppose I lie down.’ … This is the fifth ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa [M 3.0247] vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ[T 3.0320], tassa me kāyo garuko akammañño, māsācitaṃ maññe, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati…pe… idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu, while walking for alms in a village or town, obtains his fill of coarse or fine food. It occurs to him: ‘While walking for alms in a village or town, I have obtained my fill of coarse or fine food. My body is heavy and unfit for work, as if stuffed with beans. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down… This is the sixth ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno uppanno hoti appamattako ābādho, tassa evaṃ hoti [V 3.0238] – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho atthi kappo nipajjituṃ, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati…pe… idaṃ sattamaṃ kusītavatthu.

Furthermore, friends, a minor illness has arisen in a bhikkhu. It occurs to him: ‘This minor illness has arisen in me. It is allowable to lie down. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down… This is the seventh ground for laziness.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gilānāvuṭṭhito hoti aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gilānāvuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa me kāyo dubbalo akammañño, handāhaṃ nipajjāmī’ti. So nipajjati…pe… idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ kusītavatthu. Ime aṭṭha dhammā hānabhāgiyā.

Furthermore, friends, a bhikkhu has recovered from illness, not long recovered from his sickness. It occurs to him: ‘I have recovered from illness, not long recovered from my sickness. My body is weak and unfit for work. Suppose I lie down.’ So he lies down… This is the eighth ground for laziness. These eight qualities partake of decline.

(Ca) “katame aṭṭha dhammā visesabhāgiyā? Aṭṭha ārambhavatthūni. Idhāvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ hoti, tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘kammaṃ kho me kātabbaṃ bhavissati, kammaṃ kho pana me karontena na sukaraṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasikātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa [T 3.0321] sacchikiriyāyā’ti. So vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

What are the eight qualities that partake of distinction? The eight grounds for arousing effort. Here, friends, a bhikkhu has work to do, and it occurs to him: ‘I will have work to do, and while doing it, it will not be easy to attend to the teaching of the Buddhas. Let me arouse energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized.’ So he arouses energy for attaining the unattained, achieving the unachieved, and realizing the unrealized. This is the first ground for arousing effort.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā kammaṃ kataṃ hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho kammaṃ akāsiṃ, kammaṃ kho panāhaṃ karonto nāsakkhiṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasikātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… idaṃ dutiyaṃ ārambhavatthu.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a bhikkhu has done some work. It occurs to him: ‘I have done work, but while doing it, I was unable to bear in mind the teaching of the Buddhas. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the second ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gantabbo hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘maggo kho me gantabbo bhavissati, maggaṃ kho pana me gacchantena na sukaraṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasikātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… idaṃ tatiyaṃ ārambhavatthu.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a bhikkhu has a journey to make. It occurs to him: ‘I will have a journey to make, and while traveling, it will not be easy to bear in mind the teaching of the Buddhas. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the third ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhunā maggo gato hoti. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho maggaṃ agamāsiṃ, maggaṃ kho panāhaṃ gacchanto nāsakkhiṃ buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ manasikātuṃ, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… idaṃ catutthaṃ ārambhavatthu.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a bhikkhu has gone on a journey. It occurs to him: ‘I have gone on a journey, but while traveling, I was unable to bear in mind the teaching of the Buddhas. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the fourth ground for arousing energy.

“Puna [M 3.0248] caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto na [T 3.0322] labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto nālatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ[V 3.0239], tassa me kāyo lahuko kammañño, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… idaṃ pañcamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or a town, does not obtain his fill of coarse or fine food, as much as he desires. It occurs to him: ‘While wandering for alms in a village or a town, I did not obtain my fill of coarse or fine food, as much as I desired. My body is light and fit for work. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the fifth ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto labhati lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto alatthaṃ lūkhassa vā paṇītassa vā bhojanassa yāvadatthaṃ pāripūriṃ. Tassa me kāyo balavā kammañño, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ ārambhavatthu.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a bhikkhu, while wandering for alms in a village or a town, obtains his fill of coarse or fine food, as much as he desires. It occurs to him: ‘While wandering for alms in a village or a town, I obtained my fill of coarse or fine food, as much as I desired. My body is strong and fit for work. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the sixth ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhuno uppanno hoti appamattako ābādho. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘uppanno kho me ayaṃ appamattako ābādho ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ me ābādho pavaḍḍheyya, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi…pe… idaṃ [T 3.0323] sattamaṃ ārambhavatthu.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a minor illness has arisen in a bhikkhu. It occurs to him: ‘This minor illness has arisen in me. There is a possibility that my illness might worsen. Come now, I shall arouse energy…’ This is the seventh ground for arousing energy.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, bhikkhu gilānā vuṭṭhito hoti aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā. Tassa evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ kho gilānā vuṭṭhito aciravuṭṭhito gelaññā, ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ vijjati, yaṃ me ābādho paccudāvatteyya, handāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhāmi appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāyā’ti. So vīriyaṃ ārabhati appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya asacchikatassa sacchikiriyāya. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ ārambhavatthu. Ime aṭṭha dhammā visesabhāgiyā.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a bhikkhu has recovered from illness, not long recovered from his sickness. It occurs to him: ‘I have recovered from illness, not long recovered from my sickness. There is a possibility that my illness might recur. Come now, I shall arouse energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the direct experience of the unexperienced.’ He arouses energy for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized, for the direct experience of the unexperienced. This is the eighth ground for arousing energy. These eight states partake of distinction.

(Cha) “katame aṭṭha dhammā duppaṭivijjhā? Aṭṭha akkhaṇā asamayā brahmacariyavāsāya. Idhāvuso, tathāgato ca loke uppanno hoti arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca desiyati opasamiko parinibbāniko sambodhagāmī sugatappavedito. Ayañca puggalo nirayaṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ paṭhamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

What are the eight states that are difficult to penetrate? The eight inopportune, unsuitable moments for living the holy life. Here, venerable sirs, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is taught which is conducive to peace, which leads to Nibbāna, which leads to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Well-Farer. But this person has been reborn in hell. This is the first inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ, āvuso, tathāgato ca loke uppanno hoti arahaṃ sammāsambuddho, dhammo ca desiyati opasamiko parinibbāniko sambodhagāmī [M 3.0249] sugatappavedito, ayañca puggalo tiracchānayoniṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ dutiyo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is taught which is conducive to peace, which leads to Nibbāna, which leads to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Well-Farer. But this person has been reborn in the animal realm. This is the second inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna [V 3.0240] caparaṃ…pe… pettivisayaṃ [T 3.0324] upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ tatiyo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… he has been reborn in the realm of the petas. This is the third inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… aññataraṃ dīghāyukaṃ devanikāyaṃ upapanno hoti. Ayaṃ catuttho akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… he has been reborn into a certain group of long-lived devas. This is the fourth inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… paccantimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti milakkhesu aviññātāresu, yattha natthi gati bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ. Ayaṃ pañcamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… he has been reborn in the border regions, among uncultured people who are not discerning, where there is no access for bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay-followers, or female lay-followers. This is the fifth inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… ayañca puggalo majjhimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti, so ca hoti micchādiṭṭhiko viparītadassano – ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paro loko, natthi mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person has been reborn in the central regions, but he has wrong view, a distorted perspective: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed. There is no fruit or result of good and bad actions. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There are no beings who are spontaneously reborn. There are no ascetics and brahmins in the world who are well-gone and well-practiced, who, having realized it for themselves by direct knowledge, proclaim this world and the other world.’ This is the sixth inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… ayañca puggalo majjhimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti[T 3.0325], so ca hoti duppañño jaḷo eḷamūgo, nappaṭibalo subhāsitadubbhāsitānamatthamaññātuṃ. Ayaṃ sattamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya.

Furthermore… this person has been reborn in the central regions, but he is unwise, dull, and mentally defective, unable to understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and badly spoken. This is the seventh inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life.

“Puna caparaṃ…pe… ayañca puggalo majjhimesu janapadesu paccājāto hoti, so ca hoti paññavā ajaḷo aneḷamūgo, paṭibalo subhāsitadubbhāsitānamatthamaññātuṃ. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo akkhaṇo asamayo brahmacariyavāsāya. Ime aṭṭha dhammā duppaṭivijjhā.

Furthermore, a Tathāgata has not arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma is not taught which is conducive to peace, which leads to Nibbāna, which leads to enlightenment, proclaimed by the Well-Farer. But this person has been reborn in the central regions, and he is wise, not dull, not mentally defective, and is able to understand the meaning of what is well-spoken and badly spoken. This is the eighth inopportune, unsuitable moment for living the holy life. These eight states are difficult to penetrate.

(Ja) “katame aṭṭha dhammā uppādetabbā? Aṭṭha mahāpurisavitakkā – appicchassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo mahicchassa. Santuṭṭhassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo asantuṭṭhassa. Pavivittassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo saṅgaṇikārāmassa. Āraddhavīriyassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo kusītassa. Upaṭṭhitasatissāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo muṭṭhassatissa. Samāhitassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo asamāhitassa[M 3.0250][V 3.0241]. Paññavato paññāvato (sī. pī.) ayaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo duppaññassa. Nippapañcassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo papañcārāmassāti nippapañcārāmassa ayaṃ dhammo nippapañcaratino, nāyaṃ dhammo papañcārāmassa papañcaratinoti (sī. syā. pī.) aṅguttarepi tatheva dissati. aṭṭhakathāṭīkā pana oloketabbā ime aṭṭha dhammā uppādetabbā.

What eight qualities are to be developed? The eight reflections of a great man: This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires. This Dhamma is for the contented, not for the discontented. This Dhamma is for one who delights in seclusion, not for one who delights in company. This Dhamma is for one with aroused energy, not for the lazy. This Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with lapsed mindfulness. This Dhamma is for one with a concentrated mind, not for one with an unconcentrated mind. This Dhamma is for one with wisdom, not for one without wisdom. This Dhamma is for one who does not delight in proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation. These eight qualities are to be developed.

(Jha) “katame aṭṭha dhammā abhiññeyyā? Aṭṭha abhibhāyatanāni – ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni[T 3.0326], ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti – evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

What eight qualities are to be directly known? The eight bases of mastery. One, percipient of form internally, sees external forms that are limited, of good and bad appearance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the first base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti – evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ dutiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

One, percipient of form internally, sees external forms that are immeasurable, of good and bad appearance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the second base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ tatiyaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are limited, of good and bad appearance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the third base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ catutthaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are immeasurable, of good and bad appearance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fourth base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma umāpupphaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ. Seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ nīlaṃ nīlavaṇṇaṃ nīlanidassanaṃ nīlanibhāsaṃ, evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati nīlāni nīlavaṇṇāni nīlanidassanāni nīlanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ pañcamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance. Just as a flax flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance, or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance; even so, not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, blue in radiance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the fifth base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma kaṇikārapupphaṃ pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ. Seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ [M 3.0251] ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ pītaṃ pītavaṇṇaṃ pītanidassanaṃ pītanibhāsaṃ[T 3.0327], evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati pītāni pītavaṇṇāni pītanidassanāni pītanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance. Just as a kaṇikāra flower is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance, or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance; even so, not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, yellow in radiance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the sixth base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ [V 3.0242] arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma bandhujīvakapupphaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ lohitakaṃ lohitakavaṇṇaṃ lohitakanidassanaṃ lohitakanibhāsaṃ, evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati lohitakāni lohitakavaṇṇāni lohitakanidassanāni lohitakanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ sattamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, red in radiance. Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, red in color, red in appearance, red in radiance, or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is red, red in color, red in appearance, red in radiance; even so, not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, red in radiance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the seventh base of mastery.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni. Seyyathāpi nāma osadhitārakā odātā odātavaṇṇā odātanidassanā odātanibhāsā, seyyathā vā pana taṃ vatthaṃ bārāṇaseyyakaṃ ubhatobhāgavimaṭṭhaṃ odātaṃ odātavaṇṇaṃ odātanidassanaṃ odātanibhāsaṃ, evameva ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati odātāni odātavaṇṇāni odātanidassanāni odātanibhāsāni, ‘tāni abhibhuyya jānāmi passāmī’ti evaṃsaññī hoti. Idaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ. Ime aṭṭha dhammā abhiññeyyā.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in radiance. Just as the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, white in radiance, or just as a cloth from Benares, smoothed on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, white in radiance; even so, not percipient of form internally, one sees external forms that are white, white in color, white in appearance, white in radiance. Having overpowered them, one is percipient thus: ‘I know, I see.’ This is the eighth base of mastery. These eight qualities are to be directly known.

(Ña) “katame [T 3.0328][P 3.0288] aṭṭha dhammā sacchikātabbā? Aṭṭha vimokkhā – rūpī rūpāni passati. Ayaṃ paṭhamo vimokkho.

What eight qualities are to be realized? The eight liberations: One possessing form sees forms. This is the first liberation.

“Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati. Ayaṃ dutiyo vimokkho.

Not percipient of form internally, one sees forms externally. This is the second liberation.

“Subhanteva adhimutto hoti. Ayaṃ tatiyo vimokkho.

One becomes intent only on the beautiful. This is the third liberation.

“Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ catuttho vimokkho.

With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite space. This is the fourth liberation.

“Sabbaso [M 3.0252] ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ pañcamo vimokkho.

Having entirely transcended the dimension of infinite space, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ one enters and dwells in the dimension of infinite consciousness. This is the fifth liberation.

“Sabbaso [V 3.0243] viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ chaṭṭho vimokkho.

Having entirely transcended the dimension of infinite consciousness, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ one enters and dwells in the dimension of nothingness. This is the sixth liberation.

“Sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ sattamo vimokkho.

Having entirely transcended the dimension of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the dimension of neither perception nor non-perception. This is the seventh liberation.

“Sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ aṭṭhamo vimokkho. Ime aṭṭha dhammā sacchikātabbā.

Having entirely transcended the base of neither perception nor non-perception, one enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This is the eighth liberation. These eight states are to be realized.

“Iti ime asīti dhammā bhūtā tacchā tathā avitathā anaññathā sammā tathāgatena abhisambuddhā.

Thus, these eighty states are actual, real, true, not false, not otherwise, rightly fully realized by the Tathāgata.

Nava dhammā

The Nine States

359. “Nava dhammā bahukārā…pe… nava dhammā sacchikātabbā.

359. Nine states are of great benefit... nine states are to be realized.

(Ka) “katame [T 3.0329] nava dhammā bahukārā? Nava yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā, yonisomanasikaroto pāmojjaṃ jāyati, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedeti, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati, samāhite citte yathābhūtaṃ jānāti passati, yathābhūtaṃ jānaṃ passaṃ nibbindati, nibbindaṃ virajjati, virāgā vimuccati. Ime nava dhammā bahukārā.

(Ka) What nine states are of great benefit? The nine states rooted in wise attention. For one who attends wisely, gladness arises. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. With a concentrated mind, one knows and sees things as they really are. Knowing and seeing things as they really are, one becomes disenchanted. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. These nine states are of great benefit.

(Kha) “katame nava dhammā bhāvetabbā? Nava pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgāni – sīlavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, cittavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, diṭṭhivisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, kaṅkhāvitaraṇavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, maggāmaggañāṇadassana – visuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, paṭipadāñāṇadassanavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, ñāṇadassanavisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, paññāvisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ, vimuttivisuddhi pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅgaṃ. Ime nava dhammā bhāvetabbā.

(Kha) What nine states are to be developed? The nine factors of the endeavor for purity: purity of virtue is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity of mind is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity of view is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity by overcoming doubt is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity of knowledge and vision of what is path and what is not path is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity of knowledge and vision of the way is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity of knowledge and vision is a factor of the endeavor for purity; purity of wisdom is a factor of the endeavor for purity; and purity of liberation is a factor of the endeavor for purity. These nine states are to be developed.

(Ga) “katame nava dhammā pariññeyyā? Nava sattāvāsā – santāvuso, sattā nānattakāyā [V 3.0244] nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi manussā ekacce ca devā ekacce ca vinipātikā. Ayaṃ paṭhamo sattāvāso.

(Ga) What nine states are to be fully understood? The nine abodes of beings. Friends, there are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans, some devas, and some of those in states of deprivation. This is the first abode of beings.

“Santāvuso[M 3.0253], sattā nānattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā brahmakāyikā paṭhamābhinibbattā. Ayaṃ dutiyo sattāvāso.

Friends, there are beings with diverse bodies and unified perception, such as the devas of Brahmā's retinue who are first reborn there. This is the second abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā [T 3.0330] nānattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā ābhassarā. Ayaṃ tatiyo sattāvāso.

Friends, there are beings with unified bodies and diverse perceptions, such as the Ābhassara devas. This is the third abode of beings.

“Santāvuso, sattā ekattakāyā ekattasaññino, seyyathāpi devā subhakiṇhā. Ayaṃ catuttho sattāvāso.
